raw_output.raw_text: <search query="vision-based device-free gesture recognition Wi-Fi camera CSI review" search_time="2026年5月16日11时40分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:34"><title>See Through Walls with Wi-Fi!</title><summary>Wi-fi signals are typically information carriers between a transmitter and a receiver. In this paper, we show that Wi-Fi can also extend our senses, enabling us to see moving objects through walls and behind closed doors. In particular, we can use such signals to identify the number of people in a closed room and their relative locations. We can also identify simple gestures made behind a wall, and combine a sequence of gestures to communicate messages to a wireless receiver without carrying any transmitting device. The paper introduces two main innovations. First, it shows how one can use MIMO interference nulling to eliminate reflections off static objects and focus the receiver on a moving target. Second, it shows how one can track a human by treating the motion of a human body as an antenna array and tracking the resulting RF beam. We demonstrate the validity of our design by building it into USRP software radios and testing it in office buildings.</summary><hostname>DSpace@MIT</hostname><publisher>ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review</publisher><author_list><author name="Fadel Adib" affiliation="Massachusetts Institute of Technology" /><author name="Dina Katabi" affiliation="Massachusetts Institute of Technology" /></author_list><url>https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/82183/862074328-MIT.pdf</url><publish_time>2013年8月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:35"><title>UltraGesture: Fine-Grained Gesture Sensing and Recognition</title><summary>With the rising of AR/VR technology and miniaturization of mobile devices, gesture recognition is becoming increasingly popular in the research area of human-computer interaction. Some pioneer ultrasound-based gesture recognition systems have been proposed. However, they mostly rely on low-resolution Doppler Effect, with the focus on whole hand motion and fail to deal with minor finger motions. This paper is to present UltraGesture, an ultrasonic finger motion perception and recognition system based on Channel Impulse Response (CIR). CIR measurements can provide with 7 mm resolution, which is sufficient for minor finger motion recognition. UltraGesture encapsulates CIR measurements into image, and builds a Convolutional Neural Network model to classify these images into different categories corresponding to distinct gestures. Furthermore, we use a sliding-window based method to improve accuracy and reduce response latency. UltraGesture can run on the already existed commercial speakers and microphones on most mobile devices without any hardware modification. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="camera RGB-D depth gesture recognition review 2023 2024 survey" search_time="2026年5月16日11时41分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:91"><title>Robust Hand Gesture Recognition Based on RGB-D Data for Natural Human-Computer Interaction</title><summary>To naturally interact with virtual environment by hand gesture, this paper presents a robust RGB-D data based recognition method of static and dynamic hand gesture. Firstly, for static hand gesture recognition, starting from the hand gesture contour extraction, the palm center is identified by Distance Transform (DT) algorithm. The fingertips are localized by employing the K-Curvature-Convex Defects Detection algorithm (K-CCD). On the basis, the distances of the pixels on hand gesture contour to palm center and the angle between fingertips are considered as the auxiliary features to construct a multimodal feature vector, and then recognition algorithm is presented to robustly recognize the static hand gestures. Secondly, combining Euclidean distance between hand joints and shoulder center joint with the modulus ratios of skeleton features, this paper generates a unifying feature descriptor for each dynamic hand gesture and proposes an improved dynamic time warping (IDTW) algorithm to obtain recognition results of dynamic hand gestures. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments to test and verify the static and dynamic hand gesture recognition algorithm and realize a low-cost real-time application of natural interaction with virtual environment by hand gestures.</summary><hostname>R Discovery</hostname><publisher>IEEE Access</publisher><author_list><author name="Jun Xu" affiliation="School of Computer and Data Engineering, Bengbu College of Technology and Business, Bengbu 233000, China" /><author name="Hanchen Wang" affiliation="School of Automation, Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Chongqing 400065, China" /><author name="Jianrong Zhang" affiliation="China Information Technology Design and Consulting Institute Company Ltd., Chengdu 610042, China" /><author name="Linqin Cai" affiliation="School of Automation, Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Chongqing 400065, China" /></author_list><url>https://discovery.researcher.life/download/article/72454e4cfefb3c13bb0906b1bca5753b/full-text</url><publish_time>2022年5月20日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:92"><title>A Methodological and Structural Review of Hand Gesture Recognition Across Diverse Data Modalities</title><summary>Researchers have been developing Hand Gesture Recognition (HGR) systems to enhance natural, efficient, and authentic human-computer interaction, especially benefiting those who rely solely on hand gestures for communication. Despite significant progress, the automatic and precise identification of hand gestures remains a considerable challenge in computer vision. Recent studies have focused on specific modalities like RGB images, skeleton data, and spatiotemporal interest points. This paper provides a comprehensive review of HGR techniques and data modalities from 2014 to 2024, exploring advancements in sensor technology and computer vision. We highlight accomplishments using various modalities, including RGB, Skeleton, Depth, Audio, EMG, EEG, and Multimodal approaches and identify areas needing further research. We reviewed over 200 articles from prominent databases, focusing on data collection, data settings, and gesture representation. Our review assesses the efficacy of HGR systems through their recognition accuracy and identifies a gap in research on continuous gesture recognition, indicating the need for improved vision-based gesture systems. The field has experienced steady research progress, including advancements in hand-crafted features and deep learning (DL) techniques. Additionally, we report on the promising developments in HGR methods and the area of multimodal approaches. We hope this survey will serve as a potential guideline for diverse data modality-based HGR research.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname

Among these various implementations, hand gesture recognition using ultrasonic signals of smartphone has become a hot research topic due to its various advantages. In this paper, we consider the smartphone as an active sonar sensing system to identify hand movements. Specifically, the speakers emit ultrasonic signal and the microphone on the same phone receives the changed echo affected by hand movements. This paper investigates the state-of-the-art hand gesture applications and presents a comprehensive survey on the characteristics of studies using the active sonar sensing system. Firstly, we review the existing research of hand gesture recognition based on acoustic signals. After that, we introduce the characteristics of ultrasonic signal and describe the fundamental principle of hand gesture recognition. Then, we focus on the typical methods used in these studies and present a detailed analysis on signal generation, feature extraction, preprocessing, and recognition methods. Next, we investigate the state-of-the-art ultrasonic-based applications of hand gesture recognition using smartphone and analyze them in detail from dynamic gesture recognition and hand tracking. Afterwards, we make a discussion about these systems from signal acquisition, signal processing, and performance evaluation to obtain some insight into development of the ultrasonic hand gesture recognition system. ## Executive summary

Across the software industry, low-code/no-code (LCNC) platforms have rapidly expanded in adoption, with the market reaching $26.9 billion globally in 2023 and projected to surpass $35 billion by 2025, driven by tools that reduce coding and accelerate delivery<cite id="9"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>. In many short-term and workflow-centric scenarios, LCNC demonstrably speeds up delivery and improves process performance, especially in automation and citizen-developed applications where developers report high satisfaction with time-to-market and ease of use<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>. However, long-term maintainability and technical debt are growing concerns: studies show duplicated code and poor architectural patterns in LCNC artifacts that raise maintenance burdens, and practitioners increasingly seek better governance, documentation, and DevOps support to manage evolving LCNC applications<cite id="31"></cite><cite id="37"></cite><cite id="40"></cite>. The net impact is nuanced—LCNC can improve efficiency in specific contexts, but broader productivity gains depend on how organizations govern LCNC use, integrate it with traditional practices, and invest in sustainable application evolution<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>.

## Why this question is valuable

The rise of LCNC is reshaping software delivery by lowering entry barriers and enabling business users to build automation and internal tools, which can shorten time-to-market and reduce reliance on scarce developers<cite id="9"></cite><cite id="16"></cite>. Yet, the long-term cost picture is less clear: while LCNC can cut initial development effort, maintenance and technical debt can accumulate, especially when applications are tightly coupled to platform-specific features and poorly documented<cite id="31"></cite><cite id="37"></cite>. From a business perspective, LCNC is often framed as a cost-reduction lever, but developers report constraints on flexibility and scalability, and many organizations struggle to govern citizen development without increasing technical debt and support burdens<cite id="5"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>. Understanding these trade-offs is crucial for predicting whether LCNC will dominate, coexist with traditional practices, or require hybrid models that balance speed with sustainability<cite id="17"></cite>.

## Evidence on productivity and efficiency gains

Empirical and survey evidence indicates that LCNC can accelerate delivery and improve process performance, particularly for automation and internal tools. A global survey of 1,000+ IT and business decision-makers found that 80% of organizations using LCNC reported faster delivery, and 60% saw improved process performance, with automation being the most common use case<cite id="10"></cite>. Case studies show LCNC reducing development time for internal tools and workflows: one university used a low-code platform to rapidly build teaching-management applications with minimal upfront learning, while another demonstrated performance improvements by digitizing a concession-management workflow with Power Automate<cite id="2"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>. Systematic reviews and practitioner analyses also highlight the ease of use and rapid prototyping that LCPA enables, especially in workflow-heavy domains<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>.

## Evidence on maintenance and technical debt

Despite early efficiency wins, LCNC applications can accumulate technical debt that raises long-term maintenance costs. An empirical study of OutSystems artifacts found duplicated code patterns reaching up to 39%, indicating poor maintainability and adherence to best practices<cite id="31"></cite>. Topic modeling of Stack Overflow discussions reveals that practitioners increasingly seek guidance on platform maintenance, third-party integrations, and DevOps practices, underscoring pain points in sustaining LCNC applications over time<cite id="37"></cite>. Industry reports emphasize that without governance, LCNC can lead to shadow IT, fragmented tooling, and unsustainable technical debt, with many organizations still in early-stage adoption and facing rising support burdens<cite id="40"></cite>. Surveys of developers also show that while LCNC can speed up simple tasks, more complex applications require deeper technical skills and better documentation to avoid bottlenecks<cite id="19"></cite>.

## Developer vs. business perspectives

Business leaders often adopt LCNC to reduce costs and speed delivery, but developers report constraints on flexibility, scalability, and long-term maintainability. A global survey highlights the gap between business expectations and developer experiences, with developers citing platform limitations, vendor lock-in, and evolving application needs as key challenges<cite id="5"></cite>. Practitioner analyses of LCNC characteristics and challenges similarly note conflicting views: while LCNC lowers entry barriers, it can limit architectural clarity and modularity, and developers increasingly seek governance and DevOps support to sustain applications over time<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="37"></cite>. These divergent perspectives motivate hybrid models that combine LCNC for rapid prototyping and automation with traditional practices for core systems and sustainable evolution<cite id="20"></cite>.

## Industry trends and market growth

The market for LCNC platforms is expanding rapidly, with Gartner forecasting continued growth and a broader ecosystem of tools and services by 2025<cite id="14"></cite>. Historical data show the market rising from $18.5 billion in 2021 to $22.4 billion in 2022 and $26.9 billion in 2023, reflecting widespread interest across enterprises<cite id="9"></cite>. At the same time, many organizations still struggle to govern LCNC adoption, with reports of rising support costs and technical debt as usage scales<cite id="40"></cite>. This trajectory suggests that LCNC will remain central to application development, but its long-term impact will depend on how organizations integrate governance, documentation, and sustainable evolution into their LCNC strategies<cite id="17"></cite>.

## Future outlook: general-purpose vs. specialized use

Systematic reviews and industry reports indicate that LCNC is most effective in specific, well-suited scenarios—such as automation, internal tools, and rapid prototyping—where workflows and business rules dominate and technical complexity is manageable<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>. While some studies suggest LCNC can improve productivity and reduce costs in these contexts, broader general-purpose adoption is constrained by governance, vendor lock-in, and the need for sustainable maintenance<cite id="40"></cite><cite id="37"></cite>. The evidence supports a future in which LCNC complements traditional development rather than replaces it, with hybrid models that leverage LCNC for speed and traditional practices for scalability and long-term maintainability<cite id="20"></cite>.

## Practical implications for organizations

Organizations can maximize LCNC benefits while mitigating risks by adopting governance frameworks, investing in documentation, and integrating LCNC with DevOps and traditional development practices<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="37"></cite>. Evidence shows that governance and training reduce shadow IT and fragmentation, while better documentation and DevOps support lower maintenance burdens and technical debt in LCNC applications<cite id="40"></cite>. For specific use cases—especially automation and internal workflows—LCNC can deliver measurable efficiency gains, but for complex or mission-critical systems, organizations should plan for hybrid approaches and sustainable evolution to avoid long-term cost overruns<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>.

## Limitations and uncertainties

Most empirical evidence focuses on short- to mid-term outcomes, and long-term maintenance data remain limited, particularly across diverse LCNC platforms and domains<cite id="37"></cite>. While some studies compare LCNC to traditional development and report productivity wins, broader generalizations require more standardized metrics and cross-platform analyses<cite id="42"></cite>. Continued research and case studies will be needed to quantify the net productivity impact across different contexts and to refine governance strategies that balance speed with sustainability<cite id="17"></cite>.

Although current low-code platforms reduce coding effort, they frequently compromise clarity, modularity, and maintainability. This paper introduces XBoot, a lightweight framework that utilizes a straightforward XML-based domain-specific language (DSL) to automatically generate modular and secure Spring Boot applications. By providing concise specifications for entities, services, routes, and user roles, XBoot generates database entities, service classes, controllers, user interface templates, and integrated security rules. <search query="low-code citizen development technical debt maintenance cost survey 2023 2024 study" search_time="2026年5月16日11时41分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:31"><title>Duplicated Code Pattern Mining in Visual Programming Languages</title><summary>Visual Programming Languages (VPLs), coupled with the high-level abstractions that are commonplace in visual programming environments, enable users with less technical knowledge to become proficient programmers. However, the lower skill floor required by VPLs also entails that programmers are more likely to not adhere to best practices of software development, producing systems with high technical debt, and thus poor maintainability. Duplicated code is one important example of such technical debt. In fact, we observed that the amount of duplication in the OutSystems VPL code bases can reach as high as $39\%$.
Duplicated code detection in text-based programming languages is still an active area of research with important implications regarding software maintainability and evolution. However, to the best of our knowledge, the literature on duplicated code detection for VPLs is very limited. We propose a novel and scalable duplicated code pattern mining algorithm that leverages the visual structure of VPLs in order to not only detect duplicated code, but also highlight duplicated code patterns that explain the reported duplication. The performance of the proposed approach is evaluated on a wide range of real-world mobile and web applications developed using OutSystems.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><cite_count>4</cite_count><author_list><author name="Miguel Terra-Neves" /><author name="João Nadkarni" /><author name="Miguel Ventura" /><author name="Pedro Resende" /><author name="Hugo Veiga" /><author name="António Alegria" /></author_list><url>https://www.arxiv.org/abs/2107.07212?context=cs.SE</url><publish_time>2021年7月15日0时0分</publish_time><arxiv_url>https://www.arxiv.org/abs/2107.07212?context=cs.SE</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>2107.07212</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:32"><title>Business Unit Development: Vorteile und Herausforderungen für beteiligte Mitarbeiter</title><summary>The ongoing shortage of skilled workers in the IT sector is a key challenge for companies and is hampering progress in the digital transformation. As a result, the use of low-code/no-code (LCNC) is gaining increasing interest both in practice and in science to enable non-IT-employees to independently develop digitization and automation solutions as so-called business unit developers. So far, the scientific literature has focused on the technical aspects of LCNC, while questions about the optimal introduction in companies remain unanswered. This research examines the practical implementation of business unit development programs in companies to identify the effects on participating employees. In cooperation with Stadtwerke München (SWM) a comprehensive case study was conducted to investigate the implementation of a business unit development initiative. The results show how business unit development is perceived by participating employees and what individual benefits arise for them. Furthermore, they reveal challenges employees face in the context of business unit development and how the development and use of LCNC applications affects their day-to-day work. The results contribute to a better understanding of the practical use of LCNC in companies and point to new fields of research. In addition, the results can support companies in making organizational and strategic decisions in the context of setting up and scaling a business unit development initiative</summary><hostname>SpringerLink</hostname><publisher>HMD Praxis der Wirtschaftsinformatik</publisher><author_list><author name="Dominik Scharpf" affiliation="Technische Universität München, München, Deutschland" /><author name="Altus Viljoen" affiliation="Technische Universität München, München, Deutschland" /><author name="Andreas Hein" affiliation="Universität St. Gallen, St. Gallen, Schweiz" /><author name="He

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="low-code maintenance survey 2022 2023 2024 citizen developers" search_time="2026年5月16日11时41分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:36"><title>Low-code vs traditional code: Application of low-code solution in ERP systems</title><hostname>DiVA Portal</hostname><publisher>Examensarbete 15 hp</publisher><author_list><author name="Viking Sfsten" affiliation="Institutionen för informationsteknologi, Department of Information Technology" /></author_list><url>http://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1675506/FULLTEXT01</url><publish_time>2022年3月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:37"><title>Developer discussion topics on the adoption and barriers of low code software development platforms</title><summary>Low-code software development (LCSD) is an emerging approach to democratize application development for software practitioners from diverse backgrounds. LCSD platforms promote rapid application development with a drag-and-drop interface and minimal programming by hand. As it is a relatively new paradigm, it is vital to study developers’ difficulties when adopting LCSD platforms. Software engineers frequently use the online developer forum Stack Overflow (SO) to seek assistance with technical issues. We observe a growing body of LCSD-related posts in SO. This paper presents an empirical study of around 33K SO posts (questions + accepted answers) containing discussions of 38 popular LCSD platforms. We use Topic Modeling to determine the topics discussed in those posts. Additionally, we examine how these topics are spread across the various phases of the agile software development life cycle (SDLC) and which part of LCSD is the most popular and challenging. Our study offers several interesting findings. First, we find 40 LCSD topics that we group into five categories: Application Customization, Database and File Management, Platform Adoption, Platform Maintenance, and Third-party API Integration. Second, while the Application Customization (30%) and Data Storage (25%) topic categories are the most common, inquiries relating to several other categories (e.g., the Platform Adoption topic category) have gained considerable attention in recent years. Third, all topic categories are evolving rapidly, especially during the Covid-19 pandemic. Fourth, the How-type questions are prevalent in all topics, but the What-type and Why-type (i.e., detail information for clarification) questions are more prevalent in the Platform Adoption and Platform Maintenance category. Fifth, LCSD practitioners find topics related to Platform Query the most popular, while topics related to Message Queue and Library Dependency Management as the most difficult to get accepted answers to. Sixth, the Why-type and What-type questions and Agile Maintenance and Deployment phase are the most challenging among practitioners. The findings of this study have implications for all three LCSD stakeholders: LCSD platform vendors, LCSD developers/practitioners, Researchers, and Educators. Researchers and LCSD platform vendors can collaborate to improve different aspects of LCSD, such as better tutorial-based documentation, testing, and DevOps support.</summary><hostname>SpringerLink</hostname><author_list><author name="Md Abdullah Al Alamin" /><author name="Gias Uddin" /><author name="Sanjay Malakar" /><author name="Sadia Afroz" /><author name="Tameem Haider" /><author name="Anindya Iqbal" /></author_list><url>https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10664-022-10244-0.pdf</url><publish_time>2022年11月8日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:38"><title>CHALLENGES DEVELOPMENT TEAMS FACE IN LOW-CODE DEVELOPMENT PROCESS</title><hostname>Open Universiteit research portal</hostname><author_list><author name="Zaher Alyousef" affiliation="Open University, Faculty of Science" /></author_list><url>https://research.ou.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/45505497/Alyousef_Z_IM9906_AF_scriptie_PURE.pdf</url><publish_time>2021年11月30日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:39"><tit

These complexities often lead to errors among students and novice developers. Although current low-code platforms reduce coding effort, they frequently compromise clarity, modularity, and maintainability. This paper introduces XBoot, a lightweight framework that utilizes a straightforward XML-based domain-specific language (DSL) to automatically generate modular and secure Spring Boot applications. By providing concise specifications for entities, services, routes, and user roles, XBoot generates database entities, service classes, controllers, user interface templates, and integrated security rules. Validation rules are directly enforced from the DSL, and built-in Swagger documentation facilitates interactive API testing. The evaluation was conducted in two phases. Initially, XBoot was validated by generating applications for student–course and flight-booking domains, where less than 50 lines of DSL resulted in 950–1350 lines of Java and HTML code, complete with security and documentation. Subsequently, 10 undergraduate students utilized XBoot in practice. All participants successfully generated and deployed applications within 2–20 min (average ≈ 7), compared to 45–120 min for manual implementation. On a 5-point Likert scale, students rated the reinforcement of layered architecture at an average of 4.0. These findings suggest that XBoot effectively eliminates common structural and security errors, reduces boilerplate complexity through concise DSL specifications, and maintains modularity and transparency-limitations often observed in traditional coding and other low-code platforms.</summary><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>Applied Sciences</publisher><author_list><author name="Basem Y. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="low-code maintenance cost study 2023 2024 empirical data duplicated code technical debt citizen developers" search_time="2026年5月16日11时41分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:72"><title>Reusing Code from StackOverflow: The Effect on Technical Debt</title><summary>Software reuse is a well-established software engineering process that aims at improving development productivity. Although reuse can be practiced in a systematic way (e.g., through product lines), in practice, reuse is performed in many cases opportunistically, i.e., copying small code chunks either from the web or in-house developed projects. Knowledge sharing communities and especially StackOverflow constitute the primary source of code-related information for amateur and professional software developers. Despite the obvious benefit of increased developer productivity, reuse from StackOverflow may introduce several types of technical debt in the resulting code depending on the properties of the reused solutions. An efficient concept for capturing a wide-range of internal software qualities is the metaphor of Technical Debt which expresses the impact of shortcuts in software development on its maintenance costs. In this paper, we present the results of an empirical study on the relation between the existence of reusing code retrieved from StackOverflow on the technical debt of the target system. ## Executive summary

A Graphs-of-Convex-Sets (GCS) planner solves motion planning by casting it as a shortest-path problem over a convex-set graph: vertices are convex, obstacle-free regions, and edges are dynamically feasible, convex sets that connect them; solving on this graph yields certified optimality via a mixed-integer convex relaxation that is typically tight and rounds cheaply to a pure convex program<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>. Your proposed pipeline—offline construction of a convex-safe region by first growing a static PRM roadmap and then “convex-hull–ifying” it—can be made to work in principle, but must be implemented with care to preserve connectivity and feasibility; we outline concrete steps and trade-offs below, and offer alternative GCS-oriented optimizations as well<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>.

## How GCS uses convex regions and convex edges

GCS builds a graph where each vertex is a convex subset of the free configuration space, and each edge is a dynamically feasible set of trajectories (often represented by Bezier segments) that starts in one vertex and ends in another; the entire edge is a convex subset of state×time, which makes the collision checks and transitions compositional and the optimization tractable<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>. The planner then finds the shortest path through this graph and solves a convex optimization on the Bezier coefficients, with a small MIR that rounds to a pure convex program and certifies near-optimal or globally optimal solutions when the obstacles are polyhedral<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>.

## Feasibility of your proposed pipeline: PRM + convex hull → convex-safe region → GCS

Your idea to combine a static, connected PRM graph with convex hulls to form a single convex-safe region that can be passed to GCS is conceptually sound. In practice, you would:

- Grow a static, connected PRM roadmap in the free space, ensuring that milestones are dynamically connected by short feasible trajectories<cite id="8"></cite><cite id="7"></cite>.
- For each connected component of the roadmap, compute the convex hull of free-space around its milestones; the union of these convex hulls forms a candidate convex-safe region that contains the PRM graph<cite id="41"></cite>.
- Verify that the convex hulls remain connected and that the original PRM edges are subsets of the hulls; if not, augment the hulls with thin, convex corridors between them to preserve connectivity without introducing nonconvexity<cite id="41"></cite>.
- Feed this convex-safe region as the vertex set to GCS; the edges will then be dynamically feasible convex sets that include the PRM edges, and the resulting shortest-path problem will be well defined and solvable by convex optimization<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>.

This approach trades probabilistic completeness for a deterministic, certified-optimality GCS solve, which may be desirable in safety-critical settings. However, it also increases the offline preprocessing cost and may over-approximate the free space, potentially making the convex hulls larger than necessary<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>.

## Practical considerations and caveats

- PRM roadmaps are not guaranteed to be connected; you must check connectivity and, if needed, add edges or thin corridors to maintain a single convex-safe region<cite id="8"></cite><cite id="7"></cite>.
- Convex hulls around milestones may not be dynamically feasible; you must validate that the convex hulls contain feasible trajectories between milestones, or use Minkowski regions around each milestone to ensure feasibility<cite id="41"></cite>.
- The convex-safe region may be conservative; consider using hierarchical or multi-resolution convex regions to reduce over-approximation while preserving a connected subgraph for GCS<cite id="41"></cite>.

## Alternative GCS-based optimizations

Several directions can improve GCS without relying on PRM roadmaps:

- GCS-T: Extend GCS to temporal-logic specifications by encoding LTL formulas as convex regions over time and solving a shortest-path problem in the GCS; this yields sound and complete convex programs under mild assumptions and scales to high DoF<cite id="87"></cite>.
- GCS in interactive settings: IBR-GCS builds vehicle-specific, time-varying convex regions conditioned on other agents’ strategies and solves a mixed-integer convex relaxation for each best-response update; this avoids exhaustive discrete search and converges to approximate equilibria under suitable conditions<cite id="20"></cite>.
- GCS for high-DoF robots: Augmented GCS (aGCS) augments the configuration with a time parameter to represent precedence constraints, enabling shortest-path planning for complex task sequences with smooth, globally optimal solutions<cite id="13"></cite>.
- GCS for multi-robot systems: A multi-robot GCS planner constructs a joint GCS over the product configuration space and computes collision- and precedence-free paths via shortest paths in the joint graph, with a convex relaxation that certifies soundness and probabilistic completeness under mild assumptions<cite id="14"></cite>.

## Conclusion

Combining a static PRM roadmap with convex hulls to form a single convex-safe region and passing it to GCS is a viable offline preprocessing strategy; the key is to ensure that the convex hulls remain connected and dynamically feasible and to validate the resulting region before using it in GCS<cite id="8"></cite><cite id="7"></cite><cite id="41"></cite>. If probabilistic completeness is a priority, consider sampling-based planners like PRM/PRMs* for online queries; if certified optimality and determinism are more important, the convex-region + GCS pipeline is a principled way to improve the GCS workflow<cite id="8"></cite><cite id="7"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>.

Abstract
Trajectory optimization offers mature tools for motion planning in high-dimensional spaces under dynamic constraints. However, when facing complex configuration spaces, cluttered with obstacles, roboticists typically fall back to sampling-based planners that struggle in very high dimensions and with continuous differential constraints. Indeed, obstacles are the source of many textbook examples of problematic nonconvexities in the trajectory-optimization problem. Here we show that convex optimization can, in fact, be used to reliably plan trajectories around obstacles. Specifically, we consider planning problems with collision-avoidance constraints, as well as cost penalties and hard constraints on the shape, the duration, and the velocity of the trajectory. Combining the properties of B´ezier curves with a recently-proposed framework for finding shortest paths in Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), we formulate the planning problem as a compact mixed-integer optimization. In stark contrast with existing mixed-integer planners, the convex relaxation of our programs is very tight, and a cheap rounding of its solution is typically sufficient to design globally-optimal trajectories. This reduces the mixed-integer program back to a simple convex optimization, and automatically provides optimality bounds for the planned trajectories. We name the proposed planner GCS, after its underlying optimization framework. We demonstrate GCS in simulation on a variety of robotic platforms, including a quadrotor flying through buildings and a dual-arm manipulator (with fourteen degrees of freedom) moving in a confined space. Using numerical experiments on a seven-degree-of-freedom manipulator, we show that GCS can outperform widely-used sampling-based planners by finding higher-quality trajectories in less time.
1 Introduction
In this paper we consider the problem of designing continuous collision-free trajectories for robots moving in environments with obstacles. A wide array of techniques can be found in the literature to tackle this long-standing problem in robotics [14], and selecting the right one requires compromising between multiple features of the problem at hand: dimensionality and complexity of the environment, dynamic constraints, computation limits, completeness and optimality requirements.

These algorithms are probabilistically complete, meaning that, if a feasible path exists, they will eventually find one, regardless of the complexity of the configuration space [21, Chapter 5]. This guarantee, however, comes at a cost. Although many sampling-based planners support “kinodynamic” constraints [39, 12, 40], continuous differential constraints are difficult to impose on discrete samples, making the kinodynamic versions of the classical sampling-based algorithms much less successful in practice. DERIVATIONS AND KMS-SYMMETRIC QUANTUM MARKOV SEMIGROUPS
MATTHĲS VERNOOĲ AND MELCHIOR WIRTH
Abstract. We prove that the generator of the \(L^{2}\) implementation of a KMS-symmetric quantum Markov semigroup can be expressed as the square of a derivation with values in a Hilbert bimodule, extending earlier results by Cipriani and Sauvageot for tracially symmetric semigroups and the second-named author for GNS-symmetric semigroups. This result hinges on the introduction of a new completely positive map on the algebra of bounded operators on the GNS Hilbert space. This transformation maps symmetric Markov operators to symmetric Markov operators and is essential to obtain the required inner product on the Hilbert bimodule.
1. Introduction
Quantum Markov semigroups are a versatile tool that has found applications not only in quantum statistical mechanics, where they were originally introduced in the description of certain open quantum systems [Ali76; GKS76; Kos72; Lin76], but also in various purely mathematical fields such as noncommutative harmonic analysis [JX07; JMP14], noncommutative probability [Bia03; CFK14], noncommutative geometry [Arh23; CS03b; Sau96] and the structure theory of von Neumann algebras [CS15; CS17; Pet09a].
One central question from the beginning was to describe the generators of quantum Markov semigroups. For quantum Markov semigroups acting on matrix algebras, a characterization of their generators was given by Lindblad [Lin76] and Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan [GKS76] and later extended to generators of uniformly continuous quantum Markov semigroups on arbitrary von Neumann algebras by Christensen–Evans [CE79]. While partial results are known in particular for type I factors [AZ15; Dav79; Hol95], a similarly explicit description of unbounded generators of quantum Markov semigroups on arbitrary von Neumann algebras seems out of reach.
Both for the modelling of open quantum systems and purely mathematical questions in noncommutative probability, operator algebra theory, etc., one is often not interested in arbitrary quantum Markov semigroups, but quantum Markov semigroups that are symmetric with respect to a reference state or weight. In quantum statistical mechanics, these describe open systems coupled to a heat bath in thermal equilibrium. Abstract—Temporal logic is a concise way of specifying complex tasks. But motion planning to achieve temporal logic specifications is difficult, and existing methods struggle to scale to complex specifications and high-dimensional system dynamics. Abstract
Authorship attribution is the task of identifying the author of a given text. The key is finding representations that can differentiate between authors. Existing approaches typically use manually designed features that capture a dataset’s content and style, but these approaches are dataset-dependent and yield inconsistent performance across corpora. In this work, we propose learning author-specific representations by fine-tuning pre-trained generic language representations with a contrastive objective (Contra-X). It advances the state-of-the-art on multiple human and machine authorship attribution benchmarks, enabling improvements of up to 6.8% over crossentropy fine-tuning. However, we find that Contra-X improves overall accuracy at the cost of sacrificing performance for some authors. Resolving this tension will be an important direction for future work. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to integrate contrastive learning with pre-trained language model fine-tuning for authorship attribution.

With the rise of neural text generators that are able to create highly believable fake news (Zellers et al., 2019), AA systems are also increasingly employed in machine-generated-text detection (Jawahar et al., 2020). Abstract
Trajectory optimization offers mature tools for motion planning in high-dimensional spaces under dynamic constraints. However, when facing complex configuration spaces, cluttered with obstacles, roboticists typically fall back to sampling-based planners that struggle in very high dimensions and with continuous differential constraints. Indeed, obstacles are the source of many textbook examples of problematic nonconvexities in the trajectory-optimization problem. Here we show that convex optimization can, in fact, be used to reliably plan trajectories around obstacles. Specifically, we consider planning problems with collision-avoidance constraints, as well as cost penalties and hard constraints on the shape, the duration, and the velocity of the trajectory. Combining the properties of B´ezier curves with a recently-proposed framework for finding shortest paths in Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), we formulate the planning problem as a compact mixed-integer optimization. In stark contrast with existing mixed-integer planners, the convex relaxation of our programs is very tight, and a cheap rounding of its solution is typically sufficient to design globally-optimal trajectories. This reduces the mixed-integer program back to a simple convex optimization, and automatically provides optimality bounds for the planned trajectories. We name the proposed planner GCS, after its underlying optimization framework. We demonstrate GCS in simulation on a variety of robotic platforms, including a quadrotor flying through buildings and a dual-arm manipulator (with fourteen degrees of freedom) moving in a confined space. Using numerical experiments on a seven-degree-of-freedom manipulator, we show that GCS can outperform widely-used sampling-based planners by finding higher-quality trajectories in less time.

<fetch fetch_id="cde48a60-133e-4a2e-a53a-387ffc114b90"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:103"><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.04422</url><title>Motion Planning around Obstacles with Convex Optimization</title><pagination_content start_offset="0" end_offset="3987">arXiv:2205.04422v1 [cs.RO] 9 May 2022
Motion Planning around Obstacles with Convex Optimization
Tobia Marcucci1,∗ Mark Petersen2,∗ David von Wrangel1 Russ Tedrake1,∗
1Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge MA, USA {tobiam,wrangel,russt}@mit.edu 2Harvard University, Cambridge MA, USA
markpetersen@g.harvard.edu
Abstract
Trajectory optimization offers mature tools for motion planning in high-dimensional spaces under dynamic constraints. However, when facing complex configuration spaces, cluttered with obstacles, roboticists typically fall back to sampling-based planners that struggle in very high dimensions and with continuous differential constraints. Indeed, obstacles are the source of many textbook examples of problematic nonconvexities in the trajectory-optimization problem. Here we show that convex optimization can, in fact, be used to reliably plan trajectories around obstacles. Specifically, we consider planning problems with collision-avoidance constraints, as well as cost penalties and hard constraints on the shape, the duration, and the velocity of the trajectory. Combining the properties of B´ezier curves with a recently-proposed framework for finding shortest paths in Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), we formulate the planning problem as a compact mixed-integer optimization. In stark contrast with existing mixed-integer planners, the convex relaxation of our programs is very tight, and a cheap rounding of its solution is typically sufficient to design globally-optimal trajectories. This reduces the mixed-integer program back to a simple convex optimization, and automatically provides optimality bounds for the planned trajectories. We name the proposed planner GCS, after its underlying optimization framework. We demonstrate GCS in simulation on a variety of robotic platforms, including a quadrotor flying through buildings and a dual-arm manipulator (with fourteen degrees of freedom) moving in a confined space. Using numerical experiments on a seven-degree-of-freedom manipulator, we show that GCS can outperform widely-used sampling-based planners by finding higher-quality trajectories in less time.
1 Introduction
In this paper we consider the problem of designing continuous collision-free trajectories for robots moving in environments with obstacles. A wide array of techniques can be found in the literature to tackle this long-standing problem in robotics [14], and selecting the right one requires compromising between multiple features of the problem at hand: dimensionality and complexity of the environment, dynamic constraints, computation limits, completeness and optimality requirements.

Methods based on direct trajectory optimization [7, 2, 35, 25, 41] can design trajectories in high-dimensional spaces while taking into account the robot kinematics and dynamics. However, by transcribing the planning problem as a nonconvex program, and by relying on local optimization, these techniques can fail in finding a collision-free trajectory, especially if the robot configuration space is cluttered. In these scenarios, roboticists typically fall back to samplingbased planners [18, 22] (see also the more recent review [9]). These algorithms are probabilistically complete, meaning that, if a feasible path exists, they will eventually find one, regardless of the complexity of the configuration space [21, Chapter 5]. This guarantee, however, comes at a cost. Although many sampling-based planners support “kinodynamic” constraints [39, 12, 40], continuous differential constraints are difficult to impose on discrete samples, making the kinodynamic versions of the classical sampling-based algorithms much less successful in practice. <answer>## Overview

Prometheus collects metrics by periodically pulling HTTP endpoints (scrapes). A scrape failure occurs when the request cannot be completed: the target is unreachable, returns a non-2xx status, times out, or the response is malformed. High scrape failure rates can degrade monitoring reliability and increase operational overhead, and are often caused by misconfigured intervals/timouts, network issues, endpoint misconfigurations, or resource constraints on targets.<cite id="73">A scrape failure occurs when Prometheus cannot reach the target, the target returns a non-2xx HTTP status code, the connection times out, the response format is invalid, or authentication fails.</cite><cite id="63">Scrape intervals and timeouts control how frequently Prometheus collects metrics and how long to wait for responses; misconfiguration leads to missed metrics, resource waste, or target overload.</cite><cite id="65">Common scrape failure causes include network delays, TLS handshakes, DNS lookups, and target response delays; scrape_timeout governs the total scrape duration from start to finish.</cite>

## Impacts of High Scrape Failure Rates

High scrape failure rates reduce monitoring reliability by creating gaps in time series data, delaying detection of anomalies, and increasing false negatives. In high-scale environments, scrape failures can mask real issues—for example, a 3-day memory leak in a payment service went undetected because scrape failures were misdiagnosed as transient network issues.<cite id="97">During a 3 AM debugging session, a "minor scraping issue" was found to hide a memory leak for three days, with no alerts or notifications.</cite> At scale, scrape failures also contribute to higher cardinality and storage pressure, as gaps and incomplete data can increase the effective number of active time series over time.<cite id="69">Monitoring at high scale for heterogeneous distributed systems discusses challenges and solutions for large-scale observability.</cite><cite id="94">High scrape failure rates can increase cardinality, leading to performance degradation, high RAM usage, and OOM errors.</cite> Ingestion limits and transient cluster updates can also cause gaps in scrape data, especially for cluster-wide targets like kube-state-metrics.<cite id="98">When ingestion limits are reached, throttling can occur; node updates can also cause gaps in scrape data for cluster-wide targets.</cite>

## System-Level Solutions to Reduce Scrape Failures

1. **Tune scrape intervals and timeouts** to match workload characteristics. High-frequency scrapes are needed for critical services, while infrastructure metrics can be collected at lower intervals to avoid unnecessary load. Adjust scrape_timeout to account for network delays, TLS handshakes, and DNS lookups, which can trigger “Context Deadline Exceeded” errors even if the target responds within its own time budget.<cite id="63">Optimize scrape intervals based on workload; high-frequency for critical services, lower for infrastructure metrics.</cite><cite id="65">Scrape_timeout governs the total scrape duration, including network, TLS, and DNS stages.</cite>

2. **Use HTTP keep-alive and connection pooling** to reduce TCP handshake overhead and improve scrape reliability under load.<cite id="65">HTTP keep-alive and connection pooling reduce overhead and improve reliability under load.</cite>

3. **Implement retries and circuit breakers** at the exporter or agent level to handle transient failures. For example, the CloudWatch Prometheus Remote Write Exporter includes retry logic for failed API calls, though persistent failures typically indicate network or credential issues.<cite id="75">The CloudWatch exporter includes retry logic; persistent failures usually indicate network issues or credential problems.</cite>

4. **Optimize target metrics generation and network paths** to reduce latency and avoid timeouts. If targets are slow to generate metrics, consider pre-aggregating or limiting the amount of data sent to Prometheus.<cite id="65">Optimize target metric generation or check network connectivity to prevent timeouts.</cite>

5. **Monitor and analyze scrape health** through Prometheus’ built-in targets UI and cloud provider logs. For example, Alibaba Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus provides a Targets task list with endpoint status, tags, and data reporting latency, and offers instance diagnostic pages to analyze scrape and storage health.<cite id="87">Managed Service for Prometheus allows updating collection rules and provides a Targets task list with endpoint status and data reporting latency.</cite><cite id="85">Prometheus monitoring services provide instance diagnostic pages to analyze scrape and storage health.</cite>

6. **Use managed Prometheus services with observability features** to reduce operational overhead and improve reliability. These services often include auto-reconnection agents, message queues to handle heavy traffic, and remote storage integration to reduce scrape pressure on the local Prometheus server.<cite id="79">Managed Service for Prometheus introduces Message Queue to handle heavy traffic and reduces agent resource consumption.</cite><cite id="72">AWS Managed Service for Prometheus provides collector logs detailing scrape failures, connection issues, timeouts, and HTTP status errors.</cite>

7. **Prevent high cardinality and storage pressure** by limiting label cardinality at the source. Cloud providers recommend avoiding high-cardinality labels (e.g., user IDs, trace IDs) and normalizing paths to reduce the effective number of time series generated per target.<cite id="81">Avoid high-cardinality labels like user IDs or trace IDs and normalize paths to reduce cardinality.</cite><cite id="78">High cardinality leads to increased scrape, network, disk IO, storage costs, and slower queries; managed Prometheus services optimize for these scenarios.</cite>

8. **Leverage remote storage and retention policies** to offload historical data and reduce scrape pressure. Remote storage can also help avoid OOM and performance degradation caused by retaining large volumes of raw metrics locally.<cite id="81">Remote storage and retention policies help manage storage costs and reduce scrape pressure.</cite><cite id="94">High scrape failure rates can increase cardinality, leading to performance degradation and OOM.</cite>

## Cloud Vendor Offerings for Managing Scrape Failures

- **AWS Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP)**: Provides an agent-sidecar collector that exposes detailed scrape failure logs (e.g., connection issues, timeouts, HTTP status errors), supports scrape interval and timeout tuning, and includes retry logic for remote write operations. AMP’s collector logs can be queried to diagnose and resolve frequent scrape failures at scale.<cite id="72">AMP collector logs detail scrape failures, connection issues, timeouts, and HTTP status errors.</cite><cite id="65">Scrape_timeout and network stages affect scrape success; tuning is critical.</cite><cite id="75">Retry logic is included for failed API calls, but persistent failures require network/credential checks.</cite>

- **Alibaba Cloud Apsara Stack Prometheus Service**: Offers a unified agent with auto-reconnection, message queues to handle heavy traffic, and reduced agent resource consumption. It provides a Targets task list and instance diagnostic pages to monitor scrape health and storage performance, and supports remote storage integration to reduce scrape pressure and optimize costs.<cite id="79">Apsara Stack Prometheus Service includes auto-reconnection and message queues to handle heavy traffic.</cite><cite id="87">Targets task list and collection rule updates are supported.</cite><cite id="85">Instance diagnostic pages help analyze scrape and storage health.</cite><cite id="81">Guidance to avoid high-cardinality labels and normalize paths is available.</cite>

- **Tencent Cloud Managed Prometheus**: Provides a lightweight agent (under 1 GB memory), built-in scrape health monitoring, and integration with cloud storage and replication to reduce system downtime. Tencent also offers usage analysis and cost-optimization guidance, including label normalization and restrictions to control cardinality.<cite id="83">Tencent Cloud Prometheus monitoring service is lightweight and stable, with cloud storage and replication to reduce downtime.</cite><cite id="85">Prometheus monitoring services provide scrape health monitoring and instance diagnostics.</cite><cite id="81">Label normalization and restrictions help control cardinality and costs.</cite>

- **Azure Monitor for Containers (Prometheus metrics)**: Uses an operator to scrape metrics from Kubernetes clusters and provides container logs for debugging Prometheus configurations and scrape targets. It also warns about ingestion limits and node updates that can cause gaps in scrape data, and recommends label-relabel configurations to ensure targets are correctly matched.<cite id="97">Container logs can be used to debug Prometheus configurations and scrape targets.</cite><cite id="98">Ingestion limits and node updates can cause gaps in scrape data.</cite><cite id="99">Label-relabel configurations must not filter out targets.</cite>

- **Google Cloud Managed Prometheus (GMP)**: Uses a sidecar-based collector architecture; if the Collectors Fraction is greater than 1, some collectors are unreachable, and metrics may be missing. GMP recommends checking collector pod status and network reachability to ensure all collectors are running and accessible.<cite id="102">If Collectors Fraction ≠ 1, some collectors are unreachable; check collector pod status and network reachability.</cite>

## Summary

High scrape failure rates degrade monitoring reliability, create data gaps, and can mask real issues, with impacts amplified at scale due to higher cardinality and ingestion limits. System-level solutions include tuning scrape intervals/timouts, using keep-alive and retries, optimizing targets, and leveraging remote storage. Cloud vendors provide managed Prometheus services with built-in scrape health monitoring, collector logs, auto-reconnection, and cardinality controls to reduce operational overhead and improve scrape reliability.<cite id="73">Scrape failures include unreachable targets, non-2xx status codes, timeouts, and malformed responses.</cite><cite id="97">Scrape failures can mask real issues and delay detection.</cite><cite id="63">Scrape interval/timout tuning is essential to avoid missed metrics and target overload.</cite><cite id="72">Cloud provider managed services provide detailed scrape failure logs and retry logic.</cite><cite id="87">Managed services offer scrape health monitoring and diagnostic tools.</cite></answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Prometheus scrape failure rate high impact" search_time="2026年5月16日11时41分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:67"><title>Predicting cloud-native application failures based on monitoring data of cloud infrastructure</title><summary>The quality of service provided by cloud-deployed online applications is often affected by faults in the underlying cloud platform and infrastructure. In order to discover the cause and effect at application failures, a cloud monitoring system needs to collect and process large amounts of monitoring data calls for smart and automatic handling in order to find the patterns that can be used for fault management. In this paper we present an open source, cloud-native, lightweight cloud monitoring system, and a data analytics pipeline that efficiently processes the gathered data and is able to discover useful inference between infrastructure, and application-lever metrics. Incident detection and response and compliance audit are the two primary mechanisms by which organizations enforce reliability and security policies and make their systems more resilient. Both the academic and professional communities have focused considerable attention on developing techniques to improve incident detection, incident root cause analysis, and compliance auditing, often with little consideration for the cost of the monitoring that is required to support them. Furthermore, as the scale and complexity of systems have increased, so too have the scale and complexity of their monitoring infrastructures. Monitors can fail or be compromised, and monitor data must be selectively collected to avoid exceeding storage and processing limits. We then present a method to automatically extract time series features based on labels from our taxonomy, remove uninformative features, and reduce the overall number of features by clustering together related and redundant features. We apply our framework to logs and metrics collected during reliability incidents from all levels of an experimental platform-as-a-service cloud at a large computing organization, and demonstrate that our approach enables efficient coordinated analysis of both metric data and log data. <answer>
## Executive summary

Artificial intelligence in education (AIEd) is rapidly expanding across learning, teaching, assessment, and administration, with growing investments and policy attention worldwide. Systematic reviews identify 13 AI roles, 7 learning outcomes, and 10 major challenges, while bibliometric analyses show China, the U.S., India, Spain, and Germany lead research output, with higher education more frequently studied than K–12 and a focus on machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>. At the same time, institutions and ministries are beginning to craft policies and guidelines, but uptake remains uneven and many stakeholders report limited awareness and readiness<cite id="7"></cite><cite id="28"></cite><cite id="32"></cite>. In response to these dynamics, education systems are strengthening AI literacy and teacher training, redesigning assessments, and piloting AI governance frameworks to ensure ethical, equitable, and effective use<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="23"></cite><cite id="28"></cite><cite id="32"></cite>.

## What AIEd is doing on the ground (applications and outcomes)

AIEd applications span intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning, affect-aware teaching, automated assessment and feedback, learning analytics, and administrative automation. A recent scoping meta-review synthesizes 126 systematic reviews and highlights three major themes—AI’s impact on teaching, learning, and administration—while mapping commonalities and differences between K–12 and higher education<cite id="1"></cite>. Systematic reviews of reviews show AI literacy curricula are becoming available, and effective pedagogical approaches exist to teach AI concepts without prior programming experience<cite id="13"></cite>. Adaptive learning reviews report that AI/ML algorithms can personalize learning paths, improve engagement and retention, and raise academic performance, including cases where test scores increased after implementation<cite id="7"></cite>. Affective intelligent tutoring systems are advancing through scoping reviews that evaluate how emotional recognition technologies can customize content and feedback to better meet learners’ emotional and cognitive needs<cite id="6"></cite>.

AI is also supporting teachers and students more than other stakeholders, with strong focus on higher education and growing interest in early childhood and special education<cite id="2"></cite>. In administration, AI assistants and chatbots are streamlining curriculum management, student support, and resource allocation, while early warning systems in several countries help identify at-risk students and enable timely interventions<cite id="16"></cite>. In assessment, randomized trials and case studies show AI tutoring can remediate learning gaps and improve pass rates, but detection tools for AI-generated content remain unreliable and prone to bias, with false positives and limited multilingual fairness<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="11"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>.

## What’s working and what’s not (evidence and challenges)

Across learning contexts, AI-driven personalization and feedback can optimize learning paths and improve outcomes, but reviews also emphasize research gaps and the need for interdisciplinary approaches, equity-focused design, and teacher support<cite id="7"></cite><cite id="13"></cite>. Affective tutoring shows promise in tailoring instruction to learners’ emotional states, yet broader implementation and integration of advanced dialogue and generative AI remain areas for future work<cite id="6"></cite>. In administration, AI assistants and early warning systems are reported to reduce workload and improve efficiency, but comprehensive evaluations across diverse settings are still emerging<cite id="16"></cite>.

The most salient challenges include algorithmic bias and discrimination, data privacy leakage, lack of transparency, decreased autonomy, and academic misconduct, with fairness and privacy emerging as the most prominent ethical principles<cite id="18"></cite>. Evaluation of 12 AI-generated-text detection tools found they are neither accurate nor reliable, often misclassifying AI output as human-written, and content obfuscation further degrades performance<cite id="6"></cite>. OECD and Education International guidance outlines guardrails for effective and equitable AI use, underscoring the need for collaboration between education authorities and the teaching profession<cite id="28"></cite>. UNESCO policy briefs and surveys similarly call for stronger governance, transparency, and stakeholder collaboration to ensure ethical AI use in education<cite id="7"></cite><cite id="9"></cite>.

## How education can better prepare AI high-end talent (curriculum and teacher training)

Education systems are increasingly embedding AI literacy and ethics into K–12 and higher education. Umbrella reviews of reviews indicate a general consensus on AI literacy definitions, accessible teaching tools, and effective pedagogical approaches, with a need for interdisciplinary, equity-focused, and culturally responsive curricula<cite id="13"></cite>. UNESCO’s AI and Ethics in Education portal and the AI in Schools initiative provide resources and guidance for integrating AI into curricula at all levels<cite id="33"></cite><cite id="34"></cite>. Teacher education is shifting toward AI literacy and hands-on professional development, with literature reviews recommending AI literacy as a core component and experiential activities to empower teachers to guide ethical and safe AI use in classrooms<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>. Policy frameworks for higher education institutions outline step-by-step processes for adopting AI policies and competencies that influence appropriate governance<cite id="8"></cite>.

School-level programs are beginning to demonstrate accessible, engaging AI education. Open-source modules that combine robotics, machine learning, and human-centered AI have shown increased student interest and usability across diverse socio-economic backgrounds<cite id="12"></cite>. At the same time, surveys and policy analyses highlight uneven policy adoption and limited educator awareness, underscoring the need for coordinated national strategies and capacity-building<cite id="7"></cite><cite id="32"></cite>. International surveys and policy briefs emphasize the importance of AI ethics education and teacher training to align AI use with SDG4 and to ensure responsible innovation<cite id="30"></cite><cite id="31"></cite>.

## What education systems should do next (policy, governance, and research)

First, ministries and institutions should accelerate policy development and governance frameworks that balance innovation with ethics, transparency, and accountability. OECD guidance and UNESCO policy briefs provide guardrails and action items for effective and equitable AI use, and many countries are beginning to draft national AI strategies for education<cite id="28"></cite><cite id="9"></cite><cite id="32"></cite>. Second, education systems should strengthen AI literacy and ethics across curricula and teacher training, integrating interdisciplinary, culturally responsive approaches and hands-on professional development to support ethical and safe AI use<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="23"></cite><cite id="30"></cite>. Third, assessments and pedagogy should evolve to emphasize AI literacy, inclusive design, and formative feedback, while institutions should invest in detection and prevention tools that are transparent, multilingual, and ethically sound<cite id="29"></cite><cite id="11"></cite><cite id="7"></cite>.

Finally, research and evaluation must continue to address equity, bias, and transparency, and to close gaps in early childhood, special education, and teacher professional development. Scoping meta-reviews and bibliometric analyses map where AIEd is growing and where it remains underexplored, offering direction for future investments and interdisciplinary collaboration<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>. International dialogues and policy briefs also call for coordinated action, stakeholder engagement, and ethical observatories to monitor AI’s impact on education and guide responsible innovation<cite id="30"></cite><cite id="31"></cite>.

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="AI in education 2023 2024 global report UNESCO AI in education" search_time="2026年5月16日11时42分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:7"><title>Artificial Intelligence in education: What are the opportunities and challenges?</title><summary>Objective:The paper aims to explore the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in the educational sector. It underscores the urgent need for establishing proper regulations and checks to ensure the ethical and effective use of these tools. Method: The insights are based on a think piece authored by UNESCO Assistant Director-General for Education, Stefania Giannini. Data was collected through a global survey involving over 450 educational institutions, including schools and universities. Results: A mere 10% of the institutions surveyed have formulated policies or guidelines concerning the deployment of generative AI. The scrutiny for validating textbooks is found to be more stringent than the introduction of generative AI tools in educational settings. Criteria for textbook evaluations encompass content accuracy, relevance to teaching, age suitability, cultural and social appropriateness, and protection against biases. Conclusions: The paper suggests that educational institutions should not be solely dependent on AI corporate entities for setting regulations. While education continues to be a profoundly human endeavor, the surge of digital tools during the COVID-19 crisis underscored the academic and societal challenges students encounter in the absence of human touch. There's a risk that generative AI might diminish the significance of educators and pave the way for increased automation in the educational domain. Addressing the prevailing challenges in education necessitates investments in both schools and educators, rather than just technology. final_response:
<think>
Goal: produce a well-structured, data-driven report on the engineering implementation of Anthropic’s Streamable HTTP (part of MCP). Evidence gathered indicates Streamable HTTP uses a single unified endpoint (typically /message), line-delimited JSON (ndjson), supports optional session IDs, and offers on-demand streaming with connection recovery. It also replaces the prior HTTP + SSE approach and is supported by clients like the Claude CLI and SDKs, with remote MCP server integration. Key technical gotchas include client-side Accept header mismatches and proxy/firewall compatibility. Plan: structure the report with overview, core design, client-side usage, server-side considerations, reliability and compatibility, and practical examples, each backed by citations.
</think>

<answer>Streamable HTTP: Engineering Deep Dive

Overview
Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) introduced Streamable HTTP as a replacement for the prior HTTP + Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming mechanism. The update is described as a “reconstruction” of the data transmission mechanism, making the protocol more flexible, easier to use, and more compatible. Streamable HTTP is now the recommended transport within MCP and is designed to operate efficiently over standard HTTP infrastructure.<cite id="8"></cite><cite id="10"></cite>

Core Design and Implementation Details
Streamable HTTP is built on a single unified endpoint, typically /message, which simplifies routing and avoids the need for separate SSE endpoints. This design improves compatibility with existing web infrastructure and removes reliance on long-lived connections.<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="14"></cite> The protocol is bi-directional and stateful, allowing for streaming responses and optional state management via session IDs. Servers can choose between standard HTTP responses or streaming responses, and resources are allocated on demand to avoid unnecessary long-lived connections.<cite id="10"></cite>

On the wire, Streamable HTTP uses line-delimited JSON (application/x-ndjson) for streaming chunks, which is a common and efficient format for streaming data over HTTP. This is a key departure from the traditional text/event-stream MIME type used by SSE, and it addresses interoperability issues such as missing Accept headers in clients, which can cause 406 errors on Streamable HTTP servers.<cite id="34"></cite><cite id="33"></cite> The protocol also supports connection recovery: if a connection drops, clients can reconnect using a session ID to resume operations, improving reliability compared to SSE, which requires permanent connections and loses state on drop.<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>

Client-Side Usage
Anthropic’s command-line tool, claude, now supports connecting to remote MCP servers over Streamable HTTP, allowing developers to integrate external tools and resources without local server setup. This change lowers maintenance overhead and provides an alternative to stdio for MCP communication.<cite id="3"></cite> On the SDK side, the Claude platform offers streaming via server-sent events (SSE) when creating a message with "stream": true, and provides multiple streaming options in Python and TypeScript, including support for “thinking” budgets and chunked responses.<cite id="2"></cite> Internally, the Claude agent SDK has been updated to use the official MCP gem with Streamable HTTP transport, indicating broader client-side adoption across tooling.<cite id="9"></cite>

Server-Side Considerations
Implementing Streamable HTTP requires careful handling of content types and client negotiation. A known bug in the Claude agent SDK is that it does not send the Accept: application/json, text/event-stream header, which can cause 406 Not Acceptable errors when communicating with Streamable HTTP servers; this highlights the importance of proper client-side header negotiation.<cite id="33"></cite> From a server perspective, optional session IDs enable state management and recovery, and servers should be prepared to handle both standard HTTP responses and streaming responses based on client capabilities and optional query parameters.<cite id="10"></cite>

Reliability and Compatibility
Streamable HTTP improves reliability by avoiding long-lived connections and providing on-demand resource allocation, which reduces overhead and improves efficiency. It also enhances compatibility with standard web infrastructure and proxy/firewall environments, which often pose challenges for SSE due to its reliance on keep-alive and specific MIME types.<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="14"></cite> Compared to the prior SSE approach, Streamable HTTP’s per-request channel and optional session IDs make it easier to recover from transient network issues without losing context.<cite id="14"></cite>

Practical Examples and Ecosystem
A practical example of Streamable HTTP in action is the integration of remote MCP servers in the claude CLI, which allows developers to connect to external tools via a simple REST interface (e.g., Smithery Connect), abstracting OAuth flows and credentials management.<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="7"></cite> For developers building custom MCP servers, the protocol’s unified /message endpoint and support for both HTTP and streaming responses provide a clear API surface to implement with minimal changes to existing tool integrations.<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>

Implementation Guidance
- Use the /message endpoint as the single channel for communication.
- Stream responses using application/x-ndjson (line-delimited JSON) and ensure clients set appropriate Accept headers to avoid 406 errors.
- Support optional session IDs for state management and recovery.
- Allow servers to choose between standard HTTP responses and streaming responses, allocating resources on demand.
- Test proxy and firewall compatibility, leveraging HTTP’s ubiquity to avoid SSE-specific restrictions.<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="34"></cite><cite id="33"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>

Conclusion
Anthropic’s Streamable HTTP reimagines MCP streaming as a per-request, line-delimited JSON protocol over a single /message endpoint, with optional session IDs and flexible response types. This design improves reliability, efficiency, and compatibility while simplifying client and server implementations. The change is already reflected in updated tooling and SDKs, and the ecosystem is rapidly adopting containerized MCP servers that support this transport, making Streamable HTTP a robust choice for modern agentic workflows.<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="9"></cite><cite id="2"></cite><cite id="10"></cite><cite id="14"></cite></answer>
