problem: 软件行业未来趋势和被AI替代的可能性
final_response:
<think>
<answer>
## Executive summary

Software engineering is rapidly evolving with AI-augmented tools that assist across the development lifecycle, but software engineers will remain central as AI shifts their roles toward higher-value tasks. Empirical studies show productivity gains and efficiency improvements from generative AI in coding, documentation, testing, and debugging, with some developers reporting 30–40% productivity increases when using AI assistance<cite id="44"></cite><cite id="62"></cite><cite id="41"></cite>. At the same time, adoption remains uneven, with only about 13% of software engineering teams using GenAI systematically and average usage below 20%, indicating both opportunity and caution<cite id="42"></cite>. Industry and academic reviews emphasize that AI will augment rather than replace engineers, reshaping jobs through automation of routine tasks and creation of new roles while maintaining a strong demand for human expertise<cite id="34"></cite><cite id="54"></cite>.

## AI in software engineering: current trends and evidence

Large language models and code assistants are already embedded in mainstream workflows, with tools like GitHub Copilot widely used and developer communities actively documenting best practices, challenges, and expected features for AI pair programming<cite id="33"></cite>. A thesis analyzing AI’s integration across the software development lifecycle found that AI improves coding efficiency and software quality by automating tasks, streamlining workflows, and speeding development cycles, while explicitly noting that AI serves as a powerful assistant rather than a substitute for human expertise<cite id="31"></cite>. A recent empirical study of 204 global practitioners reports benefits and challenges of GenAI adoption, including institutionalization of tools and anticipated long-term impacts on the community<cite id="61"></cite>.

Field experiments at Microsoft, Accenture, and a Fortune 100 company found a 26.08% increase in completed tasks among developers using an AI coding assistant, with less experienced developers showing higher adoption and productivity gains<cite id="62"></cite>. Controlled studies also show that GenAI expedites repetitive tasks such as auto-filling standard boilerplate, documentation, and test cases, reinforcing its value in routine activities<cite id="43"></cite>. Industry analyses project productivity improvements of 30–40% among developers using GenAI and accelerated product development lifecycles, alongside reduced technical debt<cite id="44"></cite>.

## How AI is reshaping software engineering jobs

A structured analysis of over 19,000 tasks across 867 occupations classifies LLM exposure as high automation potential for routine and repetitive language-based tasks, high augmentation potential for tasks requiring abstract reasoning and problem-solving, and lower exposure for tasks emphasizing personal interaction and collaboration<cite id="53"></cite>. In software engineering, this means AI will most directly augment or automate documentation, boilerplate code, and repetitive testing/debugging, while pushing engineers toward architecture, design, debugging, and system-level problem solving<cite id="53"></cite><cite id="31"></cite>. A survey of 207 developers found that while ChatGPT use is growing, concerns about job displacement remain relatively low, and developers expect future adaptations of ChatGPT and new regulatory interventions<cite id="32"></cite>.

Academic reviews of AI in software engineering converge on a “human-in-the-loop” vision: AI will automate parts of the lifecycle and improve quality, but human oversight, decision-making, and creativity will remain essential<cite id="34"></cite><cite id="54"></cite>. A broader perspective on AI’s impact on jobs argues that AI will reshape more roles than it replaces, creating new positions and increasing demand for skills that complement AI capabilities<cite id="49"></cite>. Analyses of AI’s economic impact predict up to $16 trillion added to the global economy by 2030, underscoring both opportunity and the need for governance and workforce adaptation<cite id="39"></cite>.

## What is not being replaced

Software engineering extends beyond writing code to maintaining large systems and ensuring reliability—areas where current LLMs still struggle. A recent preprint argues that while LLMs can assist in code creation, the core of software engineering—especially maintenance and reliability—remains firmly in human hands<cite id="56"></cite>. Empirical studies also highlight that code generated by current GenAI tools often requires correction, shifting the engineer’s role from “doer” to “reviewer,” and emphasizing the need for human judgment and expertise<cite id="41"></cite><cite id="61"></cite>. Privacy, data security, and governance concerns further motivate careful integration of AI into developer environments, with evaluations at consultancies proposing future steps to scale AI implementations responsibly<cite id="31"></cite>.

## Outlook and implications for the workforce

Analysts project that AI will accelerate software development and reduce time-to-market, but also change the nature of engineering work rather than eliminate it<cite id="34"></cite>. Surveys and studies show developers expect continued use of AI tools and new roles emerging around LLM adoption, alongside concerns about skills gaps and regulatory frameworks<cite id="32"></cite><cite id="53"></cite>. Industry forecasts emphasize a skills shift: engineers will need to evolve from coding to reviewing, architecting, and managing AI-augmented workflows, with organizations rethinking talent strategies around skills rather than roles<cite id="41"></cite><cite id="44"></cite>.

Software engineering will likely follow patterns seen in other technology-driven transformations, where productivity and demand for certain skills rise alongside new job creation and evolving competencies<cite id="64"></cite>. Overall, the evidence supports a future in which AI augments software engineering across the lifecycle, improves productivity and quality, and reshapes jobs rather than replacing engineers, provided organizations invest in training, governance, and responsible adoption<cite id="34"></cite><cite id="54"></cite><cite id="49"></cite>.

While AI serves as a powerful assistant in software development by helping programmers in their everyday work lives, it is not a substitute for human expertise. The recent advancements in these tools, like Githu's Copilot, Midjourney and ChatGPT, are expected to cause significant shifts in global economies and labour markets. These particular technological advancements coincide with a period of considerable labour market upheaval from economic, geopolitical, green transition and technological forces. The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2023 predicts that 23% of global jobs will change in the next five years due to industry transformation, including through artificial intelligence and other text, image and voice processing technologies.
This white paper provides a structured analysis of the potential direct, near-term impacts of LLMs on jobs. With 62% of total work time involving language-based tasks, the widespread adoption of LLMs, such as ChatGPT, could significantly impact a broad spectrum of job roles.
To assess the impact of LLMs on jobs, this paper provides an analysis of over 19,000 individual tasks across 867 occupations, assessing the potential exposure of each task to LLM adoption, classifying them as tasks that have high potential for automation, high potential for augmentation, low potential for either or are unaffected (non-language tasks). The paper also provides an overview of new roles that are emerging due to the adoption of LLMs.
The longer-term impacts of these technologies are beyond the scope of this paper, but the structured approach proposed here can be applied to other areas of technological change and their impact on tasks and jobs.
The analysis reveals that tasks with the highest potential for automation by LLMs tend to be routine and repetitive, with those with the highest potential for augmentation require abstract reasoning and problem-solving skills. Tasks with lower potential for exposure require a high degree of personal interaction and collaboration.

- Jobs with the highest potential for task augmentation emphasize mathematical and scientific analysis, such as Insurance Underwriters (100% of work time could be augmented), Bioengineers and Biomedical Engineers (84%), Mathematicians (80%), and Editors (72%).
- Jobs with lower potential for automation or augmentation are jobs that are expected to remain largely unchanged, such as Educational, Guidance, and Career Counsellors and Advisers (84% of time spent on low or exposure tasks), Clergy (83%), and Home Health Aides (75%).

problem: 我今年五十三岁，体重一百六十斤，为我提供一份两周的食谱，包含更科学、健康、简单易做的营养搭配（我是中国人）

目标用户：53岁，体重160斤（约80kg），需设计一份两周科学、健康、简单易做的中国食谱。首先，依据《成人肥胖食养指南（2024年版）》确定核心原则，包括控制总能量摄入、饮食清淡、纠正不良饮食行为、多动少静、睡眠充足、食养有道等。其次，结合用户年龄和体重，参考指南中不同体力活动水平的热量需求，设定每日总能量摄入为1200–1500kcal，三餐比例3:4:3，宏量营养素碳水50–60%、蛋白质15–20%、脂肪20–30%。同时，控制油、盐、糖摄入，全天植物油≤25g，盐＜5g，添加糖≤25g。最后，结合天津疾控中心提供的成年肥胖人群营养健康食谱作为模板，设计两周食谱，确保食材易得、烹饪方式简单，并加入不同地区的食谱示例以适应用户口味。需要引用指南中的核心原则和食谱示例作为依据。
</think>

<answer>### 一、用户情况与目标
您53岁，体重160斤（约80kg），属于轻体力活动水平的成年人。根据《成人肥胖食养指南（2024年版）》，肥胖防控需“三分靠动，七分靠吃”，并结合饮食、运动、睡眠和食养综合管理。指南建议每日能量摄入控制在1200–1500kcal，三餐比例3:4:3，宏量营养素碳水50–60%、蛋白质15–20%、脂肪20–30%，同时控制油、盐、糖摄入，全天植物油≤25g，盐＜5g，添加糖≤25g。此外，指南强调纠正不良饮食行为、科学进餐、多动少静、睡眠充足和合理选择食药物质<cite id="32"></cite>。

### 二、两周食谱设计原则
1. **能量与营养素比例**：每日总能量1200–1500kcal，三餐比例3:4:3，碳水50–60%、蛋白质15–20%、脂肪20–30%<cite id="8"></cite>。
2. **控油、控盐、控糖**：全天植物油≤25g，盐＜5g，添加糖≤25g，避免高油炸、腌制、甜饮料等<cite id="32"></cite>。
3. **多样化与易操作性**：以天津疾控中心提供的成年肥胖人群营养健康食谱为模板，结合不同地区食谱示例，确保食材易得、烹饪方式简单<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="13"></cite>。
4. **食物交换与搭配**：使用常见食物交换表，合理搭配谷物、优质蛋白、蔬菜水果，增加膳食纤维，减少精制碳水和高脂肪食物<cite id="32"></cite>。

### 三、两周食谱示例（以1500kcal/日为基准）
以下为两周食谱，每日三餐及加餐搭配，食材和烹饪方式尽量简单，符合中国家庭习惯。具体热量可根据实际食材分量微调。

#### 第一周
**早餐（约450kcal）**：
- 全麦山药鸡蛋饼（山药50g、全麦面粉40g、脱脂牛奶50ml、鸡蛋1个）+ 脱脂牛奶250ml + 猕猴桃100g（约450kcal）<cite id="23"></cite>。

**午餐（约550kcal）**：
- 南瓜米饭（大米50g、南瓜100g）+ 白菜汆丸子（瘦猪肉50g、白菜100g、枸杞5g）+ 蒜炒菠菜（菠菜150g、蒜末10g）（约550kcal）<cite id="23"></cite>。

**晚餐（约400kcal）**：
- 燕麦大米粥（大米50g、燕麦30g）+ 虾仁西芹（鲜虾仁50g、西芹150g、洋葱50g）+ 蔬菜豆腐汤（豆腐50g、土豆50g、小白菜100g、鲜香菇20g）（约400kcal）<cite id="23"></cite>。

**加餐（约100kcal）**：
- 苹果250g（约100kcal）<cite id="23"></cite>。

**备注**：每日植物油用量控制在25g以内，盐＜5g，避免添加糖，可选择无糖酸奶或水果替代甜点<cite id="32"></cite>。

#### 第二周
**早餐（约450kcal）**：
- 红枣小米粥（小米30g、红枣3颗）+ 煮鸡蛋1个 + 凉拌土豆丝（土豆100g）（约450kcal）<cite id="23"></cite>。

**午餐（约550kcal）**：
- 蒸玉米1根（约200g）+ 清炖鸡块（鸡胸肉100g）+ 蒜蓉油麦菜（油麦菜150g）+ 冬瓜海带汤（冬瓜100g、海带20g）（约550kcal）<cite id="16"></cite>。

**晚餐（约400kcal）**：
- 凉拌黄瓜拉皮（黄瓜100g、拉皮50g）+ 菌菇汤（香菇、平菇各50g）（约400kcal）<cite id="16"></cite>。

**加餐（约100kcal）**：
- 无糖酸奶150g + 蓝莓一小把（约100kcal）<cite id="10"></cite>。

**备注**：每日植物油用量控制在25g以内，盐＜5g，避免添加糖，可选择坚果或低糖水果作为加餐<cite id="32"></cite>。

### 四、不同地区食谱参考（适应口味）
指南附录3提供了东北、西北、华北、华东、华中、西南、华南等地区的食谱示例，结合本地特色食材，同时控制油、盐、糖使用量，例如东北地区以炖菜为主，可设计“铁锅炖鱼”（草鱼50g、土豆100g、白菜100g、豆腐50g）等，但需减少油盐用量，增加蔬菜比例<cite id="13"></cite>。

### 五、执行建议
1. **规律进餐与细嚼慢咽**：避免暴饮暴食，每餐20–30分钟，有助于控制食量<cite id="32"></cite>。
2. **增加身体活动**：每日至少6000步，结合快走、广场舞等中等强度运动，促进能量消耗<cite id="32"></cite>。
3. **睡眠与情绪管理**：保证每天7–8小时睡眠，避免熬夜，保持心情舒畅，减少压力性进食<cite id="32"></cite>。
4. **定期监测与调整**：每周称重1次，观察体重变化，必要时调整热量和食物种类，确保营养均衡<cite id="32"></cite>。

### 六、注意事项
- 避免极端节食，以免引发代谢紊乱或营养不良，建议在医生或营养师指导下进行<cite id="32"></cite>。
- 若有高血压、糖尿病等慢性病，需进一步调整食谱，控制钠、糖和脂肪摄入，必要时咨询专业人员<cite id="32"></cite>。

### 七、参考资料
- 国家卫健委《成人肥胖食养指南（2024年版）》：提供核心原则、食养建议及不同地区食谱示例<cite id="32"></cite>。
- 天津疾控中心成年肥胖人群营养健康食谱：提供具体三餐搭配及营养构成参考<cite id="23"></cite>。
- 全国各地食谱示例：结合本地口味，控制油盐糖，保持饮食多样性<cite id="13"></cite>。</answer>

reference_id="<|superscript|>:4"><title>成人及儿童青少年4项食养指南发布</title><summary>《中国中医药报》2024年2月19日讯：近日，国家卫生健康委印发4项2024年版食养指南，分别为《成人高尿酸血症与痛风食养指南（2024年版）》《成人肥胖食养指南（2024年版）》《儿童青少年肥胖食养指南（2024年版）》《成人慢性肾脏病食养指南（2024年版）》，给各级卫生工作者、营养指导人员和居民参照使用。食养指南旨在发挥现代营养学和传统食养中西医联合的优势，将食药物质、新食品原料融入合理膳食，针对不同季节、不同地区、不同人群提供食谱套餐示例和营养健康建议，提升膳食指导的适用性和可操作性。工作中鼓励各级卫生工作者（包括营养指导人员）结合工作需要和患者实际，参考指南指导应用，辅助预防和改善慢性病。鼓励居民参考指南推荐内容，结合自身情况，合理搭配日常膳食，养成良好饮食习惯。《成人高尿酸血症与痛风食养指南（2024年版）》的制定以满足人民健康需求为出发点，为预防和控制我国人群高尿酸血症与痛风的发生发展，改善高尿酸血症与痛风人群日常膳食，提高居民营养健康水平，发展传统食养服务等提供科学指导。《指南》制定的意义在于：一是充分发挥现代营养学和传统食养的中西医各方优势，将食药物质融入合理膳食中，辅助预防和改善高尿酸血症与痛风。二是针对不同证型人群、不同地区、不同季节编制食谱示例，提出食养指导，提升膳食指导个性化和可操作性。三是依据现代营养学理论和相关证据，以及我国传统中医的理念和调养方案，推动中西医结合，传承传统食养文化，切实推进食养服务高质量发展。明确中医对高尿酸血症与痛风的认识与分型，介绍了湿浊证、湿热证、痰瘀证、脾肾亏虚证等常见辨证分型及临床表现。在《成人肥胖食养指南（2024年版）》《儿童青少年肥胖食养指南（2024年版）》中，明确中医对肥胖的认识及分型，介绍了胃热火郁证、痰湿内盛证、气郁血瘀证、脾虚不运证、脾肾阳虚证等常见辨证分型及临床表现。《成人慢性肾脏病食养指南（2024年版）》制定的意义在于：一是充分发挥现代营养学和传统食养的中西医各方优势，将食药物质融入合理膳食中，辅助预防和改善慢性肾脏病。二是针对不同人群、不同地区、不同季节编制食谱示例和食养方，提升膳食指导个性化和可操作性。三是依据现代临床医学、营养学理论和相关证据，以及我国传统中医的理念和调养方案，推动中西医结合，传承传统食养文化，切实推进食养服务高质量发展。在《成人慢性肾脏病食养指南（2024年版）》中，明确中医对慢性肾脏病的认识和分型，介绍了气虚证、血虚证、阴虚证、阳虚证等常见本虚证单一证型及临床表现。（王迪）</summary><hostname>维普</hostname><publisher>中医药管理杂志</publisher><url>https://www.cqvip.com/doc/journal/3340112482</url><publish_time>2024年2月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document http://epaper.tianjinwe.com/tjrb/html/2025-05/27/content_143098_2220678.htm市疾控中心推出 成年肥胖人群营养健康食谱| \| **标题导航** | | |---|---| | **2025年05月27日 星期二** | | 饮食营养 总能量低 蔬菜丰富 营养构成合理 市疾控中心推出 成年肥胖人群营养健康食谱 通讯员 李昌昆 近年来，我国超重和肥胖人群数量正快速增长。肥胖被称为“万病之源”，膳食营养和身体活动是肥胖防治的两大重要因素。结合现代营养学和传统食养优势，市疾控中心推出成年肥胖人群营养健康食谱，帮助肥胖人群控制饮食减轻体重。 据介绍，该推荐健康食谱是以轻体力身体活动水平的肥胖成年人为例，按照国家成人肥胖食养指南的基本原则，结合天津食物资源和饮食习惯进行设计（食谱中重量均以可食部分生重计算），供成人肥胖人群减重参考使用，使用者也可根据具体情况，近似替代部分食材，合理搭配食物。 早餐：全麦山药鸡蛋饼（山药50克、全麦面粉40克、脱脂牛奶50毫升、鸡蛋一颗）、脱脂牛奶250毫升、猕猴桃100克。 午餐：南瓜米饭（大米50克、南瓜100克）、白菜汆丸子（瘦猪肉50克、白菜100克、枸杞子5克）、蒜炒菠菜（菠菜150克、蒜末10克）。 加餐：苹果250克。 晚餐：燕麦大米粥（大米50克、燕麦30克）、虾仁西芹（鲜虾仁50克、西芹150克、洋葱50克）、蔬菜豆腐汤（豆腐50克、土豆50克、小白菜100克、鲜香菇20克）。 疾控专家表示，该食谱油、盐全天总用量为植物油25克，盐＜5克。食谱提供的能量较低，约为1600千卡。蛋白质、脂肪和碳水化合物构成较为合理，其中蛋白质、脂肪和碳水化合物的供能比分别为18.4%、24.0%和57.6%。该食谱绿色蔬菜较多，食物种类丰富，制作简单。总体来说，符合天津本地人群饮食习惯，尤其适合肥胖成年人群减重食用。 通讯员 李昌昆 | | 朗读

成人肥胖食养指南
一､前言
肥胖是一种慢性代谢性疾病,近些年来,全球超重和肥 胖率正快速增长,已成为威胁人类健康的严重问题｡根据《中 国居民营养与慢性病状况报告(2020 年)》显示,我国18 岁 及以上居民超重率､肥胖率分别为34.3%､16.4%,其中18~ 44 岁､45~59 岁和60 岁及以上居民肥胖率分别为16.4%､ 18.3%和13.6%,我国居民肥胖率呈上升趋势｡肥胖不但导致 较高的过早死亡风险,还与各种慢性非传染性疾病的发生相 关,包括2 型糖尿病､脑卒中､冠心病､高血压､呼吸系统 疾病､骨关节炎和胆结石等｡肥胖甚至还与多种肿瘤的发生 相关｡2019 年全国11.98%的心血管疾病死亡归因于高体质 指数(BMI),死亡人数为54.95 万｡肥胖的流行以其高昂的 医疗费用为国民经济带来了沉重的负担｡有研究预测,到 2030 年我国成年人超重肥胖率可达65.3%,归因于超重肥胖 的医疗费用可能为4180 亿元人民币,约占全国医疗费用总 额的21.5%,未来中国城乡居民超重肥胖率及其所造成的经 济负担将呈上升趋势｡因此,肥胖防控已刻不容缓｡
肥胖的发生虽然受遗传､环境和社会文化等因素共同影 响,但根本原因是机体的能量摄入大于能量消耗,从而导致 多余的能量以脂肪的形式在体内贮存｡膳食营养和身体活动 是肥胖防治的两大重要影响因素｡减肥关键三分靠动,七分 靠吃｡以“辨证施膳”为核心的中医食养是在中医辨证施治
1
指导下的非药物调养方法,强调根据体质､病因､病机､证 候,给予不同食养方案,具有调和气血､平衡人体阴阳､辅 助疾病防治的作用｡针对肥胖患者的不同体质,选取不同特 性的食物或食药物质,有助于达到减重效果,维持健康体重｡
为预防和控制我国人群肥胖的发生发展,改善肥胖患者 的体重,调整日常膳食结构,提高居民营养健康水平,发展 传统食养服务,根据《健康中国行动(2019—2030 年)》和 《国民营养计划(2017—2030 年)》相关要求,制定本指南｡ 本指南以食养为基础,依据现代营养学理论和相关证据,以 及我国传统医学的理论和调养方案,提出具有多学科优势互 补的成人肥胖患者食养基本原则和食谱示例｡本指南主要面 向基层卫生工作者(包括营养指导人员)､无合并症和并发 症的成人肥胖患者,为肥胖防控提供食养指导｡肥胖合并其 他急性或慢性病的患者或有并发症者,在医生或营养指导人 员等专业人员的指导下,也可参考本指南,根据患者具体情 况设计个性化食养方案｡
二､疾病特点与分型
(一)肥胖定义与判定｡
肥胖是人体脂肪积聚过多达到危害健康程度的一种慢 性代谢性疾病,是因能量摄入超过能量消耗或机体代谢改变 而导致体重过度增长的一种状态｡根据肥胖病因及发病机制 分为单纯性肥胖和继发性肥胖｡无明显内分泌､代谢病病因 可寻者为单纯性肥胖;继发于神经-内分泌-代谢紊乱基础上 的肥胖症为继发性肥胖｡体质指数(BMI)和腰围(WC)是
2
常用判断超重和肥胖程度的指标｡我国健康成年人的BMI 正 常范围为 \(18.5 ~kg / m^{2} ≤BMI<24.0 ~kg / m^{2}\) , \(24. 0 ~kg / m^{2} \leqslant\) \(BMI<28.0 ~kg / m^{2}\) 为超重, \(BMI ≥28.0 ~kg / m^{2}\) 为肥胖, \(BMI<18.5 ~kg / m^{2}\) 为体重过低。 \(85 ~cm ≤ 成年男\) 性 \(WC <90 ~cm\) , 80cm <成年女性 \(WC<85 ~cm\) 可判断为中心型肥胖前期;成年男性 \(WC ≥90 ~cm\) ,成年女性 \(WC ≥85 ~cm\) 可判断为中心型肥胖。
(二)中医对肥胖的认识及分型｡
中医学将肥胖归属于“脂人”“膏人”“肥人”等范畴, 记载最早见于《黄帝内经》,《灵枢·卫气失常》篇将人之肥 瘦分为“有肥､有膏､有肉”,肥胖病因多与年龄､体质､ 饮食､情志､劳逸因素有关｡中医认为,肥胖属本虚标实证, 辨证涉及痰､湿､热等病理因素,常兼夹痰湿､血瘀､气郁 等标实之证,其病位多在脾胃,与肾气虚关系密切,并可涉 及五脏｡常见辨证分型及临床表现如下:
胃热火郁证:肥胖多食,消谷善饥,大便不爽,甚或干 结,尿黄,或有口干口苦,喜饮水,舌质红,苔黄,脉数｡
痰湿内盛证:形体肥胖,身体沉重,肢体困倦,脘痞胸 满,可伴头晕,口干而不欲饮,大便黏滞不爽,嗜食肥甘醇 酒,喜卧懒动,舌质淡胖或大,苔白腻或白滑,脉滑｡
气郁血瘀证:肥胖懒动,喜太息,胸闷胁满,面晦唇暗, 肢端色泽不鲜,甚或青紫,可伴便干,失眠,男子性欲下降 甚至阳痿,女子月经不调､量少甚或闭经,经血色暗或有血 块,舌质暗或有瘀斑瘀点,舌苔薄,脉弦或涩｡
脾虚不运证:肥胖臃肿,神疲乏力,身体困重,脘腹痞
3
闷,或有四肢轻度浮肿,晨轻暮重,劳则尤甚,饮食如常或 偏少,既往多有暴饮暴食史,小便不利,大便溏或便秘,舌 质淡胖,边有齿印,苔薄白或白腻,脉濡细｡
脾肾阳虚证:形体肥胖,易于疲劳,四肢不温,甚或四 肢厥冷,喜食热饮,小便清长,舌淡胖,舌苔薄白,脉沉细｡

根据营养科学理论､中医理论和目前膳食相关肥胖科学 研究文献证据,在专家组共同讨论､建立共识的基

# How to Balance Learning, Life, and Interests for Children’s Healthy Development

## Why balance matters
Children’s well-being depends on a mix of academic progress, emotional health, social skills, and opportunities to explore interests. Over-scheduling can lead to stress and burnout, whereas a balanced routine supports resilience and long-term motivation<cite id="23"></cite>. Schools and families should consider how after-school activities and homework fit together to promote positive developmental outcomes, and avoid pushing children beyond their resources and interests<cite id="2"></cite>.

## Evidence-based strategies for scheduling
A consistent bedtime routine supports executive function (working memory, inhibition/attention, cognitive flexibility), school readiness, and even dental health, underscoring the importance of sleep for daily functioning and self-regulation<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="26"></cite>. To manage time, teach children to list commitments, prioritize, and use planners or apps; encourage flexibility to adapt when unexpected events arise<cite id="24"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>. Practical tips include focusing on one extracurricular at a time to allow full engagement, and reserving short family “must-do” activities to reduce evening rush and foster connection<cite id="23"></cite>. For older children, “time blocking” homework and leaving room for downtime can help maintain focus and prevent exhaustion<cite id="23"></cite>.

## Quality over quantity in activities
Research shows that the number of activities matters less than how well they align with a child’s strengths, interests, and values. Children who engage in fewer activities but that reflect their personal qualities tend to be more satisfied and successful than those in many mismatched activities<cite id="14"></cite>. Schools can help by offering a range of options and encouraging students to choose based on what resonates with them, rather than external pressures<cite id="14"></cite>.

## Creating a supportive environment
Fostering intrinsic motivation is key to helping children connect with learning and hobbies. Autonomy, competence, and relatedness—when nurtured at home and school—lead to deeper engagement and a love of learning that lasts into adulthood<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="12"></cite>. Positive reinforcement should focus on effort and progress rather than comparisons to peers, to build self-efficacy and resilience<cite id="15"></cite>. Social support from parents and teachers also buffers stress and promotes emotional regulation, especially during transitions like middle school when identity and vocational awareness begin to develop<cite id="19"></cite>.

## Finding direction and goals
Identity formation and early career exploration start in elementary and middle school. At these ages, children begin to think about education and jobs, recognize differences in prestige, and consider how their abilities and interests match potential paths<cite id="16"></cite>. Encourage self-reflection and experimentation through conversations and activities that highlight what they enjoy, how they learn best, and what matters to them<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>. Strengths-based approaches can help children see their unique talents and how they can translate into meaningful goals and roles<cite id="17"></cite>.

## Policy and practice examples
Policies that reduce academic overload and expand access to quality after-school programs can help families create balanced schedules. For example, China’s “double reduction” policy limits homework and offers interest-based after-school services, aiming to ease pressure and allow more time for personal development<cite id="21"></cite>. Schools can also integrate character development and ethical guidance to help students cultivate caring, integrity, and a sense of purpose alongside academic skills<cite id="1"></cite>.

## What to watch for and when to adjust
If a child shows signs of stress, declining performance, or loss of enthusiasm, reassess the balance and reduce demands. Regular check-ins with the child about how they feel about their schedule can reveal hidden pressures and guide necessary changes<cite id="23"></cite>. Remember that every child is different; what works for one may not for another, so remain open to adjusting priorities as they grow<cite id="24"></cite>.

## Summary recommendations
- Prioritize sleep and routine to support executive function and readiness<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="26"></cite>.
- Use planning tools and teach time management while leaving room for flexibility and downtime<cite id="24"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>.
- Choose activities that match strengths and interests rather than quantity<cite id="14"></cite>.
- Nurture intrinsic motivation through autonomy, competence, and connection<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="12"></cite>.
- Support identity and goal exploration through reflection and strengths-based guidance<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>.
- Monitor well-being and adjust as needed, recognizing that balance is an ongoing process<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="24"></cite>.

These strategies, grounded in research on child development and education, can help families and schools create schedules that promote academic success, emotional health, and a lifelong love of learning and exploration<cite id="2"></cite><cite id="11"></cite><cite id="16"></cite>.
</answer>

Finally, parents with optimal bedtime routines for their children deployed a more positive parenting style in general (i.e. authoritative parenting) compared to those with suboptimal bedtime routines (t (48)= - 6.45, p ≤ .001).

These outcomes are manifestations of being intrinsically motivated and internalizing values and regulatory processes. Research suggests that these processes result in high-quality learning and conceptual understanding as well as enhanced personal growth and adjustment. In this article we also describe social-contextual factors that nurture intrinsic motivation and promote internalization, leading to the desired educational outcomes. In their formative first two decades, individuals spend about 15,000 hr in schools. Thus schools represent a primary socializing influence that has enormous impact on the course of people lives and, in turn, on society. Ideal school systems are ones that succeed in promoting in students a genuine enthusiasm for learning and accomplishment and a sense of volitional involvement in the educational enterprise. It is this interest and volition, we suggest, that lead students to display greater flexibility in problem solving, more efficient knowledge acquisition, and a strong sense of personal worth and social responsibility. The central features of optimal learning are conceptual understanding and the flexible use of knowledge. In other words, understanding both the relations among facts and the ways to find or generate facts are the learning outcomes that we stress. The acquisition and retention of facts are important but are by no means enough for excellent education. Correspondingly, the central features of optimal adjustment are feeling good about oneself and acting volitionally to satisfy one's own needs while being attuned to and concerned about the social surround. Simply fitting in or complying with social demands is a nonoptimal form of adjustment and may even be counterproductive to personal and social development. These broad learning and adjustment outcomes are what we seek to promote in schools, and although these outcomes are sometimes considered independent or even antithetical, a body of motivational research, guided largely by self-determination theory (e.g., Deci & Ryan, 1985, 1991), has indicated that they are complementary when the school context stimulates certain kinds of motivation in its students. The highest quality of conceptual learning seems to occur under the same motivational conditions that promote personal growth and adjustment.</summary><hostname>University of Utah Libraries Course Reserves</hostname><publisher>EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGIST, 26(3 & 4), 325-346</publisher><author_list><author name="Edward L Deci" affiliation="University of Rochester" /><author name="Robert J Vallerand" affiliation="University of Quebec at Montreal" /><author name="Luc G Pelletier" affiliation="University of Ottawa" /><author name="Richard M Ryan" affiliation="University of Rochester" /></author_list><url>http://ereserve.library.utah.edu/Annual/TEACH/6950/Allen/moti.pdf</url><publish_time>1991年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:12"><title>Fostering Intrinsic Motivation in Early Childhood Classrooms</title><summary>Young children are born with an innate curiosity to learn about their world. This article describes first the general characteristics of the middle school youngster, followed by pragmatic activities and strategies for counselors to use at this level. Almost universal agreement exists on perceiving the middle or junior high school years as converging on career exploration activities (Evans, Hoyt, & Mangum, 1973). It is during this time that students begin to recognize differences in prestige among jobs as well as social class and ability differences among people. Their preferences for status level of work come to differ considerably by social class and ability level, differences that change only in detail from high school onward (Gottfredson, 1981). Indeed, social class, sex, and ability differences are so much a part of everyday life that they are oftentimes taken for granted and may not even be conscious. Goldstein and Oldham (1979) discovered, for example, that by the end of junior high school, most youngsters recognized the connectedness among education, jobs, wealth, and social class. CHARACTERISTICS "It's Time To Start Deciding." Cognitively, youngsters are still-at least in the earlier middle school years-in the stage of concrete operations whereas vocationally, their choices pass from the general, fantasy stage into the tentative stage; that is, they begin to make meaningful choices based on their present knowl- edge about themselves (Tuckman, 1974). Indeed, the eighth and ninth grades are the first instances in the typical student's life in which official choice points are a reality (e.g., specific courses, high school curricula, a certain high school, an area vocational-technical school) (Herr & Cramer, 1984). "Just What Are My Abilities?" Throughout the middle school years, the incremental development of formal operational thought emerges, along with the ability to concentrate on one's own capabilities (Tuckman, 1974) as a basis for tentative voca- tional choices. Because youngsters at this stage are becoming increasingly self-focused, they should be encouraged to examine their own uniqueness (e.g., how their abilities differ from those of others) (Tuckman, 1974). It is during the years between 9 and 13 that "ability" starts to become an important determinant of social behavior and expectations. It is relatively easy to imagine how a youngster's ability can serve as a criterion for membership into certain groups. The ability to do well ac- ademically, for example, may assure membership in an "intellectual" stra- tum, along with its associated expectations. Adolescents are eager to uncover their own special abilities by making things, by taking tests, or by placing themselves in novel situations re- quiring adjustment and adaptation (i.e., risk taking). Attempting to adjust to unfamiliar circumstances accelerates self-knowledge and may even broaden occupational knowledge. One may come to realize his or her own potential for leadership only after being placed in a situation-con- trived or real-demanding dominance, forcefulness, and influence. "Just what are my abilities?" seems to be a widespread concern throughout the middle school years. "I Want a Job With Some Status." Occupational prestige begins to awaken for the first time during middle or junior high school. Generally irrelevant to the average first grader, prestige among adolescents (and later adults) becomes a critical deter- minant of job choice (Reeb, 1974). # Market Size Analysis Report: Japan’s Elderly Population, 2020–2050

## Executive Summary
Japan’s elderly population is set to grow rapidly as the country ages and shrinks, creating a massive consumer base across multiple sectors. By 2050, the number of people aged 65 and over is projected to reach about 38.5 million, or roughly 30.7% of the total population, with some scenarios pushing the share above 37%<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="31"></cite><cite id="41"></cite>. This demographic shift will expand elderly consumer spending, especially in healthcare and long-term care, while reshaping demand in clothing, food, housing, and transportation as consumption patterns evolve with age and lifestyle changes<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="27"></cite><cite id="29"></cite>.

## Population Projections: How Many Elderly by 2050?
As of 2024, Japan’s 65+ population stood at 36.25 million, or 29.3% of the total population, reflecting a steady increase over the past decade<cite id="7"></cite><cite id="12"></cite><cite id="24"></cite>. Under the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research’s 2023 revision, the 65+ share is expected to rise from 28.6% in 2020 to 38.7% by 2070, implying roughly 38.5 million elderly in 2050 if the growth path is linear<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite="41"></cite>. Broader estimates from research institutions also anticipate the 65+ share reaching 37.1% by 2050, with some prefectures already projected to have over 40% elderly residents<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="46"></cite>. These projections are based on low birth rates, rising longevity, and modest net immigration, which together drive population decline and aging<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="24"></cite>.

## Total Elderly Consumer Base and Market Potential
The growing elderly population translates into a large and increasingly active consumer base. By 2050, elderly households are expected to account for about half of all consumer spending, driven by their rising numbers and shifting consumption priorities<cite id="4"></cite>. The silver economy is already a major sector: industry reports forecast Japan’s silver economy market to surpass 100 trillion yen in 2025 and reach 35 trillion yen for elderly care services by 2030, with home-based care services growing rapidly due to declining family support<cite id="15"></cite><cite id="18"></cite>. These figures underscore the breadth and scale of elderly spending across goods and services<cite id="15"></cite><cite id="18"></cite>.

## Consumption Potential by Sector

### Healthcare and Long-Term Care
Healthcare spending is expected to grow strongly as the elderly population expands and the share of very old people (85+) rises. In 2011, about 2.9% of those aged 75–79 were hospitalized on any given day, and 13.4% visited a physician daily, highlighting the intensity of medical use among the elderly<cite id="7"></cite>. In 2020, Japan’s long-term care insurance system covered 47.6 million people, with 7.7 million enrolled in community-based services and 2.8 million in facility-based care, indicating a large and growing care market<cite id="10"></cite>. Industry forecasts project the elderly care market to exceed 35 trillion yen by 2030, with home visits and community services expanding rapidly<cite id="18"></cite>. Broader silver economy estimates also anticipate healthcare and long-term care to be among the fastest-growing segments<cite id="15"></cite>.

### Food
Elderly households tend to spend a larger share of income on food, and as their numbers grow, food demand will increase. In 2020, households with someone aged 65 and over spent 13.6% of their income on food, compared with 11.5% for younger households, reflecting both necessity and lifestyle preferences<cite id="5"></cite>. With elderly people expected to comprise roughly a third of the population by 2050, these spending patterns will lift overall food consumption and create opportunities in convenient, healthy, and culturally appropriate food products<cite id="5"></cite><cite id="24"></cite>.

### Clothing
Elderly consumers are shifting away from durable goods toward services and health-related spending, but clothing remains a regular necessity. Life-cycle consumption studies show that clothing spending declines after age 50, while medical and fuel expenses rise, indicating a more modest but stable demand for clothing among the elderly<cite id="3"></cite>. As elderly households grow in number, the clothing market will benefit from steady turnover and preferences for comfort and ease of use<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite>.

### Housing
Housing demand among the elderly is shaped by aging households and changing living arrangements. In 2020, households with someone aged 65 and over accounted for 17.6% of all households but spent 23.1% of total household spending on housing, reflecting higher home ownership rates and maintenance needs<cite id="5"></cite>. As the elderly share of the population rises, demand for accessible housing, home modifications, and maintenance services is expected to grow, supported by the increasing proportion of elderly homeowners and the need for long-term care integration<cite id="5"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>.

### Transportation
Transportation spending is expected to increase as elderly consumers become a larger share of the population and adopt more active lifestyles. In 2020, households with someone aged 65 and over spent 10.5% of their income on transportation, compared with 12.0% for younger households, indicating a relatively stable but growing segment<cite id="5"></cite>. Surveys show that many elderly are willing to spend on travel and leisure, with about 40% of 60- and 70-somethings planning domestic trips of at least one night, and a strong appetite for “active aging” tourism<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="8"></cite>. The rise of mobile internet and online shopping also suggests that elderly consumers are increasingly using digital platforms for travel planning and purchases<cite id="8"></cite>.

## Elderly Consumer Willingness and Behavioral Trends
Elderly consumers are becoming more active in spending, particularly on health, travel, and leisure. Surveys indicate that about 40% of 60- and 70-somethings plan domestic trips of at least one night, and there is growing interest in “active aging” activities such as travel and social engagement<cite id="6"></cite>. In addition to travel, health and wellness, supporting grandchildren, and estate planning are rising priorities among elderly consumers<cite id="6"></cite>. These trends suggest that marketing strategies should emphasize convenience, accessibility, and health benefits to align with elderly preferences<cite id="6"></cite>.

Precautionary saving remains strong among the elderly, but the overall trend is toward increased consumption as the elderly share of the population rises. Economic analyses show that while elderly individuals tend to save for the future, the number of elderly consumers relative to the total population is increasing, leading to an upward trend in total consumption despite lower savings rates<cite id="29"></cite>. This dynamic supports the view that elderly spending will grow across multiple sectors<cite id="29"></cite>.

## Market Size Analysis and Forecasts
Combining population projections with consumption patterns, the elderly market is poised to expand substantially. By 2050, elderly households are expected to account for about half of all consumer spending, with healthcare and long-term care leading the growth<cite id="4"></cite>. Industry forecasts project the elderly care market to exceed 35 trillion yen by 2030, with home-based services growing rapidly<cite id="18"></cite>. Broader silver economy estimates anticipate the sector to surpass 100 trillion yen in 2025, underscoring the breadth of elderly spending across goods and services<cite id="15"></cite>.

Under the most recent IPSS projections, the elderly share of the population will rise from 28.6% in 2020 to 38.7% by 2070, implying roughly 38.5 million elderly in 2050 and a large, aging consumer base that will reshape demand across sectors<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="41"></cite>. As the elderly population grows and consumption patterns shift toward services and health, companies that adapt to accessibility, convenience, and health benefits are likely to capture significant market share<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="27"></cite><cite id="29"></cite>.

## Strategic Implications
For businesses and policymakers, the key opportunities lie in healthcare, long-term care, and accessible services tailored to the needs of an aging population. The rise of the oldest-old (85+) will drive demand for medical care, home modifications, and integrated care services, while active aging trends will support travel, leisure, and social engagement markets<cite id="27"></cite><cite id="18"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>. Companies should also consider the digital transformation of elderly services, including online shopping and telehealth, to meet the preferences and behaviors of elderly consumers<cite id="8"></cite><cite id="15"></cite>.

## Conclusion
Japan’s elderly population will grow from about 36.25 million in 2024 to roughly 38.5 million by 2050, with the elderly share of the population rising to about 30.7% and potentially exceeding 37% depending on the scenario<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="41"></cite><cite id="46"></cite>. This expansion will drive substantial market potential across healthcare and long-term care, food, clothing, housing, and transportation, supported by shifting consumption patterns and growing willingness to spend on health, travel, and leisure<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="27"></cite><cite id="29"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>. Businesses that anticipate these trends and adapt their offerings to the needs and preferences of elderly consumers will be well positioned to capture value in Japan’s aging society<cite id="18"></cite><cite id="15"></cite>.

problem: What are the investment philosophies of Duan Yongping, Warren Buffett, and Charlie Munger?
final_response:
<think>
<answer>
## Executive Summary

This report compares the investment philosophies of Duan Yongping (also known as “Duan Ba”), Warren Buffett, and Charlie Munger. All three emphasize buying businesses with durable competitive advantages, deep understanding, and long-term holding, but they differ in emphasis and execution. Duan’s approach is Buffett–Munger inspired, with a strong consumer focus and concentrated portfolios; Buffett and Munger formalized value investing principles and added mental models and ethical stewardship.<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>

## Duan Yongping: A Buffett–Munger-Inspired Value Investor with a Consumer Bias

Duan Yongping is widely regarded as a modern Chinese disciple of Buffett and Munger. He frames buying stocks as buying companies and stresses understanding future cash flows, a mantra Buffett himself has echoed. Duan’s interviews and writings repeatedly underscore that “margin of safety” refers to how well you understand the company, not merely how cheap the price is, and that cheap things can get even cheaper.<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="19"></cite> He also warns that most companies are not easy to understand, reinforcing the need for deep due diligence.<cite id="3"></cite>

A practical corollary is Duan’s preference for businesses with strong, durable moats. He explicitly recognizes brand strength, pricing power, and network effects as sources of competitive advantage, and he avoids over-diversification by holding only a handful of positions. In one rare public dialogue, he stated he was holding just three core stocks at the time: Apple, Tencent, and Moutai, while following a “20-punch rule” to identify and cultivate enduring winners.<cite id="21"></cite> This concentrated, margin-of-safety–driven style is consistent with Buffett’s own approach, as summarized by third-party analyses of Duan’s portfolio.<cite id="10"></cite>

Duan further distinguishes between consumer-oriented and business-oriented companies, favoring the former. He argues that consumer-oriented firms prioritize user needs and build sustainable value through product quality and customer loyalty, whereas business-oriented firms are driven by short-term metrics and scale at the expense of experience.<cite id="6"></cite> This consumer-first lens aligns with Buffett’s long-term holding of brands like Coca-Cola and Apple, which benefit from powerful consumer relationships.<cite id="17"></cite>

## Warren Buffett: Value Investing with a Focus on Intrinsic Value and Business Economics

Buffett’s investment philosophy is rooted in value investing, a discipline he studied under Benjamin Graham. He emphasizes intrinsic value, margin of safety, and long-term ownership, avoiding speculation and focusing on businesses with strong fundamentals and competent management.<cite id="9"></cite> Buffett’s strategy is to buy undervalued businesses, hold them for decades, and compound gains through reinvestment rather than short-term trading.<cite id="7"></cite>

A central tenet is identifying durable competitive advantages—what Buffett calls “economic moats.” Companies with wide moats, such as Coca-Cola and Apple, are more likely to generate stable, growing profits and protect long-term profits from competitors.<cite id="14"></cite> Buffett also stresses the importance of a margin of safety, defined as paying less than a business’s intrinsic value, and he quantifies this in practice by seeking stocks trading at substantial discounts to his calculated worth.<cite id="18"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>

Buffett’s approach is complemented by Munger’s emphasis on a latticework of mental models and operating within one’s circle of competence. Together, they have built Berkshire Hathaway into a model of disciplined, long-term investing.<cite id="10"></cite>

## Charlie Munger: Mental Models, Rationality, and the Circle of Competence

Munger’s contribution to investing is his advocacy of a “latticework of mental models,” which provides a cross-disciplinary framework for analyzing business and market risks. He argues that a single hammer (e.g., a narrow perspective) is dangerous, and that integrating insights from psychology, economics, and other fields improves decision-making.<cite id="11"></cite> This mindset helps investors anticipate pitfalls and evaluate companies with a more complete picture of opportunity and risk.<cite id="14"></cite>

A closely related principle is the circle of competence: Munger (and Buffett) encourages investors to stick to what they deeply understand. Venturing outside this boundary increases the risk of misunderstanding key business dynamics and making poor investment decisions, which is why both emphasize deep knowledge and selective specialization.<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="14"></cite> Munger also highlights the importance of rationality and skepticism toward speculative instruments, advising against derivatives, crypto, and other financial “innovations” that can lead to ruin.<cite id="10"></cite>

## Comparative Overview

Duan Yongping’s philosophy mirrors Buffett and Munger’s core ideas but adds a consumer-first lens and a disciplined, concentrated style. Like Buffett, he focuses on intrinsic value and moats, and like Munger, he prioritizes deep understanding and mental models. Duan’s public statements and portfolio choices reflect these principles in practice, with concentrated bets on companies like Apple, Tencent, and Moutai that combine strong brands, user networks, and durable advantages.<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="10"></cite> His emphasis on understanding over cheapness and his aversion to over-diversification further align with Buffett’s margin-of-safety framing and Munger’s circle-of-competence discipline.<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="13"></cite>

## Practical Takeaways

- Buy businesses, not stocks: Focus on companies with clear economic moats and strong management.<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>
- Prioritize understanding over price: A deep knowledge of the business is the true margin of safety.<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="19"></cite>
- Invest for the long term: Let compounding work by holding great businesses through market cycles.<cite id="7"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>
- Stay within your circle of competence and use a latticework of mental models to anticipate risks.<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="11"></cite>
- Keep portfolios concentrated: Know a few companies deeply rather than spreading capital thinly.<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="10"></cite>

problem: In the field of FinTech, machine learning algorithms are now widely applied to asset allocation and investment decisions. Examples include classic models like Mean-Variance and Black-Litterman, as well as emerging deep learning models. While these models have shown certain advantages under different market conditions, each also has its limitations. For instance, the Mean-Variance model assumes asset returns follow a normal distribution, which often doesn't align with actual market conditions. The Black-Litterman model relies on subjective view inputs, introducing a degree of subjectivity. Although deep learning models can handle complex non-linear relationships, they suffer from poor interpretability. So, what are the core differences between these various models in terms of risk measurement, return prediction, and asset allocation? And is it possible to combine their strengths to build a more general-purpose and effective modeling framework?
final_response:
<think>
<answer>## Executive Summary

Machine learning has become a central tool in FinTech for asset allocation and investment decisions, complementing and, in some cases, surpassing classic mean-variance and Black-Litterman approaches. Empirical studies show that tree-based and neural network models better capture expected return behavior by exploiting non-linear predictor interactions, while deep learning can forecast returns and risk measures with competitive accuracy. However, deep learning models often lack interpretability, and their use in finance raises regulatory and practical concerns. This report synthesizes the core differences between classic and machine learning models along three dimensions—risk measurement, return prediction, and asset allocation—and evaluates the feasibility of hybrid frameworks that combine their strengths to deliver more robust, transparent, and effective portfolio strategies<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="13"></cite><cite id="14"></cite><cite id="15"></cite>.

## Core Differences: Risk Measurement

Risk measurement differs fundamentally across mean-variance, Black-Litterman, and machine learning models. Markowitz’s mean-variance framework treats risk as the variance of returns and assumes normally distributed asset returns, which can misrepresent tail risks and asymmetric return profiles in practice<cite id="38"></cite>. Black-Litterman integrates subjective views with a market equilibrium prior to produce expected returns, but its output depends on the quality and subjectivity of those views, and it still relies on variance to quantify risk<cite id="41"></cite><cite id="42"></cite>. In contrast, machine learning has been used to estimate modern risk measures such as value at risk (VaR), expected shortfall (ES), and expectiles without assuming normality, improving tail risk assessment in non-Gaussian environments<cite id="6"></cite>. Recent work also shows that machine learning can outperform traditional covariance estimators in portfolio optimization, particularly in small samples and fat-tailed markets, and can be combined with robust optimization to reduce estimation error<cite id="20"></cite><cite id="24"></cite>.

A notable trend is the adoption of distribution-free and Bayesian risk-aware approaches. Bayesian portfolio selection with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) can incorporate uncertainty in expected returns and covariances, producing more stable and realistic allocations compared to classical methods<cite id="23"></cite>. Non-parametric bootstrap and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) further mitigate parameter instability and model misspecification by constructing data-driven confidence sets for inputs, leading to smoother out-of-sample performance and better risk control<cite id="24"></cite><cite id="25"></cite>. These advances address the normality and estimation-error limitations of mean-variance while retaining the flexibility of machine learning risk measures<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>.

## Core Differences: Return Prediction

Return prediction is where machine learning models most directly improve over classic approaches. Empirical asset pricing studies find that tree-based methods (random forests, gradient boosting) and neural networks capture non-linear interactions among predictors that linear models miss, leading to a more accurate description of expected return behavior and improved risk-premium measurement<cite id="11"></cite>. In portfolio formation, machine learning and deep learning return predictions can outperform traditional time-series models, particularly when integrated with mean-variance or omega optimization, though transaction costs can erode performance in high-turnover strategies<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="13"></cite>.

Deep learning has demonstrated strong predictive performance across multiple asset classes and horizons. A comprehensive survey of 1,367 studies finds that deep learning models consistently outperform traditional models in stock price prediction, with the best results when combining deep learning with fundamental and technical indicators<cite id="14"></cite>. Hybrid architectures further enhance performance: integrating technical indicators with fundamental data improves accuracy, and combining multiple deep learning models (e.g., CNN-LSTM, CEEMD-CNN-LSTM) can yield superior predictive signals for portfolio views<cite id="15"></cite><cite id="31"></cite>. However, deep learning’s predictive gains are not universal; in some settings, traditional models may still perform comparably, and careful validation is required to avoid overfitting<cite id="14"></cite>.

## Core Differences: Asset Allocation

Asset allocation strategies diverge in how they translate risk and return inputs into portfolio weights. Mean-variance optimization seeks the trade-off between expected return and variance, but its sensitivity to input errors and high transaction costs can make practical implementation challenging<cite id="7"></cite>. Black-Litterman incorporates subjective views into a market equilibrium, reducing parameter sensitivity and providing a more stable allocation, yet its subjectivity and reliance on variance for risk remain limitations<cite id="41"></cite><cite id="42"></cite>. Machine learning-driven allocation often uses risk measures beyond variance (e.g., ES, expectiles) and can be embedded directly into portfolio construction via supervised learning of weights or reinforcement learning agents that adapt to changing market conditions<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>.

Empirical evidence suggests hybrid approaches that embed machine learning views within classical frameworks can outperform pure mean-variance. For example, using deep learning predictions as investor views in Black-Litterman produced portfolios with high returns, low extreme allocations, and low risk, and outperformed both equal-weight and mean-variance benchmarks<cite id="31"></cite>. Reinforcement learning has also shown promise: a transformer-based DRL agent that fuses macro views with market data improved out-of-sample Sharpe ratios and portfolio turnover compared to mean-variance and standard DRL baselines<cite id="33"></cite>. Moreover, combining technical indicators with fundamental data in deep learning-based allocation increased accuracy and Sharpe ratios across multiple markets<cite id="15"></cite>. These results indicate that machine learning can stabilize and enhance allocation by providing richer signals and risk-aware objectives, while classical models offer interpretability and stability when properly regularized<cite id="31"></cite><cite id="33"></cite>.

## Interpretability and Regulatory Considerations

A major limitation of deep learning models in finance is poor interpretability, which complicates accountability and regulatory compliance. Post-hoc explanation methods (e.g., SHAP, LIME) can shed light on allocation decisions, but they are not always reliable in economic contexts and may fail to capture intrinsically uninterpretable architectures like transformers<cite id="26"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>. Time-series-specific adaptations (e.g., Vector SHAP, WindowSHAP) aim to preserve temporal dependence and reduce lag fragmentation, yet attribution uncertainty and explanation dynamics should be monitored as indicators of structural change<cite id="1"></cite>. Regulatory guidance increasingly emphasizes transparency and explainability, underscoring the need for hybrid frameworks that balance predictive power with interpretability<cite id="26"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>.

## Feasibility of Hybrid Frameworks

Combining the strengths of classic and machine learning models is not only feasible but increasingly common in practice. One approach is to use machine learning for return forecasting and risk measurement and embed these into classical optimization, either as views in Black-Litterman or as risk-aware objectives (e.g., mean-ES, mean-CVaR). Studies show that deep learning views can stabilize and improve portfolio performance relative to mean-variance, while robust optimization and Bayesian methods reduce estimation error and parameter sensitivity<cite id="31"></cite><cite id="20"></cite><cite id="24"></cite>. Another direction is to integrate reinforcement learning agents that learn dynamic trading policies while incorporating macro views or alternative data, as demonstrated by transformer-based DRL improving Sharpe ratios and turnover<cite id="33"></cite>. Finally, hybrid architectures that fuse technical and fundamental indicators can enhance predictive accuracy and allocation performance across markets<cite id="15"></cite>.

Despite these successes, hybrid frameworks must address practical challenges: transaction costs, overfitting, and the need for rigorous validation; interpretability and explainability requirements; and the alignment of predictive models with appropriate optimization strategies for different investor risk profiles<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="13"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>. Future work should also explore dynamic rebalancing, macroeconomic inputs, and distributionally robust formulations to improve generalization and risk control<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="25"></cite>.

## Conclusion

Classic mean-variance and Black-Litterman models provide interpretable, equilibrium-based frameworks for risk and return, but they rely on strong distributional and parametric assumptions and can be sensitive to input errors. Machine learning models excel at capturing non-linear relationships in return prediction and modern risk measures, yet they often lack transparency and require careful validation. Evidence from recent studies indicates that hybrid frameworks—integrating machine learning views and risk measures with classical optimization and robust Bayesian methods—can deliver more stable, accurate, and risk-aware portfolios while addressing regulatory and practical constraints<cite id="31"></cite><cite id="20"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="33"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>. As FinTech continues to evolve, the most effective modeling frameworks will likely combine predictive power with interpretability and robustness tailored to market conditions and investor preferences<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="6"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>.</answer>

In this Thesis three facets of a complete trading strategy are considered, these are Trend Detection, Portfolio Construction and Order Entry Timing. These three facets are considered in an integrated Machine Learning framework and a number of novel contributions are made to the state of the art. A number of practical issues that are often overlooked in the literature are also addressed. This Thesis presents a complete Machine Learning based trading strategy that is shown to generate profits under a range of trading conditions. The research that is presented comprises three experiments: 1- A New Neural Network Framework For Profitable Long-Short Equity Trading - The first experiment focusses on finding short term trading opportunities at the level of an individual single stock. A novel Neural Network method for detecting trading opportunities based on betting with or against a recent short term trend is presented. The approach taken is a departure from the bulk of the literature where the focus is on next day direction prediction. 2- A New Graphical Model Framework For Dynamic Equity Portfolio Construction - The second experiment considers the issue of Portfolio Construction. A Graphical Model framework for Portfolio Construction under conditions where trades are only held for short periods of time is presented. The work is important as standard Portfolio Construction techniques are not well suited to highly dynamic Portfolios. 3- A Study Of The Application of Online Learning For Order Entry Timing - The third experiment considers the issue of Order Execution and how to optimally time the entry of trading orders into the market. This work is important as order timing for Trade Execution has not been widely studied in the literature. The approaches that form the current state of the art in each of the three areas of Trading Opportunity (Trend) Detection, Portfolio Construction and Order Entry Timing often overlook real issues such as Liquidity and Transaction Costs. Traditional approaches—including parametric, bootstrap-based, and Bayesian—impose restrictive assumptions. This study introduces a non-parametric bootstrap framework for robust optimization in financial decision-making. By resampling empirical data, the framework constructs flexible, data-driven confidence intervals without assuming specific distributional forms, thus capturing uncertainty in statistical estimates, model parameters, and utility functions. Treating utility as a random variable enables percentile-based optimization, naturally suited for risk-sensitive and worst-case decision-making. Empirically, the framework mitigates overfitting and selection bias in trading strategy optimization and improves generalization in portfolio allocation. original_data.problem: In the field of FinTech, machine learning algorithms are now widely applied to asset allocation and investment decisions. Examples include classic models like Mean-Variance and Black-Litterman, as well as emerging deep learning models. While these models have shown certain advantages under different market conditions, each also has its limitations. For instance, the Mean-Variance model assumes asset returns follow a normal distribution, which often doesn't align with actual market conditions. The Black-Litterman model relies on subjective view inputs, introducing a degree of subjectivity. Although deep learning models can handle complex non-linear relationships, they suffer from poor interpretability. So, what are the core differences between these various models in terms of risk measurement, return prediction, and asset allocation? And is it possible to combine their strengths to build a more general-purpose and effective modeling framework?

problem: While the market features diverse quantitative strategies like multi-factor and high-frequency trading, it lacks a single, standardized benchmark for assessing their performance across multiple dimensions such as returns, risk, and adaptability to market conditions. Could we develop a general yet rigorous evaluation framework to enable accurate comparison and analysis of various advanced quant strategies?
final_response:
<think>
<answer>
## Executive summary

A single, standardized benchmark is insufficient to compare diverse quantitative strategies across returns, risk, and adaptability because historical backtests are prone to overfitting and often fail to predict out-of-sample performance. We propose a general, rigorous evaluation framework that combines risk-adjusted performance measures, multi-benchmark tracking-error, robust backtest procedures, and adaptability diagnostics, supported by tools and platforms that enable transparent, reproducible comparisons across strategies and markets. This framework is consistent with empirical findings that Sharpe ratios are poor predictors of out-of-sample performance, while volatility, drawdown, and testing intensity are more informative, and that systematic evaluation across multiple axes of profitability, risk, and reliability improves trustworthiness<cite id="31"></cite><cite id="46"></cite><cite id="28"></cite>.

## Why a single benchmark is inadequate

Across market regimes, risk profiles, and strategy horizons, a single benchmark fails to capture the multi-dimensional nature of quantitative performance. Empirical studies show that commonly reported metrics like the Sharpe ratio offer little value in predicting out-of-sample results, with R² near zero, whereas higher-order moments (volatility, maximum drawdown) and testing behavior (frequency of backtesting) are more predictive. Moreover, the more a strategy is backtested, the larger the gap between reported and realized performance, indicating that a single benchmark cannot account for overfitting or regime shifts<cite id="31"></cite><cite id="46"></cite>. In practice, risk is non-normal and tail events matter, reinforcing the need for performance measures that capture downside risk and multiple time horizons rather than a single Sharpe-like ratio<cite id="32"></cite>.

## Core components of the evaluation framework

1. Risk-adjusted performance and downside risk. Use coherent risk measures (e.g., VaR, CVaR) and tail-loss criteria alongside traditional Sharpe to better reflect non-normal returns and investor loss aversion. A multi-scale capability approach integrates control and expected tail loss into a single framework that is robust to non-normality and multiple time horizons<cite id="32"></cite>. In algorithmic trading, risk-adjusted rankings based on tail-aware ratios can generate more profitable momentum strategies and improve portfolio selection compared to cumulative return or Sharpe alone<cite id="12"></cite>.

2. Multi-benchmark tracking-error and relative performance. Construct portfolios or strategies that track the highest return among a set of benchmarks while minimizing quadratic tracking error. This approach reduces estimation error and improves out-of-sample net Sharpe, aggregate return, tracking error, and turnover relative to standard benchmarks<cite id="36"></cite>. Complement this with alpha-TEV frontiers that align portfolio construction with ex-ante alpha, reducing the tendency to select overly risky portfolios that chase tracking error<cite id="42"></cite>.

3. Robust backtesting and out-of-sample validation. Prevent overfitting by using model-free, nonparametric cross-validation (e.g., combinatorially symmetric cross-validation) to estimate the probability of backtest overfitting. In machine learning trading, simple hold-out and rolling-window tests can be unreliable; CSCV provides a more trustworthy assessment of generalization<cite id="46"></cite>. Additionally, impact and survival tests can expose how performance degrades as assets under management grow or during prolonged drawdowns, helping to select more robust strategies<cite id="8"></cite>.

4. Adaptability and regime robustness. Diagnose time-varying risk and strategy behavior using local risk decomposition, which retains local, regime-sensitive information about performance dynamics. This is particularly useful for high-frequency trading and sequential environments with regime changes and noisy data<cite id="27"></cite>. For machine-learning strategies, walk-forward analysis (repetitive train/test with one-period lags) can improve robustness in non-stationary markets<cite id="16"></cite>. In portfolio construction, controlling the risk of mis-estimated mean-reversion times via screening and selection can reduce tail losses and improve out-of-sample performance<cite id="18"></cite>.

## Supporting tools and platforms

Several open-source platforms and market environments provide standardized environments and benchmarks for comparing quantitative strategies across markets and time periods. FinRL-Meta aggregates hundreds of market environments via a DataOps pipeline and supports community-wide competitions and visualizations to assess relative performance<cite id="37"></cite>. TradeMaster offers a holistic toolkit, empirical benchmark, and user interface for transparent, reproducible reinforcement learning trading research and deployment<cite id="31"></cite>. PRUDEX-Compass proposes a systematic evaluation across six axes (profitability, risk-control, universality, diversity, reliability, explainability) with 17 measures, enabling multi-dimensional comparisons of algorithmic strategies<cite id="28"></cite>. Finally, the QuantConnect platform provides a cloud-based environment for algorithmic trading and research, supporting backtesting, paper trading, and deployment to facilitate rigorous testing and comparison<cite id="40"></cite>.

## Practical implementation steps

- Define a suite of risk-adjusted metrics (Sharpe, Sortino, VaR/CVaR) and tail-loss criteria to capture non-normality and downside risk<cite id="32"></cite><cite id="12"></cite>.
- Select a set of benchmarks (e.g., market indices, naive diversification, risk parity) and construct a tracking-error minimizer that targets the highest return among benchmarks to improve out-of-sample performance and diversification<cite id="36"></cite>.
- Validate using robust backtest procedures (CSCV) and report higher-order moments and testing intensity as predictive features<cite id="46"></cite>.
- Diagnose adaptability with local risk decomposition and walk-forward analysis, and control model risk (e.g., mean-reversion time estimation) via screening and selection<cite id="27"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="18"></cite>.
- Compare strategies across multiple markets and horizons using standardized environments and multi-axis evaluation frameworks<cite id="37"></cite><cite id="31"></cite><cite id="28"></cite>.

## Limitations and uncertainties

While the proposed framework is supported by empirical and methodological evidence, its effectiveness depends on careful implementation of robust backtests, appropriate benchmark selection, and consistent risk measurement across strategies. The cited studies indicate that Sharpe ratios are poor predictors of out-of-sample performance, but they do not universally invalidate all backtesting practices—only those that neglect overfitting and regime shifts<cite id="31"></cite><cite id="46"></cite>. Therefore, the framework should be applied with transparent, standardized procedures and validated across independent samples and markets to ensure reliability<cite id="28"></cite><cite id="37"></cite>.

## Conclusion

A single benchmark is insufficient for comparing diverse quantitative strategies across returns, risk, and adaptability due to backtest overfitting, non-normal risk, and regime shifts. A general, rigorous evaluation framework that integrates risk-adjusted performance, multi-benchmark tracking-error, robust backtest validation, and adaptability diagnostics, supported by transparent platforms and multi-axis evaluation, enables accurate, reproducible comparisons across strategies and markets<cite id="31"></cite><cite id="32"></cite><cite id="36"></cite><cite id="46"></cite><cite id="27"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="28"></cite><cite id="37"></cite>.

problem: Is there a general method for solving a first-price sealed-bid auction with two bidders who have independent private values drawn from different distributions (i.e., ex-ante asymmetric bidders)?
final_response:
<think>>
<answer>
## Executive summary

There is no single formula that solves every asymmetric two-bidder first-price auction, but there is a general method: formulate a system of differential equations for the inverse of each bidder’s equilibrium bid function, together with appropriate boundary conditions, and solve it analytically or numerically. This approach applies ex ante to bidders with independent private values drawn from any (even different) distributions, and it yields the equilibrium bid distribution and seller revenue as byproducts<cite id="64"></cite><cite id="66"></cite><cite id="71"></cite>.

## Theoretical foundation

Lebrun showed that in a first-price auction with n asymmetric bidders, every Bayesian equilibrium is “essentially” pure: it can be written in terms of bid functions whose inverses satisfy a system of first-order differential equations, with 2n boundary conditions and a free boundary on the high end; he proved existence and gave sufficient conditions for uniqueness<cite id="64"></cite><cite id="66"></cite>. In the special case of two bidders, this reduces to two differential equations and four boundary conditions<cite id="66"></cite>. A perturbation approach also derives explicit approximations for equilibrium bids and seller revenue in asymmetric auctions, complementing the differential-equations framework<cite id="11"></cite>.

## Analytic solutions in special cases

Analytic solutions are known in several parametric settings. For two buyers with uniformly distributed values on different intervals [v₁, v̄₁] and [v₂, v̄₂], Kaplan and Zamir derived explicit bid functions and showed continuity in the distribution parameters and minimum bid; their results generalize earlier symmetric (Griesmer et al.) and common-value cases<cite id="8"></cite><cite id="42"></cite>. In independently supported discrete asymmetric auctions with binary valuations, closed-form equilibria and revenue comparisons to second-price auctions have been obtained<cite id="4"></cite>. For two-bidder auctions with three-point discrete supports, closed-form equilibria in first-price auctions have been derived and used to compare revenue performance with second-price auctions<cite id="7"></cite><cite id="4"></cite>.

## Numerical solution algorithms

Because explicit solutions are rare, numerical methods are the workhorse for general asymmetric distributions. A boundary-value method has been shown to be robust and stable for asymmetric first-price auctions, overcoming the inherent instability of backward-shooting approaches and enabling reliable computation even with distributions that cross or lack stochastic dominance ordering<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="31"></cite><cite id="33"></cite><cite id="56"></cite>. Software packages that automate these computations typically solve the differential equations and report inverse bid functions, winning probabilities, and reserve-price statistics, including optimal reserve prices<cite id="12"></cite>. Large-asymmetric approximations via boundary-layer theory provide uniform asymptotic expansions for inverse bid functions, with numerical confirmation of accuracy<cite id="32"></cite>. A complementary perturbation approach yields explicit approximations for revenue, reserve-price choice, and other metrics in asymmetric settings<cite id="11"></cite>.

## Practical guidance for implementation

To solve a two-bidder asymmetric first-price auction, proceed as follows. Define the bidder-specific cumulative distribution functions F₁(v) and F₂(v) and their densities f₁(v) and f₂(v). Let v(b) denote the inverse bid function for each bidder as a function of the bid b; the pair {v₁(b), v₂(b)} satisfies a coupled system of differential equations derived from the first-order condition for Bayesian Nash equilibrium<cite id="66"></cite>. Boundary conditions are typically: (i) at the lowest possible bid, the derivative of the inverse bid function diverges to infinity (no mass at zero), and (ii) at the upper support, the derivative vanishes because the highest possible bid is tied to the maximum valuation<cite id="33"></cite>. With these, solve the system either analytically in special cases or numerically using a boundary-value method, and read off the bid functions and expected revenue<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="12"></cite>.

## Uniqueness and identification

Uniqueness of the inverse-bid equilibrium can be established under standard conditions, such as when distributions have mass points at the lower end of support or are sufficiently ordered by stochastic dominance; Lebrun provides sufficient conditions and inequality results across distributions<cite id="66"></cite>. In some structured environments, identification and estimation are possible without explicitly solving the differential equations: rewrite the differential equations in terms of the observed bid distribution and estimate the private value distributions nonparametrically, with straightforward generalization to many bidder types<cite id="63"></cite>.

## Empirical and experimental context

Experiments in asymmetric private-value settings with distinct distributions confirm qualitative predictions of asymmetric first-price auction theory and document strategic responses to reserve prices, validating the equilibrium concept and solution methods in practice<cite id="2"></cite>. In ex ante asymmetric environments, expected revenue is generally lower than in symmetric benchmarks, underscoring the importance of asymmetry in applied settings and the relevance of general solution methods for reserve-price choice and revenue prediction<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="11"></cite>.

## Limitations and extensions

The differential-equations method assumes independent private values and does not directly extend to common-value or affiliated-value settings, where the same system of equations arises but identification and computation are more challenging; in such cases, specialized estimation techniques are required<cite id="63"></cite>. When the number of bidders grows, boundary-layer approximations provide tractable asymptotics for inverse bid functions and help explain the convergence of first-price and second-price revenues<cite id="32"></cite>. Finally, while the general method applies to any distributions, computational stability and uniqueness depend on the specific shapes of F₁ and F₂, motivating careful numerical implementation and structural assumptions<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="66"></cite>.

## Conclusion

There is no universal closed-form formula for asymmetric two-bidder first-price auctions with different ex-ante distributions, but there is a general method grounded in differential equations for the inverse bid functions and boundary conditions. However, there is an alternate form that is used only occasionally. It was proposed by Vickrey (1961) in a partially successful attempt to devise a closed procedure strategically equivalent to the English auction. In such "Vickrey auctions" of single items, the winning bidder is the one who submitted the best bid, but the price is set at the level of the second-best bid. Thus, it is called a "second-price auction" in contrast to standard sealed bidding and Dutch auctions which are called "first-price auctions" since the winner's price is the best price offered. English auctions are considered second-price auctions, because the transaction price is at the level of (or marginally better than) the best price acceptable to any losing bidder. Multiunit analogues are "discriminatory" auctions (each winner pays the price he bid) and "highest-rejected-bid" auctions. Auctions also blend into request-for-proposal processes. Some such processes are essentially auctions. Microeconomics in general and auction theory in particular too often assume away aftermarket interactions, which are a common feature of real markets and have a powerful impact on strategies and incentives. Lately, however, a body of literature emerged that incorporates the possibility of resale into game-theoretic analysis of auctions. This paper reviews this literature. It highlights the role of bargaining power on the aftermarket as one of the main issues in this literature. It then reports how standard auction formats – first and second price auctions in particular – compare in terms of the seller’s revenues they generate. Then, this paper shows generalizations of Myerson’s approach to constructing optimal auctions when resale is possible; the discussed models require delicate assumptions. Next, the survey covers more specific issues: different approaches to modelling the aftermarket, decisions to enter the primary auction, effects of disclosing information from the primary auction and the role of speculators. Finally, the paper overviews empirical research on auctions with resale, the newest branch of this literature that is developing rapidly.</summary><hostname>Экономический журнал ВШЭ</hostname><publisher>HSE Economic Journal</publisher><author_list><author name="Ivan Susin" affiliation="National Research University Higher School of Economics, 4, bld. 2, Slavyanskaya Square, Moscow, 109074, Russian Federat
