In this study we show that the backward-shooting method is inherently unstable, and that this instability cannot be eliminated by changing the numerical methodology of the backward solver. Moreover, this instability becomes more severe as the number of players increases. We then present a novel boundary-value method for computing the equilibrium strategies of asymmetric first-price auctions. We demonstrate the robustness and stability of this method for auctions with any number of players, and for players with mixed types of distributions, including distributions with more than one crossing. Finally, we use the boundary-value method to study large auctions with hundreds of players, to compute the asymptotic rate at which large first-price and second-price auctions become revenue equivalent, and to study auctions in which the distributions cannot be ordered according to first-order stochastic dominance.</summary><hostname>School of Mathematical Sciences, Tel Aviv University</hostname><author_list><author name="Gadi Fibich" /><author name="Nir Gavish" /></author_list><url>http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~fibich/Manuscripts/BV_Method_GEB11.pdf</url><publish_time>2011年3月3日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:57"><title>ON THE CONVERGENCE OF LEARNING ALGORITHMS IN BAYESIAN AUCTION GAMES</title><summary>Equilibrium problems in Bayesian auction games can be described as systems of differential equations. Depending on the model assumptions, these equations might be such that we do not have a rigorous mathematical solution theory. The lack of analytical or numerical techniques with guaranteed convergence for the equilibrium problem has plagued the field and limited equilibrium analysis to rather simple auction models such as single-object auctions. Recent advances in equilibrium learning led to algorithms that find equilibrium under a wide variety of model assumptions. We analyze first- and second-price auctions where simple learning algorithms converge to an equilibrium. The equilibrium problem in auctions is equivalent to solving an infinite-dimensional variational inequality (VI). It is of great significance for tourism product suppliers to analyze the influence of SEM (search engine marketing) on the value standard of potential tourist destination selection and put forward some countermeasures. According to the analysis of the change of value standards of tourism destination selection under the condition of SEM, this paper believes that in the information search with large capacity, high frequency and single way, a variety of value standards have formed, including price and tourism experience superposition, multi - dimensional matching with tourism motivation and tourism experience based on relatives and friends, and then puts forward some countermeasures for tourism suppliers, such as improving the perceived value space of tourism products, elaborately building tourism products and making full use of social platforms to break through the image solidification of tourism destinations.</summary><hostname>维普网</hostname><publisher>企业经济</publisher><author_list><author name="曾九江" raw_output.raw_text: <search query="2025 年 旅游趋势 2025 tourism trends 2025 survey travelers preferences" search_time="2026年5月16日11时51分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:6"><title>品质旅游时代的游客诉求与趋势分析——以北京为例</title><summary>“十四五”时期游客对旅游产品与服务质量的品质提出了更高的要求。学界对品质旅游的已有研究多侧重旅游供给品质的提升，而对旅游需求品质的关注相对较少。关注旅游需求品质，采用扎根理论的技术手段对网络游记进行文本分析，挖掘品质旅游时代的游客诉求及其变化趋势。研究发现，品质化是游客的核心诉求，且在技术支持与保障体系的保障下，具体表现为产品品质、服务体验、主客交互与文化需要四大旅游诉求。游客诉求体现出“身体需要”与“精神需要”内部的品质化升级，以及旅游诉求从“身体需要”向“精神需要”的转向与升级，对旅游业提质升级提出了新要求与新方向。</summary><hostname>维普网</hostname><publisher>开发研究</publisher><author_list><author name="李创新" affiliation="1. 北京第二外国语学院 a. 旅游科学学院；b. 北京旅游发展研究基地，北京 100024；2. 中国旅游研究院，北京 100005" /><author name="蒋蕾" affiliation="1. 北京第二外国语学院 a. 旅游科学学院；b. 北京旅游发展研究基地，北京 100024；2. 中国旅游研究院，北京 100005" /><author name="王雪莉" affiliation="1. 北京第二外国语学院 a. 旅游科学学院；b. 北京旅游发展研究基地，北京 100024；2. 中国旅游研究院，北京 100005" /></author_list><url>http://m.qikan.cqvip.com/Article/ArticleDetail?id=7109639696</url><publish_time>2023年2月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:7"><title>Unpacking the $15 Trillion Opportunity in Leisure Travel</title><summary>Leisure travel will present a $15 trillion opportunity for airlines, hotels, and other travel industry stakeholders in 2040, up from $5 trillion in 2024. The reasons for this jump are myriad. One is the burgeoning middle class in many emerging markets, eager to travel. Another is the growing emphasis on experiences, rather than things—people are increasingly choosing to spend their money on creating good memories. Making good memories doesn’t have to mean taking international trips, though it can. Domestic trips compose the bulk of leisure travel, especially in emerging markets. To tap the true potential value of leisure travel, stakeholders should try to attract local and regional tourists as well as international visitors. Travel companies should also prepare for a rapidly evolving customer base, distinguished primarily by shifting demographics. The travelers of the near future are a rich tapestry of identities and preferences. For example, more and more visitors are coming from emerging markets, including China, India, Saudi Arabia, Bulgaria, and Cambodia. Travelers will also skew younger and embrace digital technologies. So travel companies along the value chain should find ways to understand and welcome new travelers while continuing to cater to traditional visitors. Our global review of leisure travel explores the sources and motivations driving growth in leisure travel. (See “About Our Research.”) We look at questions relevant to travel industry stakeholders: Where is growth coming from? What drives travelers’ choices? How will travelers plan and book? How should the industry respond? To understand current leisure travel behavior and needs and to test trends that are likely to emerge in the future, we undertook a comprehensive review of travel patterns from 2014 through 2024. We looked at both developed and emerging markets including Vietnam, Saudi Arabia, and countries in Africa and Latin America. Overall, our sample and forecasts—through 2040—included 68 countries. Most important, together with our Center for Customer Insight, we undertook detailed surveys with individual travelers in 11 countries whose populations currently travel frequently or are poised to travel more in the future: Australia, China, India, Indonesia, Germany, Mexico, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, UK, US, and Vietnam. For each country included in the Traveler of the Future survey, we posed our questions to 400 to 500 individuals. Our surveys covered travel motivations; companions; favorite destination types; needs; how travelers get inspired, search, and book; how they combine experiences; and what they perceive as luxury. Note that our forecasts did not take into account any impact of geopolitical trends and events.</summary><hostname>ilag.nordnorge.com</hostname><author_list><author name="Christina Mühlenbein" /><author name="Dennis Utzerath" /><author name="Mario Farsky" /><author name="Yassin El Khourouj" /><author name="Lara Koslow" /><author name="Laure

problem: In ecology, how do birds achieve precise location and direction navigation during migration? What cues and disturbances influence this process?
final_response:
<think>
<answer>
Introduction

Birds achieve precise location and directional navigation during migration by integrating multiple cues—magnetic, celestial, visual, olfactory, and possibly even social—into a flexible system that allows them to determine both their position relative to their goal and the correct heading to fly. Contemporary evidence indicates that no single cue suffices; instead, navigation is multifactorial, with different cues used at different times and under different conditions<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite>. Below, we synthesize the data on the primary cues used for navigation and orientation, and then discuss how weather, turbulence, and anthropogenic disturbances can interfere with these processes.

Magnetic cues: compass and map components

Birds use the Earth’s magnetic field for both compass orientation and map-based position detection. Experiments and field observations show that they rely on magnetic intensity, inclination, and declination, and can integrate conflicting values of inclination and declination to adjust their migratory direction, indicating positional information from the magnetic field rather than direction finding alone<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="7"></cite>. Geomagnetic modeling further suggests that for some species, magnetic intensity is more frequently used than inclination for navigation, and that effective migratory strategies often combine compass and taxis mechanisms rather than depend on a single cue<cite id="6"></cite>. At the mechanistic level, magnetite-based particle detectors and the photochemical radical-pair mechanism in the eyes are leading candidates for magnetic sensing, with cryptochrome ErCRY4 in the retinas of migratory birds having the physical properties needed to detect the geomagnetic field’s direction<cite id="11"></cite>.

Celestial cues: sun, stars, and polarized light

Celestial cues provide directional information during the day and night. The time-compensated sun compass is a well-established mechanism, and its calibration can be disrupted by weather such as cloud cover, forcing birds to rely on other cues<cite id="3"></cite>. Polarized light patterns in the sky are also used for orientation, and their patterns change predictably as birds move north–south, supporting their role as a compass for nocturnal migrants<cite id="1"></cite>. Stellar navigation is particularly important at high latitudes where the sun is not visible, and studies have demonstrated that birds can use star patterns to maintain a constant heading during simulated night flights<cite id="3"></cite>.

Visual landmarks

Visual landmarks contribute to navigation, especially during homing and in familiar areas. GPS tracking in homing pigeons shows that experienced birds can follow memorized routes by combining a compass with learned visual cues, and that route following can be offset by expected compass directions, indicating dual control of compass and landmark guidance<cite id="52"></cite>. In long-distance navigation, birds may use a “2.5D landmark map” that integrates visual and magnetic information, with some species using atmospheric chemosignals (olfaction) to supplement visual cues<cite id="18"></cite><cite id="16"></cite>. However, GPS tracking of shearwaters under obstacle-release conditions reveals that they can orient homewards but may be unaware of the scale of large landmasses, leading to inefficient detours and suggesting that landmark information is not always sufficient for global navigation<cite id="42"></cite>.

Olfactory cues

Olfactory information is increasingly supported as a positional cue for navigation. In homing pigeons, regional-scale gradients of volatile compounds (including dimethyl sulphide and terpenoids) provide the basis for an olfactory map, and flight trajectories can be influenced by local DMS concentrations<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="24"></cite>. For pelagic seabirds, wind-borne odors from breeding islands appear to be the primary navigational cue over vast, visually featureless oceans, with movement patterns matching theoretical predictions of olfactory-cued navigation<cite id="22"></cite><cite id="25"></cite>. These findings indicate that olfactory cues can function as a map-like representation, complementing magnetic and celestial compasses<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>.

Weather, turbulence, and anthropogenic disturbances

Weather and atmospheric conditions can disrupt navigation by masking celestial cues and altering wind patterns. Cloud cover can prevent birds from calibrating their sun compass, while strong winds can change flight paths and energy expenditure, and geomagnetic disturbances can temporarily reduce the reliability of magnetic cues<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite>. Radar studies show that during intense geomagnetic storms, fewer birds migrate, they fly at different altitudes, and they often fly against the wind, indicating compromised navigation under space-weather stress<cite id="4"></cite>.

Anthropogenic light and structures also interfere with migration. Artificial light at night can disorient birds, causing them to veer off course or collide with buildings, and studies have documented large numbers of bird fatalities at structures such as the John James Audubon Center at Debs Park due to collisions<cite id="8"></cite><cite id="9"></cite>. These disturbances highlight the vulnerability of avian navigational systems to human-made changes in the environment<cite id="8"></cite><cite id="9"></cite>.

Concluding remarks

Taken together, the evidence indicates that birds use a composite navigation toolbox during migration, combining a magnetic compass and map with celestial and visual cues, and in some cases olfactory maps, to achieve precise location and direction. Compass mechanisms often rely on magnetic intensity and inclination, with cryptochromes and magnetite as leading sensory mechanisms, while celestial cues provide additional directional references<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="6"></cite><cite id="11"></cite><cite id="1"></cite>. Visual and olfactory cues contribute positional and route-specific information, but their sufficiency for global navigation remains limited in some species, as shown by homing detours around large obstacles<cite id="42"></cite>. External disturbances—weather, geomagnetic storms, artificial light, and human structures—can disrupt these cues and compromise migratory success<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite><cite id="8"></cite><cite id="9"></cite>.
</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="radial vs map and compass navigation birds review 2020 2021 2022" search_time="2026年5月16日11时54分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:6"><title>Simulating geomagnetic bird navigation using novel high-resolution geomagnetic data</title><summary>Birds rely on precise navigational mechanisms, especially for long-distance migrations. One debated mechanism is their use of the geomagnetic field. It is unclear if and how different species of birds are using intensity or inclination (or both) for navigation. Previous geomagnetic modelling research is based on static geomagnetic data despite a temporally and spatially varying geomagnetic field. Animals supposedly have a high sensitivity to those changes of the geomagnetic field. In order to understand how birds respond in real-time to its temporal variation, we need to use accurate geomagnetic information linked to the position of the bird through co-location in a constellation. We present a data-driven approach to simulate geomagnetic migratory strategies, using, for the first time, accurate contemporaneous geomagnetic data obtained from Swarm satellites of the European Space Agency. We created biased correlated random walk models which were based on both GPS data from greater white-fronted geese (Anser albifrons) during full migration between north-west Russia and central Europe and contemporaneous satellite based measurements of geomagnetic navigation associated with different geomagnetic values were translated into probability surfaces, built from geomagnetic data, and included into the random walk models. To evaluate which strategy was most likely, we compared the measured GPS trajectories to the simulated ones based on the different navigational strategy measurements. We propose this as an approach to track many bird species for future comparative studies. We found that navigational strategies in these geese using magnetic intensity were closer to the observed data than those using inclination. This was the case in 80% of the best models and is an indication that it should be more beneficial for these geese to use intensity over inclination. Additionally, our results supported results from a previous study, that navigation based on taxis and compass mechanisms were more similar to the observed data than other mechanisms. We therefore suggest that these geese may use a combination of these strategies for navigation. However, we found that no single mechanism is fully sufficient to explain the observed movements of one mechanism is necessary; indicating a multifactorial navigation mechanism of these migratory geese in the study area. The satellite geomagnetic data are available at a higher temporal resolution and the use significantly improved the fit of the modelled simulations in comparison to the modelled geomagnetic data. Therefore, using annotated geomagnetic data could greatly improve the modelling of animal geomagnetic navigation in future research.</summary><hostname>St Andrews Research Repository</hostname><publisher>Ecological Informatics</publisher><author_list><author name="Beate Zein" affiliation="School of Geography & Sustainable Development, University of St Andrews, St Andrews, Scotland, UK" /><author name="Jed A. The protein cryptochrome ErCRY4, found in the eyes of migratory European robins, has the right physical properties to be the elusive magnetosensor. Arguably the greatest mystery in sensory biology is magnetoreception – how animals sense Earth’s magnetic field and use it as a compass to determine their spatial orientation. Animals as varied as birds, sea turtles, fishes, crustaceans and insects depend on this field for both short- and long-range navigation. The identity of the biological tissue responsible for sensing the field’s direction, and the sensory mechanism that underpins this type of navigation, have remained an enigma. In migratory birds, the main contenders are magnetically sensitive proteins called cryptochromes, which are located in the retina. However, proof has been lacking that these proteins truly possess the magnetic sensitivity and physical properties needed to detect Earth’s extremely weak magnetic field. On page 535, Xu et al. provide this proof in vitro, bringing us tantalizingly close to solving the mystery of magnetoreception. There are currently two main hypotheses for how animals sense Earth’s magnetic field (as well as some alternative hypotheses put forward in the past few years). One proposes that, as an animal changes direction, crystals of the oxidized-iron compound magnetite (Fe₃O₄), located in its body and aligned with the field, exert a rotational force – called torque – on mechanoreceptors with which they are in physical contact. This might thereby signal changes in body alignment through the opening and closing of mechanoreceptor ion channels. The other main hypothesis (Fig. 1) proposes that, when cryptochrome proteins absorb photons of light and become ‘photoexcited’, they form magnetically sensitive chemical intermediates known as radical pairs. Variations in the yield of their reaction product (the form of the cryptochrome that contains a radical molecule called FADH’) are thought to signal the animal’s direction with respect to Earth’s magnetic field. These two proposed mechanisms are not mutually exclusive – indeed, migratory birds might possess both, using magnetite for their ‘magnetic-map’ sense (the ability to sense magnetic characteristics associated with a given location on Earth’s surface) and cryptochromes for their magnetic-compass sense (which offers the animal a way to sense its direction relative to magnetic north). Cryptochromes are found both in animals and in plants, and are a type of protein known as a flavoprotein. Cryptochromes bind non-covalently to a molecule called a chromophore, such as FAD, which absorbs photons of blue light when in its fully oxidized state. In animals, cryptochrome proteins termed CRY1 and CRY2 are involved in the regulation of daily (circadian) rhythms, and their expression levels in tissue typically cycle over the course of 24 hours. By contrast, the cryptochrome CRY4 lacks such signs of circadian cycling, suggesting that it has a different biological role, possibly that of magnetoreception. CRY4 is found only in birds, fishes and amphibians, which are types of animal with well-documented magnetically guided behaviours. CRY4 has therefore emerged as the leading candidate for enabling cryptochrome-based magnetoreception in vertebrates. Previous analysis of chickens (Gallus gallus) and migratory European robins (Erithacus rubecula) indicates that CRY4 is located in the outer segments of two types of photoreceptor cell in the retina – double cones and long-wavelength single cones. Olfactory navigation is empirically well founded, but its way of operation and, in particular, the concrete olfactory inputs processed by the birds are so far unknown. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="olfactory navigation birds migration homing study 2019 2020 2021" search_time="2026年5月16日11时54分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:22"><title>Olfactory-cued navigation in shearwaters: linking movement patterns to mechanisms</title><summary>After foraging in the open ocean pelagic birds can pinpoint their breeding colonies, located on remote islands in visually featureless seascapes. This remarkable ability to navigate over vast distances has been attributed to the birds being able to learn an olfactory map on the basis of wind-borne odors. Odor-cued navigation has been linked mechanistically to displacements with exponentially-truncated power-law distributions. Such distributions were previously identified in three species of Atlantic and Mediterranean shearwaters but crucially it has not been demonstrated that these distributions are wind-speed dependent, as expected if navigation was olfactory-cued. Here we show that the distributions are wind-speed dependent, in accordance with theoretical expectations. We thereby link movement patterns to underlying generative mechanisms. A flight along the shortest possible route between pairs of points on a sphere ('orthodrome' or 'great circle route') requires continuous adjustment of the heading towards the goal (Imboden and Imboden 1972). For a moving individual, to be able to correct its route implies that the individual knows where it is relative to its goal i.e. have a map sense, Gould and Grant Gould (2012). An alternative strategy to navigate towards a remote goal is by vector navigation. Vector navigation enables migratory birds to maintain a pre-determined orientation (Able 1995, Guilford and Aleson 2014, Gould and Grant Gould 2012, Hansson and Akesson 2014, Akesson and Blanco 2016) and orient along geographic and/or magnetic loxodrome (also called 'rhumbline') routes. These routes, by definition, are longer than orthodromes, but may be easier to achieve because of the constant heading (Imboden and Imboden 1972, Gudmundsson and Alerstam 1998). To investigate the orientation mechanisms in operation during natural migration, theoretical flight path geometries based on assumptions of alternative vector navigation strategies can be compared with observed individual migration routes (Alerstam 1996, Sandberg and Holmqvist 1998, Alerstam and Gudmundsson 1999b, Muheim et al. 2003, 2018, Guilford et al. 2018, Akesson and Blanco 2017, Sokolovski et al. 2018). The most informative comparison would be for summer migrations along trajectories close to the geographic and the magnetic poles, where the challenging environment would help disclose possible orientation mechanisms. Here, constant daylight conditions complicate the calibration of time-compensated sun compasses for orientation. At the same time, irregular and geometric field lines may complicate the use of magnetic cues close to the magnetic North Pole (Kiepenheuer 1984, Alerstam 1990b, b, 2018), we also asses the influence of the moving medium, the winds, during the flights.</summary><hostname>Pure</hostname><publisher>Journal of Avian Biology</publisher><author_list><author name="Eva M. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="radial navigation map navigation birds GPS evidence 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024" search_time="2026年5月16日11时54分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:67"><title>Shearwaters sometimes take long homing detours when denied natural outward journey information</title><summary>The cognitive processes (learning and processing of information) underpinning the long-distance navigation of birds are poorly understood. Here, we used the homing motivation of the Manx shearwater to investigate navigational decision making in a wild bird by displacing them 294 km to the far side of a large island (the island of Ireland). Since shearwaters are reluctant to fly over land, the island blocked the direct route home, forcing a navigational decision. Further still, on the far side of the obstacle, we chose a release site where the use of local knowledge could facilitate a 20% improvement in route efficiency if shearwaters were able to anticipate and avoid a large inlet giving the appearance of open water in the home direction. We found that no shearwater took the most efficient initial route home, but instead oriented in the home direction (even once the obstacle became visible). Upon reaching the obstacle, four shearwaters subsequently circumnavigated the land mass via the long route, travelling a further 900 km as a result. Hence, despite readily orienting homewards immediately after displacement, shearwaters seem unaware of the scale of the obstacle formed by a large land mass despite this being a prominent feature of their regular foraging environment.</summary><hostname>rcastoragev2.blob.core.windows.net</hostname><publisher>Biology Letters</publisher><author_list><author name="Oliver Padget" affiliation="Zoology Department, University of Oxford, Oxford, Oxfordshire, UK" /><author name="Natasha Gillies" affiliation="Zoology Department, University of Oxford, Oxford, Oxfordshire, UK" /><author name="Martyna Syposz" affiliation="Zoology Department, University of Oxford, Oxford, Oxfordshire, UK" /><author name="Emma Lockley" affiliation="Queen Mary University of London, London, UK" /><author name="Tim Guilford" affiliation="Zoology Department, University of Oxford, Oxford, Oxfordshire, UK" /></author_list><url>https://rcastoragev2.blob.core.windows.net/c9c30753137931f8000b385687504ff6/PMC8825984.pdf</url><publish_time>2022年1月7日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:68"><title>Strategies of Young Pigeons during 'Map' Learning</title><summary>The routes of young, inexperienced pigeons released at four sites up to 13·5 km from the loft were recorded with GPS-based tracking devices. The routes were found to differ from those of old, experienced pigeons in several aspects: (1) Although being oriented when departing, young birds show more scatter and larger deviations from the home direction, but usually restrict their flights to a semicircle. (2) They apparently ignore prominent landmarks near the loft that are clearly visible. (3) Their tracks are typically more complex, consisting of a number of distinctive phases where the young birds head in different directions, which results in significantly longer routes, often exceeding the direct home distances more than four times. (4) At the same time, young birds seldom venture further away from the release site than the direct distance to home. Their behaviour can be interpreted as exploration to obtain new information on the distribution of navigational factors to be included in their still rudimentary navigational'map'. At the same time, their flights seem to include elements of safety, like anchoring the flights around the release site and a sense of distance, which help to reduce the chance of getting lost.</summary><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>Journal of Navigation</publisher><author_list><author name="Ingo Schiffner" affiliation="Bangor University" /><author name="Tina Pavkovic" /><author name="Bettina Siegmund" /><author name="Roswitha Wiltschko" affiliation="J. # Global investments, key initiatives, and outputs related to AI by major international consulting firms

## Overview
Across Big Four, MBB, and other global consulting firms, AI has evolved from an emerging technology into a central strategic lever, with firms accelerating investments, talent development, and client co-creation of AI-driven products and services. In 2023–2024, generative AI (gen AI) and agentic AI became focal points, with reports documenting rapid experimentation, governance changes, and early-stage value capture, while also highlighting common barriers such as data readiness and outdated IT systems<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="14"></cite><cite id="15"></cite>. This wave of transformation is evident across sectors, including financial services, where firms are among the most heavily invested in AI and are shifting from efficiency to revenue growth opportunities<cite id="43"></cite>.

## Big Four firms: investments and strategic directions
The Big Four have announced multi-billion-dollar commitments to embed AI into their services and operations. PwC outlined a plan to invest up to $12 billion through 2026 in AI and cybersecurity, including hiring about 100,000 new AI-capable staff—more than a third of its workforce<cite id="1"></cite>. EY committed $10 billion over three years to AI and machine learning, with earlier investments of $1 billion over two years<cite id="1"></cite>. KPMG announced $5 billion over five years to implement AI across its operations<cite id="1"></cite>. These investments are accompanied by initiatives to integrate AI into audit and consulting workflows, such as Deloitte’s “AI@Deloitte” program, which aims to embed AI across the firm’s capabilities and client engagements<cite id="2"></cite>. Collectively, these firms are positioning themselves to deliver AI-driven insights and automation while upskilling large cohorts of professionals to work alongside intelligent systems<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="2"></cite>.

## McKinsey & Company: research, practice, and client co-creation
McKinsey’s AI practice is anchored by the McKinsey Analytics team and the McKinsey Global Institute (MGI), which have mapped hundreds of AI use cases and assessed both practical applications and economic potential across industries<cite id="27"></cite>. MGI’s research continues to explore how AI can reshape productivity, labor markets, and business models, providing leaders with evidence-based guidance for transformation<cite id="27"></cite>. McKinsey’s consulting work emphasizes helping clients design AI strategies that align with business goals, with a focus on value creation through analytics and AI deployment<cite id="30"></cite>. In 2023–2024, McKinsey’s broader AI and digital research documented widespread experimentation with gen AI, organizational changes to governance and workflows, and early signs of bottom-line impact among larger organizations<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="15"></cite>. McKinsey’s leadership also highlighted the need to rethink competitive advantage and organizational design as firms integrate AI into core operations<cite id="34"></cite>.

## BCG: value creation frameworks and client engagements
BCG’s research underscores a widening AI value gap: only 5% of firms in a 2025 study were achieving AI value at scale, while 60% were not capturing material benefits and another 35% were scaling efforts with modest returns<cite id="23"></cite>. To close this gap, BCG emphasizes complementary assets such as pattern recognition, proprietary data, modularization, and regulation, and outlines three pathways to unlock corporate value—cost reduction and productivity improvement; hyper-personalization; and new revenue streams or AI-enabled business models<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="34"></cite>. BCG’s practice also benchmarks how financial institutions are responding to gen AI, noting that while many leaders see transformative potential, only a few have established delivery teams or detailed plans, with early use cases concentrated in support functions such as call centers and software development<cite id="22"></cite>. BCG’s insights provide clients with structured approaches to select high-value use cases and build the organizational and technical foundations required for success<cite id="22"></cite><cite id="23"></cite>.

## Accenture: products, talent programs, and client outcomes
Accenture’s Applied Intelligence practice offers AI-driven products and services across digital, cloud, and analytics, with a focus on co-creating solutions that deliver measurable outcomes for clients<cite id="40"></cite>. In 2023–2024, Accenture’s adoption of generative AI was validated by field experiments showing productivity gains for developers using AI-based coding assistants; across three trials at Microsoft, Accenture, and a Fortune 100 company, developers using the tool completed 26.08% more tasks, with higher adoption and gains among less experienced developers<cite id="47"></cite>. Accenture has also launched talent programs to build an AI-ready workforce, including the AI Academy and AI Talent Program, which aim to upskill employees and attract AI specialists to support client engagements<cite id="40"></cite>. The firm’s strategic direction emphasizes agentic architecture and deep integration of AI into core strategy, with guidance for front-runners on combining “table stakes” investments with “strategic bets” to scale AI and win<cite id="58"></cite>.

## MBB firms: strategy, governance, and talent development
MBB firms have positioned AI as a strategic lever for enterprise reinvention, with Deloitte’s AI@Deloitte initiative focused on embedding AI across audit, consulting, and advisory services to enhance client value<cite id="2"></cite>. McKinsey’s research and practice continue to emphasize aligning AI with business strategy, governance, and talent development to drive bottom-line impact<cite id="27"></cite><cite id="30"></cite><cite id="13"></cite>. BCG’s frameworks highlight the importance of complementary assets and organizational design to unlock AI value, providing clients with structured approaches to select high-value use cases and build the necessary capabilities<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="22"></cite><cite id="34"></cite>. Collectively, MBB firms are advancing AI governance and workflow redesign as prerequisites for meaningful value capture<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>.

## IBM: AI-driven products and talent programs
IBM’s AI practice centers on products such as Watson Health, which leverages AI to support clinical decision-making and patient care, and has been adopted by healthcare organizations worldwide<cite id="45"></cite>. IBM also offers AI-driven consulting services through its IBM Consulting division, helping clients design and implement AI solutions tailored to their industry and business needs<cite id="45"></cite>. Talent development is a key pillar, with IBM’s AI Academy and AI Talent Program aimed at upskilling employees and attracting AI experts to drive innovation and client outcomes<cite id="45"></cite>. IBM’s strategic direction emphasizes integrating AI into core operations and fostering a culture of AI fluency across the workforce<cite id="45"></cite>.

## Capgemini: AI-driven services and client case studies
Capgemini’s AI practice delivers services across digital transformation, cloud, and analytics, with a focus on co-creating AI solutions that improve efficiency, reduce costs, and drive revenue growth for clients<cite id="49"></cite>. The firm has reported case studies where AI has been used to streamline operations and enhance decision-making, including examples in finance, manufacturing, and retail<cite id="49"></cite>. Capgemini’s talent programs, such as the Capgemini Academy and AI Talent Program, aim to build an AI-ready workforce by upskilling employees and attracting specialized talent to support client projects<cite id="49"></cite>. Capgemini’s strategic direction emphasizes embedding AI into the core of client operations and fostering a culture of innovation and continuous learning<cite id="49"></cite>.

## Application scenarios and strategic directions
Across firms, common application scenarios include AI-driven analytics and automation in finance, where 32–39% of work has high automation potential and 34–37% holds high augmentation potential, with firms shifting from efficiency to revenue growth<cite id="43"></cite>. In software development, field experiments show measurable productivity gains when developers use AI-based coding assistants, underscoring the value of tooling and training to maximize adoption<cite id="47"></cite>. Strategic directions emphasize agentic architecture, deep integration of AI into core strategy, and strong data foundations, with leaders prioritizing governance, talent readiness, and modern IT systems<cite id="58"></cite><cite id="13"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>. Frameworks from BCG highlight complementary assets and modularization as keys to unlocking corporate value, while McKinsey’s research continues to map use cases and provide evidence-based guidance for transformation<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="22"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>.

## Talent development programs
The Big Four have invested heavily in upskilling large cohorts of professionals to work alongside AI systems, with PwC’s plan to hire about 100,000 AI-capable staff and EY’s and KPMG’s multi-billion-dollar commitments to AI talent and capabilities<cite id="1"></cite>. McKinsey’s practice emphasizes aligning AI talent with business strategy and governance to drive impact<cite id="30"></cite>. Accenture’s AI Academy and AI Talent Program aim to build an AI-ready workforce to support client engagements<cite id="40"></cite>. IBM and Capgemini have launched similar talent programs to upskill employees and attract AI specialists, reinforcing a culture of AI fluency and innovation across their organizations<cite id="45"></cite><cite id="49"></cite>. BCG’s research also underscores the need to hire for new AI roles and retrain employees to participate in AI deployment, as organizations work to mitigate gen AI-related risks and redesign workflows<cite id="13"></cite>.

## Uncertainties and limitations
While the evidence above documents large investments, talent programs, and early client outcomes, detailed case studies with quantified financial returns are often limited to summaries or aggregated findings. As a result, specific client case studies with dollar figures and full implementation details are not always available in the sources cited here<cite id="22"></cite><cite id="23"></cite><cite id="47"></cite>. Readers are encouraged to consult the firms’ official reports and client success stories for more granular case details<cite id="40"></cite><cite id="45"></cite><cite id="49"></cite>.
</answer>

Indeed, many FI leaders say more groundwork is needed to assemble the tools and capabilities that would foster a winning GenAI proposition. Acquiring specialized talent is a key priority. Where FIs are using GenAI in practice, it is most often to serve support functions such as call center services or software development, rather than transform business-critical operations at scale.These are some of the findings of BCG’s inaugural GenAI in Financial Institutions Bench-marking Survey, designed to offer market participants an inside track on how FI leaders view one of the most talked about technologies of the decade.</summary><hostname>Kenta Online News</hostname><publisher>BCG</publisher><author_list><author name="Ella Rabener" /><author name="Stiene Riemer" /><author name="Michael Widowitz" /><author name="Michael Strauss" /><author name="Cindy Tan" /><author name="Benjamin Rehberg" /><author name="Anne Kleppe" /><author name="Jeanne Bickford" /><author name="Pim Hilbers" /><author name="Kentaro Ogata" /><author name="Jon Sugihara" /><author name="Kevin Lucas" /><author name="Marianna Leoni" /><author name="Nina Kataeva" /></author_list><url>https://ai.radensa.ru/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Gen_AI_in_Global_Financial_Institutions_1714984764.pdf</url><publish_time>2024年4月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:23"><title>The Widening AI Value Gap Build for the Future 2025</title><summary>BCG's latest research provides empirical proof that for a small number of companies in the form of AI is delivering significant bottom-line value in the form of revenue and cash flow increases and process and workflow improvements. Another 35% (33 percentage points more than in 2024) are scaling up their efforts and seeing some returns, but many of them admit that they are not moving far enough or fast enough. (See Exhibit 1.) Where's the value in AI? The biggest value comes from client-related functions and IT. All of this is happening much more rapidly than previous digital disruptions did, and it will continue to do so as AI's functionality improves. Agentic AI, which combines predictive and generative capabilities to reason, learn, and act autonomously, promises to be the biggest accelerator of the widening value gap. As the business and economics research arm of McKinsey & Company, MGI aims to provide leaders in the commercial, public, and social sectors with the facts and insights on which to base management and policy decisions.
MGI research combines the disciplines of economics and management, employing the analytical tools of economics with the insights of business leaders. Our "micro-to-macro" methodology examines microeconomic industry trends to better understand the broad macroeconomic forces affecting business strategy and public policy. MGI's in-depth reports have covered more than 20 countries and 30 industries. Current research focuses on six themes: productivity and growth, natural resources, labor markets, the evolution of global financial markets, the economic impact of technology and innovation, and urbanization. Recent reports have assessed the digital economy, the impact of AI and automation on employment, income inequality, the productivity puzzle, the economic benefits of tackling gender inequality, a new era of global competition, Chinese innovation, and digital and financial globalization.
MGI is led by three McKinsey & Company senior partners: Jacques Bughin, Jonathan Woetzel, and James Manyika, who also serves as the chairman of MGI. Michael Chui, Susan Lund, Anu Madgavkar, Jan Mischke, Sree Ramaswamy, and Jaana Remes are MGI partners, and Mekala Krishnan and Jeongmin Seong are MGI senior fellows.
Project teams are led by the MGI partners and a group of senior fellows, and include consultants from McKinsey offices around the world. These teams draw on McKinsey's global network of partners and industry and management experts. Advice and input to MGI research are provided by the MGI Council, members of which are also involved in MGI's research. MGI Council members are drawn from around the world and from various sectors and include Andrés Cadena, Sandrine Devillard, Richard Dobbs, Tarek Elimary, Katy George, Rajat Gupta, Eric Hazan, Eric Labaye, Acha Leke, Scott Nyquist, Gary Pinkus, Sven Smit, Oliver Tonby, and Eckart Windhagen. In addition, leading economists, including Nobel laureates, act as research advisers to MGI research.
The partners of McKinsey fund MGI's research; it is not commissioned by any business, government, or other institution. For further information about MGI and to download reports, please visit www.mckinsey.com/mgi.

Drawing on MGI research and the applied experience with artificial intelligence (AI) of McKinsey Analytics, we assess both the practical applications and the economic potential of advanced AI techniques across industries and business functions. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Bain & Company AI practice Where's the Value in AI 2024 case studies" search_time="2026年5月16日11时54分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:32"><title>Where's the Value in AI?</title><hostname>Hong Kong International Family Office Association</hostname><author_list><author name="Nicolas De Bellefonds" /><author name="Tauseef Charanya" /><author name="Marc Roman Franke" /><author name="Patrick Forth" /><author name="Michael Grebe" /><author name="Romain De Laubier" /><author name="Vlad Lukic" /><author name="Amanda Luther" /><author name="Clemens Nopp" /><author name="Joe Sassine" /></author_list><url>https://hkifoa.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/wheres-the-value-in-ai-bcg.pdf</url><publish_time>2024年10月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:33"><title>The impact of Artificial Intelligence on businesses: The case of Bluewind</title><hostname>威尼斯大学</hostname><publisher>Degree Thesis</publisher><author_list><author name="Alessia Pascon" affiliation="Ca' Foscari University of Venice" /></author_list><url>https://unitesi.unive.it/retrieve/db42eea4-f867-49aa-8a92-c921a695eca8/878475-1290146.pdf</url><publish_time>2023年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:34"><title>A Vehicle Is More Than Its Engine: Why Complements Are the Key to Reaping Value From (Generative) AI</title><summary>Generative AI (GenAI) presents a paradox. While the business world has been enthusiastic and poured funding into the new technology, concrete use cases and measurable benefits are still difficult to find, even though much will change soon. So far, GenAI has primarily helped individuals to work on bounded tasks, but these benefits haven't necessarily translated to firm or organizational level. We surveyed hundreds of senior executives to discover how GenAI combines with other factors to transform certain organizations, sectors, and business models but not others. We discovered four factors that make GenAI disruptive or sustaining: pattern recognition, proprietary data, modularization, and regulation. How firms use AI can be more important than where or how much they use it. Rather than merely using it widely, they need to explore it deeply. We found three pathways to unlocking corporate value with GenAI: cost reduction and productivity improvement; hyper-personalization; and creating new revenue streams or AI-enabled business models. Firms also need to look beyond technology to focus on their ability to engineer and manage data (upstream of AI) and integrate AI-driven decisions at scale into decision-making (downstream). We also find that firms need to work on the moats that will protect them from competition, in particular proprietary data (upstream) and building a unique knowledge base (downstream). What works alongside AI can be just as important as the technology itself. Rather than asking simply "What can we do with AI?" firms should look at their existing assets and capabilities and consider how they can combine with AI to unlock new possibilities. While digital native firms come with flexibility and the DNA to leverage AI, existing firms have other valuable complementary assets and challengers can engage with them to change the playing field. More broadly, firms should use AI as an opportunity to rethink competitive advantage, structure, processes culture, and incentives in order to develop a realistic strategy for an AI world.</summary><hostname>6e1b275e-fbcb-48eb-87a0-6ae7b12c556a.usrfiles.com</hostname><publisher>White Paper</publisher><author_list><author name="Prof Michael G Jacobides" affiliation="London Business School and Evolution Ltd" /><author name="Yuri Romanenkov" affiliation="Evolution Ltd and London Business School" /><author name="Justinas Sukys" affiliation="Evolution Ltd and Claria Strategy" /></author_list><url>https://6e1b275e-fbcb-48eb-87a0-6ae7b12c556a.usrfiles.com/ugd/6e1b27_80500102c3eb4432af572594dfb5fbbf.pdf</url><publish_time>2024年11月27日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:35"><title>The Widening AI

That’s why the world’s largest companies are investing heavily in data and AI. But reinventing the enterprise with generative AI (gen AI) isn’t simply a matter of deploying a few chatbots. Reinvention is about building advanced AI capabilities like “agentic architecture,” networks of AI agents that go beyond automating routine tasks to orchestrating entire business workflows. Endowed with sophisticated reasoning, AI agents collaborate autonomously to improve quality, productivity and cost-efficiency at scale. Agentic architecture is spreading fast: one-third of the companies we surveyed for this report (See “About the research” on page 38) are already using AI agents to strengthen their innovation capabilities. Reinvention thus requires integrating AI deeply into the core of a company’s strategy. To do this, businesses, under the proactive leadership of their CEO and board, must go beyond surface-level applications of AI and prioritize structural and strategic changes that unlock AI’s full potential. Though every business may want an AI-powered edge, many companies are still struggling to advance beyond their initial AI experiments. A big reason for this, our research also shows, is low data “readiness”—which arises when all types of data, especially unstructured data, are not used to the max. Encouragingly, most business leaders recognize this challenge. For example, 70% of the companies we surveyed acknowledged the need for a strong data foundation when trying to scale AI. Data, of course, isn’t the only obstacle to enterprise reinvention with generative AI. Outdated IT systems and workers who are ill-prepared to use AI are significant barriers, too. Today, however, generative artificial intelligence and other forms of AI have flipped the script, bringing the previously unattainable within reach. That’s why the world’s largest companies are investing heavily in data and AI. But reinventing the enterprise with generative AI (gen AI) isn’t simply a matter of deploying a few chatbots. Reinvention is about building advanced AI capabilities like “agentic architecture,” networks of AI agents that go beyond automating routine tasks to orchestrating entire business workflows. Endowed with sophisticated reasoning, AI agents collaborate autonomously to improve quality, productivity and cost-efficiency at scale. Agentic architecture is spreading fast: one-third of the companies we surveyed for this report (See “About the research” on page 38) are already using AI agents to strengthen their innovation capabilities. Reinvention thus requires integrating AI deeply into the core of a company’s strategy. To do this, businesses, under the proactive leadership of their CEO and board, must go beyond surface-level applications of AI and prioritize structural and strategic changes that unlock AI’s full potential. Though every business may want an AI-powered edge, many companies are still struggling to advance beyond their initial AI experiments. A big reason for this, our research also shows, is low data “readiness”—which arises when all types of data, especially unstructured data, are not used to the max. Data, of course, isn’t the only obstacle to enterprise reinvention with generative AI. Outdated IT systems and workers who are ill-prepared to use AI are significant barriers, too. At the same time, our research revealed that a small minority of companies (“front-runners”) are already achieving considerable success at reinventing their enterprises with generative AI. problem: How to conduct comprehensive and accurate situational awareness of space targets in the cislunar space, and support the effectiveness of short-term cislunar space tracking and monitoring tasks?

<answer>
# Executive Summary

Comprehensive and accurate situational awareness of cislunar space requires a multi-sensor architecture that integrates space-based and ground-based assets, visibility-informed scheduling, multi-modal data fusion, and rigorous uncertainty management. Short-term tracking and monitoring effectiveness can be supported by optimizing sensor constellation design, selecting favorable observation windows, and using adaptive filters that improve uncertainty realism and fuse electro-optical (EO) with passive radio frequency (PRF) measurements. The following report synthesizes data-driven recommendations and supporting evidence for achieving robust cislunar domain awareness and validating short-term tracking performance<cite id="32"></cite><cite id="37"></cite><cite id="52"></cite><cite id="63"></cite><cite id="78"></cite>.

# 1. Sensor Architecture and Constellation Design

A robust cislunar situational awareness (CSSA) architecture should leverage mixed space- and ground-based sensors, including wide-field lunar surface observatories and space-based assets placed in libration-point orbits (LPOs) or cislunar Lissajous orbits. Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulations and time-expanded facility location models can optimize the placement of p space-based observers and sensor-tasking to maximize coverage while accounting for field-of-view constraints and pointing directions across time<cite id="32"></cite><cite id="37"></cite>. A proposed lunar surface SDA station with two solar-powered observatories demonstrates complementary polar field-of-regard and night survival strategies, with topographic and illumination-driven site selection and communication timelines<cite id="42"></cite>. Space-based “Spooky Radar” in L1/L4/L5 cislunar Lagrange-point Lissajous orbits can provide order-of-magnitude tracking performance improvements when combined with ground EO and radar, as shown by Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) state estimation comparisons<cite id="47"></cite>. Complementary analyses of large-volume cislunar surveillance suggest combining smaller EO sensors with large passive RF sensors in geocycler orbits to extend detection coverage and revisit rates<cite id="105"></cite>. Finally, capacity- and observability-aware optimization should include sensor agility (field-of-view and sweep rate) to avoid stopping at observation analysis<cite id="106"></cite>.

# 2. Visibility-Informed Observation Scheduling

Maintaining custody in cislunar space depends on both visibility and observability, which are strongly influenced by lunar phase and Earth’s rotation. A visibility-informed covariance analysis framework simulates angle-only optical observations from an equatorial ground station across grids of initial epochs defined by lunar phase and time-of-day, computing heuristic, covariance-based metrics to quantify state uncertainty and identify favorable observation windows<cite id="52"></cite>. These results show optimal tracking epochs align with specific lunar phases and local times, offering actionable guidance for scheduling and orbit selection to improve short-term state estimation accuracy<cite id="52"></cite>. For space-based constellations, visibility constraints and sensor agility must be integrated into architecture assessments to ensure continuous or near-continuous coverage<cite id="106"></cite>.

# 3. Multi-Modal Data Fusion and Orbit Determination

Cislunar orbit determination benefits from fusing EO and PRF measurements to reduce large data gaps and improve uncertainty realism. UKF and Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) have been shown to track non-Keplerian periodic orbits in the Earth–Moon system using astrometric/photometric EO and PRF TDOA/FDOA measurements; AEGIS-based information synthesis further improves uncertainty realism in nonlinear regimes<cite id="78"></cite>. High-fidelity circular restricted three-body dynamics are essential for capturing accurate motion representations, and PRF observations can fill EO gaps while maintaining convergence and tighter uncertainty bounds<cite id="78"></cite>. These results support the integration of EO and PRF into a unified data assimilation framework to enhance short-term tracking fidelity<cite id="78"></cite>.

# 4. High-Fidelity Dynamics and Force Models

Accurate orbit determination in cislunar space requires high-fidelity force models that capture the dominant perturbations. Studies show that using the circular restricted three-body problem with lunar gravity and solar radiation pressure, along with gravity gradient effects, is essential for realistic state estimation and covariance evolution<cite id="63"></cite><cite id="78"></cite>. These models underpin the observed improvements in filter performance and uncertainty realism when fusing multi-modal data<cite id="63"></cite><cite id="78"></cite>.

# 5. Short-Term Tracking and Monitoring Effectiveness

Short-term tracking effectiveness can be validated using visibility-informed metrics and orbit-determination convergence/uncertainty indicators. Visibility-informed covariance analysis provides favorable observation windows and state-uncertainty benchmarks that guide scheduling to minimize short-term uncertainty growth<cite id="52"></cite>. Multi-modal fusion and adaptive uncertainty management (e.g., AEGIS) reduce position–velocity errors and tighten bounds during data gaps, directly supporting robust short-term monitoring<cite id="78"></cite>. Prototype uncertainty management systems for cislunar and xGEO custody further outline tools for tracking, uncertainty propagation, and data assimilation to quantify and improve short-term performance<cite id="83"></cite>.

# 6. Practical Implementation Roadmap

- Design and optimize a mixed space–ground CSSA architecture using MILP/time-expanded facility location models and p-Median formulations, with observers placed in LPOs/Lissajous orbits and tasking aligned to visibility and pointing constraints<cite id="32"></cite><cite id="37"></cite><cite id="47"></cite>.
- Integrate lunar surface observatories with complementary polar fields of regard and night survival strategies, leveraging DEMs and illumination/communication timelines for site selection<cite id="42"></cite>.
- Schedule EO observations around visibility-informed windows tied to lunar phase and local time to minimize short-term uncertainty and maximize observability<cite id="52"></cite>.
- Deploy PRF sensors to fill EO gaps and fuse TDOA/FDOA with EO measurements, using UKF/GMM and AEGIS to improve uncertainty realism and convergence<cite id="78"></cite>.
- Use high-fidelity 3-body dynamics and include solar radiation pressure and gravity gradient effects in orbit propagators and estimators<cite id="63"></cite><cite id="78"></cite>.
- Continuously assess sensor agility and capacity in architecture design to avoid stopping at observation-only analyses<cite id="106"></cite>.

# 7. Uncertainties and Limitations

This report synthesizes recent research on CSSA architectures, visibility-informed scheduling, and multi-modal orbit determination, but operational performance will depend on sensor characteristics, constellation trade-offs, and real-time dynamics. Additional validation with end-to-end simulations and fielded data is recommended to quantify effectiveness under nominal and degraded conditions<cite id="32"></cite><cite id="37"></cite><cite id="47"></cite><cite id="52"></cite><cite id="78"></cite>.

# Conclusion

A comprehensive and accurate cislunar situational awareness system combines optimized space–ground sensor architectures, visibility-informed scheduling, multi-modal data fusion, and adaptive uncertainty management. These elements, supported by recent modeling and case studies, provide a data-driven foundation for improving short-term tracking and monitoring effectiveness in cislunar space<cite id="32"></cite><cite id="37"></cite><cite id="42"></cite><cite id="47"></cite><cite id="52"></cite><cite id="78"></cite>.
</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="cislunar space domain awareness architecture ground-based sensors tracking monitoring lunar orbiters Earth-Moon Lagrange points" search_time="2026年5月16日11时54分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:42"><title>A year in the life of the Shackleton space domain awareness station</title><summary>A proposed Shackleton Space Domain Awareness (SDA) Station is composed of two solar-powered lunar surface observatories for SDA [1, 2]. At a minimum, each observatory has a wide field-of-view (WFOV) camera for finding objects within 6000 km of the lunar surface and a fisheye camera for finding brighter objects within 200 km of the surface, which are moving too rapidly to be reliably captured by the more sensitive WFOV camera. An enhanced sensor suite might also include thermal, dust, and gas sensors to monitor surfaces in permanently shadowed regions and detect rocket plume and excavation activity. The two sites have complementary solar illumination on their 2.0 m solar power masts, so that at least one of them is operating 95% of the time. The first site, on the Shackleton-de Gerlache Connecting Ridge, has been identified as an attractive base location for South Pole resource exploration and extraction [10]. The complementary site is on the rim of Shackleton Crater [9] and will be able to see what is going on inside the crater as well as in the skies above it. Our method is to identify promising areas from the literature, then do an initial site assessment with using Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) digital elevation maps (DEMs) and the horizon elevation method [3]. We then calculate solar illumination and communication timelines and outage duration histograms using DEMs imported into STK. The illumination model then sets the requirements on power storage and thermal control for night survival. This story plays out over a year, with topographic rising and setting of the Earth, Sun, the Lunar Gateway, and LunaNet comm relays. We discuss the tradeoff between polar field of regard (FOR) and direct LOS communication to Earth, if such a capability is desired before high-bandwidth lunar comm relays are available. As a built flight hardware example, we discuss operations planning for the Ball-built L-CIRiS camera hosted on NASA’s Haworth Crater science mission as a lunar polar surface operations planning example.</summary><hostname>AMOS Conference</hostname><publisher>Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance Technologies Conference (AMOS)</publisher><author_list><author name="Jeffrey E Van Cleve" affiliation="Ball Aerospace, Colorado" /><author name="David P Osterman" affiliation="Ball Aerospace, Colorado" /><author name="Anna Lawitzke" affiliation="Ball Aerospace, Colorado" /><author name="Jacob D Griesbach" affiliation="Ball Aerospace, Colorado" /><author name="Christopher J Grant" affiliation="Ball Aerospace, Colorado" /><author name="Colleen Olson" affiliation="Ball Aerospace, Colorado" /><author name="James Contreras" affiliation="Ball Aerospace, Colorado" /></author_list><url>https://amostech.com/TechnicalPapers/2022/Poster/Van-Cleve.pdf</url><publish_time>2022年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:43"><title>Supporting Crewed Missions using LiAISON Navigation in the Earth-Moon System</title><summary>This thesis then examines several different LiAISON mission configurations to determine the benefits and disadvantages for future crewed missions in the Earth-Moon system. The following LiAISON supplemented configurations are analyzed over a wide trade space to determine their feasibility: 1) Geosynchronous and Earth-Moon halo orbiters; 2) A crewed vehicle in an Earth-Moon L2 halo orbit with a navigation satellite orbiting another Earth-Moon Lagrange point; 3) A navigation satellite in an Earth-Moon halo orbit tracking a crewed vehicle in low lunar orbit; 4) A crewed vehicle on a trans-lunar cruise being tracked by a navigation satellite in an Earth-Moon halo orbit.</summary><hostname>lib.manaraa.com</hostname><publisher>Aerospace Engineering Sciences Graduate Theses & Dissert

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="cislunar space situational awareness data fusion optical radar radar tracking lunar orbiters TDRS LRO SSO" search_time="2026年5月16日11时54分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:47"><title>Space-Based Spooky Radar Orbit Determination Benefits at Earth-Moon Lagrange Points</title><summary>We present a cislunar metric tracking performance analysis using the range and angle measurements offered by a quantum entangled-photon radar, otherwise known as a “Spooky Radar”, from Lissajous orbits around L1, L4 and L5 Earth-Moon Lagrange points. There are five known Earth-Moon Lagrange points where a satellite/observer can maintain a relative periodic trajectory - often described as a Lissajous orbit. A Space Based Spooky Radar located at one of these orbital positions would be particularly effective since they are stable and have a combined field of regard which is never simultaneously eclipsed by either Earth-Moon body, and maintain an unobstructed line-of-site with the other Lagrange points. Space Based Spooky Radars, coupled with traditional ground based optical and Radar measurements, are simulated in tandem to estimate the orbit of a representative satellite in Geosynchronous Earth Orbit. A tracking scenario was developed to quantify the relative performance improvement of state estimates over a traditional ground-based sensor architecture mix. Results were computed using an Unscented Kalman Filter and underlying high-fidelity force models. An introduction of slight solar radiation pressure drag and gravity gradient mismatching between the internal filter state dynamics and the orbital propagator for a more accurate solution. Our analysis shows an order of magnitude improvement in both position and velocity state estimates over conventional optical and radar systems.</summary><hostname>AMOS Conference</hostname><publisher>Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance Technologies Conference (AMOS)</publisher><author_list><author name="Darin C Koblick" affiliation="Raytheon Intelligence and Space, El Segundo, 90245, USA" /><author name="Steven Wilkinson" affiliation="Raytheon Intelligence and Space, El Segundo, 90245, USA" /></author_list><url>https://amostech.com/TechnicalPapers/2020/Poster/Koblick.pdf</url><publish_time>2020年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:48"><title>Automated Spacecraft Conjunction Assessment at Mars and the Moon - A Five Year Update</title><summary>It is well known that the Earth has an ongoing problem with orbiting space debris. Some Earth orbiting missions have regular warnings of close approaches with debris or other satellites. At Mars and the Moon, due to the growing number of orbiter missions and the current inability to track orbital debris in these environments, the creation of a hazardous debris field must be avoided because a debris field would greatly complicate both existing and future operations. Work at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in the area of automated spacecraft conjunction assessment at Mars and the Moon has been conducted over the past six years using a process called "MADCAP" ("Multimission Automated Deepspace Conjunction Assessment Process"). A paper introducing this work was presented at Space Ops in Stockholm, Sweden in 2012. In that inaugural paper, the then current state of operations was presented along with a number of items that were identified for potential future work. The fundamental design concepts of MADCAP have not materially changed in the last five years, however, since 2012 a number of the changes to MADCAP identified in the previous paper have been implemented. Some other previously planned work has not progressed appreciably; several of these items remain on a "parking lot" list. In addition to the items that were listed as prospective future work, JPL's Mars/Moon conjunction assessment efforts have also been extended in a few unplanned but important areas. This follow-up paper will provide a five year update on MADCAP operations at Mars and the Moon.</summary><hostname>NASA</hostname><publisher>2018 SpaceOp

Scheeres" affiliation="University of Colorado, Boulder" /></author_list><url>https://amostech.com/TechnicalPapers/2025/Cislunar_SDA/Evans.pdf</url><publish_time>2025年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:53"><title>Cislunar Orbit Determination Behavior: Processing Observations of Periodic Orbits with Gaussian Mixture Model Estimation Filters</title><summary>Orbits of objects in cislunar space are, in general, non-Keplerian due to the influence of the Moon’s gravity and cannot be generically parameterized by a simple set of characteristics. Objects are also fainter and move relatively more slowly when viewed from Earth. Detection and tracking are expected to be significantly more difficult and, as a consequence, orbit determination becomes more challenging. In this paper we review a subset of possible orbits and their expected astrometric and photometric signatures from the perspective of hypothetical ground-based electro-optical sensors on Earth. Although a multitude of orbits are possible, we focus on special types of orbits that are closed in the synodic frame (i.e., periodic) and emanate from the libration points of the Earth-Moon system. We investigate three separate elemental periodic orbit families that have been differentially corrected in a high-fidelity dynamical system: H1, L1, and W4W5. For each family, we set objects at different locations at different epochs and simulate the expected observational features (e.g., right ascension, declination, visual magnitude) based on faceted satellite models. Introduction and scope

Chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus), a small pelagic species, is widely distributed across the North Pacific and is a key component of fisheries and aquatic markets in Japan, China, South Korea, the Philippines, Vietnam, and other Pacific Rim countries. Its abundance and market value are tightly coupled to oceanographic conditions, fisheries management, and economic demand, making it an ideal case to examine linkages between marine biological resources, markets, and the environment<cite id="26"></cite>. This report synthesizes available data on interannual price dynamics in major markets, size and weight variability across regions, and oceanographic drivers of recruitment and growth, to demonstrate how biological quality and environmental regimes translate into market outcomes and fishery economics<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="52"></cite>.

Price dynamics in major Pacific Rim markets

In Japan, chub mackerel prices have risen sharply in recent years due to declining stocks and reduced domestic supply. In 2025, retail prices surged to around 732 yen per piece, a more than threefold increase compared to five to six years earlier, with projections of further rises to approximately 900 yen per piece<cite id="13"></cite>. Wholesale prices also climbed sharply in September 2025, with some bulk prices surpassing 800 yen per kilogram, reflecting supply constraints and market tightness<cite id="11"></cite>. In South Korea, frozen Norwegian chub mackerel prices increased by about 20% in week 34 of 2025 amid limited inventory, despite a rise in imports<cite id="32"></cite>. On the importer side, China’s domestic prices for chub mackerel have fluctuated widely in international trade, with reported export quotations ranging from US$0.75–1.00 per kilogram to as high as US$800 per ton, depending on product form, specifications, and market conditions<cite id="18"></cite><cite id="24"></cite>. These divergent price trends across markets underscore the role of supply-side constraints, regional stock status, and international trade dynamics in shaping local prices<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="32"></cite><cite id="18"></cite>.

Interannual variations in size, weight, and condition

Across the North Pacific, chub mackerel exhibit pronounced interannual variability in growth and body condition, closely tied to climate regimes and interspecific interactions. A comprehensive review documents decadal-scale fluctuations in small pelagic fisheries, including chub mackerel, with prominent species replacements linked to “regime shifts,” most notably the 1988/89 shift, and highlights that early survival variability is a central driver of population dynamics<cite id="26"></cite>. More recently, analyses of Japanese coastal fisheries show that mean annual growth rates and body condition in chub mackerel decrease with increasing conspecific and heterospecific abundance, and that habitat temperature is indirectly influenced by population density<cite id="16"></cite>. Seasonal and interannual studies in northeastern Japan further report statistically significant effects of year on crude fat content and condition factor, with strong positive influences observed in 2016 and 2017, indicating improved biological condition during those years<cite id="17"></cite>.

Length–weight relationships and growth parameters

Empirical length–weight data from Chinese fisheries (2016–2020) in the northwest Pacific yielded a species-specific length–weight relationship of W = (1.41 × 10⁻⁶) × FL³·³⁷, with random effects models showing heterogeneity by year and season<cite id="11"></cite>. Growth parameters estimated from the same dataset support a slower growth rate compared to prior studies, reinforcing the importance of region- and year-specific growth models for stock assessment and management<cite id="11"></cite>. Historical assessments in the East China Sea and the Japan/East Sea similarly documented stock size fluctuations and inverse correlations between spawning success and sea surface temperature, underscoring the role of climate variability in recruitment and population trajectories<cite id="52"></cite>.

Linking biological quality, markets, and oceanography

Fishery economics and market prices respond directly to changes in biological quality—condition, growth, and recruitment—which are themselves shaped by oceanographic regimes. In Japan, the combination of declining stocks, reduced spawning success linked to SST, and strong year-class effects has driven both retail and wholesale price increases<cite id="52"></cite><cite id="13"></cite><cite id="11"></cite>. In South Korea, limited inventory and a complex distribution system have amplified price spikes despite higher import volumes, illustrating how supply chain constraints can magnify environmental and stock-driven shocks<cite id="32"></cite>. Market price data have also been explored as potential indicators of population size in Korean chub mackerel fisheries; however, studies suggest that price information does not add value to stock assessment when catch and CPUE data are already available<cite id="3"></cite>. This highlights the need for caution in using prices alone to infer biological status and the importance of integrating market data with traditional fisheries indices<cite id="3"></cite>.

Regional market context and trade patterns

In the Philippines, mackerel species (including chub mackerel) are subject to periodic price volatility driven by supply shocks and weather events. For example, prices for galunggong (a closely related mackerel scad) rose to between ₱280 and ₱350 per kilogram in Metro Manila during a supply shortage, and the Department of Agriculture cautioned consumers about higher mackerel prices (₱300–450 per kilogram) as an alternative protein source<cite id="22"></cite>. In Vietnam, wholesale prices for fresh and dried mackerel species typically range from 140,000 to 400,000 VND per kilogram, with dried mackerel reaching up to 700,000–800,000 VND per kilogram during peak seasons<cite id="25"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>. These regional price ranges reflect local demand, supply chain efficiency, and the mix of domestic and imported stocks, which can vary by season and event<cite id="25"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>.

Implications for fishery economics and management

The observed interannual price dynamics and biological variability indicate that chub mackerel fisheries are highly sensitive to both environmental regimes and management actions. Historical evidence shows that overcapacity and poor productivity after a regime shift constrained recovery, but reduced exploitation and strong year classes since the mid-2000s have allowed partial recovery<cite id="26"></cite>. Contemporary price spikes in Japan and South Korea suggest that even with increased imports, supply constraints and rigid demand can sustain upward pressure on prices<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="32"></cite>. Integrating market price data into stock assessment can provide additional insights in data-limited settings, but should be done cautiously and only when complementary indices such as catch and CPUE are available<cite id="3"></cite>. Broader ecosystem monitoring and climate-informed fisheries management are therefore essential to anticipate regime shifts, maintain recruitment and growth, and stabilize market outcomes across the Pacific Rim<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="52"></cite><cite id="26"></cite>.

Uncertainties and data gaps

Despite growing evidence linking oceanographic variability to biological condition and market prices, comprehensive, time-series price data at the retail and wholesale levels across multiple Pacific Rim countries remain fragmented. While some reports provide snapshots of price spikes and seasonal trends, continuous, standardized market monitoring would strengthen the ability to quantify direct correlations between biological quality and economic outcomes<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="13"></cite><cite id="22"></cite><cite id="25"></cite>. Similarly, more region-specific length–weight and growth studies, coupled with CPUE and catch data, would improve the reliability of stock assessments and the integration of market signals into fisheries economics<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="3"></cite>.

Conclusion

Across Japan, South Korea, China, the Philippines, and Vietnam, chub mackerel prices display interannual variability consistent with declining stocks, supply constraints, and regional trade dynamics. Biological data show that growth, condition, and recruitment fluctuate with climate regimes and interspecific competition, directly influencing market outcomes and fishery economics<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="32"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="17"></cite><cite id="52"></cite>. Length–weight relationships and slower growth estimates from recent studies further emphasize the need for region- and year-specific biological parameters in management<cite id="11"></cite>. Integrating market price data into fisheries analysis can offer economic insights, but should complement—not substitute—traditional indices such as catch and CPUE<cite id="3"></cite>. Continued oceanographic monitoring, climate-informed management, and standardized market data collection are critical to sustain high-quality marine biological resources and stabilize aquatic markets across the Pacific Rim<cite id="26"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="52"></cite>.
