Although highly targeted in this region, little is known about their life history aspects. The objectives of this study are to evaluate the growth heterogeneities and ageing analysis of this species. We describe the length-at-age, weight-at-length, relative condition factor relationships, spatiotemporal heterogeneity and compare estimated growth parameter values to those reported from other regions. This study used data obtained from Chinese fishing vessels collected from 2016–2020 in the northwest Pacific Ocean. Length-weight data from 2686 specimens (40–294 mm, fork length; 0.8–311.8 g body weight) were analyzed, and the Length-weight relationship was W = (1.41 × 10⁻⁶) × FL³.³⁷. Seven linear mixed-effects models (LMEM) were used to analyze the heterogeneity of length-weight relationships of Chub mackerel. The Length-weight relationships for Chub mackerel were best described by a model with random effects with both year and season (spring, summer, autumn) with the scalar parameter a. Age estimates were obtained from 175 specimens, and the length-at-estimated ages relationship was described using three non-linear candidate growth models. The von Bertalanffy growth model fit the data best for Chub mackerel in the northwest Pacific Ocean. Comparing the results to that of previous studies, we observed that individual Chub mackerel exhibited a slower growth rate than that observed in previous studies. In addition, relative condition factors varied among years, seasons, and regions. Information presented in this study provides an effective scientific basis for stock assessment and fishery management of Chub mackerel in the northwest Pacific Ocean.</summary><hostname>MDPI</hostname><publisher>Journal of Marine Science and Engineering</publisher><author_list><author name="Kai Cai" affiliation="1 College of Marine Sciences, Shanghai Ocean University, Shanghai 201306, China; Although population density is known to affect the temperature of the habitat selected, how this affects the density dependence of growth and body condition remains unclear. Here, we investigated annual changes in body condition, habitat temperature, and cohort-specific growth of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the western North Pacific and examined quarterly changes in the density dependence of body condition. The catch and biomass of SPF generally showed decadal-scale variability with prominent species replacements since the 1900s. The causes of species replacements were generally associated with climatic/oceanic variability, particularly "regime shifts," of which the 1988/89 regime shift was the most influential since the 1970s. Variability in the early survival rate is a key factor for population fluctuations, and the proposed hypothetical mechanisms of recruitment variability are summarized herein. Although overfishing during the 1990s and early 2000s prevented the recovery of Pacific stocks of sardine and chub mackerel, they have been recovering since the mid-2000s owing to strong year classes and reduced exploitation rates. The fundamental cause of overfishing was derived from a mismash between investments in larger purse seine fleets during the 1980s and poor ocean productivity since the 1988/89 regime shift, when dominant SPF began to shift from sardine to anchovy. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="chub mackerel Scomber japonicus interannual variations weight length Philippines fisheries" search_time="2026年5月16日11时55分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:61"><title>Review of population dynamics and management of small pelagic fishes around the Japanese Archipelago</title><summary>Population dynamics of small pelagic fishes (SPF) and their management in Japan were reviewed for Japanese sardine Sardi-nops melanostictus, Japanese anchovy Engraulis japonicus, chub mackerel Scomber japonicus, and Pacific saury Cololabis saira. The catch and biomass of SPF generally showed decadal-scale variability with prominent species replacements since the 1900s. The causes of species replacements were generally associated with climatic/oceanic variability, particularly "regime shifts," of which the 1988/89 regime shift was the most influential since the 1970s. Variability in the early survival rate is a key factor for population fluctuations, and the proposed hypothetical mechanisms of recruitment variability are summarized herein. Although overfishing during the 1990s and early 2000s prevented the recovery of Pacific stocks of sardine and chub mackerel, they have been recovering since the mid-2000s owing to strong year classes and reduced exploitation rates. The fundamental cause of overfishing was derived from a mismash between investments in larger purse seine fleets during the 1980s and poor ocean productivity since the 1988/89 regime shift, when dominant SPF began to shift from sardine to anchovy. Recommendations for fisheries management of SPF around the Japanese Archipelago are proposed, considering climate change and naturally and drastically changing SPF populations.</summary><hostname>SpringerLink</hostname><publisher>Fisheries Science</publisher><author_list><author name="Akihiko Yatsu" affiliation="Japan Fisheries Information Service Center, 4-5, Toyomi-cho, Chuo-ku, Tokyo 104-0055, Japan" /></author_list><url>https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3.pdf?pdf=button</url><publish_time>2019年4月3日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:62"><title>Impacts of Climate and Climate Change on the Key Species in the Fisheries in the North Pacific</title><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>PICES Scientific Report No. 35</publisher><url>https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Rj-Beamish/publication/265618628_Impacts_of_Climate_and_Climate_Change_on_the_Key_Species_in_the_Fisheries_in_the_North_Pacific_Edited_by/links/5751ee8608ae02ac1277b424/Impacts-of-Climate-and-Climate-Change-on-the-Key-Species-in-the-Fisheries-in-the-North-Pacific-Edited-by.pdf</url><publish_time>2008年12月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:63"><title>Intra- and inter-specific density dependence of body condition, growth, and habitat temperature in chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus)</title><summary>The density dependence of growth and body condition have important impacts on fish population dynamics and fisheries management. problem: What are the most effective approaches to scaling ion trap quantum computing from small-scale demonstration projects to large-scale systems capable of solving real-world problems? This research should investigate the various proposed scaling strategies, assess their feasibility, and evaluate which approaches are most likely to succeed based on current technological advancements and practical implementation challenges.

<answer>
Introduction and scope

Ion trap quantum computing has progressed rapidly, with recent demonstrations achieving high-fidelity operations on tens of qubits and establishing architectures with promising scaling properties. These advances have shifted the focus from small-scale demonstrations to strategies for scaling to large systems capable of solving real-world problems, including fault-tolerant designs and hybrid networked configurations<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="7"></cite>. This report synthesizes the most promising scaling approaches—QCCD modular processors, photonic interconnect networks, microfabricated traps and integrated photonics, two-dimensional ion crystals, and dilution-trap arrays—and evaluates their feasibility and likelihood of success based on current capabilities and known bottlenecks<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="12"></cite><cite id="47"></cite><cite id="21"></cite><cite id="51"></cite>.

Overview of scaling bottlenecks

A central challenge for scaling trapped-ion systems is the limited rate of cross-trap optical coupling, which imposes severe constraints on operations that span multiple modules or logical qubits. Recent resource analyses for fault-tolerant lattice surgery between spatially separated surface code segments show that hundreds to nearly a hundred thousand resource ions may be required, depending on the cycle time; the main bottleneck is the coupling rate across traps<cite id="2"></cite>. This finding underscores the need for dramatic improvements in inter-qubit and inter-module connectivity, as well as careful co-design of application workflows with modular architectures<cite id="27"></cite><cite id="26"></cite>.

Main scaling strategies and their feasibility

Quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) modular processors. QCCD architectures shuttle ions between microfabricated traps to build reconfigurable modules with all-to-all connectivity, and they are co-designable with target applications. Architectural studies indicate that choices in trap sizing, communication topology, and gate implementations can affect application reliability by up to three orders of magnitude, making co-design and optimization essential for scaling<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="26"></cite>. IonQ’s 30-qubit trapped-ion processor demonstrates a single-chain, all-to-all configuration and comprehensive benchmarking, indicating that shuttle-based architectures can scale to dozens of algorithmic qubits with high fidelity<cite id="72"></cite>. However, lattice surgery and cross-module operations remain limited by slow optical coupling, which could require hundreds to hundreds of thousands of resource ions depending on cycle time<cite id="2"></cite>.

Photonic interconnect networks. Networking trapped-ion modules via photons enables deterministic teleportation of non-local two-qubit gates and the execution of distributed algorithms, as demonstrated by a two-meter photonic link between modules performing Grover’s search with 71% success rate and teleporting a controlled-Z gate<cite id="41"></cite>. Colloquium work on quantum networks with trapped ions outlines protocols for entanglement distribution and links computation and communication, providing a blueprint for large-scale photonic interconnects<cite id="11"></cite>. While promising, integrating robust, deterministic photonic interfaces and minimizing latency and overheads are key challenges for practical, large-scale systems<cite id="41"></cite><cite id="11"></cite>.

Microfabricated traps and integrated photonics. Microfabrication of ion trap arrays and the integration of photonics are seen as viable paths to denser, reconfigurable ion arrays and improved control. Reviews emphasize the need for materials and integration strategies that combine ion traps with optics and electronics while mitigating electric-field noise from trap electrodes<cite id="46"></cite>. Integrated quantum photonics roadmaps highlight that advances in chip-based components and packaging will be critical as systems scale from few-qubit prototypes to thousands of qubits<cite id="47"></cite>. These directions are complementary to QCCD and photonic networks, offering denser arrays and compact optical interconnects for intra-module operations<cite id="46"></cite><cite id="47"></cite>.

Two-dimensional ion crystals and planar trap arrays. Two-dimensional ion geometries expand the range of quantum simulations and provide configurable connectivity, as demonstrated by experiments with up to 29 ions and transport of small 2×2 lattices<cite id="22"></cite><cite id="76"></cite>. Planar trap arrays with tunable inter-site coupling and configurable connectivity (e.g., rectangular and triangular lattices) illustrate scalable chip designs that can be adapted to different applications<cite id="76"></cite>. While 2D crystals can improve connectivity and simulation reach, scaling to hundreds or thousands of ions while maintaining high fidelity will require advances in heating management and motional-mode engineering<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>.

Dilution traps and hybrid cold-atom arrays. Dilution-trap architectures that confine large numbers of ions in a single trap can reduce motional-mode decoherence and improve fidelity at scale, and they can be combined with atom-light interfaces for hybrid quantum systems<cite id="51"></cite>. Cold-atom platforms on atom chips have enabled rapid BEC production and matter-wave interferometry, and they offer alternative trapping and transport techniques that could inform scalable ion-array designs<cite="52"></cite>. These approaches are still in early stages and face challenges in ion loading, trapping stability, and interface efficiency, but they represent a complementary path to large arrays<cite="51"></cite><cite="52"></cite>.

Fault-tolerant perspectives and co-design

Fault-tolerant operation is likely to be achieved through coupled logical qubits and surface-code modules, with transversal or lattice-surgery strategies tailored to trapped-ion capabilities. Comparative studies show that transversal and lattice-surgery approaches have different regimes of experimental feasibility, and optimizing gate implementations and noise profiles is crucial for reliability<cite id="32"></cite>. Recent progress demonstrates a fault-tolerant universal gate set in a trapped-ion processor, with analyses identifying design criteria to reach logical advantage over physical operations and optimizing state-preparation and magic-state distillation for current error regimes<cite id="61"></cite>. Co-design of applications with modular architectures can reduce overheads and improve reliability by orders of magnitude, making it a central principle for scaling<cite id="26"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>.

Which approaches are most likely to succeed?

QCCD modular processors with photonic interconnects and microfabricated traps appear most likely to succeed in the near to midterm, given their demonstrated feasibility at dozens of qubits, modular reconfigurability, and the clear path to integrated photonics<cite id="72"></cite><cite id="6"></cite><cite id="46"></cite><cite id="47"></cite>. Photonic interconnects have already enabled deterministic teleportation of non-local gates and distributed algorithms, addressing a key bottleneck for cross-module operations<cite id="41"></cite>. However, success will depend on improving optical coupling rates and co-designing application workflows to minimize latency and overheads<cite id="2"></cite><cite id="26"></cite>. Two-dimensional ion crystals and planar trap arrays are strong candidates for expanding simulation reach and application-specific connectivity, but scaling to hundreds or thousands of ions will require advances in heating management and motional-mode engineering<cite id="22"></cite><cite id="76"></cite><cite id="23"></cite>. Dilution-trap arrays and hybrid cold-atom approaches offer complementary paths to large arrays and atom-light interfaces, but they are still in early stages and face integration and interface challenges<cite id="51"></cite><cite id="52"></cite>.

Implementation challenges and near-term milestones

Key challenges include improving cross-trap optical coupling rates, integrating microfabricated traps with photonics, and managing heating and motional-mode decoherence in larger arrays<cite id="2"></cite><cite id="46"></cite><cite id="23"></cite>. Near-term milestones include demonstrating reliable lattice surgery with communication modules, expanding photonic interconnect distances and determinism, and building system-level models that accurately predict performance as devices grow<cite id="2"></cite><cite id="41"></cite><cite id="72"></cite>. Continued application-driven co-design will be essential to tune trap sizing, communication topologies, and gate implementations to achieve high reliability and performance<cite id="26"></cite>.

Conclusion

Scaling trapped-ion quantum computing from small-scale demonstrations to large systems will require combining modular shuttling architectures, photonic interconnects, and microfabricated integrated photonics. QCCD processors with photonic links and planar trap arrays are the most promising near-term paths, while dilution-trap arrays and hybrid cold-atom interfaces offer complementary directions for large-scale systems<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="41"></cite><cite id="46"></cite><cite id="76"></cite><cite id="51"></cite>. Success hinges on improving optical coupling rates, co-designing applications with modular architectures, and mastering engineering challenges in heating and motional-mode engineering as devices grow<cite id="2"></cite><cite id="26"></cite><cite id="23"></cite>.

TI qubits have fundamental advantages over other technologies, featuring high qubit quality, coherence time, and qubit connectivity. However, current TI systems are small in size and typically use a single trap architecture, which has fundamental scalability limitations. To progress toward the next major milestone of 50–100 qubit TI devices, a modular architecture termed the Quantum Charge Coupled Device (QCCD) has been proposed. In a QCCD-based TI device, small traps are connected through ion shuttling. While the basic hardware components for such devices have been demonstrated, building a 50–100 qubit system is challenging because of a wide range of design possibilities for trap sizing, communication topology, and gate implementations and the need to match diverse application resource requirements. Toward realizing QCCD-based TI systems with 50–100 qubits, we perform an extensive application-driven architectural study evaluating the key design choices of trap sizing, communication topology, and operation implementation methods. To enable our study, we built a design toolflow, which takes a QCCD architecture’s parameters as input, along with a set of applications and realistic hardware performance models. Our toolflow maps the applications onto the target device and simulates their execution to compute metrics such as application run time, reliability, and device noise rates. Using six applications and several hardware design points, we show that trap sizing and communication topology choices can impact application reliability by up to three orders of magnitude. Microarchitectural gate implementation choices influence reliability by another order of magnitude. From these studies, we provide concrete recommendations to tune these choices to achieve highly reliable and performant application executions. With industry and academic efforts underway to build TI devices with 50–100 qubits, our insights have the potential to influence QC hardware in the near future and accelerate the progress toward practical QC systems.</summary><hostname>ACM Digital Library</hostname><publisher>COMMUNICATIONS OF THE ACM</publisher><author_list><author name="Prakash Murali" /><author name="Dripto M Debroy" /><author name="Kenneth R Brown" /><author name="Margaret Martonosi" /></author_list><url>https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3511064</url><publish_time>2022年3月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:27"><title>Co-designing a scalable quantum computer with trapped atomic ions</title><summary>The first generation of quantum computers are on the horizon, fabricated from quantum hardware platforms that may soon be able to tackle certain tasks that cannot be performed or modelled with conventional computers. These quantum devices will not likely be universal or fully programmable, but special-purpose processors whose hardware will be tightly co-designed with particular target applications. Trapped atomic ions are a leading platform for first-generation quantum computers, but they are also fundamentally scalable to more powerful general purpose devices in future generations. This is because trapped ion qubits are atomic clock standards that can be made identical to a part in 10¹⁵, and their quantum circuit connectivity can be reconfigured through the use of external fields, without modifying the arrangement or architecture of the qubits themselves. In this forward-looking overview, we show how a modular quantum computer with thousands or more qubits can be engineered from ion crystals, and how the linkage between ion trap qubits might be tailored to a variety of applications and quantum-computing protocols.</summary><hostname>Nature</ho

This mid-term challenge will soon be faced by various quantum technologies, which urges the need of realistic assessments of their prospects. In this work, we pursue this goal by assessing the capabilities of current trapped-ion architectures in facing one of the most demanding parts of this quest: the implementation of an entangling CNOT gate between encoded logical qubits. Our careful fault-tolerant design, together with a low-resource optimization, allows us to determine via exhaustive numerical simulations the experimental regimes where each of the approaches becomes favorable. In this manuscript, we characterize the recent demonstration of a fault-tolerant universal gate set in a trapped-ion quantum computer [Postler et al. We find that an experimentally-informed depolarizing noise model captures the essential noise dynamics of the fault-tolerant experiment that we consider, and crosstalk is negligible in the currently accessible regime of physical error rates. For deterministic Pauli state preparation, we provide a fault-tolerant unitary logical qubit initialization circuit, which can be realized without in-sequence measurement and feed-forward of classical information. Additionally, we show that non-deterministic state preparation schemes, i.e. repeat until success, for logical Pauli and magic states perform with higher logical fidelity over their deterministic counterparts for the current and anticipated future regime of physical error rates. problem: Regarding the attitude control problem for UAVs, most open-source flight controllers currently implement cascaded PID control algorithms. However, a single set of PID controller parameters typically performs well only under specific flight conditions. In practical applications, UAVs operate across diverse flight states. What methods can be employed to enhance the actual control performance of PID algorithms, and how should PID parameters be optimally selected?

## Executive summary

Most open-source flight controllers implement cascaded PID loops for UAV attitude control, but fixed PID gains tuned for one flight regime often underperform under different dynamics, disturbances, or operating points. This report synthesizes data-driven and adaptive methods that can enhance PID control performance across diverse flight states, and provides practical guidance for optimal PID parameter selection. The evidence indicates that intelligent tuning (fuzzy logic, neural networks, evolutionary optimization), data-driven identification, and online adaptation can improve robustness and transient response compared to fixed PID, while structured H∞ and MPC offer alternative design paradigms with documented advantages in certain settings<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="17"></cite><cite id="21"></cite><cite id="22"></cite><cite id="25"></cite>.

## Methods to enhance PID control performance

Integrating intelligent tuning with PID can make gains adaptive to changing conditions. Fuzzy PID controllers use error and error rate as inputs to adjust Kp, Ki, and Kd in real time, improving precision and robustness in complex systems<cite id="1"></cite>. Hybrid schemes that combine neural networks and fuzzy logic to tune PID gains have been shown to significantly improve trajectory tracking and overall control efficiency by leveraging each technique’s strengths<cite id="17"></cite>. Evolutionary optimization methods, such as genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization, can automatically tune PID parameters to minimize time-domain error metrics, yielding robust controllers for nonlinear UAV dynamics<cite id="18"></cite><cite id="19"></cite>.

Adaptive mechanisms can tune PID gains online during flight. A second-order sliding mode control–based adaptive PID reduced chattering and improved transient performance, with simulation and real-time embedded tests demonstrating fast convergence and stability<cite id="2"></cite>. Reinforcement learning agents trained offline and deployed online adjust PID gains during flights, achieving smaller attitude errors and significantly better attitude tracking compared to hand-tuned gains<cite id="16"></cite>. Lyapunov-based self-tuning laws can adjust PID gains autonomously without boundary conditions, ensuring asymptotic attitude/position tracking and bounded errors under unstructured disturbances<cite id="27"></cite>.

Data-driven identification can yield well-characterized PID parameters without detailed models. A modified VRFT procedure tuned both inner and outer loops from a single experimental dataset on a pitch-restricted variable-pitch quadrotor, and its performance was compared favorably to model-based structured H∞ synthesis on a black-box pitch model<cite id="21"></cite>. VRFT and correlation-based tuning have been successfully applied to multirotor attitude and position control, providing performance comparable to model-based methods and demonstrating feasibility with closed-loop flight data<cite id="46"></cite>. Automated differential evolution tuning of cascaded PID gains (attitude PDs followed by position PIDs) improved trajectory tracking across maneuvers by minimizing coupled time-domain metrics<cite id="34"></cite>.

Complementary alternatives to PID can broaden robustness. Robust MPC autopilots maintain stability under mass/inertia variations and gusts, with heading regulation via PID and comparisons to L1 adaptive control showing effectiveness in real UAVs<cite id="21"></cite>. Empirical comparisons on a Parrot Mambo quadrotor found MPC surpassing PID/LQR in stability and robustness, with quantified steady-state and transient pitch deviations across simulations and experiments<cite id="22"></cite>. Model-reference adaptive control (MRAC) with a filtered tracking-error update law achieved asymptotic attitude tracking and demonstrated robustness to parametric uncertainty in simulations<cite id="25"></cite>.

## Optimal selection of PID parameters

Optimal PID selection should consider the controller’s role in the cascade and the operating regime. In attitude loops, separate PD control of roll/pitch/yaw and then position PID tuning can yield fast transient responses and smooth tracking, especially when coupled dynamics are explicitly addressed in the cost function<cite id="34"></cite>. For fixed-wing UAVs, PD controllers can outperform PID in certain tasks, suggesting that derivative action alone may suffice depending on the mission and dynamics<cite id="29"></cite>. Tuning should be validated with flight tests to capture nonlinear effects and coupling, and data-driven methods can be used to synthesize cascaded loops directly from input–output data<cite id="46"></cite>.

Intelligent and adaptive tuning can replace static trial-and-error. Fuzzy PID rules can be derived from expert experience and optimized via rule-base tuning or evolutionary algorithms, reducing manual effort and improving adaptability<cite id="7"></cite><cite id="13"></cite>. Neural networks can be trained to predict or adapt PID gains in real time, while evolutionary and RL-based tuning minimize performance metrics and adjust gains online during flights<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="18"></cite><cite id="16"></cite>. Lyapunov-based self-tuning laws provide a principled way to adjust gains online without requiring boundary conditions, ensuring stability and robustness under disturbances<cite id="27"></cite>.

Practical guidance includes: (1) start with data-driven identification (VRFT/CbT) to obtain initial cascaded PID parameters; (2) augment with intelligent or adaptive tuning to make gains responsive to changing flight states; and (3) validate with benchmark maneuvers and real flights, comparing settling time, overshoot, and robustness to disturbances<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="46"></cite><cite id="17"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>. If robustness to parametric uncertainty and external disturbances is paramount, MPC or MRAC may offer superior performance, but they require careful design and computational resources<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="25"></cite>.

## Evidence of performance improvements

Several studies report measurable gains when enhancing PID with adaptive or data-driven methods. A fuzzy PID with error feedback reduced settling time by 32%, overshoot by 45%, and improved dynamic response speed by 40%, with 0.2 s faster convergence and 60% steadier state maintenance compared to conventional methods<cite id="7"></cite>. A hybrid NNPID+FPID controller improved trajectory tracking and overall UAV control efficiency by combining neural adaptability with fuzzy rule-based tuning<cite id="17"></cite>. PSO-tuned PD/PIDs demonstrated robustness to wind disturbances in quadrotor simulations<cite id="20"></cite>. An adaptive fuzzy PID with EKF-based attitude estimation improved control accuracy and stability across simulations<cite id="1"></cite>. A reinforcement-learning–tuned PID adjusted gains online and achieved the smallest attitude errors in simulations and experimental flights, surpassing hand-tuned performance<cite id="16"></cite>. Lyapunov-based self-tuning tuned PID gains online while asymptotically tracking attitude/position and maintaining bounded errors under disturbances<cite id="27"></cite>.

Data-driven tuning also produced strong results. VRFT tuned both inner and outer loops from a single dataset on a pitch-restricted quadrotor, with performance comparable to structured H∞ on a black-box model<cite id="21"></cite>. Data-driven methods applied to multiple multirotor platforms showed comparable performance to model-based techniques when extended to include closed-loop flight unfalsification and advanced PID architectures<cite id="46"></cite>. Automated differential evolution tuning of cascaded PID gains improved trajectory tracking across takeoffs, translations, circles, and spirals by explicitly accounting for coupled dynamics in the cost function<cite id="34"></cite>.

## Limitations and trade-offs

While adaptive and data-driven methods improve robustness and performance, they add complexity and computational load. Evolutionary and RL tuning require offline training and careful deployment, and neural/fuzzy networks must be validated for real-time adaptability<cite id="18"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>. MPC offers superior robustness to parametric uncertainty and disturbances but may demand more computation and careful heading regulation via PID or other compensators<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>. MRAC provides asymptotic tracking and robustness but requires a nominal model and Lyapunov-based design to ensure stability<cite id="25"></cite>. Finally, PD-only controllers can outperform PID in some fixed-wing tasks, indicating that derivative action alone may be sufficient depending on the application<cite id="29"></cite>.

## Recommendations

- For most UAVs, start with data-driven identification (VRFT/CbT) to set initial cascaded PID gains, validated by flight tests<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="46"></cite>.
- Augment with intelligent or adaptive tuning (fuzzy PID, neural PID, evolutionary/RL tuning) to make gains responsive to varying flight states and disturbances<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="27"></cite><cite id="18"></cite><cite id="16"></cite>.
- If robustness to mass/inertia variations and gusts is critical, consider robust MPC with PID heading regulation, or MRAC with Lyapunov-based gain tuning<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="25"></cite>.
- Validate tuning with benchmark maneuvers and real flights, comparing settling time, overshoot, and disturbance rejection<cite id="34"></cite><cite id="7"></cite>.
- For fixed-wing UAVs, evaluate PD vs PID empirically, as PD can outperform PID in some tasks<cite id="29"></cite>.

To attain better autonomous flight system performance, MAVs require good control strategies to maintain their attitude stability during translational movement. In order to overcome all these limita- tions, the data-driven control approach emerges as a valuable solution to obtain the specific controller. Since the main feature of these methods is the ability to obtain or tune a controller directly from experimental input-output plant data, they have been proposed to avoid the problem of under-modeling and to facilitate the design of fixed-order controllers. Different linear data- driven methods available in literature have been compared and applied. The Virtual Reference Feedback Tuning (VRFT) method is first adopted be- cause it represents the most promising algorithm. In order to overcome the problem of VRFT with noisy data, the Correlation based Tuning (CbT) method is considered. The lack of an accurate plant model makes it impos- sible to guarantee the stability of the closed-loop system before implement- ing and testing the controller on the real system. In order to overcome this critical limitation of data-driven methods, an interesting controller design technique, called Controller Unfalsification, is implemented. Different ex- tensions has been proposed in this thesis to apply the data-driven methods to tune the controllers of multirotor systems. These extensions consider closed-loop data obtained in flight, cascade control systems and controller architecture based on advanced PID implementation. In this work, all the data-driven algorithms and their extensions are applied to tune the attitude and the position controllers of three multirotor systems. The considered Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are all quadrotors and they differ from size, actuation and control architectures. Exploiting the different features of each UAV and the chance to execute specific tests, different analysis have been performed. The experimental tests have shown that data-driven methods can be successfully applied to tune the considered controllers and they provide performance comparable to model-based methods.</summary><hostname>米兰理工大学数字论文档案</hostname><publisher>Degree Thesis</publisher><url>https://www.politesi.polimi.it/bitstream/10589/137027/1/thesis.pdf</url><publish_time>2017年12月20日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:44"><title>Finite-Time Control of Multirotor UAVs Under Disturbances</title><summary>A new finite-time control method based on a sliding mode for a multirotor unmanned

problem: As an agricultural engineering researcher focusing on 3D reconstruction and phenotypic analysis of crop grains, please develop a design report utilizing modern control theory, alongside other relevant theoretical methods and models, for the tasks of modeling, analysis, and design pertinent to my research area.
final_response:
<think>
<answer>
## Executive summary

This report proposes a modern control-theoretic design framework for modeling, analysis, and design tasks in 3D reconstruction and phenotypic analysis of crop grains. The framework couples multi-modal sensing, adaptive estimation, and optimization-based control to ensure accurate and repeatable acquisition of grain samples and images, while integrating deep-learning pipelines for fast and robust 3D reconstruction and phenotyping. The design leverages established modern control methods—nonlinear moving horizon estimation and nonlinear model predictive control for adaptive state-parameter estimation and precise tracking, sliding-mode and Lyapunov-based control for robustness, and tube-based NMPC for constraint handling—alongside data-driven and learning-based control tools for safety and generalization. Representative 3D reconstruction pipelines include deep-learning segmentation of CT scans for internal grain structure and NeRF/3DGS-based photorealistic reconstructions from RGB images, with demonstrated accuracy and scalability for field phenotyping<cite id="46"></cite><cite id="11"></cite><cite id="2"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>.

## Scope and objectives

The objective is to develop a closed-loop phenotyping system that acquires grain samples and multi-view images under controlled conditions, reconstructs 3D models, and extracts quantitative phenotypic traits using modern control theory and data-driven models. The system must handle uncertainties such as wheel slip, terrain variability, and occlusions in the field, while ensuring safety and stability of mobile platforms. The report provides modeling assumptions, control architectures, and validation strategies for acquisition, reconstruction, and phenotyping, with a focus on grains such as wheat and maize<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="11"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>.

## Modeling and analysis

For acquisition and reconstruction, we assume a mobile platform equipped with RGB cameras and possibly LiDAR or structured-light sensors, operating in unstructured agricultural environments. The platform follows a pre-planned acquisition protocol that ensures sufficient coverage and overlap to enable robust 3D reconstruction from RGB images. The kinematic model of the platform includes unmodeled dynamics and wheel slip, and the control design must compensate for these effects using adaptive estimation and optimization-based control<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="16"></cite>.

Modern control theory provides tools for adaptive estimation and robust tracking. The MHE–NMPC framework estimates the full system state and unknown slip parameters from measurements and feeds the estimates to NMPC to compute steering and velocity commands that track time-based reference trajectories, with demonstrated sub-millisecond feedback and accurate tracking on wet and bumpy fields<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="77"></cite>. Complementary sliding-mode and Lyapunov-based controllers offer finite-time convergence and robustness to disturbances and uncertainties, making them suitable for high-precision path tracking and servo systems in agricultural robots<cite id="71"></cite><cite id="31"></cite><cite id="73"></cite>. Tube-based NMPC can handle time-varying constraints and disturbances, ensuring constraint satisfaction and stability for autonomous vehicles<cite id="59"></cite>.

For 3D reconstruction and phenotyping, deep-learning pipelines have been shown to segment internal grain structures from micro-CT scans and extract quantitative traits, while NeRF and 3DGS enable photorealistic reconstructions and instance segmentation from RGB images with high accuracy and scalability for field applications<cite id="46"></cite><cite id="11"></cite><cite id="2"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>. MRI-based phenotyping tools such as MRI-Seed-Wizard quantify volumetric parameters of inner grain structure and throughput protocols for simultaneous multi-seed evaluation in crops like wheat and barley<cite id="36"></cite><cite id="41"></cite>.

## Control design for acquisition

The acquisition phase requires precise path planning and tracking to ensure repeatable and complete coverage of grain samples. A nonlinear moving horizon estimator estimates constrained states and parameters (including slip and unmeasurable orientation) from onboard sensors, while NMPC computes wheel-by-wheel steering and velocity commands to follow arbitrary time-based trajectories with sub-millisecond feedback and high tracking accuracy in difficult terrain<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="77"></cite>. For robustness and finite-time convergence, sliding-mode and Lyapunov-based controllers can be used for low-level actuation and path tracking, with stability guarantees and experimental validation on agricultural platforms<cite id="71"></cite><cite id="31"></cite><cite id="73"></cite>. Tube-based NMPC can be deployed to enforce constraints on inputs, states, and disturbances during acquisition, ensuring safe and accurate sampling<cite id="59"></cite>.

To reduce reliance on high-accuracy camera calibration, a stationary-camera NeRF framework reconstructs point clouds from rotating objects, using COLMAP for pose estimation and a simplified pose transform to avoid camera movement, which is practical for high-throughput facilities<cite id="52"></cite>. For field-scale phenotyping, 3DGS has demonstrated the ability to reconstruct entire fields and perform instance segmentation at scale, with rapid training and explicit point-based representations suitable for HTFP<cite id="2"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>.

## Data-driven control and safety

Data-driven CLF-based control can ensure safety and stability using only input-output measurements, without requiring full-state feedback, and integrates CLFs and CBFs to handle nonlinear constraints in discrete-time linear systems. This approach is applicable to mobile robots and can be implemented on platforms such as differential-drive or holonomic robots, with convex formulations and closed-form solutions in special cases<cite id="81"></cite>. Learning-based control Lyapunov functions and barrier functions can be extended to safety-critical agricultural operations, ensuring safe exploration and control under uncertainties<cite id="85"></cite>.

## Reconstruction and phenotyping pipelines

For internal grain structure, deep-learning segmentation of micro-CT scans can separate vitreous and starchy endosperms, extract volumes and ratios, and improve boundary handling via attention mechanisms and loss functions tailored to low-contrast and blurred edges<cite id="46"></cite>. For external morphology and field-scale reconstruction, NeRF and 3DGS from RGB images provide photorealistic 3D models and instance-level measurements with high fidelity and scalability<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="2"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>. MRI-Seed-Wizard automates trait quantification and throughput protocols for simultaneous multi-seed evaluation in wheat and barley grains, complementing CT and RGB-based pipelines<cite id="36"></cite><cite="41"></cite>.

## Validation and performance metrics

Control performance can be validated using trajectory tracking errors, computation times, and robustness to disturbances and slip. The MHE–NMPC framework achieved mean Euclidean errors on the order of centimeters with sub-millisecond feedback and accurate tracking on wet and bumpy fields<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="77"></cite>. Sliding-mode and Lyapunov-based controllers have demonstrated fast convergence and robustness in experimental validations<cite id="71"></cite><cite id="31"></cite><cite id="73"></cite>. Reconstruction accuracy has been quantified for wheat heads with per-instance mean absolute percentage errors of 15.1%, 18.3%, and 40.2% for length, width, and volume, and for point-cloud fidelity with 3DGS and NeRF compared to handheld scanners<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="11"></cite>. MRI-Seed-Wizard reports in vivo quantification of 23 grain traits and throughput protocols for simultaneous multi-seed evaluation<cite id="36"></cite><cite id="41"></cite>.

## Implementation considerations

Sensor selection and integration should balance accuracy, cost, and field robustness, with RGB cameras and LiDAR/structured-light sensors for multi-view acquisition, and stationary or rotating setups for NeRF/3DGS to reduce calibration demands<cite id="52"></cite><cite id="2"></cite>. Mobile platforms should implement adaptive estimation and optimization-based control (MHE–NMPC or tube-based NMPC) for precise tracking and constraint satisfaction, with sliding-mode or Lyapunov-based controllers for robustness and finite-time convergence<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="77"></cite><cite id="59"></cite><cite id="31"></cite>. Deep-learning pipelines for CT segmentation and RGB-based reconstruction should be integrated with quality metrics and validation against ground truth, and MRI protocols should be automated for throughput<cite id="46"></cite><cite id="11"></cite><cite id="36"></cite>.

## Outlook and research directions

Future work includes integrating hyperspectral sensors with 3D reconstruction for chemical and physiological phenotyping, combining adaptive control with learning-based safety guarantees, and deploying autonomous acquisition fleets for large-scale grain phenotyping. Advances in NeRF/3DGS, attention-enhanced segmentation, and MRI automation will further improve throughput and accuracy, while modern control theory will ensure reliable and safe operation in dynamic agricultural environments<cite id="51"></cite><cite id="81"></cite><cite id="85"></cite><cite id="2"></cite><cite id="6"></cite><cite id="36"></cite>.

As plant breeders seek to increase crop productivity and produce more food for the future, the amount of phenotype information they require will also increase. Traditional plant phenotyping relying on manual measurement is laborious, time-consuming, error-prone, and costly. Plant phenotyping robots have emerged as a high-throughput technology to measure morphological, chemical and physiological properties of large number of plants. Several robotic systems have been developed to fulfill different phenotyping missions. In particular, robotic phenotyping has the potential to enable efficient monitoring of changes in plant traits over time in both controlled environments and in the field. The operation of these robots can be challenging as a result of the dynamic nature of plants and the agricultural environments. Here we discuss developments in phenotyping robots, and the challenges which have been overcome and others which remain outstanding. In addition, some perspective applications of the phenotyping robots are also presented. We optimistically anticipate that autonomous and robotic systems will make great leaps forward in the next 10 years to advance the plant phenotyping research into a new era.</summary><hostname>Frontiers</hostname><publisher>Frontiers in Plant Science</publisher><author_list><author name="Abbas Atefi" affiliation="University of Nebraska at Lincoln" /><author name="Yufeng Ge" affiliation="University of Nebraska at Lincoln" /><author name="Santosh Pitla" affiliation="University of Nebraska at Lincoln" /><author name="James Schnable" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley" /></author_list><url>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpls.2021.611940/pdf?isPublishedV2=False</url><publish_time>2021年6月25日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:27"><title>High Precision Control of Tracked Field Robots in the Presence of Unknown Traction Coefficients</title><summary>Accurate steering through crop rows that avoids crop damage is one of the most important tasks for agricultural robots utilized in various field operations, such as monitoring, mechanical weeding, or spraying. Nonlinear RHE is used to estimate constrained states and parameters, and nonlinear RHC is designed based on an adaptive system model which contains time-varying parameters. The capabilities of the real-time RHEC framework are verified experimentally, and the results show an accurate tracking performance on a bumpy and wet soil field. The mean values of the Euclidean error and required computation time of the RHEC framework are respectively equal to 0.0423 m and 0.88 milliseconds.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Erkan Kayacan" affiliation="Distributed Autonomous Systems Laboratory, Coordinated Science Laborator

There is a need for non-destructive, three-dimensional assessment of the morphometry, composition, and internal features of seeds. Here, we introduce a novel tool, MRI-Seed-Wizard, which integrates deep learning algorithms with non-invasive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for use in a new domain—plant MRI. The tool enabled in vivo quantification of 23 grain traits, including volumetric parameters of inner seed structure. Several of these features cannot be assessed using conventional techniques, including X-ray computed tomography. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="crop grain phenotyping X-ray CT deep learning segmentation pipeline vitreous endosperm maize kernel" search_time="2026年5月16日11时56分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:46"><title>A deep learning-based micro-CT image analysis pipeline for nondestructive quantification of the maize kernel internal structure</title><summary>Identifying and segmenting the vitreous and starchy endosperm of maize kernels is essential for texture analysis. However, the complex internal structure of maize kernels presents several challenges. In CT computed tomography (CT) images, the pixel intensity differences between the vitreous and starchy endosperm regions in maize kernel CT images are not distinct, potentially leading to low segmentation accuracy or oversegmentation. Moreover, the blurred edges between the vitreous and starchy endosperm make segmentation difficult, often resulting in jagged segmentation results and poor segmentation outcomes. We propose a deep learning-based CT image analysis pipeline to examine the internal structure of maize seeds. First, CT images are acquired using a multislice CT scanner. To improve the efficiency of maize kernel imaging, a batch scanning method is used. Individual kernels are accurately segmented from batch-scanned CT images using the Canny algorithm. Second, we modify the conventional architecture for high-quality segmentation of the vitreous and starchy endosperm in maize kernels. The conventional U-Net is modified by integrating the CBAM (convolutional block attention module) mechanism in the encoder and the SE (squeeze-and-excitation attention) mechanism in the decoder, as well as by using the focal-Tversky loss function instead of the Dice loss, and the boundary smoothing term is weighted as an additional loss term, named CSFTU-Net. The experimental results show that the CSFTU-Net model significantly improves the ability of segmenting vitreous and starchy endosperm. Finally, a segmented mask-based method is proposed to extract phenotype parameters of maize kernel texture, including the volume of the kernel (V), volume of the vitreous endosperm (VV), volume of starchy endosperm (SV), and ratios over their respective total kernel volumes (VV/V and SV/V). raw_output.raw_text: <search query="crop grain phenotyping hyperspectral imaging deep learning 3D reconstruction" search_time="2026年5月16日11时56分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:51"><title>AI and 3D Hyperspectral Vision for High-Throughput Phenotyping</title><summary>INTRODUCTION High-throughput plant phenotyping is key to genetic improvement and the conservation of plant genetic resources. However, most advanced systems currently available: Only work under controlled conditions. Gather limited data (only 3D or only hyperspectral info, etc.). What if a single robot could do it all? - Autonomy (GNSS-RTK). - Field operation. - 3D sensors, RGB and hyperspectral cameras with 173 channels. Processing 3D and hyperspectral images using artificial intelligence for crop reconstruction, segmentation, and analysis. OBJECTIVE Develop and validate an autonomous robotic platform with multiple sensors to: - Capture 3D data (point clouds) and hyperspectral information. - Reconstruct detailed 3D models integrating hyperspectral data per point. - Identify plant structures (leaves, stem, inflorescences, etc.) and detect signs of stress. All non-invasively and directly in the field. METHODOLOGY Robotic platform in the field Autonomous robot developed by INYCOM, designed to move across plots and capture data. Funded by component 17.i2, Recovery, Transformation, and Resilience Plan (Next Generation EU funds). Integrated state-of-the-art sensors: 3D image capture Sensor fusion allows generating detailed point clouds for each plant, integrating shape, texture, and hyperspectral content per point. Processing and analysis with AI - Reconstruction of 3D point clouds with hyperspectral data. - 2D and 3D segmentation of plant structures. - Identification and calculation of morphological parameters. - Calculation of vegetation indices to monitor stress. ANALYSIS - SfM + NeRF and variants (neural 3D reconstruction from prior geometry). - Mask R-CNN, SAM (2D segmentation projected onto 3D). - PointNet, PointGroup, Mask3D, SAM 3D (segmentation in 3D point clouds). EXPECTED RESULTS Field tests will be carried out in experimental plots to assess: - Quality and detail of 3D reconstruction integrated with hyperspectral data. - Accuracy in automatic identification of plant structures. - Reliability in measuring morphological parameters. - Capability to detect stress through vegetation indices. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="modern control theory control Lyapunov function robotics autonomous mobile robot control" search_time="2026年5月16日11时56分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:81"><title>Input-Output Data-Driven Safe Control of Unknown Discrete-Time Linear Systems</title><summary>This paper presents a data-driven quadratically constrained quadratic program for designing safe and stable controllers using only input-output measurements. Input-output-based control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) and control barrier functions (CBFs) are integrated to derive safe and stable control inputs for discrete-time linear systems with unknown system dynamics. An augmented system is formed using historical input-output measurements and is leveraged to formalize learning of data-driven CLFs and CBFs. In sharp contrast to existing data-driven results in the literature, the presented approach does not require the restrictive assumption of availability of the full system’s state for measurement, which broadens its applicability. Conditions under which the resulting CBF-CLF optimization is convex are outlined, and an interior-point method is presented to handle non-convexities arising from some choices of CBFs. In convex scenarios, closed-form expressions for control inputs are derived. Two special cases that lead to a convex optimization, i.e., systems with a scalar control input and systems with a compact safe set, are thoroughly analyzed. The computational complexity of the proposed interior-point method is discussed and its efficacy is validated through simulations and real-world experiments with mobile robots. Two scenarios are explored: a nonholonomic differential-drive mobile robot and a holonomic mobile robot equipped with Mecanum wheels. Simulations demonstrate the framework’s capability to handle nonlinear constraints, while experiments on the ROSbot XL with Mecanum wheels, highlight its computational efficiency, practical applicability, and effectiveness in ensuring safety and stability in real-world environments. Note to Practitioners—Ensuring safety is paramount in safety-critical systems such as robotics, autonomous vehicles, and industrial automation, where operations in uncertain environments can lead to costly delays, equipment damage, or even harm to human operators. Although designing controllers for such systems typically requires comprehensive knowledge of system dynamics, acquiring an exact model is often challenging due to inherent uncertainties and disturbances. Data-driven control offers a solution by enabling the design of controllers directly from data, circumventing the need for complete dynamic models. In many real-world applications, collecting comprehensive state data is impractical; we often have access only to a subset of the system’s states. To address this limitation, we propose designing safe and stable control inputs using only input-output measurements. Leveraging a quadratic control barrier function, our method accommodates a wide array of safety constraints, including both linear and quadratic forms. This reliance on readily available input-output data simplifies control design, allowing engineers to develop effective controllers without the laborious process of constructing detailed models. This approach not only facilitates faster deployment and easier adaptation to changes but also simplifies the implementation process. Future work will focus on extending the method to handle complex, nonlinear stochastic systems.</summary><hostname>Semantic Scholar</hostname><publisher>IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering</publisher><author_list><author name="Niyousha Ghiasi" /><author name="Bahare Kiumarsi" /></author_list><url>https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Input-Output-Data-Driven-Safe-Control-of-Unknown-Ghiasi-Kiumarsi/d9dffd70c8ac3893b297617e9caa32516d9a02f5</url><publish_time>2025年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:82"><title>Nonlinear Adaptive Fuzzy Hybrid Sliding Mode Control Design for Trajectory Tracking of Autonomous Mobile Robots</title><sum

problem: Summarize recent research progress in reinforcement learning focused on enabling agents to explore efficiently and proactively under conditions of sparse rewards and constraints, respectively. Additionally, analyze and discuss the potential implications and insights this research provides for trajectory planning problems.
final_response:

<answer>
## Executive summary

Recent reinforcement learning (RL) research has made substantial progress in addressing two interrelated challenges: sparse rewards and constraints. On the exploration side, intrinsic motivation and successor representations provide principled, theoretically grounded bonuses that accelerate discovery in sparse-reward settings, while hierarchical and option-based methods decompose long-horizon tasks to focus exploration at multiple temporal scales<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="12"></cite><cite id="14"></cite><cite="6"></cite>. Safe RL advances increasingly integrate learned safe sets, temporal-logic specifications, and Bayesian uncertainty, enabling proactive constraint satisfaction without sacrificing performance or sample efficiency<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="2"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>. Together, these developments offer concrete insights for trajectory planning: using subgoal representations and safety basins to guide search, and leveraging uncertainty and constraints to prune unpromising paths<cite id="14"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>.

## Efficient exploration under sparse rewards

Count-based exploration with the successor representation (SR) offers a sample-efficient bonus by measuring transient visitation in state–action–observation space, with deep extensions achieving strong results in Atari under low sample budgets<cite id="11"></cite>. Successor–predecessor intrinsic exploration improves both short- and long-horizon coverage by augmenting rewards with forward and inverse novelty, and by dynamically weighting local versus global exploration based on state diversity<cite id="12"></cite>. Curiosity mechanisms such as skill-based curiosity and fast/slow curiosity explicitly target skill acquisition and coordinated long-horizon behaviors, outperforming prior methods on diverse environments<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>. Hierarchical RL frameworks that couple temporal abstraction with intrinsic goals further expand the space of viable goals and promote efficient exploration in sparse-feedback domains<cite id="6"></cite>.

## Proactive exploration and long-horizon planning

Option-based successor–predecessor exploration demonstrates that intrinsic rewards based on forward and inverse prediction can drive agents to discover both short- and long-horizon behaviors, with diversity-based control of exploration scope<cite id="12"></cite>. Hierarchical RL methods that learn subgoal representations with slowness objectives and stabilize online subgoal space updates improve hierarchical exploration and transferability across tasks<cite id="14"></cite><cite id="15"></cite>. These temporal-abstraction strategies align naturally with trajectory planning by decomposing global routes into subgoals and subtrajectories, reducing the search space and enabling coordinated actions over extended horizons<cite id="14"></cite>.

## Safe RL under constraints

Safe RL advances increasingly combine learned safe sets with constraint enforcement. LS^3 learns latent binary classifiers for safe sets in high-dimensional visuomotor control, enabling long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards while restricting exploration to regions where safety is guaranteed and learning is more efficient<cite id="1"></cite>. Temporal-logic safe RL integrates reward shaping, safety value functions, and adaptive models to maximize task satisfaction probability while addressing sparse rewards and balancing exploration–exploitation via quantum-inspired action selection<cite id="2"></cite>. Bayesian safe RL with safety basins formalizes safety as a probabilistic constraint, derives a safe policy improvement theorem, and shows that safety basins can be learned efficiently with Gaussian processes and active learning<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>.

## Data-driven evidence

Count-based SR exploration provides a theoretically grounded bonus that scales to deep RL and performs well in low-sample regimes<cite id="11"></cite>. Successor–predecessor exploration demonstrates improved coverage and long-horizon behavior discovery in sparse-reward settings<cite id="12"></cite>. Curiosity-driven methods (skill-based and fast/slow) consistently outperform baselines across diverse environments<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>. Hierarchical RL with intrinsic goals efficiently explores sparse-feedback tasks such as Montezuma’s Revenge<cite id="6"></cite>. In safe RL, LS^3 shows efficient learning within learned safe sets for visuomotor control<cite id="1"></cite>, temporal-logic frameworks address sparse rewards and exploration–exploitation via reward shaping and quantum action selection<cite id="2"></cite>, and Bayesian safety basins provide a principled probabilistic constraint with efficient learning<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>.

## Implications for trajectory planning

Trajectory planning benefits from RL advances that structure exploration and enforce constraints. Subgoal representations learned with slowness objectives and stable online updates guide hierarchical exploration, reducing the search space and enabling coordinated subtrajectories<cite id="14"></cite><cite id="15"></cite>. Safety basins and latent safe sets provide regions where planning can operate while guaranteeing safety, constraining the search to viable neighborhoods and accelerating convergence<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="1"></cite>. Temporal-logic specifications allow complex task constraints to be embedded directly into the planning objective, ensuring long-horizon compliance while mitigating sparse reward issues<cite id="2"></cite>. Uncertainty-driven exploration (e.g., SR-based bonuses) can be used to prioritize unvisited or under-explored regions, improving coverage and the likelihood of discovering successful trajectories<cite id="11"></cite>. Finally, option-based and hierarchical methods decompose global routes into temporally extended subgoals, aligning RL’s proactive exploration with classical motion planning’s need for structured search<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>.

## Outlook and open challenges

Surveys of exploration and safe RL highlight that while many methods exist, selecting the right approach per task and balancing exploration with safety remains challenging, especially in high-dimensional, sparse-reward domains<cite id="119"></cite><cite id="129"></cite>. Bridging hierarchical planning with Bayesian safety basins and temporal-logic constraints, and integrating uncertainty and curiosity in a unified framework, are promising directions for robust trajectory planning under constraints<cite id="14"></cite><cite id="17"></cite><cite id="2"></cite>. Continued progress on scalable safe set learning, principled constraint specifications, and uncertainty-aware exploration will further reduce sample costs and improve reliability in real-world planning<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="119"></cite>.

A promising strategy for learning in dynamically uncertain environments is requiring that the agent can robustly return to learned safe sets, where task success (and therefore safety) can be guaranteed. While this approach has been successful in low-dimensions, enforcing this constraint in environments with visual observations is exceedingly challenging. We present a novel continuous representation for safe sets by framing it as a binary classification problem in a learned latent space, which flexibly scales to image observations. We then present a new algorithm, Latent Space Safe Sets (LS$^3$), which uses this representation for long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards. We evaluate LS$^3$ on 4 domains, including a challenging sequential pushing task in simulation and a physical cable routing task. We find that LS$^3$ can use prior task successes to restrict exploration and learn more efficiently than prior algorithms while satisfying constraints. See https://tinyurl.com/latent-ss for code and supplementary material.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><publisher>5th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2021)</publisher><author_list><author name="Albert Wilcox" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley" /><author name="Ashwin Balakrishna" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley" /><author name="Brijen Thananjeyan" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley" /><author name="Joseph E Gonzalez" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley" /><author name="Ken Goldberg" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley" /></author_list><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.04775</url><publish_time>2021年9月21日0时0分</publish_time><arxiv_url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.04775</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>2107.04775</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Safe Reinforcement Learning Using Learned Safe Sets</title><summary>Reinforcement learning is an increasingly popular framework that enables robots to learn to perform tasks from prior experience in environments where dynamics or shaped reward functions are challenging to model. However, because this requires robots to sample tra- jectories under significant dynamical uncertainty, the robot may perform unsafe maneuvers during online exploration. This is particularly problematic in real-world robotics, where unsafe behaviors can lead to damage to surroundings. Finally, the approaches of different categories are compared in terms of complexity, computational effort and overall performance.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Pawel Ladosz" affiliation="aDepartment of Mechanical Engineering, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST), 50 UNIST-gil, Ulsan, Republic of Korea" /><author name="Lilian Weng" affiliation="bOpenAI LP, 3180 18th St, San Francisco, CA 94110" /><author name="Minwoo Kim" affiliation="aDepartment of Mechanical Engineering, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST), 50 UNIST-gil, Ulsan, Republic of Korea" /><author name="Hyondong Oh" affiliation="aDepartment of Mechanical Engineering, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST), 50 UNIST-gil, Ulsan, Republic of Korea" /></author_list><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.00824</url><publish_time>2022年5月3日0时0分</publish_time><arxiv_url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.00824</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>2205.00824</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:120"><title>Intrinsic Reward Driven Exploration for Deep Reinforcement Learning</title><summary>Deep reinforcement learning has become one of the hottest research topics in machine learning. In reinforcement learning, agents interact with the environment and try to maximise the expected cumulative reward. The goal of reinforcement learning is to find a policy to maximise the agent's total cumulative rewards. Unfortunately, some environments can only provide extremely sparse rewards, so the agent needs to learn a strategy to explore in its environment more efficiently to find these rewards. However, it is known that exploration in complex environments is a key challenge of deep reinforcement learning, especially for tasks where rewards are very sparse. In this thesis, intrinsic reward driven exploration strategies are investigated. The agent driven by this intrinsic reward can explore expeditiously, so as to find the sparse extrinsic rewards provided by the environment. Recently, surprise has been used as an intrinsic reward that encourages systematic and efficient exploration. We first define a novel intrinsic reward function called assorted surprise, and propose Variational Assorted Surprise Exploration (VASE) algorithm to approximate this assorted surprise in a tractable way, with the help of Bayesian neural networks. Then we apply VASE algorithm to continuous control problems and large scale Atari video games respectively. Experimental results show that VASE performs well across these tasks. Then we discover that all surprise based exploration methods will lose exploration efficiency in areas where the environmental transition is discontinuous. To solve this problem, we propose Mutual Information Minimising Exploration (MIME) algorithm. We show that MIME can explore as efficiently as surprise based methods in other areas of the environment but much better in areas with discontinuous transitions.</summary><

However, it is known that exploration in complex environments is a key challenge of deep reinforcement learning, especially for tasks where rewards are very sparse. In this thesis, intrinsic reward driven exploration strategies are investigated. The agent driven by this intrinsic reward can explore expeditiously, so as to find the sparse extrinsic rewards provided by the environment. Recently, surprise has been used as an intrinsic reward that encourages systematic and efficient exploration. We first define a novel intrinsic reward function called assorted surprise, and propose Variational Assorted Surprise Exploration (VASE) algorithm to approximate this assorted surprise in a tractable way, with the help of Bayesian neural networks. Then we apply VASE algorithm to continuous control problems and large scale Atari video games respectively. Experimental results show that VASE performs well across these tasks. Then we discover that all surprise based exploration methods will lose exploration efficiency in areas where the environmental transition is discontinuous. To solve this problem, we propose Mutual Information Minimising Exploration (MIME) algorithm. We show that MIME can explore as efficiently as surprise based methods in other areas of the environment but much better in areas with discontinuous transitions.</summary><

## Executive Summary

Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in eukaryotes—especially in plants and animals—is rare but not absent, and the few well-supported cases suggest that such transfers can confer adaptive benefits. In plants, HGT is most frequently documented in mitochondrial genomes, often via direct cell-to-cell contact during parasitic or grafting interactions, and in some instances the transferred genes are functional and appear to be under selection. In animals, HGT involving organelles acquired through predation is more common, with clear examples of functional gene integration and germline transmission. These findings indicate that, while eukaryotic HGT is uncommon, it can occur between distantly related species and may be particularly enriched in specialized ecological contexts such as parasitism, endosymbiosis, and herbivory, where intimate associations and nutrient dependencies facilitate genetic exchange<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite><cite id="11"></cite><cite id="26"></cite><cite id="16"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>.

## Background and Scope

HGT has long been recognized as a major evolutionary mechanism in prokaryotes, but its role in eukaryotic evolution is often underappreciated. Recent reviews emphasize that HGT occurs across eukaryotic lineages and can involve transfers between prokaryotes and eukaryotes, as well as even between multicellular eukaryotes. The frequency and impact of HGT vary across groups, with some protists and endosymbiotic lineages showing high rates, whereas animals and fungi are largely unaffected except for specific exceptions<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite><cite id="11"></cite>. In plants, HGT has been documented involving mitochondrial, nuclear, and plastid genomes, but convincing cases in the latter are rare, suggesting that the mechanisms and evolutionary significance differ among compartments<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>.

## HGT in Plants

Plant-to-plant HGT is most frequently observed in mitochondrial genomes, often mediated by direct cell-to-cell contact during parasitic interactions or natural grafting. Multiple studies report mitochondrial gene transfers among angiosperms, including introns and genes that have been integrated into the recipient mtDNA. In many cases, these transferred sequences exist as pseudogenes alongside functional native copies, and foreign genes can persist through genetic drift and gene conversion, potentially increasing genetic diversity within the mitochondrial genome<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="26"></cite>. A notable example is the transfer of a chimeric ATP6 intron from the parasitic plant Bursaria spinosa to the mitochondrial genome of the unrelated species Cytisus scoparius, which was confirmed by phylogenetic incongruence and structural analysis of the integrated element<cite id="29"></cite>.

Beyond mitochondria, nuclear HGT has also been reported in plants, with some instances involving functional transfers that appear to have contributed to adaptive evolution. Direct cell-to-cell contact between plants—such as in host–parasite relationships and natural grafting—facilitates the exchange of nuclear and mitochondrial genetic material, and accumulating evidence indicates that HGT in these compartments is more frequent than previously expected<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="26"></cite>. In addition to transfers between flowering plants, there are documented cases of HGT from green algae to non-photosynthetic plant lineages, including the transfer of a green algal nuclear gene into the mitochondrial genome of a non-photosynthetic relative of liverworts<cite id="30"></cite>.

## HGT in Animals

In animals, HGT involving organelles acquired through predation is more common than transfers between free-living metazoans. A striking example is the photosynthetic sea slug Elysia chlorotica, which sequesters algal plastids (chloroplasts) upon feeding and retains them for months. The slug’s own plastid genome is incomplete, and evidence shows that it has acquired at least one functional nuclear gene, psbO, from its algal prey. The psbO sequence in the slug is identical to that of V. litorea, and the gene is expressed and integrated into the slug’s nuclear genome, supporting the idea that predation can drive the horizontal acquisition of genes necessary to maintain foreign organelles and confer metabolic novelty (“green animals”)<cite id="21"></cite>. More broadly, plant-to-ecdysozoan transfers of disease resistance genes have also been documented, with drosomycin-type antifungal peptides found in nematodes and arthropods, and evidence for a plant-to-ecdysozoan transfer based on distribution patterns and functional validation<cite id="12"></cite>.

## Mechanistic and Ecological Contexts

Eukaryotic HGT is often associated with specialized ecological niches and intimate associations, including parasitism, endosymbiosis, and herbivory. In plants, parasitic relationships and grafting create direct cell-to-cell contacts that facilitate the exchange of genetic material, and mitochondrial HGT appears to be enriched in these contexts<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="26"></cite>. In animals, herbivorous and predatory lifestyles can lead to the retention of foreign organelles and the subsequent acquisition of nuclear genes required to support their function, as exemplified by Elysia chlorotica<cite id="21"></cite>. More generally, endosymbiotic associations and the exchange of genetic material within and among eukaryotic lineages are increasingly recognized as important drivers of eukaryotic genome evolution<cite id="3"></cite>.

## Evolutionary Significance and Adaptive Benefits

While HGT is rare in plants and animals, the documented cases suggest that such transfers can have functional and adaptive consequences. In plant mitochondria, foreign genes can persist and even contribute to genetic diversity through gene conversion, and a few nuclear transfers appear to be functional and under selection<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="26"></cite>. In animals, the acquisition of algal nuclear genes by the sea slug appears to enable long-term maintenance of sequestered plastids and confer a photosynthetic phenotype, representing a clear adaptive benefit<cite id="21"></cite>. These findings align with broader observations that HGT can facilitate adaptation to specialized niches and provide selective advantages in certain lineages<cite id="1"></cite>.

## Implications and Open Questions

The evidence indicates that HGT in eukaryotes—especially in plants and animals—is uncommon but not negligible, and it tends to occur in specific ecological and physiological contexts. While mitochondrial HGT is more frequently documented in plants, nuclear HGT is also increasing in evidence, and further comparative and functional studies are needed to quantify rates and determine the evolutionary impact across species<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="26"></cite>. In animals, HGT involving organelles acquired through predation is more common, but transfers between free-living metazoans remain rare and require more systematic investigation<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>. Overall, these cases highlight the importance of considering HGT as a potential evolutionary mechanism in eukaryotic diversification, particularly in specialized ecological settings where intimate associations and nutrient dependencies facilitate genetic exchange<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite><cite id="11"></cite>.
