Involvement of plastid, mitochondrial and nuclear genomes in plant-toplant horizontal gene transfer
Maria Virginia Sanchez-Puerta*
IBAM-CONICET & FCA, FCEN, Universidad Nacional de Cuyo, Chacras de Coria, Mendoza 5505, Argentina
Abstract
This review focuses on plant-to-plant horizontal gene transfer (HGT) involving the three DNA-containing cellular compartments. It highlights the great incidence of HGT in the mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) of angiosperms, the increasing number of examples in plant nuclear genomes, and the lack of any convincing evidence for HGT in the well-studied plastid genome of land plants. Most of the foreign mitochondrial genes are non-functional, generally found as pseudogenes in the recipient plant mtDNA that maintains its functional native genes. The few exceptions involve chimeric HGT, in which foreign and native copies recombine leading to a functional and single copy of the gene. Maintenance of foreign genes in plant mitochondria is probably the result of genetic drift, but a possible evolutionary advantage may be conferred through the generation of genetic diversity by gene conversion between native and foreign copies. Conversely, a few cases of nuclear HGT in plants involve functional transfers of novel genes that resulted in adaptive evolution. Direct cell-to-cell contact between plants (e.g. host-parasite relationships or natural grafting) facilitate the exchange of genetic material, in which HGT has been reported for both nuclear and mitochondrial genomes, and in the form of genomic DNA, instead of RNA. A thorough review of the literature indicates that HGT in mitochondrial and nuclear genomes of angiosperms is much more frequent than previously expected and that the evolutionary impact and mechanisms underlying plant-to-plant HGT remain to be uncovered.
Keywords: angiosperm; horizontal gene transfer; chimeric; gene conversion; parasitic
Introduction
Horizontal gene transfer (HGT), the exchange of genetic material between non-mating organisms, is widespread in prokaryotes and, to a lesser extent, in unicellular eukaryotes [1–3]. Most of the evidence for HGT in eukaryotes comes from genes derived from bacteria, describing transfers between phagotrophic, unicellular eukaryotes and their bacterial prey [1,4]. In the last few years, horizontal transfer in multicellular eukaryotes has been increasingly reported [5–8]. Plants in particular have been recognized as donors and targets of HGT involving the three domains of life [5,9]. Of the genetic exchanges reported between multicellular eukaryotes, the frequency of HGT between flowering plants is surprisingly elevated [10–16]. Most cases of plant-to-plant HGT comprise mitochondrial sequences (introns or genes) that were transferred to the mitochondrial genome of another angiosperm [15–20].
This review focuses on plant-to-plant HGT events involving the three DNA-containing compartments in plant cells,
with emphasis on transfers between angiosperm mitochondria, especially those involving host-parasite relationships.
HGT among plants: impact in each of the three genomes
Horizontal transfers among angiosperms has been increasingly recognized and slowly accepted by the scientific community. HGT between two plants may involve any of the three DNA-containing compartments, though certain genomes are more prone to genetic exchanges than others (Fig. 1).

##  Abstract  

  The sea slug Elysia chlorotica acquires plastids by ingestion of its algal food source Vaucheria litorea. Organelles are sequestered in the mollusc's digestive epithelium, where they photosynthesize for months in the absence of algal nucleocytoplasm. This is perplexing because plastid metabolism depends on the nuclear genome for >90% of the needed proteins. Two possible explanations for the persistence of photosynthesis in the sea slug are (i) the ability of V. litorea plastids to retain genetic autonomy and/or (ii) more likely, the mollusc provides the essential plastid proteins. Under the latter scenario, genes supporting photosynthesis have been acquired by the animal via horizontal gene transfer and the encoded proteins are retargeted to the plastid. We sequenced the plastid genome and confirmed that it lacks the full complement of genes required for photosynthesis. In support of the second scenario, we demonstrated that a nuclear gene of oxygenic photosynthesis, psbO, is expressed in the sea slug and has integrated into the germline. The source of psbO in the sea slug is V. litorea because this sequence is identical from the predator and prey genomes. Evidence that the transferred gene has integrated into sea slug nuclear DNA comes from the finding of a highly diverged psbO 3' flanking sequence in the algal and mollusc nuclear homologues and gene absence from the mitochondrial genome of E. chlorotica. We demonstrate that foreign organelle retention generates metabolic novelty ("green animals") and is explained by anastomosis of distinct branches of the tree of life driven by predation and horizontal gene transfer.

problem: I need to dynamically adjust Kubernetes (K8S) cluster node counts based on fluctuating business request volumes, ensuring resources are scaled up proactively before peak loads and scaled down promptly during troughs. The standard Cluster Autoscaler (CA) isn't suitable as it relies on pending pods and might not fit non-elastic node group scenarios. What are effective implementation strategies, best practices, or existing projects that address predictive or scheduled autoscaling for K8S nodes?
final_response:
<think>
<answer>
## Executive Summary

Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler (CA) scales nodes only when pods become unschedulable, which makes it unsuitable for proactive scaling or non-elastic node groups. Predictive and scheduled node autoscaling can be implemented using time-series forecasting for near-future load, workload prediction models, and cloud-native schedulers that launch nodes ahead of demand. Scheduled scaling is also practical via Kubernetes CronHPA, custom CronJobs, or cloud provider node pools with minimum/maximum sizes and scheduled resizing, yielding substantial cost savings during off-hours<cite id="139"></cite><cite id="141"></cite>. Best practices include setting time-based or demand-based thresholds, tuning scale-down grace periods, and combining node and pod autoscaling with fast node provisioners<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="18"></cite><cite id="151"></cite>.

## Why Cluster Autoscaler Is Not Enough

CA’s core behavior is to add or remove nodes based on pending pods and underutilization, which is reactive and unsuitable for non-elastic node groups or proactive scaling before peak loads<cite id="13"></cite>. CA also cannot scale down nodes that are no longer needed if they lack pods, and its scale-down delay is governed by provider-specific settings (e.g., AWS CA’s scale-down-unneeded-time and scale-down-delay-after-failure), which may be too conservative for short-lived peaks<cite id="147"></cite><cite id="149"></cite>. For example, CA may wait 10 minutes to scale down before reclaiming nodes, risking over-provisioning during troughs<cite id="18"></cite>.

## Predictive Kubernetes Node Autoscaling

Predictive node autoscaling uses time-series forecasting to estimate load at the time a new node would start, provisioning nodes before queues build up. One approach aggregates per-instance metrics into a cluster-wide load signal, predicts its trajectory, and converts the prediction to an instance count; experiments show this reduces violations and improves latency compared to reactive scaling<cite id="160"></cite>. LSTM-based HPA has been proposed to anticipate demand and provision pods earlier, though it consumes more resources than CPU-based HPA<cite id="161"></cite>. For latency-sensitive workloads, LA-IMR integrates a utilization-driven latency model with a custom Kubernetes autoscaler to scale replicas (and nodes) proactively before P99 delays spike<cite id="11"></cite>.

A deep-learning proactive scaler (CATScaler) predicts local and global workloads and uses an instance-counting method for serverless environments; tests on a 4-server cluster reduced response time by 1.1× and cut service violation rates by 3.2×, demonstrating the value of prediction for resource allocation<cite id="12"></cite>. In green cloud transcoding, Kubernetes HPA with Random Forest/XGBoost/CatBoost forecasts renewable energy and schedules workloads to minimize grid reliance, illustrating how predictive signals can drive node provisioning decisions<cite id="1"></cite>. For batch jobs, predictive scaling leverages machine learning to forecast CPU/memory and scale out/in, achieving up to 98% accuracy and reducing costs by 60–80% by scaling down idle nodes<cite id="17"></cite>.

## Scheduled Kubernetes Node Autoscaling

Scheduled scaling can be implemented via cloud provider node pools with explicit min/max sizes and scheduled resizing, enabling scale-downs during off-hours and weekends. Public reports indicate 60–70% cost reductions in non-production environments using automated scheduled scaling<cite id="139"></cite>. Kubernetes CronHPA supports crontab-style timing to scale deployments up/down, ideal for applications with clear daily traffic patterns<cite id="141"></cite>. Custom CronJobs can invoke kubectl scale or autoscaling APIs to adjust node pools or deployments at defined times, offering fine-grained control over peak and trough periods<cite id="142"></cite>.

## Cloud-Native Node Provisioners for Faster Scaling

Karpenter is a Kubernetes node autoscaler that watches unschedulable pods, evaluates scheduling constraints, and provisions nodes directly via cloud APIs, reducing scheduling delays and improving application performance compared to CA’s 3–5 minute node launch times<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="147"></cite>. On EKS, Karpenter’s tight integration with AWS APIs enables rapid instance launch without waiting for ASG operations, preventing pod scheduling delays and improving utilization<cite id="17"></cite>. For non-elastic node groups, Karpenter’s constraint-aware provisioning can still be used to add temporary capacity ahead of known peaks, then reclaim nodes after the event<cite id="147"></cite>.

## Best Practices for Predictive and Scheduled Node Autoscaling

- Define time-based or demand-based thresholds and set minimum/maximum node pool sizes to control capacity and costs<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="18"></cite>.
- Tune scale-down policies to match your SLAs: CA’s scale-down grace periods (e.g., 10 minutes on AWS) can be adjusted to avoid reclaiming nodes too late<cite id="18"></cite>.
- Combine node and pod autoscaling: use HPA/CronHPA to estimate pod counts and node provisioners (e.g., Karpenter) to launch nodes ahead of demand<cite id="160"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>.
- Validate with historical data: predictive models require representative training and should be tested for accuracy and lead-time alignment to the provisioning pipeline<cite id="160"></cite><cite id="12"></cite>.
- Monitor and protect: use metrics and anomaly detection to avoid scaling decisions based on noise, and implement safeguards to prevent over-provisioning<cite id="160"></cite>.

## Existing Projects and Tools

- Predictive HPA using LSTM: proactive pod provisioning based on learned demand patterns<cite id="161"></cite>.
- LA-IMR: latency-aware, predictive routing and Kubernetes-based proactive autoscaling to reduce tail latency<cite id="11"></cite>.
- CATScaler: convolution-augmented transformer predicts workload and scales resources, reducing latency and violations<cite id="12"></cite>.
- Predictive batch scaling with ML: forecasts CPU/memory and scales out/in with high accuracy and cost savings<cite id="17"></cite>.
- Karpenter: constraint-aware, fast node provisioner that can launch nodes before pods fail, improving responsiveness<cite id="17"></cite>.
- CronHPA: Kubernetes native scheduled scaling for deployments<cite id="141"></cite>.
- Scheduled node pools: cloud provider support for scaling down during off-hours (e.g., 60–70% cost reduction in non-prod)<cite id="139"></cite>.
- CronJobs: custom scripts to invoke kubectl scale or autoscaling APIs at defined times<cite id="142"></cite>.

## Implementation Strategy for Non-Elastic Node Groups

For non-elastic node groups, create a dedicated autoscaling node pool with min/max limits and scheduled resizing to handle peaks and troughs. During predictable peaks, use a predictive scaler (e.g., forecasting load and converting to instance counts) or CronHPA to trigger Karpenter or the provider’s CA to add nodes ahead of demand<cite id="160"></cite><cite id="141"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>. During troughs, enable scheduled scale-downs or adjust CA’s scale-down policies to reclaim nodes promptly<cite id="139"></cite><cite id="18"></cite>. Monitor node utilization and pending pods to validate that the combined strategy avoids over-provisioning while meeting SLAs<cite id="160"></cite>.

## Limitations and Uncertainties

The evidence shows strong benefits of predictive and scheduled scaling, but specific implementations depend on workload characteristics, provider capabilities, and model accuracy. While CA’s behavior and scale-down policies are well documented<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="18"></cite>, the exact performance gains for non-elastic node groups require case studies tailored to your environment. The cited projects demonstrate feasibility, but adoption should include rigorous testing and monitoring<cite id="160"></cite><cite id="12"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>.

problem: Which Obsidian plugins can effectively replicate Notion's multi-view database functionality (including Table, Kanban, Calendar, and List views)? Please provide a detailed comparison of the strengths and weaknesses of these plugins.
final_response:
<think>>
<answer>
# Obsidian Plugins That Replicate Notion’s Multi-View Database Functionality

Obsidian’s native support for Markdown and its recent release of the Bases core plugin make it possible to build database-like interfaces with multiple views. While Notion uses proprietary database views and linking, Obsidian relies on plugins and frontmatter to achieve similar multi-view layouts. The following plugins and native features most closely replicate Notion’s multi-view database functionality, including Table, Kanban, Calendar, and List views, and are compared by their strengths and weaknesses based on public documentation and user reports.

## 1. Obsidian Bases (Core Plugin)

Obsidian’s Bases plugin provides native database views and filtering, and integrates with other plugins that extend its display types. Bases lets users create custom table and card views, apply filters and formulas, and manage data backed by Markdown notes. It supports multiple views of the same dataset and acts as a foundation for other plugins to add additional layouts, making it a strong starting point for multi-view databases.

- Strengths: Native performance, customizable table and card views, live filtering and formulas, and seamless integration with other plugins for richer layouts. Bases also supports summaries and sorting, enabling dynamic data exploration<cite id="135"></cite><cite id="140"></cite>.
- Weaknesses: Bases alone does not provide Kanban, Calendar, or List views beyond tables and cards; additional plugins are needed to replicate Notion’s full multi-view set<cite id="140"></cite>.

## 2. TaskNotes (Task Management + Bases Views)

TaskNotes follows a “one note per task” model and stores tasks in YAML frontmatter. It exposes the same dataset through multiple Bases views, including Task List, Kanban, Calendar, Agenda, MiniCalendar, Pomodoro, and Pomodoro Stats, all of which operate as `.base` files. TaskNotes also supports external calendar subscriptions and time-blocking, and integrates with Obsidian’s inline task widgets.

- Strengths: Comprehensive multi-view support (including Calendar, Agenda, and Kanban), calendar drag-and-drop scheduling, time-block support, and calendar subscriptions (Google, Outlook, ICS). It also provides productivity-focused views (Pomodoro) and tight Bases integration<cite id="151"></cite><cite id="150"></cite>.
- Weaknesses: Relies on Bases for views, so limitations of Bases (e.g., lack of built-in Kanban or Calendar views) are inherited. It focuses on task management rather than general databases, and some advanced filtering and sorting may require DQL or additional plugins<cite id="150"></cite><cite id="140"></cite>.

## 3. Task List Kanban (Kanban Board)

Task List Kanban automatically imports task lists formatted with checkboxes or task syntax and organizes them into a Kanban board. It supports tag-based column mapping, drag-and-drop reordering, and exporting to CSV, and updates both the board and source files.

- Strengths: Lightweight and automatic task import, flexible column mapping via tags, drag-and-drop, and CSV export. It is ideal for users who already use task lists and want a Kanban interface without changing their note format<cite id="149"></cite>.
- Weaknesses: Does not provide Table, Calendar, or List views; limited to Kanban. No native calendar integration, and it is a standalone plugin that does not leverage Bases views<cite id="149"></cite>.

## 4. Obsidian Projects Plus (Table and Board Views)

Obsidian Projects Plus is a fork of Projects that adds Table and Board views for managing tasks and projects. It supports sorting, filtering, and navigation within a single plugin, with features such as inline editing and zooming.

- Strengths: Combines Table and Board views in one plugin, supports sorting and filtering, and includes inline editing and zoom controls. It is a single-plugin solution for task boards and tables<cite id="139"></cite>.
- Weaknesses: Limited to Table and Board views; lacks Calendar and List views. It may not match the breadth of Notion’s multi-view database without additional plugins<cite id="139"></cite>.

## 5. TileLineBase (Table, Kanban, Slide Views)

TileLineBase is a Markdown-driven database plugin that supports Table, Kanban, and Slide views from the same dataset. It includes filtering and sorting and aims to provide multiple interaction modes for the same data.

- Strengths: Native Markdown tables with multiple views (Table, Kanban, Slide), and built-in filtering and sorting. It offers a unified dataset across different layouts<cite id="108"></cite>.
- Weaknesses: Less mature compared to TaskNotes or Bases; limited documentation and community adoption. May require additional plugins for Calendar or advanced filtering<cite id="108"></cite>.

## 6. Obsidian Tables (Interactive Tables with Multiple Perspectives)

Obsidian Tables creates interactive JSON tables and supports multiple views within the same table file (e.g., “Active Tasks,” “Completed Items”). It also enables linked embeds and inline editing.

- Strengths: Interactive tables with multiple perspectives, linked embeds, and inline editing. It is useful for users who prefer a spreadsheet-like interface with embedded views<cite id="138"></cite>.
- Weaknesses: Limited to Table views; does not provide Kanban, Calendar, or List views out of the box<cite id="138"></cite>.

## 7. CSV Database (Multiple Views with Sort/Filter)

The CSV Database plugin provides a database view backed by CSV files with rich column types and multiple views that can be sorted and filtered. It includes a board layout with drag-and-drop editing.

- Strengths: Rich column types, multiple views with sort/filter, and inline editing with multi-select dropdowns. The board layout supports drag-and-drop, making it suitable for Kanban-like workflows<cite id="110"></cite>.
- Weaknesses: Requires CSV files instead of Markdown notes; less integrated with Obsidian’s native note linking and Bases. Limited to CSV-backed data<cite id="110"></cite>.

## 8. QueryDash (Timeline, Gallery, Table, and Other Views)

QueryDash is a multi-view database plugin that supports timeline, gallery, and table views, and includes built-in review cards and database operations. It is designed to meet diverse scenario needs with a user-friendly interface.

- Strengths: Multiple views (timeline, gallery, table) and built-in review functionality. It aims to be user-friendly and supports create/edit/delete operations<cite id="107"></cite>.
- Weaknesses: Less mature compared to TaskNotes or Bases; limited documentation and community adoption. May require additional plugins for advanced filtering and sorting<cite id="107"></cite>.

## 9. Marvis (Timeline, Calendar, Table Views)

Marvis is a community plugin that provides timeline (Gantt-style), calendar (month/week/day/year/list), and table views over vault notes, treating projects, milestones, tasks, logs, and events as first-class entities. It supports drag-and-drop scheduling and response-status cues on calendars.

- Strengths: Comprehensive timeline and calendar views with drag-and-drop and response-status cues. Table views are sortable and grouped by project/milestone<cite id="142"></cite>.
- Weaknesses: Relies on frontmatter for entities, which may require consistent formatting across notes. It does not provide List views natively and may need additional plugins for full coverage<cite id="142"></cite>.

## Comparison Summary

- Best for full Notion-like multi-view databases: TaskNotes + Bases. TaskNotes provides Calendar, Agenda, Kanban, and List views, while Bases offers filtering, formulas, and summaries. It also supports calendar subscriptions and time-blocking, making it a robust choice for task-centric databases<cite id="151"></cite><cite id="150"></cite><cite id="140"></cite>.

- Best for Kanban-only with automatic task import: Task List Kanban. It is lightweight and integrates well with existing task lists, but lacks Calendar and Table views without additional plugins<cite id="149"></cite>.

- Best for Table and Board views in one plugin: Obsidian Projects Plus. It combines Table and Board views with sorting/filtering and inline editing, but requires extra plugins for Calendar and List<cite id="139"></cite>.

- Best for Markdown tables with multiple perspectives: Obsidian Tables. It supports interactive tables and linked embeds, but is limited to Table views<cite id="138"></cite>.

- Best for CSV-backed databases with sort/filter and board layout: CSV Database. It offers rich column types and multiple views, but uses CSV instead of Markdown notes<cite id="110"></cite>.

- Best for diverse multi-view interfaces: QueryDash. It supports timeline, gallery, and table views with review cards, but may be less mature and require more plugins for advanced filtering<cite id="107"></cite>.

- Best for timeline and calendar over notes: Marvis. It provides Gantt-style timelines and calendar views with drag-and-drop, but may need additional plugins for List views and advanced filtering<cite id="142"></cite>.

## Recommendations

- If you need a comprehensive Notion-like database with Calendar, Agenda, Kanban, and List views, TaskNotes with Bases is the strongest option. It also supports external calendars and time-blocking, and leverages Obsidian’s native features for filtering and formulas<cite id="151"></cite><cite id="150"></cite><cite id="140"></cite>.

- If you already use task lists and want a Kanban board without changing your format, Task List Kanban is a good lightweight choice. Pair it with a separate calendar plugin for full multi-view coverage<cite id="149"></cite>.

- For users who prefer Table and Board views in one plugin, Obsidian Projects Plus is a solid alternative, but consider adding calendar and list views via other plugins<cite id="139"></cite>.

- For Markdown table-centric workflows with multiple perspectives and embedded views, Obsidian Tables and TileLineBase are viable, but they lack Calendar and List views natively<cite id="138"></cite><cite id="108"></cite>.

- If you work with CSV data and need sort/filter and board layouts, CSV Database is a strong option, but it uses CSV files rather than Markdown notes<cite id="110"></cite>.

- For diverse multi-view interfaces and user-friendly design, QueryDash is worth exploring, but it may require additional plugins for advanced filtering and sorting<cite id="107"></cite>.

- For timeline and calendar views over structured notes, Marvis is a good fit, but you may need to supplement it with other plugins for List views and advanced filtering<cite id="142"></cite>.

In summary, Obsidian’s plugin ecosystem can closely replicate Notion’s multi-view database functionality through combinations of Bases and TaskNotes, or via specialized plugins that add specific views. The choice depends on your primary use case (task management vs. general databases), preferred views, and willingness to integrate multiple plugins<cite id="140"></cite><cite id="151"></cite>.

<fetch fetch_id="60064484-1bfe-4713-adf0-74f59417a209"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:145"><url>https://tasknotes.dev/views/</url><title>Views</title><pagination_content start_offset="0" end_offset="563"># Views

TaskNotes provides multiple views for managing tasks and tracking productivity. All task-focused views operate as `.base` files located in the `TaskNotes/Views/` directory and require Obsidian's Bases core plugin to be enabled.

For details on Bases integration and how to enable it, see <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:145-<|link|>:1" text="Core Concepts" />. For view templates and configuration examples, see <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:145-<|link|>:2" text="Default Base Templates" />.

## Task-Focused Views

Task-focused views are different entry points into the same underlying task notes. The <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:145-<|link|>:3" text="Task List View" /> is a common starting view for day-to-day planning because it exposes filters, sorting, and grouping in list format.

When you want workflow by status, <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:145-<|link|>:4" text="Kanban View" /> organizes cards into columns and can optionally add swimlanes for an extra organizational layer. <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:145-<|link|>:5" text="Calendar Views" /> are useful when schedule and timing matter more than backlog shape, with month/week/day/year/list modes plus drag-and-drop scheduling and time-block support.

<link reference_id="<|superscript|>:145-<|link|>:6" text="Agenda View" /> is a preconfigured list-oriented calendar layout designed for short-horizon planning, while <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:145-<|link|>:7" text="MiniCalendar View" /> gives a compact month heatmap and fast keyboard navigation.





## Productivity-Focused Views

These views support time management and work tracking.

<link reference_id="<|superscript|>:145-<|link|>:8" text="Pomodoro View" /> supports focused intervals directly inside Obsidian, and <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:145-<|link|>:9" text="Pomodoro Stats View" /> summarizes completed sessions so you can see pace and consistency over time.



Screenshots in this section are captured via the Playwright docs suite (`npm run e2e:docs`).</pagination_content></document></fetch>

The Task List Kanban plugin streamlines task management in Obsidian by creating a dynamic kanban view that organizes tasks from your notes. Tasks are automatically added to the kanban board when formatted in the task list style, and users can assign them to specific columns using tags. The kanban view allows for efficient task management with features like drag-and-drop organization, task editing, archiving, and filtering based on tags. The plugin updates tasks both in the kanban and their original files, ensuring synchronization. Customizable columns and folder scopes make it adaptable to individual workflows, while its integration minimizes duplicate effort in managing and prioritizing tasks.

# TaskNotes Documentation

TaskNotes is a task and note management plugin for Obsidian that follows the "one note per task" principle. Each task is a Markdown file with structured metadata in YAML frontmatter.



## Requirements

TaskNotes requires **Obsidian 1.10.1**  or later and depends on the **Bases**  core plugin. Before you begin, open Obsidian Settings and confirm Bases is enabled under Core Plugins.

## Getting Started

### 1. Install and Enable

Install TaskNotes from Community Plugins in Obsidian settings, then enable it. If Bases is still disabled, enable it right away so TaskNotes views can open correctly.

### 2. Create Your First Task

Press Ctrl+P (or Cmd+P on macOS), run **TaskNotes: Create new task** , fill in the modal, and save. If you prefer inline workflows, start with a checkbox like `- [ ] Buy groceries` and convert it using the inline task command.



### 3. Open the Task List

Open your first view from the TaskNotes ribbon icon or by running **TaskNotes: Open tasks view**  from the command palette. This opens the default Task List `.base` file inside `TaskNotes/Views`.

### 4. Explore

Use <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:150-<|link|>:3" text="Core Concepts" /> to understand the data model, <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:150-<|link|>:4" text="Features" /> for workflow capabilities, <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:150-<|link|>:5" text="Views" /> for interface behaviour, and <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:150-<|link|>:6" text="Settings" /> to tune TaskNotes for your vault.

<think>
Goal: Write a well-structured, data-driven report comparing Google’s A2A protocol with the Model Context Protocol (MCP), highlighting differences, connections, and A2A’s innovations and targeted problems. Evidence gathered: A2A’s scope (agent-to-agent interoperability), features (AgentCards, task management, collaboration, UX negotiation, modality support), transport/standards (HTTP, SSE, JSON-RPC), security (OpenAPI-compatible auth), and async support. MCP’s scope (model-tool boundary), components (hosts, clients, servers), transport (stdio, HTTP/WebSockets), and deliberate limitations (does not address agent-to-agent communication). Direct comparisons: layered analysis and technical comparison documents explicitly contrast A2A and MCP. Innovations: A2A’s async-first design, modality agnosticism, opaque execution, standardized task lifecycle, push notifications, and enterprise-grade security. Problems addressed: vendor/framework fragmentation, long-running tasks, modality-rich interactions, secure interoperability, and data silos in enterprise workflows. Plan: Structure the report with sections—Introduction, Scope and Core Concepts, Differences and Connections, Innovative Aspects, Problems Addressed, Enterprise Implications, and Conclusion. Support each claim with localized citations to the comparison document and protocol resources.
</think>

<answer>## Overview

This report compares Google’s Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol with the Model Context Protocol (MCP), detailing their scope, core concepts, differences, and connections. It also highlights A2A’s innovative aspects and the specific problems it aims to solve, supported by data from protocol documentation and comparative analyses.

## Scope and Core Concepts

MCP is an open standard that connects AI systems to external tools, data sources, and computational resources by defining a JSON-RPC-based interface for listing, introspecting, and invoking “tools” and accessing “resources” hosted by a server. It runs over stdio, HTTP, or WebSocket, and its scope is deliberately limited to the model–tool boundary; it does not address agent-to-agent communication, discovery of remote agents, or task coordination beyond tool invocation and context access<cite id="7"></cite><cite id="11"></cite>. MCP’s ecosystem includes hosts (AI assistants, agents, or applications), clients embedded within hosts that connect to MCP servers, and servers that expose tools, prompts, and resources<cite id="12"></cite>.

A2A, in contrast, is an open protocol designed to enable seamless collaboration between AI agents, allowing them to communicate, securely exchange information, and coordinate actions even when built by different vendors or using different frameworks. A2A’s scope extends beyond the model–tool boundary to agent-to-agent interoperability, discovery, and task management<cite id="1"></cite>. Its core concepts include AgentCards (JSON metadata describing identity, capabilities, and authentication requirements), tasks (stateful units of work with a defined lifecycle), messages (communication turns with roles and parts), parts (atomic content units), artifacts (outputs composed of parts), and support for streaming via Server-Sent Events and asynchronous push notifications<cite id="22"></cite>.

## Differences and Connections

A key difference is scope: MCP focuses on connecting models to external capabilities at the model–tool boundary, while A2A focuses on agent-to-agent communication, discovery, and collaboration. As a result, MCP does not address remote agent discovery or task coordination across agents, whereas A2A explicitly targets these capabilities<cite id="7"></cite><cite id="11"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>. Both protocols, however, are built on common standards and aim to reduce integration complexity by providing unified interfaces for external capabilities<cite id="11"></cite>.

Transport-wise, MCP supports stdio, HTTP, and WebSocket, while A2A leverages HTTP, Server-Sent Events (SSE), and JSON-RPC 2.0 to achieve interoperability across systems and support real-time updates and structured interactions<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>. Functionally, MCP enables hosts to discover and invoke tools and access resources, while A2A adds capability discovery (via AgentCards), task management, collaboration through messages, UX negotiation via parts, and modality-agnostic exchange beyond text<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>.

## Innovative Aspects of A2A

A2A introduces several innovations tailored to modern agentic workflows. First, it is async-first and designed for long-running tasks and human-in-the-loop interactions, supporting both synchronous request/response, streaming via SSE, and asynchronous push notifications delivered to webhooks<cite id="22"></cite>. Second, A2A is modality agnostic, enabling the exchange of diverse content types—including text, audio/video via file references, structured data, and potentially embedded UI components (e.g., iframes)—to support rich, multimodal collaboration<cite id="22"></cite>.

Third, A2A emphasizes opaque execution: agents collaborate based on declared capabilities and exchanged information without needing to share internal thoughts, plans, or tool implementations, which enhances security and reduces coupling<cite id="22"></cite>. Fourth, A2A standardizes task negotiation and lifecycle management, including UX negotiation through parts to agree on format and user interface capabilities, and standardized task IDs and contexts to group related work<cite id="22"></cite>.

Finally, A2A aligns with enterprise-grade security and observability by supporting OpenAPI-compatible authentication and authorization schemes, and by integrating tracing and monitoring practices, making it suitable for production environments<cite id="22"></cite>. The protocol also benefits from broad industry support and contributions from over 50 technology partners and leading service providers, underscoring its interoperability goals<cite id="6"></cite>.

## Problems A2A Is Designed to Address

A2A was created to address fragmentation across agent frameworks and vendors by providing a common language and interaction model for interoperable communication and collaboration<cite id="1"></cite>. It targets the lack of standardized agent discovery and remote capability introspection, which MCP does not cover<cite id="11"></cite>. A2A also addresses the need for robust task coordination and long-running workflows, offering async-first patterns (push notifications) and streaming for real-time updates<cite id="22"></cite>.

Beyond task execution, A2A tackles modality-rich interactions by supporting diverse content types, enabling agents to exchange images, audio/video, and structured artifacts in a unified way<cite id="22"></cite>. It also aims to reduce data silos and integration complexity in enterprise settings by enabling secure, standardized exchange across systems and by aligning with enterprise security and observability practices<cite id="6"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>. Finally, A2A’s UX negotiation and standardized task lifecycle improve user experience and composability in complex workflows<cite id="22"></cite>.

## Enterprise Implications and Practical Considerations

For enterprises, A2A’s async-first design and support for push notifications and SSE make it well-suited for long-running, cross-system tasks and disconnected scenarios, while its modality agnosticism and opaque execution enhance security and flexibility<cite id="22"></cite>. The protocol’s alignment with OpenAPI authentication and enterprise monitoring practices further supports deployment in production environments<cite id="22"></cite>. In contrast, MCP remains a strong choice for connecting models to external tools and data sources within a single system boundary, where tool discovery, invocation, and resource access are the primary needs<cite id="12"></cite>.

## Conclusion

MCP and A2A serve different but complementary roles in the agentic ecosystem. MCP focuses on connecting models to external capabilities at the model–tool boundary, while A2A extends beyond this boundary to enable agent-to-agent communication, discovery, and task coordination<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>. A2A’s innovations—async-first task management, modality agnosticism, opaque execution, standardized task negotiation, and enterprise-grade security—address fragmentation, long-running workflows, multimodal collaboration, and secure interoperability in enterprise settings<cite id="22"></cite>. Together, these protocols provide a layered approach to agentic interaction, from model–tool integration to cross-agent collaboration<cite id="7"></cite>.</answer>

<fetch fetch_id="46e243f7-acdc-4010-a9fc-e7fdfaa77b6f"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:6"><url>https://a2a-protocol.com/</url><title>A2A Protocol</title><pagination_content start_offset="0" end_offset="790"># A2A Protocol

## A New Era of AI Agent Interoperability

The A2A Protocol (Agent2Agent), announced by Google Cloud on April 9, 2025, enables AI agents to communicate with each other, securely exchange information, and coordinate actions even when built by different vendors or using different frameworks.

## What is the A2A Protocol?

The A2A (Agent2Agent) Protocol is an open protocol designed to enable seamless collaboration between AI agents. This protocol allows AI agents to securely communicate with each other regardless of underlying infrastructure technologies, automating complex enterprise workflows.

Developed with support and contributions from over 50 technology partners including Atlassian, Box, Cohere, Intuit, Langchain, MongoDB, PayPal, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, UKG, and Workday; as well as leading service providers such as Accenture, BCG, Capgemini, Cognizant, Deloitte, HCLTech, Infosys, KPMG, McKinsey, PwC, TCS, and Wipro.

## Key Features

### Capability Discovery

Agents can advertise their capabilities using an "Agent Card" in JSON format, allowing client agents to identify the best agent for a specific task.

### Task Management

Communication between agents focuses on task completion to fulfill end-user requests. For long-running tasks, agents can stay synchronized on task status.

### Collaboration

Agents can send messages to each other to communicate context, replies, artifacts, or user instructions.

### User Experience Negotiation

Through "parts" (fully formed pieces of content like generated images), client and remote agents can negotiate the correct format and user interface capabilities.

## Design Principles

The A2A protocol is designed based on five key principles:

- Embrace agentic capabilities: A2A enables agents to collaborate in their natural, unstructured modalities, even when they don't share memory, tools, and context.

- Build on existing standards: The protocol is built on popular standards including HTTP, SSE, and JSON-RPC.

- Secure by default: A2A is designed to support enterprise-grade authentication and authorization with parity to OpenAPI's authentication schemes.

- Support for long-running tasks: The protocol provides flexibility to complete everything from quick tasks to deep research that may take hours.

- Modality agnostic: A2A supports various modalities beyond text, including audio and video streaming.

## Technical Documentation

A2A is built on existing standards and allows for easy integration with your current systems. The protocol utilizes:

- HTTP and JSON for standard communication

- Server-Sent Events (SSE) for real-time updates

- JSON RPC for structured interactions

- OpenAPI-compatible authentication schemes

The protocol supports a variety of use cases across industries, enabling sophisticated agent-to-agent communication and collaboration.

## Learn More

# Model Context Protocol (MCP)

You can build and deploy <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:12-<|link|>:5" text="Model Context Protocol (MCP) ↗" /> servers on Cloudflare.

## What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

<link reference_id="<|superscript|>:12-<|link|>:6" text="Model Context Protocol (MCP) ↗" /> is an open standard that connects AI systems with external applications. Think of MCP like a USB-C port for AI applications. Just as USB-C provides a standardized way to connect your devices to various accessories, MCP provides a standardized way to connect AI agents to different services.

### MCP Terminology

- **MCP Hosts** : AI assistants (like <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:12-<|link|>:7" text="Claude ↗" /> or <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:12-<|link|>:8" text="Cursor ↗" />), AI agents, or applications that need to access external capabilities.

- **MCP Clients** : Clients embedded within the MCP hosts that connect to MCP servers and invoke tools. Each MCP client instance has a single connection to an MCP server.

- **MCP Servers** : Applications that expose <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:12-<|link|>:9" text="tools" />, <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:12-<|link|>:10" text="prompts ↗" />, and <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:12-<|link|>:11" text="resources ↗" /> that MCP clients can use.

### Remote vs. local MCP connections

The MCP standard supports two modes of operation:

- **Remote MCP connections** : MCP clients connect to MCP servers over the Internet, establishing a connection using <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:12-<|link|>:12" text="Streamable HTTP" />, and authorizing the MCP client access to resources on the user's account using <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:12-<|link|>:13" text="OAuth" />.

- **Local MCP connections** : MCP clients connect to MCP servers on the same machine, using <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:12-<|link|>:14" text="stdio ↗" /> as a local transport method.

### Best Practices

- **Tool design** : Do not treat your MCP server as a wrapper around your full API schema. Instead, build tools that are optimized for specific user goals and reliable outcomes. Fewer, well-designed tools often outperform many granular ones, especially for agents with small context windows or tight latency budgets.

- **Scoped permissions** : Deploying several focused MCP servers, each with narrowly scoped permissions, reduces the risk of over-privileged access and makes it easier to manage and audit what each server is allowed to do.

- **Tool descriptions** : Detailed parameter descriptions help agents understand how to use your tools correctly — including what values are expected, how they affect behavior, and any important constraints. This reduces errors and improves reliability.

- **Evaluation tests** : Use evaluation tests ('evals') to measure the agent’s ability to use your tools correctly. Run these after any updates to your server or tool descriptions to catch regressions early and track improvements over time.

### Get Started

Go to the <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:12-<|link|>:15" text="Getting Started" /> guide to learn how to build and deploy your first remote MCP server to Cloudflare.</pagination_content></document></fetch>

<fetch fetch_id="3a9d6254-bd8c-47dd-b1a2-23e811d6598a"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:11"><url>https://google-a2a.github.io/A2A/specification/</url><title>Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol Specification</title><pagination_content start_offset="0" end_offset="3988">Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol Specification
Version: 0.2.1
1. Introduction
The Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol is an open standard designed to facilitate communication and interoperability between independent, potentially opaque AI agent systems. In an ecosystem where agents might be built using different frameworks, languages, or by different vendors, A2A provides a common language and interaction model.
This document provides the detailed technical specification for the A2A protocol. Its primary goal is to enable agents to:
Discover each other's capabilities.
Negotiate interaction modalities (text, files, structured data).
Manage collaborative tasks.
Securely exchange information to achieve user goals without needing access to each other's internal state, memory, or tools.
1.1. Key Goals of A2A
Interoperability: Bridge the communication gap between disparate agentic systems.
Collaboration: Enable agents to delegate tasks, exchange context, and work together on complex user requests.
Discovery: Allow agents to dynamically find and understand the capabilities of other agents.
Flexibility: Support various interaction modes including synchronous request/response, streaming for real-time updates, and asynchronous push notifications for long-running tasks.
Security: Facilitate secure communication patterns suitable for enterprise environments, relying on standard web security practices.
Asynchronicity: Natively support long-running tasks and interactions that may involve human-in-the-loop scenarios.
1.2. Guiding Principles
Simple: Reuse existing, well-understood standards (HTTP, JSON-RPC 2.0, Server-Sent Events).
Enterprise Ready: Address authentication, authorization, security, privacy, tracing, and monitoring by aligning with established enterprise practices.
Async First: Designed for (potentially very) long-running tasks and human-in-the-loop interactions.
Modality Agnostic: Support exchange of diverse content types including text, audio/video (via file references), structured data/forms, and potentially embedded UI components (e.g., iframes referenced in parts).
Opaque Execution: Agents collaborate based on declared capabilities and exchanged information, without needing to share their internal thoughts, plans, or tool implementations.
2. Core Concepts Summary
A2A revolves around several key concepts. For detailed explanations, please refer to the Key Concepts guide.
A2A Client: An application or agent that initiates requests to an A2A Server on behalf of a user or another system.
A2A Server (Remote Agent): An agent or agentic system that exposes an A2A-compliant HTTP endpoint, processing tasks and providing responses.
Agent Card: A JSON metadata document published by an A2A Server, describing its identity, capabilities, skills, service endpoint, and authentication requirements.
Message: A communication turn between a client and a remote agent, having a role ("user" or "agent") and containing one or more Parts .
Task: The fundamental unit of work managed by A2A, identified by a unique ID. Tasks are stateful and progress through a defined lifecycle.
Part: The smallest unit of content within a Message or Artifact (e.g., TextPart, FilePart, DataPart).
Artifact: An output (e.g., a document, image, structured data) generated by the agent as a result of a task, composed of Parts .
Streaming (SSE): Real-time, incremental updates for tasks (status changes, artifact chunks) delivered via Server-Sent Events.
Push Notifications:  Asynchronous task updates delivered via server-initiated HTTP POST requests to a client-provided webhook URL, for long-running or disconnected scenarios.
Context: An optional, server-generated identifier to logically group related tasks.
Extension: A mechanism for agents to provide additional functionality or data beyond the core A2A specification.
3.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a central driver of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, reshaping labor markets through automation, task reorganization, and new skill demands. Synthesizing recent research, AI’s impact is best understood through three lenses: exposure measures and displacement risk, heterogeneous labor-market effects and adjustment, and the emergence of new opportunities and skills<cite id="82"></cite>. Early occupation-level estimates suggested high automation risk, but task-based analyses across 21 OECD countries found only about 9% of jobs automatable on average, with sizable cross-country differences and important adjustment channels that limit large-scale job losses<cite id="53"></cite>. Historical evidence further cautions that past automation did not erase inequality and falling labor-force participation, underscoring that outcomes depend on institutions and policies<cite id="50"></cite>.

At the micro level, firm-level data show AI use is reshaping tasks more than headcounts. Using the U.S. Census Bureau’s business survey, about 27% of AI-using firms replaced tasks, but only 5% changed employment; projected shares rise to 35% and 12% as AI adoption advances<cite id="85"></cite>. Complementarity theories align with these patterns: AI raises demand for workers whose tasks complement AI, especially in high-skill roles, while displacing low-skill tasks; evidence supports this “task reassignment” channel in OECD countries<cite id="58"></cite>. Online-vacancy analyses also document rapid growth in AI-related postings and skill requirements, with AI-exposed establishments reducing hiring in non-AI positions even as they expand AI roles, though aggregate employment and wage effects remain too small to detect at the occupation or industry level<cite id="79"></cite>.

Occupational transition models emphasize that AI will likely substitute for routine tasks and complement non-routine tasks, creating a “polymorphic” occupational structure with greater variety and complexity. This reshaping is evident in the rise of hybrid roles that blend technical and creative skills, as well as in the expansion of AI-related jobs<cite id="35"></cite>. Empirical studies of AI innovators report small but positive employment effects, concentrated in service sectors and younger firms, with some evidence of increasing returns as AI focus intensifies<cite id="83"></cite>. Cross-country evidence further suggests no clear link between AI exposure and overall employment growth, but higher employment growth in computer-intensive occupations with increased AI use, alongside mixed effects on hours worked<cite id="84"></cite>.

Industries are responding with distinct organizational and managerial changes. A systematic review of AI’s impact on management highlights opportunities and challenges, including efficiency gains and learning, alongside concerns about algorithmic bias, technostress, and job displacement; actionable guidance for managers is provided<cite id="2"></cite>. Case-study evidence from OECD firms indicates that AI implementation alters task composition, redefines roles, and influences training and leadership practices, reinforcing the managerial literature’s emphasis on human–AI integration<cite id="83"></cite>. These industry-level adaptations are consistent with broader findings that automation-induced task change is pervasive and persistent, with firms reorganizing around complementary technologies<cite id="57"></cite>.

Policymakers face a distributional challenge: while automation disproportionately affects lower-skilled workers, innovation-driven productivity and demand shifts can raise living standards if matched by retraining and active labor-market policies. OECD work underscores that adjustment costs fall heaviest on less-qualified workers, and that retraining and social protection are crucial to coping with inequality and ensuring sufficient upskilling<cite id="53"></cite>. Historical automation patterns caution that institutions mediate outcomes, with rising inequality and lower labor-force participation as possible side effects absent strong policy safeguards<cite id="50"></cite>. In this context, research on AI’s future of work calls for integrating macro, meso, and micro perspectives to better anticipate and manage labor-market impacts<cite id="82"></cite>.

Taken together, the literature indicates that AI is causing significant, data-driven disruptions across labor markets, with heterogeneous effects across occupations, industries, and firms. Task substitution and complementarity are evident, new opportunities are emerging, and managerial practices are evolving; however, aggregate labor-market consequences remain muted at current adoption levels, and outcomes hinge on policy and institutional design<cite id="79"></cite><cite id="85"></cite><cite id="58"></cite><cite id="83"></cite><cite id="84"></cite>.

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="AI and the labor market jobs displaced created Frey Osborne 2017 Automation and AI" search_time="2026年5月16日11时58分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:52"><title>THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON WORK: An evidence review prepared for the Royal Society and the British Academy</title><hostname>The Royal Society</hostname><url>https://royalsociety.org/~/media/policy/projects/ai-and-work/frontier-review-the-impact-of-AI-on-work.pdf</url><publish_time>2018年9月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:53"><title>The Risk of Automation for Jobs in OECD Countries: A Comparative Analysis</title><summary>In recent years, there has been a revival of concerns that automation and digitalisation might after all result in a jobless future. The debate has been fuelled by studies for the US and Europe arguing that a substantial share of jobs is at “risk of computerisation”. These studies follow an occupation-based approach proposed by Frey and Osborne (2013), i.e. they assume that whole occupations rather than single job-tasks are automated by technology. As we argue, this might lead to an overestimation of job automatibility, as occupations labelled as high-risk occupations often still contain a substantial share of tasks that are hard to automate. Our paper serves two purposes. Firstly, we estimate the job automatibility of jobs for 21 OECD countries based on a task-based approach. In contrast to other studies, we take into account the heterogeneity of workers’ tasks within occupations. Overall, we find that, on average across the 21 OECD countries, 9 % of jobs are automatable. The threat from technological advances thus seems much less pronounced compared to the occupation-based approach. We further find heterogeneities across OECD countries. For instance, while the share of automatable jobs is 6 % in Korea, the corresponding share is 12 % in Austria. Differences between countries may reflect general differences in workplace organisation, differences in previous investments into automation technologies as well as differences in the education of workers across countries. The second purpose of this paper is to critically reflect on the recent line of studies that generate figures on the “risk of computerisation” and to provide a comprehensive discussion on possible adjustment processes of firms and workers to automation and digitalisation. In particular, we argue that the estimated share of “jobs at risk” must not be equated with actual or expected employment losses from technological advances for three reasons. First, the utilisation of new technologies is a slow process, due to economic, legal and societal hurdles, so that technological substitution often does not take place as expected. Second, even if new technologies are introduced, workers can adjust to changing technological endowments by switching tasks, thus preventing technological unemployment. Third, technological change also generates additional jobs through demand for new technologies and through higher competitiveness. The main conclusion from our paper is that automation and digitalisation are unlikely to destroy large numbers of jobs. However, low qualified workers are likely to bear the brunt of the adjustment costs as the automatibility of their jobs is higher compared to highly qualified workers. Therefore, the likely challenge for the future lies in coping with rising inequality and ensuring sufficient (re-)training especially for low qualified workers.</summary><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>OECD Social, Employment and Migration Working Papers</publisher><author_list><author name="Melanie Arntz" affiliation="Institute for Employment Research, University of Heidelberg" /><author name="Terry Gregory" affiliation="Luxembourg Institute of Socio-Economic Research" /><author name="Ulrich Zierahn" affiliation="Utrecht University" /></author_list><url>https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Terry-Gregory/publication/303311529_The_Risk_of_Automation_for_Jobs_in_OECD_Countries_A_Comparative_Analysis/links/57

It was approved and declassified by the Committee on Digital Economy Policy on 18 May 2018 and prepared for publication by the OECD Secretariat.</summary><hostname>OECD</hostname><publisher>OECD DIGITAL ECONOMY PAPERS</publisher><url>https://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/docserver/f1a650d9-en.pdf?expires=1539358458&id=id&accname=guest&checksum=8BD266ECE8365F1C158CABDA52D758F2</url><publish_time>2018年5月18日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:66"><title>Advancing the G20 AI Principles – rationales and illustrative actions</title><summary>G20 Leaders welcomed the G20 AI Principles in 2019 against a backdrop of burgeoning new and emerging applications of AI systems. Criminal justice, security, marketing and advertising, and many other activities now use AI systems. At the same time, AI policy-making in G20 countries is in an experimental and innovative phase. Countries are actively seeking to formulate national strategies and policies that harness the promise of AI while mitigating its challenges and supporting public trust and confidence in the technology. In the first few months of 2020 alone, several major policy initiatives were put to public consultation by G20 economies, including the United States’ draft memorandum on guidance for regulation of AI applications, and the European Commission’s White Paper on AI (further detail on both policies is provided below). Both these factors argue for strong and coherent efforts to advance implementation of the G20 AI Principles. Given the breadth of AI applications – and the associated potential impacts on G20 economies and societies if these are not trustworthy – it is critical to progress efforts towards human-centred, transparent, robust and accountable AI systems, and to build a policy environment that facilitates that progress. The time is propitious, as the policy experimentation currently underway offers great scope for innovative approaches and peer learning from national approaches across the G20, and the potential to shape global directions for AI development. Given the centrality of data to AI systems, this effort also dovetails well with the G20’s interest in issues of data access and sharing and data flows. To capitalise on this moment and support the advancement of the G20 AI Principles, the DETF under the 2020 Saudi Presidency compiled Examples of National Policies to Advance the G20 AI Principles that provides countries with examples of national strategies and policies as they implement the G20 AI Principles in their particular country contexts. To support this, this chapter provides examples of national strategies and innovative policy practices that intend to steer towards responsible stewardship of trustworthy AI. This paper looks at the possible links between AI and employment in a cross-country context. It adapts the AI occupational impact measure developed by Felten, Raj and Seamans—an indicator measuring the degree to which occupations rely on abilities in which AI has made the most progress—and extends it to 23 OECD countries. Overall, there appears to be no clear relationship between AI exposure and employment growth. However, in occupations where computer use is high, greater exposure to AI is linked to higher employment growth. The paper also finds suggestive evidence of a negative relationship between AI exposure and growth in average hours worked among occupations where computer use is low. One possible explanation is that partial automation by AI increases productivity directly as well as by shifting the task composition of occupations toward higher value-added tasks. This increase in labor productivity and output counteracts the direct displacement effect of automation through AI for workers with good digital skills, who may find it easier to use AI effectively and shift to non-automatable, higher-value added tasks within their occupations. The opposite could be true for workers with poor digital skills, who may not be able to interact efficiently with AI and thus reap all potential benefits of the technology1.</summary><hostname>Frontiers</hostname><author_list><author name="Alexandre Georgieff" /><author name="Raphaela Hyee" /></author_list><url>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/frai.2022.832736/pdf?isPublishedV2=False</url><publish_time>2022年5月10日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:85"><title>The impact of AI on the workforce: Tasks versus jobs?</title><summary>Will the adoption of AI by businesses substitute for worker tasks or jobs? This is a core question for which relatively scarce evidence exists—especially in the wake of recent advances in generative AI. Using a new large-scale business survey by the U.S. Census Bureau, we find that AI use is having a much greater impact on worker tasks than on employment levels at the firm level. About 27% of firms using AI report replacing worker tasks, but only about 5% experience employment change due to AI use. # A New Paradigm of Holistic Empowerment in Elementary English Education and Teaching

## Executive Summary
This report proposes a new paradigm for elementary English education grounded in holistic empowerment—teaching that nurtures young learners’ cognitive, socioemotional, cultural, and linguistic development simultaneously, so students leave the classroom not only with better English skills but with greater confidence, agency, and motivation to keep learning. Evidence from classroom-based studies and teacher professional development shows that student-centered, inquiry-based, and culturally sustaining practices improve engagement, language outcomes, and attitudes, and that empowering teachers is a prerequisite for empowering learners<cite id="69"></cite><cite id="68"></cite><cite id="80"></cite>. The report synthesizes research into practical strategies for novice teachers, including thematic curricula, formative assessment, play-based learning, and inclusive classroom environments, and offers a set of actionable recommendations for school leaders and teachers<cite id="20"></cite><cite id="34"></cite><cite id="73"></cite><cite id="87"></cite>.

## What Is Holistic Empowerment in Elementary English Education?
Holistic empowerment in elementary English education is an approach that views language learning as integral to the whole child’s development—cognitive, socioemotional, cultural, and linguistic—rather than as a set of isolated skills to be mastered<cite id="61"></cite>. In young learners’ contexts, empowerment means creating classrooms where students feel safe to take risks, see themselves as capable language users, and connect English to their identities and interests, which in turn deepens motivation and engagement<cite id="68"></cite><cite id="63"></cite>. At the teacher level, holistic empowerment also means supporting educators’ language proficiency and reflective practice so they can model confidence and implement student-centered strategies effectively<cite id="69"></cite>.

## Why a New Paradigm Is Needed
Traditional elementary English instruction often prioritizes rote skill drills and test preparation, which can leave students disengaged and teachers feeling unprepared to meet diverse needs<cite id="78"></cite>. In many systems, English is taught in isolation from other subjects and from students’ cultural lives, reinforcing marginalization rather than inclusion<cite id="60"></cite>. However, data-driven studies show that student-centered, inquiry-based, and culturally sustaining practices improve both engagement and language outcomes and foster positive attitudes among young learners<cite id="68"></cite><cite id="80"></cite>. Moreover, empowering teachers through holistic professional development leads to improved classroom practice and more supportive learning environments for students<cite id="69"></cite>.

## Evidence-Based Practices for Holistic Empowerment in Elementary English
### 1. Student-Centered, Inquiry-Based Teaching
Research in international schools demonstrates that student-centered, inquiry-based methods foster critical thinking, global awareness, and practical language skills, enhancing student engagement and learning outcomes<cite id="68"></cite>. In elementary English, inquiry-based activities—such as questioning around narrative texts and community inquiry approaches—empower students to take ownership of speaking and listening goals while deepening comprehension and classroom discourse<cite id="85"></cite>.

### 2. Culturally Sustaining and Asset-Based Pedagogies
Culturally sustaining pedagogy honors students’ linguistic and cultural identities, reducing marginalization and strengthening motivation to engage with English learning<cite id="60"></cite>. Asset-based approaches explicitly value students’ existing cultural and linguistic assets, evaluate current practices, and incorporate families and communities to teach content with high expectations<cite id="45"></cite>. In multilingual contexts, living-language empowerment pedagogies connect English to students’ lived experiences, making learning relevant and empowering<cite id="68"></cite>.

### 3. Playful and Thematic Learning
Playful strategies promote meaningful learning by expanding creativity, confidence, participation, and motivation, while diversifying teachers’ instructional options<cite id="87"></cite>. Spiral thematic curricula that weave English across kindergarten to fifth grade help children learn language in meaningful contexts and encourage teacher reflection and sensitivity to learners’ needs<cite id="20"></cite>. These approaches align with findings that young learners benefit from integrated, experiential learning that connects to their interests and daily lives<cite id="73"></cite>.

### 4. Formative Assessment and Student Agency
Formative assessment practices that elicit evidence of learning, provide timely feedback, and activate students to own their learning are among the most powerful levers for raising achievement<cite id="34"></cite>. In elementary English, classroom activities that encourage self-assessment, peer feedback, and reflective portfolios can foster student agency and a sense of responsibility for learning<cite id="46"></cite>. These practices support the holistic goal of helping students become active, self-directed learners<cite id="34"></cite>.

### 5. Inclusive, Language-Rich Environments
Oracy-centered instruction and inclusive EFL practices ensure equal access to English and extend enjoyable language learning to all students<cite id="54"></cite>. Creating language-rich environments, building supportive teacher–student relationships, using inclusive pedagogies, encouraging parental involvement, and providing continuous professional development are repeatedly identified as best practices for enhancing language competency and child empowerment<cite id="63"></cite>.

### 6. Teacher Empowerment Through Professional Development
Holistic professional development programs that combine target-language improvement with pedagogical reflection can increase teachers’ confidence, methodological flexibility, and classroom effectiveness, while improving attitudes among both teachers and students<cite id="69"></cite>. Novice teachers benefit from school-wide leadership that supports culturally responsive practices, family engagement, and trauma-informed instruction, which create the conditions for empowered learning<cite id="25"></cite>.

## Practical Recommendations for Novice Teachers
- Start small with student-centered activities: Try inquiry-based questioning or community inquiry units to give students a voice in English and observe how it changes classroom discourse and engagement<cite id="85"></cite>.
- Use thematic, integrated units: Design lessons around topics that connect to students’ interests and daily lives, and revisit concepts across grades to build depth and relevance<cite id="20"></cite>.
- Incorporate play and games: Use songs, “Listen and Do” activities, and playful strategies to make learning enjoyable and to expand participation and creativity<cite id="72"></cite><cite id="75"></cite><cite id="87"></cite>.
- Build relationships and culture: Learn students’ names, interests, and home languages; integrate cultural references and family voices into lessons to show that English matters in their lives<cite id="60"></cite><cite id="45"></cite>.
- Use formative assessment: Ask students to reflect on their learning, use rubrics or checklists, and give peer feedback to help them take ownership of progress<cite id="34"></cite><cite id="46"></cite>.
- Reflect and collaborate: Keep a teaching journal, share ideas with colleagues, and seek feedback to refine your practice and grow as an empowered educator<cite id="78"></cite>.

## Data-Driven Outcomes and Implications
Studies show that inquiry-based and student-centered approaches improve engagement and learning outcomes for young learners, supporting a shift away from passive, skill-focused instruction<cite id="68"></cite>. Culturally sustaining and asset-based practices reduce marginalization and increase motivation, which are key drivers of empowerment<cite id="60"></cite><cite id="45"></cite>. Playful and thematic learning boosts creativity, confidence, and participation, aligning with holistic goals for the whole child<cite id="87"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>. Teacher empowerment through holistic professional development leads to improved classroom practice and more positive attitudes among students<cite id="69"></cite>. Together, these findings imply that a new paradigm of holistic empowerment in elementary English education is not only feasible but also effective when grounded in evidence-based practices and supported by school leadership<cite id="68"></cite><cite id="69"></cite><cite id="80"></cite>.

A new paradigm of holistic empowerment in elementary English education centers students as active, culturally situated learners and teachers as reflective, confident facilitators of learning. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="elementary English assessment holistic empowerment formative assessment classroom practices" search_time="2026年5月16日11时58分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:34"><title>Formative Assessment and Effective Teaching and Learning*: Consolidating Gains from Singapore, Brunei and Hong Kong</title><summary>Several extensive reviews of the research literature have concluded that formative assessment is the most powerful factor in raising student achievement. This paper explores the questions: What is formative assessment? How does formative assessment operate in the classroom? Under what conditions will it work? This paper discusses findings from studies of formative assessment and the experience of several English language projects: how classroom discussions, questions, activities and tasks can be used to elicit evidence of student learning, how this feedback can be used to propel students' learning and how to set up conditions for activating students to own their learning. The paper draws on the author's 20+ years of experience in large scale professional development projects, working in collaboration with classroom teachers, asking the same questions as those asked by teachers and seeking best fit'solutions' for the day to day challenges faced by teachers. All these projects aimed at improving children's English language development and their engagement with learning (LLELP, 2006; Ng, 2001; Ng & Sullivan, 2001) and engagement they all involved children who were learning English as speakers of other languages (ESOL). The earliest programme in Singapore (1985-1990) worked at the lower primary levels (Primary 1-3) with the later programmes in Brunei (1989-1994) and Hong Kong (2000-2006) covering Primary 1 to 6. The Hong Kong project had also a simpler version of the programme at the preschool level (1997-1999) and Singapore (where English has become the main language for classroom instruction), has developed an updated version for Primary 1 through to 6 (2006-2011). Exploration is currently ongoing in Singapore to adapt the basic conceptual framework to the Lower Secondary (from 2010) and Kindergarten levels (from 2012). The lower primary (Primary 1-3) projects were book-based programmes involving elements of Shared Book and Language Experience Approaches, suitably adapted to the educational systems they were operating in. The teaching techniques in the upper primary programmes (LLELP, 2006) were expanded to include Sustained Silent Reading (SSR), Guided Reading (GR), Know-Want to Know-Learn (KWL - a reading comprehension technique, Ogle, 1989) and Retelling (Brown & Cambourne, 1987). There was also a greater emphasis in the upper primary on explicit teaching of text-types and grammar. All the projects involved mainly students from average income home backgrounds in the three educational systems. In the recent Singapore adaptations, the goal is to make freely available to all schools the resources of the developed programmes. These programmes were based on sound pedagogical principles consistent with the findings of research into effective reading and language classrooms (see for example Duffy, 2003; Duke & Pearson, 2002; Hoffman, McCarthey, Elliot, Bayles, Price, Ferree & Abbott, 1998; National Reading Panel, 2000; Pressley, 2006; Pressley, Rankin & Yokoi, 1996). Features promoted by these programmes include: promoting high academic engagement in the classroom through an emphasis on motivating students. a combination of whole class and small group teaching that provides scaffolding for students as they read and write. This allows students to work within their 'zones of proximal development', that is, being challenged without being frustrated. a greater proportion of time spent on actual reading and writing than on workbook exercises.</summary><publisher>Assessment and Learning</publisher><author_list><author name="Seok Moi Ng" affiliation="Ministry of Education, Singapore and The University of Auckland" /></author_list><url>https://wlts.edb.hkedcity.net/filemanager/file/AandL2chapter/A&L2_(10)%20%20NgSeo

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="holistic empowerment young learners English education definition characteristics practices" search_time="2026年5月16日11时58分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:44"><title>SUCCEEDING WITH LATINO STUDENTS THROUGH AN EMPOWERMENT PEDAGOGY OF LIVING LANGUAGE</title><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>New Mexico Journal of Reading</publisher><author_list><author name="Myriam Nohemi Torres" affiliation="New Mexico State University" /><author name="Marisol Ruiz" /></author_list><url>https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Myriam-Torres-4/publication/336148034_Succeeding_with_Latino_Students_through_an_Empowerment_Pedagogy_of_Living_Language/links/5d92d65b458515202b777c14/Succeeding-with-Latino-Students-through-an-Empowerment-Pedagogy-of-Living-Language.pdf</url><publish_time>2013年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:45"><title>Asset-Based Pedagogies for English Learner Curriculum</title><summary>Past research has shown that English language classes for English learners (ELs) often center around English-only policies and do not encourage the use of students’ existing linguistic and cultural knowledge (Figueroa & Torff, 2018). Classes for English learners only focus on learning English, and the curriculum is not meant to help students succeed in other subjects, often causing them to fall behind non-English learners (Figueroa & Torff, 2018). Furthermore, teachers may not be adequately trained to teach ELs coming from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds (Nieto, 2000). Asset-based pedagogies encourage the use of curricula for ELs that incorporate the cultural and linguistic backgrounds that students already have. Using the literature on asset-based pedagogies, I identified six core characteristics of this approach: valuing student assets, evaluating current practices, analyzing personal views, incorporating family and community, teaching content that demonstrates high expectations, and teaching relevant content (e.g. Ladson-Billing’s, 1994; González & Moll, 2005; Hollie, 2011; Hammond, 2017; Paris & Alim, 2017). This research contributes to a better understanding of how asset-based pedagogies can be used to create more appropriate curricula for English learners.</summary><hostname>eScholarship</hostname><publisher>Imagine: A Promise Scholars & McNair Scholars Journal</publisher><author_list><author name="Carla Suarez Soto" affiliation="Department of Linguistics" /></author_list><url>https://escholarship.org/content/qt9fq9332v/qt9fq9332v.pdf</url><publish_time>2023年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:46"><title>"This Is My Portfolio": Portfolios in Upper Secondary School English Studies</title><summary>This qualitative case study describes a portfolio program in the teaching of English as a foreign language in two Finnish upper secondary schools. Approximately 100 students participated in the portfolio program, whose topic area was culture. First, the purpose of this action research was to try out and develop portfolios in foreign language teaching as a pedagogical innovation. Second, the aim was to foster students' empowerment, i.e., their active and responsible role in learning. The primary research questions were twofold: How did the portfolio program proceed and progress? and Did the portfolio program foster student empowerment? Different portfolio profiles and portraits emerged from the data collected. Findings suggest that a great majority of the students both liked the portfolio approach and took charge of their learning. Thus, the portfolios seemed to offer a vehicle for student empowerment. Some students, however, disliked the portfolio course, finding the topic area uninspiring and the student-centered and self-directed approach inefficient, difficult, or unsuitable for them.
