In collegial relationships that thrive, teachers listen deeply to one another. Teachers are energized by these interactions; their instructional practices improve, and their students benefit. We also noticed a conundrum related to collaboration. While principals may actually support and encourage close teacher collaboration, they are often unable to provide organizational structures that offer time for collaboration (Dalton et al., 2004). A number of educators reported their schools are moving away from teaming and common planning time—a move that impedes collaboration. Without common planning time in the school day, collaboration and teaming rarely occur on any sustained basis. Collaboration must be a practice expected by the organization, and it must be valued and intentional. Collaborative approaches can promote school change that extends beyond individual classrooms. When teachers learn together, students in the school benefit (Darling-Hammond, Wei, Andree, Richardson, & Orphanos, 2009). Common planning time and professional learning communities are organizational structures through which this can happen. But organizational structures alone are not sufficient. For authentic connections among colleagues to develop over an extended period requires that participants find collaboration to be useful (Trubowitz & Longo, 1997). Teachers spend more time on test-taking strategies and less time on meaningful curriculum (Greene et al., 2008). A middle grades teacher lamented, “All my curriculum is test-preparation based. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="holistic empowerment elementary English education keywords" search_time="2026年5月16日11时58分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:54"><title>Orality, Inclusion and Equality in the EFL Primary Classroom</title><summary>This paper describes the interplay between orality and inclusive English as a Foreign Language Teaching (in the primary classroom), with reference to the Italian context. # Overview

Artificial Intelligence-Generated Content (AIGC) has rapidly entered primary and secondary school classrooms worldwide, reshaping how teachers design instruction and how students engage with learning. Across case studies, AIGC spans text-to-image tools, large language models like ChatGPT, and multimodal assistants, with educators reporting both enthusiasm and challenges as they scramble to adapt to AI’s ubiquity<cite id="9"></cite>. This report synthesizes global evidence into a practical framework, organizes applications by category, and offers actionable recommendations for integrating AIGC in K-12 settings.

# A Framework for Practical AIGC Integration

A practical framework for AIGC integration in K-12 classrooms includes: (1) teacher preparation and ethical literacy; (2) student-centered, scaffolded use of AI as an “object-to-think-with”; (3) multimodal and cross-disciplinary applications; and (4) assessment and policy aligned with digital literacy goals<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="11"></cite><cite id="1"></cite>. Teacher workshops that demystify TTIG tools and foreground ethical implications have enabled educators to design classroom-ready materials<cite id="10"></cite>. In STEM, treating ChatGPT and Bing Chat as objects-to-think-with supports reflective and critical thinking, creativity, and concept comprehension, provided AIs are integrated with collaborative learning and accuracy concerns are addressed<cite id="30"></cite>. AI literacy curricula for middle schoolers emphasize project-based, inquiry-driven learning to develop skills in AI creation, use, critique, and governance<cite id="11"></cite>.

# Categorization of Application Approaches

## 1. AI as a Creative and Design Tool (Text-to-Image)

Text-to-image generation (TTIG) has been co-designed with K–12 educators to teach technical, applied, and ethical dimensions, with pilots showing teachers’ readiness to prototype classroom materials<cite id="10"></cite>. In elementary art, an interface combining DALL-E and GPT (AskArt) supported background research, inspiration, and personalized guidance for group projects, increasing engagement while surfacing challenges in query formulation and interface suitability<cite id="2"></cite>. These cases demonstrate TTIG’s potential to scaffold creative expression and design thinking when paired with teacher-led ethical and technical instruction<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="2"></cite>.

## 2. AI as a Tutor and Feedback System (Text-to-Text)

ChatGPT-powered tutors can personalize and scale feedback, improving engagement and vocabulary use in science video learning, though they may elicit frustration when probing unnecessary details<cite id="45"></cite>. In math, detailed AI-generated feedback significantly boosted quiz performance compared to basic correctness-only feedback (Hake’s gain: 21.6% vs. 13.8%), underscoring scalable, personalized support<cite id="62"></cite>. For writing, teacher-guided ChatGPT feedback improved creative writing and writing self-efficacy in fourth graders, suggesting AI’s value when embedded in structured, guided practice<cite id="53"></cite>.

## 3. AI as a Content Creation and Curation Tool (Text-to-Text)

Teachers globally use ChatGPT to generate lesson plans, creative teaching materials, and differentiate instruction, reporting enhanced classroom interaction and motivation, alongside concerns about over-reliance and limited training infrastructure<cite id="35"></cite><cite id="70"></cite>. In test item development, AI tools accelerated reading test item creation across stages (passage creation, item generation, selection, vocabulary control, and styling), with teachers responding positively to the efficiency gains<cite id="78"></cite>. These applications highlight AI’s capacity to streamline content creation and curation when coupled with clear roles for human oversight<cite id="35"></cite><cite id="78"></cite>.

## 4. AI as a Learning Companion and Inquiry Support (Multimodal)

Multimodal assistants like Cognimates Scratch Copilot integrated into block-based coding environments support ideation, code generation, debugging, and asset creation, while revealing children’s agency in negotiating AI suggestions and learning from its limitations<cite id="59"></cite>. Inquiry-based digital story writing with AI enabled primary students to apply AI knowledge to authentic scenarios and propose AI-driven solutions, effectively fostering AI literacy beyond rote concepts<cite id="60"></cite>. These cases illustrate how multimodal AI can scaffold inquiry and creative problem-solving when aligned with constructivist pedagogy<cite id="59"></cite><cite id="60"></cite>.

## 5. AI in Subject-Specific Learning (Science, History, Evolution)

In secondary science, ChatGPT as an object-to-think-with enhanced reflective and critical thinking, creativity, and concept comprehension in simulated STEM experiences, though accuracy concerns and reduced human interaction must be mitigated<cite id="30"></cite>. For history, ChatGPT narratives were stylistically strong but lacked emotional depth; educators are advised to channel AI into task design and delivery rather than relying solely on narrative assignments<cite id="37"></cite>. In biology, ChatGPT provided limited conceptual enhancement on evolution, but students developed more positive attitudes toward AI-supported learning, underscoring the need for reflective, scaffolded use<cite id="23"></cite>.

## 6. AI in Language Learning (EFL Writing and Information Discovery)

In middle school EFL writing, structured engagement with ChatGPT-generated feedback correlated with proficiency, with mid-proficiency learners showing the highest overall engagement and high-proficiency learners demonstrating more critical cognitive engagement; instructor facilitation is essential for proficiency-differentiated scaffolding<cite id="22"></cite>. For information discovery tasks, analyses of ChatGPT responses for fourth-grade curricula revealed readability and language challenges, emphasizing the need for testing generative tools with children and robust training and supervision<cite id="69"></cite>.

# Practical Implementation Methods

- Co-design teacher workshops that demystify TTIG tools and foreground ethical implications to build educator capacity and classroom-ready materials<cite id="10"></cite>.
- Use AI as an object-to-think-with in STEM and coding, pairing AI assistance with collaborative learning and explicit attention to accuracy and reliability<cite id="30"></cite><cite id="59"></cite>.
- Scaffold AI feedback in writing and math with teacher guidance, ensuring personalized explanations, hints, and encouragement, and aligning tasks with learning objectives<cite id="45"></cite><cite id="62"></cite><cite id="53"></cite>.
- Integrate AI into content creation and assessment workflows (lesson planning, test item development) while maintaining human oversight and clear roles<cite id="35"></cite><cite id="78"></cite>.
- Design inquiry-based, multimodal projects (e.g., digital story writing, Scratch Copilot) to foster AI literacy and creative problem-solving aligned with constructivist principles<cite id="60"></cite><cite id="59"></cite>.
- Align subject-specific use (science, history, EFL) with clear learning goals, leveraging AI for task design and delivery while addressing narrative and conceptual gaps<cite id="37"></cite><cite id="23"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>.

# Evidence-Based Outcomes

Across studies, AI-assisted feedback and tutoring improved engagement, vocabulary use, and quiz performance in science and math, with statistically significant gains in math when detailed explanations and encouragement were provided<cite id="45"></cite><cite id="62"></cite>. In creative writing, teacher-guided ChatGPT feedback increased self-efficacy and creative output among fourth graders, indicating AI’s potential in formative support<cite id="53"></cite>. Teacher pilots of TTIG co-design programs demonstrated educators’ technical, applied, and ethical understanding, enabling prototype development for classroom use<cite id="10"></cite>. Inquiry-based AI projects in primary schools effectively fostered AI literacy, with students proposing authentic AI-driven solutions in digital stories<cite id="60"></cite>.

# Limitations and Risks

AI tools can produce biased, harmful, or unsafe content and may be queried in ways that yield unexpected or inaccurate results, necessitating testing with children and robust training and supervision<cite id="69"></cite>. In some cases, AI-supported learning showed limited conceptual enhancement but increased positive attitudes, highlighting the need for reflective, scaffolded use and digital literacy<cite id="23"></cite>. Teachers also report challenges such as limited digital infrastructure, lack of training, and uncertainty about AI’s role relative to traditional instruction, underscoring the importance of policy and professional development<cite id="70"></cite>.

# Future Trends

Future trends include multimodal assistants integrated into block-based coding environments that support ideation and debugging while preserving youth agency, and inquiry-based AI literacy programs that span disciplines to develop skills in AI creation, use, critique, and governance<cite id="59"></cite><cite id="60"></cite><cite id="11"></cite>. As AI becomes more prevalent, research will increasingly focus on integrating AI with collaborative learning, ensuring accuracy, and cultivating reflective practices to mitigate overreliance and misinformation risks<cite id="30"></cite><cite id="23"></cite>.

# Recommendations for Educators

- Prioritize teacher preparation and ethical literacy through co-design workshops and classroom materials that demystify TTIG and AI governance<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="11"></cite>.
- Use AI as a scaffolded learning companion, aligning it with clear learning goals and embedding teacher facilitation to support critical engagement and digital literacy<cite id="30"></cite><cite id="45"></cite><cite id="62"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>.
- Integrate AI into content creation and assessment workflows with human oversight, leveraging efficiency gains while maintaining pedagogical control<cite id="35"></cite><cite id="78"></cite>.
- Design multimodal, inquiry-based projects that connect AI to real-world problems and creative expression, fostering AI literacy and agency<cite id="60"></cite><cite id="59"></cite>.
- Align subject-specific applications with evidence-based practices, using AI to support task design and delivery while addressing narrative and conceptual gaps<cite id="37"></cite><cite id="23"></cite>.
- Establish policies and professional development to ensure infrastructure, training, and clear guidelines for classroom use, balancing innovation with safeguards<cite id="70"></cite>.

# Conclusion

Global case studies show AIGC can be a powerful resource in primary and secondary classrooms when integrated thoughtfully with teacher guidance, ethical literacy, and inquiry-based pedagogy. Evidence supports AI’s role as a tutor, feedback system, content creator, and multimodal learning companion, provided educators scaffold use, monitor accuracy, and cultivate digital literacy<cite id="45"></cite><cite id="62"></cite><cite id="53"></cite><cite id="35"></cite><cite id="78"></cite><cite id="30"></cite><cite id="59"></cite><cite id="60"></cite><cite id="11"></cite>. With careful implementation, AIGC can enhance engagement, creativity, and learning outcomes while preparing students to use and govern AI responsibly<cite id="22"></cite><cite id="23"></cite><cite id="37"></cite>.

# Evolution from Java Servlets to Spring Boot: A Data-Driven Report

## Overview
This report traces the evolution from Java Servlets to the Spring Boot framework, explaining the problems each iteration aimed to solve and detailing Spring’s core functionalities and essential developer knowledge. It synthesizes historical context, specification changes, and modern practices to provide a structured view of the Java web ecosystem’s maturation.<cite id="32"></cite>

## Servlets: The Foundation and Its Limitations
Servlets were introduced as a low-level API for handling HTTP requests and responses within a web container, requiring developers to implement lifecycle methods and manage HTTP details directly. While Servlets provided fine-grained control, they imposed boilerplate and deployment complexity, necessitating explicit configuration and servlet-container management, which increased the barrier to entry and slowed development.<cite id="55"></cite><cite id="57"></cite>

Servlet 3.0 (2009) introduced annotations and asynchronous request processing, reducing XML configuration and enabling non-blocking I/O, which improved developer productivity and application responsiveness. Servlet 3.1 (2014) added features like multipart/form-data enhancements and improved WebSocket support, reflecting a trend toward simplification and modern web capabilities.<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="60"></cite>

## Spring Framework: Abstraction and Inversion of Control
The Spring Framework emerged to address Servlets’ boilerplate and configuration complexity by providing an inversion-of-control (IoC) container and dependency injection, enabling loosely coupled, testable components. Early adopters reported reduced complexity and greater productivity by avoiding Enterprise JavaBeans (EJB) and leveraging Spring’s lightweight, non-intrusive approach for web applications.<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="41"></cite>

Spring’s core modules include the IoC container, which manages object lifecycles and dependencies, and Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP), which modularizes cross-cutting concerns. Spring MVC offers a flexible web-layer model with request mapping, handler methods, and view resolution, while Spring Data and JPA/JPQL simplify data access and persistence. Together, these components reduce boilerplate and promote separation of concerns in enterprise Java applications.<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="48"></cite><cite id="50"></cite>

## Spring Boot: Convention Over Configuration
Spring Boot was introduced to further cut down boilerplate and configuration, enabling developers to create production-ready applications with minimal setup. It automates configuration via auto-configuration and starter dependencies, eliminating the need to define dispatcher servlets, web jars, view resolvers, and component scans manually, thereby accelerating CRUD application development.<cite id="18"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>

Key Spring Boot features include embedded servers (Tomcat, Jetty, Undertow), opinionated defaults, and a rich ecosystem of starters that bundle dependencies and auto-configuration. This reduces build and deployment complexity, allowing developers to focus on business logic rather than infrastructure, and to deliver applications faster with consistent defaults.<cite id="18"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>

## Problems Each Iteration Aimed to Solve
- Servlets: Low-level control and boilerplate; developers had to handle HTTP manually and configure containers, increasing complexity and deployment overhead.<cite id="55"></cite><cite id="57"></cite>
- Spring Framework: Enterprise frameworks like EJB and heavy XML configuration raised complexity; Spring’s IoC and DI reduced coupling and simplified component assembly.<cite id="41"></cite><cite id="10"></cite>
- Spring Boot: Opinionated defaults and auto-configuration eliminated repetitive configuration, cutting down setup time and deployment friction.<cite id="18"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>

## Core Functionalities of the Spring Framework
- IoC and DI: Central to Spring, enabling declarative configuration and automated dependency injection across components.<cite id="10"></cite>
- AOP: Modularizes cross-cutting concerns such as logging and security, improving maintainability.<cite id="48"></cite>
- Spring MVC: A flexible web framework with request mapping and handler methods, supporting RESTful services and traditional views.<cite id="50"></cite>
- Data Access: Spring Data and JPA/JPQL simplify persistence, with declarative transactions and ORM capabilities that reduce boilerplate.<cite id="50"></cite><cite id="52"></cite>

## Essential Knowledge for Developers Working with Spring
Developers should understand IoC/DI principles, configuration metadata (XML, Java config, @ConfigurationProperties), and AOP concepts. Proficiency in Spring MVC is crucial, including request mapping, handler methods, and view resolution. Familiarity with Spring Data and JPA/JPQL will help manage data access efficiently, while knowledge of auto-configuration and starter dependencies streamlines project setup and maintenance.<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="48"></cite><cite id="50"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>

## Conclusion
From Servlets’ low-level APIs to Spring’s IoC-driven abstractions and Spring Boot’s convention-over-configuration paradigm, each iteration addressed specific pain points—boilerplate, configuration complexity, and deployment friction—to accelerate development and improve maintainability. Modern Spring Boot applications benefit from embedded servers, auto-configuration, and a rich ecosystem, enabling developers to focus on business logic while leveraging robust, production-ready defaults.<cite id="18"></cite><cite id="21"></cite><cite id="32"></cite>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Java Servlets evolution to Spring Boot problems solved core Spring functionalities essential knowledge for developers" search_time="2026年5月16日11时58分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:9"><title>SPRING BOOT ЯК ІНСТРУМЕНТ ДЛЯ ПРИСКОРЕННЯ РОЗРОБКИ ВЕБ-ДОДАТКІВ</title><summary>Для розробки сучасних веб-додатків можна використовувати багато різних технологій. Серед найчастіше використовуваних можна виділити наступні: • Servlet API; • Spring Framework; • Spring Boot. Кожна технологія має свої переваги та недоліки, а також використовується у різних галузях завдяки своему вбудованому функціоналу. Але враховуючи те, що ці технології призначено для розробки веб-додатків, розглянемо їх з точки зору клієнт-серверного архітектури. Servlet API - це стандартна бібліотека, яка надає можливість розробляти веб-додатки на платформі Java EE. Servlet е Java-класом, який містить ряд методів для обробки запитів від клієнтів та відправки відповідей на них. Кожен запит, що надходить на веб-сервер, передається відповідному сервілету, який генерує відповідь у вигляді HTML-сторінки, JSON-данних, або будь-якому іншому типу відповіді. Servlet API е нижчим рівнем інтерфейсу, тому для створення веб-додатків з його використанням потрібно здійснити більше зусиль. Розробка додатків на основі Servlet API вимагає знання HTTP-протоколу та Java-технологій, таких як Java Server Pages (JSP) та Java Server Faces (JSF). Створення серверної частини складається з кількох етапів. Спочатку необхідно створити клас, який реалізує інтерфейс javax.servlet.Servlet та успадковується від класу HttpServlet. Далі необхідно перевизначити методи життєвого циклу, такі як init() та destroy(), які викликаються при запуску та завершенні роботи Servlet. Для обробки запитів методи використовують два параметри - об'єкт HttpServletRequest, що містить запит від клієнта, та об'єкт HttpServletResponse, що відповідає на запит. Сервлети зберігаються в servlet-контейнерах, таких як WildFly або Tomcat, які потребують окремого встановлення та налаштування йе в окремими елементами веб-застосунку. Spring Framework – це програмний каркас з відкритим програмним кодом для платформи Java, який містить контейнери з підтримкою інверсії управління. The ends are freshly-graduated jobseekers and employers. This project introduces the best possible ways possible how a jobseeker can apply for a job and view his/her applied jobs through the system. At the same time the system provides the employers with a channel to post their vacancies in their efforts of hunting new employees and checking if there is any application to their posted jobs. apply for jobs. The following four major parts were designed and implemented. Firstly, the analysis phase the overall direction of the project was identified. Secondly, the design of the graphical user interface was implemented. Thirdly, a MySQL database that connects and communicates with spring boot was built to store all required data. Finally, Thymeleaf which is a modern server-side java template engine was written to display the data in a human-friendly way to the users of this application. The core features of this application for employers are posting jobs, editing jobs, deleting jobs and viewing applications. Other core features for jobseekers are viewing listed jobs in the system and applying for available jobs. In this application almost any employer can post a job online, the process is clear, easy to understand, less timewasting and user-friendly. Conversely, the process is very simple for jobseekers too, it makes quick and painless to apply for jobs.</summary><hostname>Theseus</hostname><author_list><author name="Said Abdirahman Mohamed" affiliation="VAASAN AMMATTIKORKEAKOULU UNIVERSITY OF APPLIED SCIENCES" /></author_list><url>https://www.theseus.fi/bitstream/handle/10024/271559/Thesis.pdf?sequence=2&isAllowed=y</url><publish_time>2019年5月16日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:18"><title>BANKING APPLICATION (BACKEND DEVELOPMENT USING SPRING BOOT)</title><summary>Web application technologies are rapidly evolving, with new features and improvements being added all the time. The level of configuration complexity in any Spring-based application is a hurdle. Spring Boot simplifies the creation and deployment of stand-alone, production-ready Spring apps with minimal Spring configuration. If we use the Spring Model-View-Controller (MVC) framework as an example, we'll need to set up a dispatcher servlet, web jars, a view resolver, and component scan, among other things. To address this, Spring Boot offers a number of Auto Configuration options for configuring the application with any required dependencies. Further, the paper discusses the improvement of enterprise solutions by using Enterprise JavaBeans (EJB), the Java Persistence API (JPA), and by use of RESTful web services via JAX-RS, the roles that they play in providing strong data handling and the communication of services. There is a special section with a microservices architecture checklist that focuses on the configuration management, fault tolerance, service discovery, automation of testing, and data consistency. Whereas Smart Store Eazy is a lighter version of the Enterprise Edition and is intended for small grocery stores. A mobile device is possible to provide useful information about user activities, interests and location. Imagine a mobile application that has the ability to recognize the exact location every time a user accesses the location service. Furthermore, think how easily a mobile application could access personal data, activities, education and interests from social media such as Facebook. There is a way to incorporate all of these features into one large company mobile application. The application will save this information in a database. An admin tool will manage this data in order to design targeted campaigns for these users. By having a lot of information, we could increase the effectiveness of the campaigns. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Spring Boot Actuator endpoints health metrics info mappings audit log management essential features" search_time="2026年5月16日11时58分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:92"><title>Monitoring Integration Traffic in Microservices Architecture</title><summary>Microservice architecture has become a widely adopted approach for building modern software systems, offering advantages such as improved scalability, maintainability, and flexibility over monolithic architectures. However, monitoring microservices remains a complex task due to their distributed nature and the intricate interactions between independent services. This thesis investigates how integration traffic in Java-based microservices can be monitored more effectively. It identifies core principles for monitoring such traffic, examines the limitations of current solutions, and defines the key requirements for tools that support observability in microservice environments. A mixed-methods approach was applied, combining literature review with semi-structured interviews of industry professionals. The study’s main contribution is a set of design criteria for integration traffic monitoring tools that address both technical and organizational needs. The results show that existing systems often lack the detail and context required to trace data across services. Effective monitoring requires human-readable logs, standardized formatting, alerting mechanisms, intuitive visualization, and message-level traceability.</summary><hostname>UTUPub</hostname><publisher>Master's thesis</publisher><author_list><author name="Elias Kinnunen" affiliation="Computer Science Faculty of Technology" /></author_list><url>https://www.utupub.fi/bitstream/handle/10024/182219/Kinnunen_Gradu_Final_muunnettu.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=-1</url><publish_time>2025年5月20日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:93"><title>Spring Boot Actuator Web API Documentation</title><hostname>Spring</hostname><publisher>Spring Boot Actuator Web API Documentation</publisher><author_list><author name="Andy Wilkinson" /><author name="Stephane Nicoll" /></author_list><url>https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/docs/2.6.11/actuator-api/pdf/spring-boot-actuator-web-api.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:94"><title>Spring Boot Actuator: Monitoring and Managing Production-Ready Applications</title><summary>Monitoring and managing production-ready applications are critical aspects of modern software engineering, especially in microservices architectures. # The role of need for closure on misinformation acceptance: a data-driven report

## Overview
Misinformation acceptance is shaped by a complex interplay of cognitive motivations, social context, and epistemic goals. Research indicates that people’s preference for information—and willingness to accept misinformation—depends not only on accuracy but also on how well the information satisfies broader psychological goals, such as reducing uncertainty and maintaining coherent worldviews. In social media environments, the design and culture of platforms can reduce the psychological cost of adhering to misinformation, enabling its proliferation alongside increased polarization and radicalization<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="18"></cite>. Within this landscape, individual differences in need for closure emerge as a key determinant of how people process, evaluate, and ultimately accept misinformation<cite id="28"></cite>.

## Need for closure theory and motivated processing
Need for Cognitive Closure (NFCC) reflects a desire for definite conclusions and a tendency to prefer structured, comprehensible information over ambiguous or uncertain options. Classic work established that higher NFCC is associated with motivated resistance to persuasion, particularly when individuals already possess some prior information or are exposed to situations that heighten urgency for closure (e.g., noise or time pressure). These effects are moderated by the presence of an informational base: closure-seeking individuals are more resistant to persuasion when they have prior support for a position, but less resistant when no prior information is available<cite id="51"></cite><cite id="52"></cite><cite id="55"></cite>. More recent theory emphasizes two tendencies under NFCC—urgency (seeking closure quickly) and permanence (maintaining it over time)—which together explain diverse social-cognitive outcomes, including impression formation, stereotyping, attribution, and group decision-making<cite id="52"></cite><cite id="55"></cite>.

## NFCC and misinformation evaluation
Empirical studies of misinformation assessment show that NFCC is linked to patterns of judgment that can favor established positions and reduce openness to disconfirming evidence. In evaluations of politically charged content, respondents high in NFCC are less aligned with expert consensus compared to those with lower NFCC, even when controlling for other cognitive traits<cite id="28"></cite>. This tendency to prioritize closure over thorough evaluation aligns with broader findings that closure motivation can lead to polarized trust judgments—low trust in distant or dissimilar others and high trust in close in-groups—further insulating individuals from counterevidence<cite id="27"></cite>. Consistent with motivated skepticism, people with stronger directional goals (including ideological commitments) tend to require less evidence for preferred conclusions and more for dispreferred ones, a bias that can be amplified when closure needs are high<cite id="31"></cite><cite id="35"></cite>.

## Moderating conditions: context and group dynamics
The impact of NFCC on misinformation acceptance is not uniform; it depends on situational and contextual factors. In online crowdsourcing experiments, higher NFCC was associated with reduced alignment with experts, but this effect was amplified by politically conservative leanings, underscoring how closure-seeking behavior interacts with partisan cues in misinformation evaluation<cite id="28"></cite>. Social identity and group dynamics further shape these effects: individuals motivated by relational goals (e.g., conformity, shared reality) are more susceptible to misinformation and homophily, creating echo-chamber environments that lower the cost of closure-seeking acceptance<cite id="17"></cite>. At the same time, interventions that increase the perceived cost of misinformation—such as highlighting source trustworthiness or leveraging balanced social networks—can counteract closure-driven acceptance by making uncertainty more tolerable and evidence evaluation more salient<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="54"></cite>.

## Implications for misinformation interventions
Because closure needs can drive both the rejection of disconfirming evidence and the preference for coherent, albeit false, narratives, effective interventions must address the psychological cost of uncertainty. Research on source-trust ratings and algorithmic amplification suggests that crowdsourced judgments of source quality can reliably differentiate reliable from unreliable outlets, and that balanced exposure to diverse perspectives can improve accuracy—offering pathways to raise the cost of accepting misinformation for closure-seeking individuals<cite id="54"></cite><cite id="56"></cite>. Laypeople’s ability to discern quality varies by cognitive traits: higher cognitive reflection is associated with better source discrimination, indicating that tailoring interventions to closure-related and analytic dispositions may enhance their effectiveness<cite id="56"></cite>. Finally, the lay epistemic literature emphasizes that closure needs can sometimes motivate more complex cognition, implying that carefully designed contexts that delay closure or encourage exploration may reduce susceptibility to misinformation without undermining motivation<cite id="20"></cite><cite id="40"></cite>.

## Limitations and open questions
While the evidence connects NFCC to motivated processing and misinformation acceptance, the relationship is context-dependent and often interacts with other motives (e.g., ideological commitment, social identity). Few studies directly test NFCC within political misinformation scenarios, and effects can be moderated by traits such as openness to experience or political orientation<cite id="35"></cite><cite id="28"></cite>. Moreover, the mechanisms linking closure needs to acceptance in echo-chamber environments remain underexplored, calling for more research on how closure interacts with group polarization, source credibility, and correction strategies in real-world settings<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>.

## Conclusion
Need for closure is a significant predictor of how people seek, evaluate, and accept information, often prioritizing closure over accuracy and insulating beliefs from disconfirming evidence. In politically charged and socially fragmented environments, closure-seeking tendencies can facilitate misinformation acceptance by aligning with ideological goals and reducing the psychological cost of holding coherent, but false, positions<cite id="28"></cite><cite id="27"></cite><cite id="12"></cite>. However, the strength and direction of these effects depend on context, social identity, and the availability of credible alternatives, offering opportunities to design interventions that raise the cost of misinformation acceptance for closure-seeking individuals<cite id="54"></cite><cite id="56"></cite>.

This could happen because the messages contained within different pieces of information may either be well-liked or repulsive. To do so, we ask whether crowdsourced trust ratings can effectively differentiate more versus less reliable sources. We ran two preregistered experiments (n = 1,010 from Mechanical Turk and n = 970 from Lucid) where individuals rated familiarity with, and trust in, 60 news sources from three categories: (i) mainstream media outlets, (ii) hyperpartisan websites, and (iii) websites that produce blatantly false content ("fake news"). Despite substantial partisan differences, we find that laypeople across the political spectrum rated mainstream sources as far more trustworthy than either hyperpartisan or fake news sources. Although this difference was larger for Democrats than Republicans—mostly due to distrust of mainstream sources by Republicans—every mainstream source (with one exception) was rated as more trustworthy than every hyperpartisan or fake news source across both studies when equally weighting ratings of Democrats and Republicans. Preferring and using health-related misinformation occur most likely when people are primarily driven by directional goals. Moreover, disconfirmation bias results in the rejection of information that challenges the existing beliefs about an issue. problem: Could the rapeutic interventions aimed at modulating plasma metal ion concentrations represent effective preventive or therapeutic strategies against cardiovascular diseases? What types of interventions—such as supplementation—have been proposed, and is there clinical evidence supporting their feasibility and efficacy?
final_response:

<answer>
Metal ions and cardiovascular disease (CVD). Epidemiologic and mechanistic evidence increasingly implicates chronic exposure to nonessential metals such as lead, cadmium, and arsenic in atherosclerosis and its sequelae. Contaminant metals interfere with critical intracellular reactions, inducing oxidative stress and inflammation that lead to endothelial dysfunction, hypertension, epigenetic dysregulation, dyslipidemia, and myocardial excitation–contractile abnormalities; they are further associated with subclinical atherosclerosis, coronary stenosis and calcification, and increased risk of ischemic heart disease, stroke, left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, and peripheral artery disease. Public health measures that reduce metal exposure have lowered cardiovascular death, supporting the premise that modulating metal body burden may be relevant to CVD prevention and treatment<cite id="38"></cite>. Reviews of atherosclerosis pathogenesis highlight that trace elements including iron, copper, zinc, and selenium play roles in the disease process, and only longitudinal studies can resolve many questions, underscoring the need to consider metal status in CVD risk<cite id="1"></cite>.

Chelation therapy targeting toxic metals. Repeated intravenous chelation with disodium EDTA mobilizes divalent cations (lead, cadmium, calcium) and enhances their urinary and biliary excretion; it is FDA-approved for metal poisoning but has been widely used off-label for CVD<cite id="12"></cite>. In the large, randomized Trial to Assess Chelation Therapy (TACT), 1708 post–myocardial infarction patients received 40 EDTA infusions versus placebo; after a median 55 months of follow-up, the composite outcome occurred in 26% of the chelation group versus 30% of placebo, with the major difference being fewer coronary revascularizations (15% vs. 18%). The authors concluded that although chelation modestly reduced adverse cardiovascular outcomes, the results were not sufficient to support routine use, and the guideline update did not recommend chelation for stable ischemic heart disease<cite id="7"></cite><cite id="50"></cite>. Safety in TACT was reassuring: treatment with edetate disodium was safe, with no excess mortality and no deaths directly attributable to hypocalcemia, and the study was not stopped for safety<cite id="9"></cite>. Biomarker data from TACT participants show that repeated EDTA chelation lowers urine lead and increases plasma zinc, consistent with mobilization of toxic metals and modulation of metal homeostasis<cite id="39"></cite>. In a cohort of patients with peripheral artery disease, chelation therapy was associated with a 40% relative risk reduction in major adverse limb and vascular events, with no excess mortality, further supporting its safety profile<cite id="10"></cite>.

Evidence for preventive and therapeutic strategies. Systematic reviews of EDTA chelation in CVD report that 17 of 24 studies found improved outcomes, with the largest gains in patients with diabetes and severe peripheral arterial disease; a meta-analysis of ankle–brachial index showed improvement of 0.08 (95% CI, 0.06–0.09) from baseline, suggesting benefit in peripheral circulation<cite id="13"></cite>. Mechanistic work links chronic toxic metal exposure to CVD morbidity and mortality and examines TACT’s findings, arguing that toxic metals contribute to atherosclerosis and that chelation may be a secondary prevention strategy<cite id="12"></cite>. A focused update of ischemic heart disease guidelines did not recommend chelation for stable disease, and a narrative review emphasizes that even in the post–MI diabetic subgroup, which appeared to benefit in TACT, evidence is insufficient for routine use; an ongoing TACT2 trial may clarify its role<cite id="14"></cite><cite id="50"></cite>. Ethical concerns have been raised about earlier chelation trials, including misrepresentation of prior evidence and risks, leading some to argue that such studies should be abandoned; however, TACT’s design and safety monitoring set a contemporary standard for evaluating chelation in CVD<cite id="6"></cite><cite="7"></cite><cite id="56"></cite>.

Supplementation and other interventions targeting metal status. Antioxidant and trace element supplementation has been explored as secondary prevention for coronary heart disease; interventional studies at pharmacologic doses showed benefit, but results were mixed, and only future longitudinal studies can resolve many questions<cite id="1"></cite>. Micronutrient supplementation meta-analyses found that n-3 fatty acids, folic acid, and coenzyme Q10 showed moderate- to high-quality evidence for reducing CVD risk factors or events, whereas vitamin C, vitamin D, vitamin E, and selenium showed no effect on CVD or type 2 diabetes risk<cite id="43"></cite>. For selenium specifically, observational studies suggest inverse associations with coronary heart disease risk, but randomized trials did not demonstrate efficacy for preventing coronary endpoints, highlighting the need for caution in translating observational findings to supplementation<cite id="24"></cite>. Zinc supplementation effects on plasma lipoproteins were largely neutral overall, but in healthy individuals it was associated with reduced HDL cholesterol, potentially increasing coronary heart disease risk, whereas broader reviews found significant lowering of triglycerides, total cholesterol, glucose, and inflammatory markers, indicating heterogeneity by population and dose<cite id="28"></cite><cite id="29"></cite>. Iron’s relationship to CVD remains controversial; epidemiologic studies show mixed support for an iron hypothesis, and the evidence is not strong enough to conclude a consistent association<cite id="34"></cite>.

Emerging mechanistic targets for modulating metal ions. Copper dyshomeostasis drives atherosclerosis, with both excess and deficiency linked to pathogenesis. Copper-induced cell death (cuproptosis) and interactions with other modes of cell death and mitochondrial dysfunction are emerging themes, and therapeutic strategies include copper balance regulators and nanotechnology to adjust body copper levels<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="18"></cite><cite id="19"></cite>. Reviews emphasize that maintaining normal copper homeostasis is crucial for cardiovascular health and that dysregulation can induce cell death linked to atherosclerosis and its complications<cite id="11"></cite><cite id="18"></cite>.

Feasibility and efficacy considerations. Clinical evidence supports the feasibility of EDTA chelation in CVD populations, with safety profiles that have improved over time and measurable changes in metal biomarkers; revascularization rates were lower in chelation-treated post–MI patients, indicating potential clinical benefit, albeit not sufficient to warrant routine use without further evidence<cite id="39"></cite><cite id="9"></cite><cite id="7"></cite>. Supplementation strategies targeting antioxidant and trace elements show mixed efficacy for CVD outcomes, with some nutrients (n-3 fatty acids, folic acid, coenzyme Q10) demonstrating benefit and others (vitamin C/D/E, selenium) lacking robust evidence in randomized trials<cite id="43"></cite>. Population-level reductions in metal exposure have lowered cardiovascular death, reinforcing the plausibility of modulating metal body burden as a preventive strategy<cite id="38"></cite>.

Conclusion. Preventive and therapeutic strategies that modulate plasma metal ion concentrations—such as EDTA chelation in patients with chronic toxic metal exposure, particularly those with diabetes and peripheral arterial disease—may offer feasible, albeit modest, benefits for secondary prevention of atherosclerotic CVD, with encouraging safety profiles and biomarker evidence of metal mobilization<cite id="13"></cite><cite id="39"></cite><cite id="9"></cite><cite id="10"></cite><cite id="7"></cite>. Supplementation with certain micronutrients (e.g., n-3 fatty acids, folic acid) has strong evidence for cardiometabolic benefits, while others (vitamin C/D/E, selenium) do not consistently reduce CVD risk in randomized trials, necessitating careful selection and individualized approaches<cite id="43"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="28"></cite><cite id="29"></cite>. Mechanistic advances in copper homeostasis and cuproptosis suggest novel therapeutic targets for adjusting metal levels, but larger, well-controlled trials are needed to establish efficacy and optimize protocols for routine clinical use<cite id="18"></cite><cite id="19"></cite><cite id="13"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>.

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="metalloestrogens cardiovascular disease copper zinc estrogen receptor alpha beta COMT polymorphisms atherosclerosis" search_time="2026年5月16日11时59分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:12"><title>VASCULAR ACTIONS OF ESTROGENS: FUNCTIONAL IMPLICATIONS</title><summary>The impact of estrogen exposure in preventing or treating cardiovascular disease is controversial. But it is clear that estrogen has important effects on vascular physiology and pathophysiology, with potential therapeutic implications. Therefore, it is the goal of this review to summarize, using an integrated approach, current knowledge of the vascular effects of estrogen, both in humans and in experimental animals. Aspects of estrogen synthesis and receptors, as well as general mechanisms of estrogenic action are reviewed with an emphasis on issues particularly relevant to the vascular system. Recent understanding of the impact of estrogen on mitochondrial function suggests that the longer lifespan of women compared to men may depend in part on the ability of estrogen to decrease production of reactive oxygen species in mitochondria. Mechanisms by which estrogen increases endothelial vasodilator function, promotes angiogenesis and modulates autonomic function are summarized. Key aspects of the relevant pathophysiology of inflammation, atherosclerosis, stroke, migraine and thrombosis are reviewed concerning current knowledge of estrogenic effects. A number of emerging concepts are addressed throughout. These include the importance of estrogenic formulation and route of administration and the impact of genetic polymorphisms, either in estrogen receptors or in enzymes responsible for estrogen metabolism, on responsiveness to hormone treatment. The importance of local metabolism of estrogenic precursors and the impact of timing for initiation of treatment and its duration are also considered. While consensus opinions are emphasized, controversial views are presented in order to stimulate future research.</summary><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>Pharmacol Rev</publisher><author_list><author name="Virginia M Miller" affiliation="Mayo Clinic College of Medicine" /><author name="Sue P Duckles" affiliation="University of California, Irvine, School of Medicine" /></author_list><url>https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Virginia-Miller-4/publication/5275997_Vascular_Actions_of_Estrogens_Functional_Implications/links/53eba8070cf250c8947a6a25/Vascular-Actions-of-Estrogens-Functional-Implications.pdf</url><publish_time>2008年6月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:13"><title>Sex-based differences in vascular function</title><summary>Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality for both men and women in the USA. However, there are differences between the sexes in age-dependent onset, severity, symptoms and outcomes. Basic research into the causes of sex-dependent differences in cardiovascular disease is ongoing and includes investigation into genetic variation in expression and distribution of receptors for the sex steroids; specificity of natural and synthetic ligands that activate the sex steroid receptors; and intracellular mechanisms that are activated by the receptors in all components of the vessel wall and blood elements, which integrate to regulate vascular tone, vascular repair and remodeling in health and disease. In this era of personalized medicine, basic research into mechanisms of sex differences in vascular function will result in improved prevention, detection and treatment of cardiovascular disease in both men and women.</summary><hostname>moscow.sci-hub.ru</hostname><publisher>Women's Health</publisher><author_list><author name="Vm Miller" affiliation="Departments of Surgery & Physiology & Biomedical Engineering, College of Medicine, Mayo Clinic, 200 First St SW, Rochester, MN 55905, USA" /></author_list><url>https://moscow.sci-hub.ru/1832/e76a3148e04a73d6cfa949df379a641f/miller2010.pdf#navpanes=0&view=FitH</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:14"

We conducted a systematic review of published studies to examine the effect of repeated EDTA on clinical outcomes in adults with CVD.

Twenty-four studies (4 randomized clinical trials, 15 prospective before/after studies, and 5 retrospective case series) of repeated infusion treatment in patients with preexistent CVD. Of these, 17 studies (1 randomized clinical trial) found improvement in their respective outcomes following repeated treatment. The largest improvement was observed in studies with high prevalence of participants with diabetes and/or severe occlusive arterial disease. A meta-analysis conducted with 4 studies reporting ankle-brachial index indicated an improvement of 0.08 (95% CI, 0.06-0.09) from baseline.
CONCLUSIONS: Overall, 17 studies suggested improved outcomes, 5 reported no statistically significant effect of treatment, and 2 reported no qualitative benefit. Repeated EDTA for CVD treatment may provide more benefit to patients with diabetes and severe peripheral arterial disease. Copper, an essential trace element in the human body, participates in various biological processes and plays a significant role in the cardiovascular system. Maintaining normal copper homeostasis is crucial for cardiovascular health, and dysregulation of copper balance is closely associated with the development of CVD. When copper homeostasis is disrupted, it can induce cell death, which has been proposed to be a novel form of "cuproptosis", distinct from traditional programmed cell death. This new form of cell death is closely linked to the occurrence and progression of AS. Polyphenols have been shown to have cardioprotective properties; however, their impact on iron bioavailability and potential impact on other aspects of health is unclear. A systematic review was undertaken to evaluate the current status of the relationship between habitual polyphenol consumption, iron status, and circulating biomarkers of CVD. Following the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2009 guidelines, searches were performed across 5 electronic databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, Scopus, Web of Science, and CINAHL) to identify randomized controlled trials which investigated the effects of polyphenol consumption on inflammatory markers, serum lipid profile, and iron absorption and bioavailability. The duration of the studies ranged from between 56 and 145 days, with total polyphenolic content of the food items and supplements ranging from 45 to 1015 mg (per 100 g). Polyphenols did not appear to interfere with iron status, and most studies reported improvements in inflammatory markers and lipid profile. problem: Please conduct a study and prepare a report on the 'Construction and Application of a Sports Intelligent Tutoring and Learning Guidance System Driven by Multimodal Data Fusion.'

<answer>
# Executive Summary

A sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system driven by multimodal data fusion integrates motion capture, wearable sensors, vision, audio, and textual instruction to provide real-time feedback, personalized learning paths, and performance analytics. Recent systems demonstrate high recognition accuracy for strokes and movements, enable natural-language coaching, and improve training outcomes and learning motivation in empirical studies. The core components include multimodal sensing, action recognition and segmentation, error detection and instruction generation, adaptive tutoring and knowledge representation, and evaluation and visualization. Evidence shows that fusing skeletal and inertial data improves action modeling, multimodal datasets with targeted suggestions support virtual coaching, and knowledge graphs organize pedagogical content for personalized instruction. The systems also benefit from multimodal fusion frameworks and interactive coaching architectures that combine motion analysis, dialogue, and virtual humans for closed-loop learning<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="28"></cite><cite id="39"></cite><cite id="40"></cite><cite id="53"></cite><cite id="63"></cite><cite id="61"></cite>.

# System Overview

A typical multimodal sports tutoring system collects data from multiple sources to capture the full spectrum of movement and context. Motion capture and skeletal tracking provide precise joint positions and velocities, while wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) record orientation and acceleration, enabling robust pose and gesture recognition even in unconstrained settings<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="24"></cite>. Vision-based pose estimation from RGB cameras, including state-of-the-art models like HRNet and OpenPose, supports real-time scoring and error pattern recognition in sports<cite id="24"></cite>. Wearables and smart garments further enable gait and posture analysis with high accuracy and comfort for long-term monitoring<cite id="42"></cite>. In table tennis, multimodal sensing fuses skeletal and inertial data to improve action modeling and recognition, addressing challenges in complex sports scenarios<cite id="17"></cite>.

Beyond kinematic data, audio and textual modalities contribute context and instruction. Systems that combine RGB-D video, depth, skeleton, and audio achieve higher action recognition performance than single-modal approaches, and multimodal fusion frameworks provide taxonomies and architectures for integrating diverse inputs<cite id="60"></cite><cite id="63"></cite>. Natural-language coaching agents map motion features to concise feedback using large language models (LLMs), supporting interactive, self-guided practice and real-time guidance<cite id="55"></cite><cite id="60"></cite>.

# Action Recognition and Segmentation

Accurate action recognition and segmentation are prerequisites for error detection and instruction. A multi-stream 3D CNN with skeletal and inertial streams achieves 98.9% top-1 accuracy on a table-tennis dataset, demonstrating the value of fusing skeleton and IMU data for fine-grained motor skill analysis<cite id="17"></cite>. In badminton, a hierarchical segmentation framework using a 3D CNN with a long short-term memory (LSTM) achieves 98.3% accuracy for stroke segmentation, enabling precise timing of feedback<cite id="20"></cite>. For volleyball, a deep multimodal fusion model combining skeletal and inertial data outperforms single-modal baselines, achieving 98.5% top-1 accuracy for action recognition and 98.3% for segmentation<cite id="21"></cite>. In tennis, a data fusion methodology using features from wrist-worn accelerometers achieves high stroke detection and classification, reducing the time coaches spend analyzing data<cite id="65"></cite>.

# Error Detection and Instruction Generation

Modern tutoring systems detect errors and generate actionable feedback tailored to the learner’s motion. A computer-vision system using HRNet-W46 for pose estimation and a Bi-LSTM with a professional rule database provides quantitative scoring and error pattern recognition for motor skills, addressing subjectivity and delayed feedback in traditional instruction<cite id="24"></cite>. An AI table-tennis coaching system with a multimodal LLM and a table-tennis knowledge base identifies common beginner errors with 73% arm-related accuracy and 82% racket-related accuracy, delivering targeted guidance at low cost and with high cost-performance<cite id="23"></cite>. A multimodal coaching system for motor skill learning integrates motion analysis, dialogue management, and virtual human animation in a motion tracking and 3D VR setup, delivering closed-loop interaction during performance<cite id="61"></cite>.

Recent advances in reference-based instruction generation analyze differences between a learner’s motion and a reference under temporal and physical aspects, producing domain-knowledge–informed feedback that outperforms general LLM baselines in figure skating and boxing<cite id="60"></cite>. A multimodal transformer with cross-attention over visual and textual information provides accurate and timely feedback from multi-modal robot data, addressing the need for real-time, comprehensive guidance in sports training<cite id="24"></cite>. In basketball, a virtual coach using 3D motion reconstruction and an LLM maps spatio-temporal joint data to natural-language cues, with participants preferring AI-generated feedback and reporting improved awareness of posture and balance<cite id="55"></cite>.

# Adaptive Tutoring and Knowledge Representation

Personalized learning paths and adaptive guidance are supported by knowledge graphs and intelligent tutoring architectures. A knowledge graph construction scheme integrating deep learning and lightweight modules improves entity recognition and linking, achieving an F1 of 91.03% for head entity detection and a composite score of 92.13% over a baseline<cite id="28"></cite>. Empirical evidence shows that the system improves physical health indicators and learning interest: lung capacity increases by 12.1%, 50-meter time improves by 0.84 seconds, standing long jump increases by 11.2%, interest positivity rises by 45.5%, and negativity declines by 71.5%, verifying the effectiveness of knowledge-graph-driven instruction<cite id="28"></cite>. In table tennis, a multimodal intelligent tutoring system with a knowledge base and rule database provides stroke recognition, error detection, and personalized guidance, with stroke recognition accuracy of 92.5% and error detection accuracy of 93.7% in experiments<cite id="25"></cite>.

# Evaluation and Visualization

System evaluation methods include controlled experiments, user studies, and comparative analyses. A multimodal teacher behavior analysis system using video, audio, and motion data achieved F1 = 0.85 for recommendations, with significant improvements in instructional clarity, demonstration quality, and feedback specificity among 124 PE teachers<cite id="40"></cite>. In basketball, user studies found that participants preferred AI-generated feedback to coach feedback and reported noticing posture and balance issues and refining movements beyond self-observation<cite id="55"></cite>. A yoga avatar with an AI-enhanced multimodal insole sensing system achieved 98.33% posture recognition and 90.06% imbalance detection, delivering personalized guidance and real-time haptic feedback<cite id="39"></cite>. In PE, a multimodal intelligent tutoring system demonstrated high stroke recognition and error detection accuracy, supporting personalized guidance for learners<cite id="25"></cite>.

# Multimodal Fusion Frameworks

Multimodal fusion frameworks provide architectures and taxonomies for integrating diverse inputs. RGB-D data fusion reviews and surveys highlight the value of RGB, depth, skeleton, and infrared modalities, and discuss challenges and future directions for multimodal action recognition<cite id="60"></cite><cite id="59"></cite>. General fusion surveys categorize early, late, and intermediate fusion techniques and analyze joint, coordinated, and encoder–decoder frameworks, offering guidance for multimodal sports tutoring systems<cite id="63"></cite>. Reviews of ITS in arts, music, and sports emphasize measuring body movements with hardware and optimizing feedback with machine learning, noting the need for ITS that address open-ended, creative skills<cite id="61"></cite>.

# Limitations and Future Directions

Despite strong empirical results, several challenges remain. Many ITS in psychomotor domains still focus on feedback rather than open-ended creative instruction, and multimodal fusion in sports often requires robust, real-time processing and personalized adaptation<cite id="61"></cite><cite id="63"></cite>. Future work includes improving accuracy for under-recognized aspects such as footwork in table tennis, expanding guidance to high-level athletes, and integrating more modalities (e.g., audio, haptics) for richer feedback<cite id="23"></cite>. Advances in neural-symbolic AI, lightweight architectures, and interactive coaching architectures can enhance interpretability, efficiency, and closed-loop learning in sports tutoring<cite id="28"></cite><cite id="61"></cite>.

# Conclusion

Multimodal data fusion has enabled sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance systems that recognize strokes and movements with high accuracy, detect errors, and deliver personalized, real-time feedback. Systems that combine skeletal and inertial sensing, vision-based pose estimation, and natural-language coaching have demonstrated measurable improvements in physical health, skill acquisition, and learning motivation in empirical studies<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="28"></cite><cite id="25"></cite><cite id="39"></cite><cite id="40"></cite>. Continued progress in multimodal fusion, knowledge representation, and adaptive tutoring will further enhance the effectiveness and accessibility of intelligent sports tutoring<cite id="63"></cite><cite id="28"></cite>.
</answer>

Hydrogel, owing to its multimodal sensing capabilities and biocompatible properties, showcases great potential for advanced plantar monitoring during exercise. This study develops an AI table tennis coaching system using a Multimodal Large Language Model with a table tennis knowledge base, aiming to provide precise training guidance and match strategies for table tennis beginners. Method: By using visual recognition technology, motion capture technology, and advanced multimodal large language models with a comprehensive professional table tennis knowledge base, the system accurately identifies common errors made by beginners and provides targeted training guidance. Result: The AI Table Tennis Coaching System demonstrates high accuracy in identifying mistakes made by beginner players, particularly in recognizing arm-related errors and racket-related errors, with accuracies reaching 73% and 82% respectively. Conclusion: The system operates at low costs, is easy to deploy, and offers a high cost-performance ratio, providing effective technological support for table tennis teaching and training. The AI table tennis coaching system is expected to play a significant role in enhancing training efficiency, promoting athlete skill improvement, and popularizing the sport. The domains of arts, music, and sports, however, have been challenging for ITS due to their open-ended, multimodal nature. We conducted a systematic, narrative literature review to investigate how ITS in arts, music, and sports address these challenges. How do ITS in arts, music, and sports individualize instruction in the face of open-ended tasks? How do they use technology to handle multimodal data? We searched eight databases (Google Scholar, PsychInfo, PsychArticles, Education Research Complete, The New Republic Archive, ProQuest, ERIC, Psyndex) using a search string that combined the term “intelligent tutoring system” and its synonyms with the terms “arts,” “music,” and “sports”. Most ITS were focused on providing feedback. However, some systems achieved individualized task selection by decomposing complex skills into component skills and mapping them to tasks. Regarding technology use, we identified two overarching issues: measuring or presenting body movements with hardware such as depth cameras, digital styluses, and robots; and optimizing feedback or task selection with machine learning algorithms. We consider the lack of ITS that address open-ended, creative skills to be a gap in the literature that should be addressed by future research and discuss the potential of artificial intelligence in tackling this challenge.</summary><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><url>https://www.researchgate.net/publication/400542064_Intelligent_Tutoring_Systems_in_Open-ended_Multimodal_Domains_Reviewing_the_Evidence_from_Arts_Music_and_Sports</url><publish_time>2026年2月5日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:55"><title>ViSTAR: Virtual Skill Training with Augmented Reality with 3D Avatars and LLM coaching agent</title><summary>We present ViSTAR, a Virtual Skill Training system in AR that supports self-guided basketball skill practice, with feedback on balance, posture, and timing. ViSTAR follows the Behavioral Skills Training (BST) framework—instructions, modeling, rehearsal, and feedback. It provides feedback through visual overlays, rhythm and timing cues, and an AI-powered coaching agent using 3D motion reconstruction. We generate verbal feedback by analyzing spatio-temporal joint data and mapping features to natural-language coaching cues via a Large Language Model (LLM). A key novelty is this feedback generation: motion features become concise coaching insights. In two studies (N=16), participants generally preferred our AI-generated feedback to coach feedback and reported that ViSTAR helped them notice posture and balance issues and refine movements beyond self-observation.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Chunggi Lee" affiliation="Harvard University" /><author name="Hayato Saiki" affiliation="University of Tsukuba" /><author name="Tica Lin" affiliation="Dolby Laboratories" /><author name="Eiji Ikeda" affiliation="University of Tsukuba" /><author name="Kenji Suzuki" affiliation="University of Tsukuba" /><author name="Chen Zhu-Tian" affiliation="University of Minnesota-Twin Cities" /><author name="Hanspeter Pfister" affiliation="Harvard University" /></author_list><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.22077</url><arxiv_url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.22077</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>2602.22077</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:56"><title>Enhancing

One of the most challenging issues for computer vision is the automatic and precise identification of human activities. A significant increase in feature learning-based representations for action recognition has emerged in recent years, due to the widespread use of deep learning-based features. This study presents an in-depth analysis of human activity recognition that investigates recent developments in computer vision. Augmented reality, human-computer interaction, cybersecurity, home monitoring, and surveillance cameras are all examples of computer vision applications that often go in conjunction with human action detection. At long last, we are able to offer some study analysis concepts and proposals for academics. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Intelligent Tutoring System sports psychomotor feedback multimodal" search_time="2026年5月16日12时0分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:60"><title>CoachMe: Decoding Sport Elements with a Reference-Based Coaching Instruction Generation Model</title><summary>Motion instruction is a crucial task that helps athletes refine their technique by analyzing movements and providing corrective guidance. Although recent advances in multimodal models have improved motion understanding, generating precise and sport-specific instruction remains challenging due to the highly domain-specific nature of sports and the need for informative guidance. We propose CoachMe, a reference-based model that analyzes the differences between a learner’s motion and the reference under temporal and physical aspects. This approach enables both domain-knowledge learning and the acquisition of a coach-like thinking process that identifies movement errors effectively and provides feedback to explain how to improve. In this paper, we illustrate how CoachMe adapts well to specific sports such as skating and boxing by learning from general movements and then leveraging limited data. Experiments show that CoachMe provides high-quality instructions instead of directions merely in the tone of a coach but with out critical information. CoachMe outperforms GPT-4o by 31.6% in G-Eval on figure skating and by 58.3% on boxing. Analysis further confirms that it elaborates on errors and their corresponding improvement methods in the generated instructions. problem: The significance of the gut microbiota in maintaining normal intestinal function has emerged as a prominent focus in contemporary research, revealing both beneficial and detrimental impacts on the equilibrium of gut health. Disruption of microbial homeostasis can precipitate intestinal inflammation and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of colorectal cancer. Conversely, probiotics have demonstrated the capacity to mitigate inflammation and retard the progression of colorectal cancer. Within this domain, key questions arise: What are the predominant types of gut probiotics? What precisely constitutes prebiotics and their mechanistic role? Which pathogenic bacteria warrant concern, and what toxic metabolites do they produce? How might these findings inform and optimize our daily dietary choices?

## Executive summary

The gut microbiota is a central determinant of intestinal health, and its disruption is linked to inflammation and colorectal cancer (CRC). Conversely, probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics can restore balance, reduce inflammation, and slow CRC progression, offering practical dietary strategies to support gut health<cite id="19"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>. This report synthesizes the evidence on predominant probiotic types, prebiotics and their mechanisms, pathogenic bacteria and their toxic metabolites, and actionable dietary recommendations<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="17"></cite><cite id="61"></cite><cite id="10"></cite>.

## Predominant types of gut probiotics

Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Saccharomyces boulardii are among the most widely used probiotics, with clinical formulations often containing multiple strains to target specific outcomes<cite id="12"></cite>. Meta-analyses of perioperative CRC patients show that microecological agents increase Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium while decreasing pathogenic E. coli, supporting their role in restoring microbial balance<cite id="6"></cite>. Mechanistically, probiotics modulate the gut microbiota, enhance mucosal immunity, and reduce inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and CRP, which are elevated in CRC and inflammatory bowel disease<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>. In CRC models and patients, probiotics can also suppress NF-κB and Wnt/β-catenin signaling, inhibit tumor proliferation, and promote apoptosis, highlighting their multifaceted antitumor effects<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>.

## What are prebiotics and their mechanistic role?

Prebiotics are selectively fermented, nondigestible food ingredients that beneficially affect the host by selectively stimulating the growth and activity of intestinal bacteria associated with health<cite id="16"></cite>. The best-characterized prebiotics include fructo-oligosaccharides (FOS), galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS), lactulose, and resistant starch (RS), which are fermented by colonic bacteria to produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>. SCFAs lower gut pH, strengthen the mucosal barrier, and exert anti-inflammatory and antitumorigenic effects, contributing to CRC prevention and improved treatment outcomes<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>. Systematic reviews recommend prebiotics such as inulin and RS, alongside lactic acid strains that produce SCFAs, as part of microbiota modulation strategies for CRC patients<cite id="6"></cite>.

## Pathogenic bacteria of concern and their toxic metabolites

Several gut bacteria are implicated in CRC through genotoxic and inflammatory pathways. Escherichia coli harboring the pks island produces colibactin, a genotoxin that induces DNA damage and is associated with colorectal tumorigenesis<cite id="61"></cite>. Bacteroides fragilis secretes BFT, which disrupts epithelial tight junctions and activates NF-κB-driven inflammation, contributing to CRC progression<cite id="61"></cite>. Salmonella species secrete typhoid toxin, which interferes with epithelial homeostasis and signaling, and S. Typhimurium can produce genotoxins that promote DNA damage and tumorigenesis<cite id="61"></cite>. Other pathogens, including Fusobacterium nucleatum, Enterococcus faecalis, and certain Helicobacter species, also drive CRC by modulating host signaling (E-cadherin/β-catenin, TLR4/NF-κB, SMAD/RAS/p38 MAPK), suppressing antitumor immunity, and creating a pro-inflammatory tumor microenvironment<cite id="61"></cite><cite id="19"></cite>.

## How to apply these findings to daily dietary choices

To support a healthy gut microbiota, prioritize fermented foods and prebiotic-rich plant foods. Fermented foods such as yogurt, kefir, miso, and sauerkraut are natural sources of probiotics and can help replenish beneficial bacteria<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>. Prebiotic-rich foods include onions, garlic, leeks, chicory root, Jerusalem artichokes, bananas, apples, berries, legumes, and whole grains; combining these with probiotic foods forms a synbiotic approach that enhances microbial colonization and function<cite id="17"></cite><cite id="13"></cite>. Dietary guidelines recommend at least 25–35 g of dietary fiber per day, primarily from whole grains, vegetables, fruits, and pulses, to promote regular bowel function and reduce CRC risk<cite id="10"></cite><cite id="14"></cite>. Public health analyses consistently link higher fiber intake to lower colorectal cancer risk and improved outcomes, reinforcing the importance of fiber-rich diets<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="13"></cite>.

In addition to fiber, limit consumption of processed red meats and ultra-processed foods, which are associated with increased CRC risk through pro-inflammatory and genotoxic pathways<cite id="12"></cite>. Synbiotic products containing well-characterized probiotic strains (Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, S. boulardii) and prebiotics such as GOS/FOS or RS may be considered under medical supervision, particularly for individuals at elevated CRC risk or undergoing CRC treatment<cite id="12"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>. Finally, individualized guidance from a healthcare provider familiar with microbiota modulation is essential to tailor recommendations to personal health needs and monitor outcomes<cite id="6"></cite>.

One of the elements directly related to lifestyle is gut microbiota. The microbial ecosystem has a vital role in colorectal cancer prevention and antitumoral response through modulation of the immune system and production of short-chain fatty acids. Numerous approaches have been used to identify healthy microbiota that can reduce the risk of cancer development, improve treatment efficacy, and reduce side effects. Scientific literature in this subject is growing exponentially and, therefore, systematic reviews and meta-analysis are required to ensure that appropriate recommendations are given to patients. This work aimed to perform a systematic analysis of the published literature to elucidate whether microbiota modulation through pre-, pro-, symbiotic treatment and/or nutritional intervention can be beneficial for patients diagnosed with colorectal cancer. Detailed analysis of published studies shows that some prebiotics, such as inulin and resistant starch, probiotics such as lactic strains producers of short-chain fatty acids, and consumption of unprocessed plant products, can be effective recommendations for patients diagnosed with colorectal cancer. Disruption of microbial homeostasis can precipitate intestinal inflammation and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of colorectal cancer. Conversely, probiotics have demonstrated the capacity to mitigate inflammation and retard the progression of colorectal cancer. Within this domain, key questions arise: What are the predominant types of gut probiotics? What precisely constitutes prebiotics and their mechanistic role? Which pathogenic bacteria warrant concern, and what toxic metabolites do they produce? How might these findings inform and optimize our daily dietary choices?
