# AI Fashion Design Tools and Creative Homogenization: A Data-Driven Report

## Executive Summary

AI fashion design tools are reshaping the industry by accelerating ideation, prototyping, and trend analysis, but they also raise concerns about creative homogenization and intellectual property (IP) disputes. Empirical and policy evidence indicates that reliance on common datasets and “prompt engineering” can push designs toward dominant visual norms, while legal analyses emphasize that originality and authorship are central to copyright protection. Independent designers increasingly face risks of unauthorized use by fast fashion and algorithmic outputs that mirror training data, spurring calls for clearer licensing, provenance, and liability frameworks<cite id="2"></cite><cite id="112"></cite><cite id="22"></cite><cite id="19"></cite>.

## The Rise of AI in Fashion Design

AI is now embedded across the fashion value chain, from trend forecasting to production, and generative AI (GenAI) is expected to contribute up to $275 billion in operating profits over the next five years. Universities and industry partners are exploring AI as a co-design tool that channels machine learning into faster, trend-informed workflows, while acknowledging risks such as IP and homogenization<cite id="2"></cite><cite id="1"></cite>. Adoption is rapid: nearly 70% of major fashion brands use AI in design or production, and adoption in marketing and inventory management is even higher<cite id="116"></cite>.

## Evidence on Creative Homogenization

Analysts warn that most AI fashion tools rely on similar public datasets (e.g., Instagram, Pinterest, and fashion websites), and prompts for common categories—such as “summer dress”—often yield statistically averaged outputs that converge toward dominant visual standards. This “echo chamber effect” can make brands using the same tool produce nearly identical results, narrowing aesthetic diversity rather than expanding it<cite id="112"></cite>. In design education, students report being steered toward “safe” trending elements, reducing motivation to explore niche cultures and reinforcing popular loops<cite id="124"></cite>. Broader critiques of AI-driven design highlight cultural bias and homogenization, arguing that reliance on historical and dominant datasets constrains creativity and replicates existing inequalities<cite id="127"></cite><cite id="140"></cite>.

## Mitigating Homogenization: Design Practices and Human Agency

Research on AI-based automated fashion design systems shows that incorporating human workflows, domain knowledge, and iterative feedback can help maintain brand identity and reduce convergence toward generic outputs<cite id="96"></cite>. Studies of AI-assisted fashion design workflows emphasize that human designers retain agency by curating prompts, refining outputs, and integrating cultural context, which can counteract tendencies toward visual uniformity<cite id="139"></cite>. Moreover, AI can be used to analyze diverse archives and support inclusive design, provided training data and prompts are curated to broaden representation<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="127"></cite>.

## Copyright Disputes and AI-Assisted Design

Legal scholarship in the UK and EU clarifies that copyright protects originality in applied art, and the use of pre-existing designs in training data can affect originality but does not automatically render AI-assisted outputs infringing. Infringement analyses focus on the right of reproduction and transformative uses, with room for derivative designs that add sufficient authorship<cite id="22"></cite>. Comparative law perspectives note that in jurisdictions such as China, AI-generated works are not protected by copyright, and data-source compliance is crucial to avoid liability when training on unlicensed designs<cite id="19"></cite>. In the United States, courts have ruled that AI-generated works without human involvement are not eligible for copyright, reinforcing the importance of human authorship in legal protection<cite id="18"></cite>.

## Independent Designers vs. Algorithms: Risks and Cases

Independent creators face heightened exposure when AI tools mirror training data or when fast fashion firms scale “copy-paste” practices. A prominent example is the Shein class-action lawsuit, which alleges a systematic, for-profit surveillance and copying system that reproduces the designs of independent creators without permission<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>. Empirical studies of AI-generated fashion imagery show that outputs can be substantially similar to training data, with Chinese courts awarding damages when AI-generated patterns are deemed to infringe original designs<cite id="19"></cite>. These cases underscore the need for licensing, watermarking, and provenance tracking to distinguish authorized use from unauthorized replication<cite id="19"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>.

## Policy and Industry Responses

Calls for legal clarity include expanding definitions of “author” to include human designers who co-create with AI, strengthening licensing for training data, and implementing provenance and watermarking to trace AI outputs<cite id="22"></cite><cite id="19"></cite>. Industry reports and legal guides recommend reviewing terms of service, avoiding unlicensed data, and monitoring for infringement as AI tools move from novelty to mainstream use<cite id="22"></cite><cite id="20"></cite>. Broader governance frameworks emphasize transparency, accountability, and human oversight to align AI’s efficiency with creative diversity and ethical standards<cite id="139"></cite>.

## Recommendations

- Encourage diverse, curated training data and cross-cultural prompts to broaden visual outputs and reduce convergence<cite id="127"></cite><cite id="140"></cite>.
- Integrate human-in-the-loop workflows that preserve brand identity and cultural context to counter homogenization<cite id="96"></cite><cite id="139"></cite>.
- Adopt licensing and provenance practices for training data and AI outputs, and use watermarking to protect independent designers’ IP<cite id="19"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>.
- Monitor and enforce terms of service and IP rights to mitigate “copy-paste” risks and algorithmic mimicry<cite id="20"></cite><cite id="16"></cite>.
- Advocate for legal reforms that recognize human authorship in AI-assisted design and clarify liability for unauthorized training data use<cite id="22"></cite><cite id="19"></cite>.

## Conclusion

AI fashion design tools offer powerful productivity gains and new creative possibilities, but they also pose measurable risks of homogenization and IP conflict. The evidence indicates that these risks arise from shared datasets, prompt-driven convergence, and weak licensing regimes, while legal analyses emphasize originality and human authorship as safeguards<cite id="112"></cite><cite id="124"></cite><cite id="22"></cite><cite id="19"></cite>. Proactive governance—combining technical, legal, and policy measures—can help align AI’s efficiency with the industry’s need for diversity and fair IP practices<cite id="139"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>.
</answer>

## Abstract

The growing use of generative artificial intelligence technology (gen-AI) technology in design creation offers valuable tool for increasing efficiency and for widening the creative perspectives of fashion designers. However, adopting AI tools in the fashion design process raises important copyright concerns, too. First, this article explores copyright implications from the use of gen-AI in fashion design creation, given that in-copyright content, including pre-existing original designs, can be part of the corpus of data mined for training gen-AI systems. In light of both UK and EU copyright law, the article analyses the circumstances under which the use of AI tools in new design generation can negate their originality as works of applied art under Infopaq and subsequent CJEU decisions, whilst enriching the discussion with elements of fashion theory.

It further examines copyright infringement concerning AI-generated fashion design outputs, focusing on the right of reproduction under the InfoSoc Directive 2001/29/EC and the UK CDPA 1988, as well as transformative uses of AI-generated derivative designs.

The article concludes that gen-AI can have a considerable impact for fostering fashion innovation. It argues that this technology can contribute to the creation of novel original works of fashion that could derive from a more diverse ‘pool’ of fashion archives and pre-existing designs as part of AI systems’ text-and-data mining.

Abstract
With the recent expansion of the applicability of artificial intelligence into the crea‑ tive realm, attempts are being made to use AI (artificial intelligence) in the garment development system in various ways, both in academia and the fashion business. Several IT companies have developed and possess AI-based garment design technolo‑ gies that utilize StyleGAN2 for image transformation. However, they are not widely utilized in the fashion business. Since fashion brands need to create numerous designs to launch new garment products for at least two seasons per year, the adop‑ tion of AI-based garment design generation technology can be one way to increase work efficiency. Therefore, this research aims to collect and analyze existing cases of AI-based garment design tools in order to identify the similarities and differences between the garment development processes of human designers and the existing AI-based garment design tools. Based on this analysis, the research aims to develop an AI-based garment development system that takes into consideration the garment development process of human designers, incorporating fashion domain knowledge. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, AI driven garment development tool, Automated garment design generation tool, GAN (Generative Adversarial Networks), Fashion domain knowledge
Introduction
Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the key drivers shaping the transformation of contemporary society alongside big data, virtual reality, and other technological advancements. The fashion industry is undergoing a transformation driven by technological innovations centered around AI (Carvalho et al., 2019; Jang & Ha, 2023; Market.US, 2023). For instance, advancements in AI technology have improved the ability to analyze big data, enabling online retailers to track consumer purchasing data and provide personalized services, thereby enhancing sales. Moreover, AI-based technologies allow for more accurate predictions of upcoming fashion trends, enabling efficient inventory management. problem: Analyze the complex issue of liability allocation in accidents involving vehicles with advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) operating in a shared human-machine driving context. Your analysis should integrate technical principles of ADAS, existing legal frameworks, and relevant case law to systematically examine the boundaries of responsibility between the driver and the system. Conclude with proposed regulatory guidelines or recommendations.
final_response:
<think>
<answer>
Introduction

Advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) have redefined the shared human–machine interface in driving, blurring traditional lines of responsibility between the driver and the automated function. Legal frameworks must adapt to allocate liability in accidents where control may shift or be distributed across both the human and the machine, depending on the level of automation and the circumstances of the incident<cite id="75"></cite>. This report synthesizes technical principles of ADAS, existing legal regimes, and relevant case law to examine liability boundaries and proposes regulatory guidelines to improve clarity and accountability.

Technical Background: Levels of Automation and Human-Machine Interaction

SAE Level 2 systems perform both longitudinal and lateral control under defined conditions, but the driver remains responsible for monitoring and taking over when needed; Level 3 systems can transition control to the driver, who may legally divert attention within the system’s operational design domain<cite id="71"></cite>. ADAS are designed to reduce workload and improve safety, yet empirical studies show automation can induce complacency and inattention, increasing the risk of delayed or failed takeovers<cite id="49"></cite>. Moreover, Level 3 systems can request transitions from hands-off to eyes-on driving, and drivers must be able to respond to these demands; failure to do so can compromise safety<cite id="49"></cite>.

Legal Frameworks: Product Liability, Holder Liability, and Fault-Based Driver Liability

German law assigns liability for damage caused by an automated vehicle to both the driver/handler (fault liability under § 18 StVG) and the registered keeper (absolute liability under § 7(1) StVG), with manufacturer liability governed by the Product Liability Act (ProdHaftG) when a defect contributes to the damage<cite id="72"></cite>. Up to Level 2, the driver is legally responsible for the driving task; at Level 3, responsibility may shift to the automated driving system, depending on the system’s capabilities and the driver’s ability to intervene<cite id="75"></cite>. In Europe, the liability of automated driving systems is governed by the liability regime for products, with the injured party able to claim from the producer if a defect caused the damage<cite id="20"></cite>. The European Commission’s proposed AI Liability Directive aims to simplify and speed up claims for damages by introducing a presumed liability for providers of high-risk AI, with the burden of proof on them to show the damage was not caused by their AI<cite id="25"></cite>.

Case Law and Emerging Trends: Manufacturer Liability and Evidence Challenges

Recent litigation involving AI-assisted driving systems in Germany highlights evidentiary and causal challenges. In a Volkswagen Travel Assist case, the claimant argued a latent defect in the autonomous parking algorithm contributed to the accident, supported by an independent software audit; the court’s analysis of causation and admissibility of crash simulation data underscores gaps in proving manufacturer fault when decisions are opaque<cite id="61"></cite><cite id="7"></cite>. Comparative perspectives show divergent approaches across jurisdictions, reinforcing the need for harmonized standards and clearer documentation practices for software updates and system architecture<cite id="7"></cite>. Empirical studies also reveal that judges may assign more liability to self-driving vehicles than human-driven ones under identical conditions, and treat identical injuries as more serious, indicating a bias that could overburden manufacturers without clear regulatory guidance<cite id="16"></cite>.

Public Perception and Blame Allocation in Shared-Control Scenarios

Public blame allocation is not strictly proportional to fault in shared-control accidents. When only one party (human or machine) errs, that party is blamed more; but when both make errors, blame attributed to the machine decreases, suggesting under-reaction to AI malfunctions and potential inadequacy of jury-based schemes for regulating safety<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>. These behavioral findings support the case for top-down legal standards rather than relying solely on common law adjudication to govern human–machine shared control<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="22"></cite>.

Regulatory Recommendations

First, harmonize definitions and operational design domain requirements across levels of automation to avoid inconsistent interpretations of when responsibility resides with the driver versus the system. This includes clarifying conditions under which a driver may legally divert attention and the obligations to remain available for takeover<cite id="71"></cite><cite id="75"></cite>. Second, mandate the creation of a “Software Liability Dossier” by manufacturers, containing standardized documentation of software updates, architecture, and testing protocols, to improve evidentiary support for causation and admissibility in litigation<cite id="7"></cite>. Third, adopt pre-production cybersecurity and AI risk testing requirements to ensure transparency and traceability of automated decisions, addressing evidentiary gaps and strengthening victim protection<cite id="7"></cite>. Fourth, align liability rules with the AI Liability Directive’s presumed liability regime for high-risk AI, reducing procedural burdens and delays for injured parties<cite id="25"></cite>. Finally, revise national laws to keep pace with Level 3 and above automation, as seen in Sweden, where legislation has not yet fully adapted to higher levels and may need to redefine the boundaries of driver responsibility<cite id="13"></cite>.

Conclusion

Liability allocation in accidents involving ADAS operating in a shared human–machine context depends on the level of automation, the driver’s attention and readiness to intervene, and the presence of system defects. Current frameworks combine fault-based driver liability, absolute keeper liability, and product liability, but gaps in evidence and public perception complicate accountability<cite id="72"></cite><cite id="75"></cite><cite id="20"></cite><cite id="16"></cite>. Proactive regulatory measures—standardized documentation, pre-production testing, presumed liability for high-risk AI, and updated national laws—can better delineate responsibility and ensure timely remedies while balancing innovation and safety<cite id="7"></cite><cite id="25"></cite><cite id="13"></cite>.
</answer>

One of them is whether or not present legislation frameworks are able to accommodate a smooth development and market implementation of ADAS. This is strongly related to the aspect of traffic safety. The various aspects related to this issue are categorised based on an exploration of the functionality and possible failure of ADAS. Next, some problem categories are more in-depth elaborated. In particular attention is paid to the need for establishing safety requirements to the design and marketing of ADAS as well as the issue of liability regulation. It is concluded that decision making on safety requirements mainly takes place at an international level. However, so far hardly any requirements regarding ADAS have been laid down in compulsory rules yet. It is further concluded that current legal frameworks in both the fields of vehicle safety standards and liability provide for (some) flexibility towards technical developments regarding ADAS, i.e. these frameworks do not contain many 'hard rules' obstructing the introduction of ADAS. Concerning the safety regulation of ADAS it is argued that the speed of technological developments and the innovative and specific nature of ADAS technology generate various tensions. These tensions should have consequences for the weight that is put on public and private intervention mechanisms and the relation between preventive safety standards and reactive regimes such as product liability and post-market controls.</summary><hostname>R Discovery</hostname><publisher>European Journal of Transport and Infrastructure Research</publisher><author_list><author name="Robert Van Der Heijden" affiliation="Radboud University" /><author name="Kiliaan Van Wees" affiliation="Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam" /></author_list><url>https://discovery.researcher.life/download/article/3ec3e54b14603e9fa2602f96deaf61b9/full-text</url><publish_time>2001年6月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Driving into the Loop: Mapping Automation Bias and Liability Issues for Advanced Driver Assistance Systems</title><summary>Advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) are transforming the modern driving experience. Today’s vehicles seem better equipped than ever to augment safety by automating routine driving activities. The assumption appears straightforward: auto- mation will necessarily improve road safety because automation replaces the human driver, thereby reducing human driving errors. But is this truly a straightforward assumption? In our contention, this assumption has potentially dangerous limits. This paper explores how well-understood and well-researched psychological and cognitive phenomena pertaining to human interaction with automation should not be properly labelled as misuse. Framing the problem through an automation bias lens, we argue that such so-called instances of misuse can instead be seen as predict- able by-products of specific engineering design choices. We engage empirical data to problematize the assumption that automating driving functions directly leads to increased safety. If judges choose poorly, they can unleash novel injuries on society without redress or stifle progress by overburdening a technological breakthrough. The emergence of self-driving, or autonomous, vehicles will present an enormous challenge of this sort to judges. This technology will alter the foundation of the largest source of civil liability in the United States. Although regulatory agencies will determine when and how autonomous cars may be placed into service, judges will likely play a central role in defining the standards of liability for them. Will judges express the same negative biases that lay people commonly express against technological innovations? In this Article, we present data from 967 trial judges showing that judges are biased against self-driving vehicles. They both assigned more liability to a self-driving vehicle than to a human-driven vehicle for an accident caused under identical circumstances and treated injuries caused by a self-driving vehicle as more serious than identical injuries caused by a human-driven vehicle. These results suggest that judges harbor suspicion or animosity towards autonomous vehicles that might lead them to burden manufacturers and consumers of autonomous vehicles with more liability than the tort system currently imposes on conventional vehicles.</summary><hostname>Yale Journal of Law & Technology</hostname><publisher>Yale Journal of Law & Technology</publisher><author_list><author name="Jeffrey J Rachlinski" affiliation="Henry Allen Mark Professor of Law, Cornell Law School" /><author name="Andrew J Wistrich" affiliation="Magistrate Judge, United States District Court, Central District of California (retired) and an Adjunct Professor of Law, Cornell Law School" /></author_list><url>https://yjolt.org/sites/default/files/6_-_rachlinski_-_judging_autonomous_vehicles_0.pdf</url><publish_time>2022年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:17"><title>Drivers are blamed more than their automated cars when both make mistakes</title><summary>When an automated car harms someone, who is blamed by those who hear about it? original_data.problem: Analyze the complex issue of liability allocation in accidents involving vehicles with advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) operating in a shared human-machine driving context. Your analysis should integrate technical principles of ADAS, existing legal frameworks, and relevant case law to systematically examine the boundaries of responsibility between the driver and the system. Conclude with proposed regulatory guidelines or recommendations.
original_data.additional_instructions: Please write a well structured, data-driven report on the given research question, and add citations when needed.

problem: Acting as a senior hardware product manager, conduct in-depth research on tablet-style devices used for payments or SaaS applications. Your report should: 1) List major manufacturers, specific device models, and their configurations. 2) Include images of these devices. 3) Analyze the primary use cases and scenarios where these devices are deployed. 4) Investigate the market penetration, common usage scenarios, typical price ranges, and estimated installed base for such devices across different regions (North America, Japan/Korea, Southeast Asia, South America).
final_response:
<think>>
I will produce a structured report listing major manufacturers and specific tablet-style payment/SaaS devices with configurations and images, analyze use cases, and synthesize market penetration, usage scenarios, price ranges, and installed base by region. I will cite only the sources already retrieved and note uncertainties where evidence is insufficient.
</think>

<answer>Executive Summary  
Tablet-style devices for payments and SaaS span purpose-built POS terminals (NCR, Ingenico, Verifone, PAX) and repurposed consumer tablets (iPad, Samsung, Microsoft Surface, Dell Wyse, Lenovo, HP) used with card readers and kiosk mounts. These devices are deployed in retail, restaurants, healthcare, hospitality, field service, and vending, with price ranges from sub-$200 to over $1,000 depending on form factor and connectivity. Evidence is limited on exact installed bases, but adoption is strong in North America and Japan/Korea, growing in Southeast Asia and South America via consumer tablets and cloud-based SaaS deployments<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="28"></cite><cite id="30"></cite><cite id="45"></cite><cite id="76"></cite><cite id="81"></cite>.

Major Manufacturers and Device Models  
NCR Voyix offers mobile-first tablet POS with a 6-inch screen and Windows 10 tablets via Aava Mobile, designed for mobility and flexibility in operations<cite id="23"></cite>. Ingenico’s iPP320 is a 10.1-inch Android tablet with a 15-key backlit keypad, LCD display, and function keys, optimized for fast checkout in intense retail environments<cite id="46"></cite><cite id="50"></cite>. Verifone’s X990 is a thin, lightweight Android 7.X smart device with uncompromised security and scalable platform support for seamless integrations and 4G connectivity<cite id="38"></cite><cite id="39"></cite>. PAX provides Android tablets such as the S60 series with EMV, NFC, MSR, and built-in printers, targeting mobile and countertop POS<cite id="41"></cite><cite id="44"></cite>.  

Consumer tablets are widely repurposed for payments and SaaS: Apple iPad models are paired with Square or Stripe card readers and kiosk mounts for restaurant POS, retail kiosks, and healthcare check-in<cite id="24"></cite><cite id="76"></cite><cite id="81"></cite>. Samsung Galaxy Tab S9 FE (Wi‑Fi and 5G) offers high-end displays and connectivity suitable for retail and hospitality when paired with payment accessories<cite id="52"></cite><cite id="53"></cite>. Microsoft Surface Go 2 is a 2‑in‑1 detachable tablet ideal for mobility and productivity tasks, often used in field service and small business POS<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="57"></cite>. Dell Wyse and HP ElitePad 900 are thin clients/tablets running Windows, used in healthcare and retail where virtualized desktops and durability matter<cite id="61"></cite><cite id="72"></cite>. Lenovo Tab P11 provides powerful performance and long battery life for work and learning, adaptable to POS setups with external peripherals<cite id="67"></cite><cite id="68"></cite>.  

Images of Representative Devices  
- NCR Voyix Axium EX8000 mobile POS: https://www.ncr.com/product-catalog/ncr-pos-terminal-p-series<cite id="23"></cite>.  
- Ingenico iPP320 tablet POS: https://www.mtpos.net/product/ingenico-ipp320-cloud-emv<cite id="50"></cite>.  
- Verifone X990 smart terminal: https://www.verifone.com/en-us/hardware-product/verifone-x990<cite id="39"></cite>.  
- PAX S60 countertop POS: https://www.paxtechnology.com/sk-series<cite id="45"></cite>.  
- iPad POS with Square Reader and AboveTEK mounts: https://squareup.com/ca/en/hardware/reader/specs<cite id="76"></cite> and https://abovetek.com/products/abovetek-retail-tablet-pos-stand-swivel-kiosk-ipad-pro-mount-holder-ts-138w<cite id="81"></cite>.  
- Samsung Galaxy Tab S9 FE: https://www.samsung.com/sg/tablets/galaxy-tab-s/galaxy-tab-s9-fe-wifi-gray-128gb-sm-x510nzaaxsp/<cite id="52"></cite>.  
- Microsoft Surface Go 2: http://www.shurl.cc/6029b023fbbc9f6de834102b82c2246e<cite id="56"></cite>.  
- HP ElitePad 900: https://support.hp.com/pt-br/document/c03689744<cite id="71"></cite>.  

Primary Use Cases and Deployment Scenarios  
- Retail payments: Mobile POS tablets (NCR, Ingenico, Verifone, PAX) enable staff to process transactions at customer locations, while consumer tablets with card readers are used for checkout and kiosks<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="46"></cite><cite id="38"></cite><cite id="41"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="76"></cite><cite id="81"></cite>.  
- Restaurants: iPad POS with kiosk mounts and card readers support order-taking, payment, and check-in, with above-the-counter and countertop POS options<cite id="24"></cite><cite id="81"></cite><cite id="45"></cite>.  
- Healthcare: Tablets and thin clients (Microsoft Surface, Dell Wyse, HP ElitePad) are used for patient check-in, telehealth, and mobile rounds, leveraging durability and Windows compatibility<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="61"></cite><cite id="72"></cite>.  
- Hospitality and kiosks: High-end consumer tablets (Samsung Galaxy Tab S9 FE) and repurposed iPads serve as digital signage, check-in, and self-service kiosks<cite id="52"></cite><cite id="53"></cite><cite id="24"></cite>.  
- Field service and small business: 2‑in‑1 tablets (Microsoft Surface Go 2) and ruggedized POS (PAX S60) support mobile workers and small retailers<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="45"></cite>.  

Market Penetration and Installed Base by Region  
North America: Strong adoption of branded POS terminals (NCR, Ingenico, Verifone, PAX) and consumer tablets for payments and SaaS, driven by retail, restaurants, and healthcare<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="46"></cite><cite id="38"></cite><cite id="41"></cite><cite id="24"></cite>.  
Japan/Korea: High penetration of consumer tablets and POS accessories for payments and kiosks, with robust infrastructure and SaaS adoption<cite id="24"></cite><cite id="76"></cite>.  
Southeast Asia: Growing use of consumer tablets and cloud-based SaaS for payments and kiosks, supported by expanding mobile networks and retail modernization<cite id="24"></cite><cite id="76"></cite>.  
South America: Increasing deployment of mobile POS tablets and consumer tablets for payments and field service, with price-sensitive markets favoring entry-level devices<cite id="24"></cite><cite id="76"></cite>.  

Price Ranges and Installed Base Estimates  
Entry-level mobile POS tablets start around $199–$242 and can reach $500–$1,000 depending on connectivity and security features<cite id="21"></cite><cite id="25"></cite>. Consumer tablets paired with card readers range from sub-$200 (iPad models) to premium prices for high-end tablets like the Galaxy Tab S9 FE<cite id="76"></cite><cite id="52"></cite><cite id="53"></cite>. Purpose-built POS terminals (e.g., Ingenico iPP320) are priced mid to high, reflecting security and durability<cite id="50"></cite><cite id="46"></cite>. Installed bases are largest in North America and Japan/Korea; exact global numbers are not readily available in the sources, but adoption is expanding in Southeast Asia and South America via consumer tablets and cloud SaaS deployments<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="76"></cite><cite id="46"></cite>.  

Uncertainties and Limitations  
The sources do not provide precise installed base figures or regional market shares beyond general adoption trends<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="76"></cite>. Some device specifications are summarized or outdated (e.g., HP ElitePad 900), and price ranges reflect third-party listings rather than official lists<cite id="71"></cite><cite id="72"></cite><cite id="21"></cite><cite id="25"></cite>. For exact regional penetration and installed base, consult recent market reports focused on POS tablets and SaaS device deployments<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="24"></cite>.</answer>

problem: Research and analyze the latest advancements and cutting-edge theories within the field of game design. Specifically include recent developments, research, and practical design applications related to established frameworks like MDA (Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics).
final_response:

# Executive Summary

The MDA framework remains a widely used tool for analyzing and designing games, but recent scholarship highlights its limitations and proposes extensions such as DDE and unified models that explicitly include player experience and interworld transfer. In parallel, serious games and gamification increasingly adopt hybrid frameworks that integrate MDA with experience-oriented and educational models, and they emphasize evaluation methods that capture intended versus actual outcomes. At the same time, systemic and emergent gameplay—often associated with indie and immersive simulation design—has become a focal point for creating player-driven experiences and meaningful emergent narratives. These trends collectively suggest a maturation of game design theory toward experience-aware, evaluation-grounded, and emergent-systems approaches that complement and extend MDA’s original three pillars.<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="27"></cite><cite id="34"></cite><cite id="47"></cite><cite id="50"></cite>

# The MDA Framework: Foundations and Limitations

MDA’s core remains useful for decomposing games into mechanics, dynamics, and aesthetics, and it continues to be taught and applied in design curricula. However, it has been criticized for overemphasizing mechanics, neglecting many design aspects, and being unsuitable for experience-oriented design and narrative design, which often require stretching the framework beyond its original definitions. These critiques have motivated alternative approaches that explicitly address experience and interworld transfer of knowledge, actions, and emotions.<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="20"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>

# Extensions and Alternatives to MDA: DDE and Unified Experience Models

In response to MDA’s shortcomings, the DDE framework re-centers design on the front end, retains dynamics, and replaces aesthetics with experience, placing the player’s actual experience at the center of analysis. DDE consolidates improvements from multiple counterproposals and aims to support both functionality- and experience-oriented design, including narrative design, without forcing it into MDA’s original structure. Complementing this, a CHI ’21 extended abstract argues that existing models miss intended versus actual player experience and the transfer of knowledge, actions, and emotions between the game world and the real world, and proposes a unified model that integrates these aspects.<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>

# MDA in Serious Games and Gamification: Integration and Evaluation

Serious games research increasingly integrates MDA with educational and experience-oriented frameworks. A multiplayer cooperative serious game development framework explicitly considers both entertainment and learning, selecting game elements to meet learning objectives while motivating players through engagement and delight—areas where MDA’s focus on mechanics and aesthetics is complemented by broader design and evaluation criteria.<cite id="33"></cite> In gamification, systematic reviews and umbrella reviews emphasize the need for a functional model of implementation to align with teaching goals, underscoring that translating game elements into effective learning experiences requires careful design beyond mechanics alone.<cite id="57"></cite><cite id="59"></cite>

Evaluation practices in serious games have also evolved. A VR-specific extension proposes metrics that combine UX features (e.g., headset choice, tutorials, comfort adaptations) with MDA features (e.g., exclusive VR aesthetics and interactions), reflecting a hybrid approach that grounds aesthetics and dynamics in measurable outcomes relevant to engagement and learning.<cite id="52"></cite> In practice, case studies show that integrating task-based learning with MDA can yield significant post-test score improvements and positive usability ratings, demonstrating how MDA can be operationalized within educational contexts when paired with clear learning goals and iterative testing.<cite id="53"></cite>

# Systemic and Emergent Gameplay: Design Trends and Theory

A growing body of research focuses on systemic and emergent gameplay, often associated with immersive simulation design. Systemic games are player-driven, rule-consistent, and offer frequent choice opportunities that cultivate self-expression; while big-budget immersive sims may be in decline, systemic elements persist across many modern titles and continue to shape indie and systemic design legacies.<cite id="40"></cite> Theoretical work distinguishes “games of emergence” from “games of progression,” arguing that emergence captures multiplicity of outcomes from small rule sets, yet its use in games research still falls short of capturing the full potential of emergent structures and their implications for player agency and narrative.<cite id="50"></cite>

Procedural content generation is increasingly used to support emergent gameplay, enabling dynamic world creation that sustains player engagement and variety. Research on procedural content generation for emergent gameplay provides practical guidance on leveraging algorithms and systems to produce emergent experiences that align with design goals, offering a concrete pathway to implement emergent dynamics within MDA-style analyses.<cite id="47"></cite>

# Practical Design Applications: Balancing Mechanics, Experience, and Emergence

Practitioners report that successful games often focus on 2–3 core aesthetics, and that tuning and balancing are central to aligning mechanics with desired player experiences. This practice aligns with DDE’s emphasis on experience and with unified experience models that distinguish intended from actual outcomes, suggesting that designers should map mechanics to dynamics that reliably produce targeted emotional and experiential responses.<cite id="44"></cite> In educational contexts, integrating MDA with task-based learning and clear learning goals can improve outcomes, reinforcing the value of frameworks that explicitly connect mechanics and dynamics to measurable learning and engagement metrics.<cite id="53"></cite>

# Outlook: Experience-Aware, Evaluation-Grounded, and Emergent Design

The field is moving toward experience-aware design models that explicitly track intended versus actual player experience and interworld transfer, alongside evaluation methods that combine UX and learning metrics with MDA-inspired lenses. At the same time, systemic and emergent gameplay is becoming a design priority, with procedural content generation and immersive simulation principles offering practical tools to create player-driven experiences. Taken together, these trends indicate that MDA’s legacy endures, but its most cutting-edge applications likely extend it with experience, evaluation, and emergent systems to better capture the complexity of modern games and gamified experiences.<cite id="27"></cite><cite id="52"></cite><cite id="47"></cite><cite id="50"></cite><cite id="16"></cite>

MDA stands for acronym which is consist of Mechanics - Dynamics - Aesthetics. MDA framework is an instrument for analyzing for games. The MDA framework was developed by Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc, Robert Zubek, as a step by step to approach video game design. Every term inside MDA framework there is meaning for each one component: Mechanics are the base components of the game - its rules, every basic action the player can take in the game, the algorithms, and data structures in the game engine etc. Dynamics are the run-time behavior of the mechanics acting on player input and "cooperating" with other mechanics. Aesthetics are the emotional responses evoked in the player. Fundamental to this framework is the idea that games are more like artifacts than media. By this we mean that the content of a game is its behaviour ñ not the media that streams out of it towards the player. Thinking about games as designed artifacts helps frame them as systems that build behaviour via interaction. This thesis conducted a literature review, and a text mining analyses on elements of game design. The thesis addresses a few major elements of game design, different typologies of gamers and the text mining analysis conducted with Leximancer software. This thesis compares the previous research to the findings of the text mining analysis. The findings include confirmation that there are multiple different player types that enjoy different aspects of gameplay experience. A systematic literature review</title><summary>This article explores the transformative role of gamification in higher education through a systematic literature review. Rooted in the concept of gamefulness, gamification involves the intentional integration of game elements to enhance student engagement and learning experiences. The systematic literature review focuses on gamification in higher education, using the PRISMA model to conduct the analysis. The search protocol employs a rigorous search strategy using five online databases, excluding non-English language articles and duplicates. Adopting an aggregative review approach, the study delves into the theoretical framework of gamification, tracing its definitions, underlying principles and potential impacts on learning outcomes. The narrative textual synthesis of the 53 selected articles reveals a diverse landscape of gamification implementations in higher education, highlighting challenges in the uniformity of theoretical and empirical analyses. Then a thematic analysis is also proposed exploiting the results of a'meta-summary' to explore the relationships among themes. Abstract
Although the Mechanics, Dynamics and Aesthetics (MDA) framework is probably the most widely accepted and practically employed approach to game design, that framework has recently been criticized for several weaknesses. Other frameworks have been proposed to overcome those limitations, but none has generated sufficient support to replace MDA. In this chapter, we improve the MDA framework, place it on new pillars, and thus present the Design, Dynamics, Experience (DDE) framework for the design of computer and video games.
Introduction
The MDA framework was designed and introduced by Robin et al. (Hunicke, Leblanc, & Zubek, 2004) to “clarify and strengthen the iterative processes of developers, scholars and researchers alike, making it easier for all parties to decompose, study and design a broad class of game designs and game artifacts.” Since then, the MDA framework has become one of the fundamental approaches to game design, being well cited and accepted especially in academia. They defined the eponymous parts of the MDA framework (Mechanics, Dynamics and Aesthetics, see Fig. 1) as follows:
• Mechanics describes the particular components of the game, at the level of data representation and algorithms.
• Dynamics describes the run-time behavior of the Mechanics acting on player inputs and each other’s outputs over time.
Aesthetics describes the desirable emotional responses evoked in the player, when she interacts with the game system.
Figure 1. The basic concept of the MDA framework by Hunicke et al. 2004.
Only recently, in 2015 and 2016, articles have been published in which MDA was deeply analyzed, criticized and challenged. MDA was first discussed in depth on Gamasutra by Luis Claudio Silveira Duarte (Duarte, 2015). In that same year, an article by Lana Polansky (Polansky, 2015) was followed by an article by Frank Lantz (Lantz, 2015), both adding further points of criticism. In summary, these three authors identified two major weaknesses in the MDA framework:
1. It neglects many design aspects of games, focusing too much on game mechanics.
2. It is (therefore) not suitable for all types of games, including particularly gamified content or any type of experience-oriented design (as opposed to functionality-oriented design).
In addition, MDA fails to provide a framework or even a coherent approach for narrative design. Are narratives a component of Mechanics in MDA? In part, but not completely. Narrative design certainly does not belong to Dynamics – and also not to Aesthetics as defined by (Hunicke et al., 2004). Inevitably, every attempt to apply MDA to narrative design stretches the framework to the breaking point.
However, MDA is not the only game design framework. Having identified weaknesses in MDA, several practitioners and scientists proposed their own approaches to game design. In this chapter, we present those counterproposals and their distinctive features, consolidating many of those improvements, along with our own developments, into a revisited MDA framework based on three new pillars: Design, Dynamics, and Experience (DDE).

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="MDA framework 2023 2024 review serious games evaluation frameworks" search_time="2026年5月16日12时5分星期六"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:33"><title>The M-SG framework: A framework for Multiplayer Cooperative Serious Game development</title><summary>Designers and developers have to consider many factors when creating Serious Games (SGs), including entertainment and education. After playing games, SGs aim to improve players’ or learners’ skills (s). In a pedagogical sense, SGs should teach players/participants. SGs should entertain players throughout the game. Thus, SGs must motivate players. Developers must analyze functional demands to select game elements for learning objectives. Developers should also consider non-functional factors like delight and entertainment to promote long-term user engagement. Another issue is that SGs are tailored to learning objectives, which makes recreating and reusing their output difficult and costly. Multiplayer cooperative SG development needs additional work. First, the gameplay must meet conventional multiplayer game needs like player participation and interaction and SG design restrictions like learning content, flexibility, and personalization. Second, players collaborate to achieve a goal in cooperative games. Design must consider both. The developers must consider embedded instructional content, mechanics that engage many players, and mechanics that encourage cooperation throughout the game. Existing research and methods are suggested to solve the challenges of building serious games. However, due to the necessity to address the remaining gaps in usability and utility, only a few of these methods were implemented in actual projects. The main goal of this research is to investigate systematic ways to develop multiplayer cooperative SGs. This thesis aims to develop a systematic method for decreasing the effort required to develop SGs while retaining the game’s entertaining and educational purposes. It presents the findings of an investigation on the effects of game elements on player experience in multiplayer cooperative entertainment and serious games. The lessons learned from producing cooperative serious games, as well as the results of user research conducted for developing "The M-SG framework," a framework to support multiplayer cooperative serious games. To fulfill the primary purpose of this thesis, a user evaluation of the framework was conducted. The results indicate that the M-SG framework can benefit the research of multiplayer cooperative serious games and improve the reuse of games from previous projects by modifying the games’ premises. These findings show the value of the M-SG framework as a tool for supporting the development of cooperative serious games.</summary><hostname>MEDIA</hostname><publisher>Degree Thesis</publisher><author_list><author name="Supara Grudpan" affiliation="Universität Bremen" /></author_list><url>https://media.suub.uni-bremen.de/bitstream/elib/7465/3/The_M_SG_framework_for_Publishing.pdf</url><publish_time>2023年11月13日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:34"><title>An Evidence-Based Framework for Optimizing Serious Game Design in Software Engineering Education</title><hostname>Universidad de Murcia</hostname><publisher>Degree Thesis</publisher><author_list><author name="Manal Kharbouch" affiliation="Universidad de Murcia - Escuela Internacional de Doctorado" /></author_list><url>https://digitum.um.es/digitum/bitstream/10201/147062/1/Kharbouch%2c%20Manal.pdf</url><publish_time>2024年10月3日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:35"><title>The Rosetta Wheel: Towards a Shared Language and Framework for Game Design for Health Behaviour Change</title><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>Degree Thesis</publisher><author_list><author name="Jane Cocks" affiliation="School of Social Sciences, University of the Sunshine Coast" /></author_list><url>https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Jane-Cocks/publication/344206609_The_Rosetta_Wheel_Towards_a_Shared_Language_and_Framew

problem: For a research project titled 'Analysis and Study of Singles Badminton Player Actions Using Sports Videos,' please refine and optimize the following four research components: 1) Object Detection and Tracking within Badminton Videos; 2) Recognition of Technical Actions performed by Singles Players; 3) Recognition of Tactical Intent behind Singles Players' Actions; 4) Prediction of Singles Players' Subsequent Actions.

# Overview

This report refines and optimizes a research project on “Analysis and Study of Singles Badminton Player Actions Using Sports Videos” by structuring the four core components—object detection and tracking, technical action recognition, tactical intent recognition, and action prediction—around data-driven, turn-based modeling and evaluation. The optimization leverages rally segmentation, skeleton and shuttlecock trajectories, and stroke-level annotations to improve accuracy and interpretability, while aligning with public benchmarks and datasets such as ShuttleSet and ShuttleSet22<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>.

# 1) Object Detection and Tracking within Badminton Videos

Optimized pipeline: (a) segment rallies to isolate turn-based units; (b) detect and track players and shuttlecock with pose estimation; (c) use shuttlecock trajectories to trigger hit-frame detection and improve temporal alignment; (d) integrate rally progress and player positions for context-aware tracking. Rally segmentation has achieved 95.44% accuracy across 10 Olympic matches, player detection 97.38% mAP@0.5, player identification 97.98%, and stroke segmentation edit scores of 80.48%, establishing a robust foundation for per-rally tracking<cite id="2"></cite>. Skeleton-based keyframe detection can precisely locate strikes (≈0.033 s error) and supports spatiotemporal modeling of player movements<cite id="23"></cite>. Hit-frame detection and shuttlecock trajectory extraction, coupled with court-aware trimming, enable accurate rally boundaries and player pose alignment during flight<cite id="59"></cite><cite id="31"></cite>. ShuttleNet demonstrates that fusing rally progress and player styles improves stroke forecasting, underscoring the value of context-aware tracking and position conditioning<cite id="28"></cite>. For deployment, lightweight models like YOLOv8 and TrackNet can be tuned for singles-specific court geometry and occlusion patterns, with real-time analysis validated in professional leagues<cite id="20"></cite><cite id="71"></cite>.

# 2) Recognition of Technical Actions performed by Singles Players

Optimized modeling: (a) use skeleton joints, shuttlecock trajectories, and player positions as inputs to stroke-type classifiers; (b) adopt transformer architectures (e.g., BST) that leverage ball trajectory to outperform prior baselines; (c) incorporate rally-aware fusion and stroke embeddings (e.g., from LLMs) to capture technical nuances. BST reports state-of-the-art performance on ShuttleSet by combining pose estimation and shuttlecock trajectories, highlighting the importance of ball motion in racket sports action recognition<cite id="1"></cite>. RallyTemPose conditions predictions on rally contexts and player positions, with improved forecasting accuracy over sequential baselines and stroke embeddings from pre-trained LLMs<cite id="30"></cite>. FineBadminton introduces multi-level annotations (Foundational Actions, Tactical Semantics, Decision Evaluation) and Hit-Centric Keyframe Selection to focus on pivotal moments, aiding technical analysis and MLLM evaluation<cite id="17"></cite>. For evaluation, ShuttleSet provides stroke-level labels (18 shot types, hitting locations, and player positions), enabling per-stroke accuracy and influence analyses<cite id="16"></cite>.

# 3) Recognition of Tactical Intent behind Singles Players’ Actions

Optimized modeling: (a) forecast strokes and player movements using rally progress and style embeddings; (b) condition predictions on hit locations and player positions; (c) integrate movement forecasting to infer strategic footwork and coverage. ShuttleNet’s position-aware fusion of rally progress and player styles significantly outperforms prior methods, validating the feasibility of modeling strategic and technical contexts in forecasting<cite id="28"></cite>. RallyTemPose’s rally-aware fusion blocks provide strategic considerations that improve informed predictions, demonstrating the value of conditioning on rally state and spatial positioning<cite id="30"></cite>. FineBadminton’s multi-level annotations (Tactical Semantics and Decision Evaluation) and visualization platforms offer structured labels and interactive interfaces for dissecting players’ tactical preferences, with national teams using the platform in high-ranking matches<cite id="17"></cite>. Complementary vision–language pipelines (ChatMatch) extract meta-features (locations, actions, gestures) with high accuracy and enable LLM-based agents to infer higher-level insights, supporting tactical inference and video retrieval<cite id="6"></cite>.

# 4) Prediction of Singles Players’ Subsequent Actions

Optimized modeling: (a) sequence prediction with encoder–decoder transformers conditioned on skeleton poses, court positions, and player-specific embeddings; (b) incorporate rally-aware fusion and stroke embeddings; (c) forecast both strokes and movements to capture tactical intent. RallyTemPose improves forecasting accuracy over traditional sequential methods by conditioning on rally contexts and integrating stroke embeddings from LLMs<cite id="30"></cite>. ShuttleNet’s fusion network integrates rally contexts and player positions, showing feasibility and empirical gains in stroke forecasting<cite id="28"></cite>. Movement forecasting (e.g., footwork and coverage) can be modeled with skeleton-based keyframes and transformer architectures, aligning predicted movements with stroke outcomes to infer tactical intent<cite id="23"></cite><cite id="21"></cite>. Benchmarks like ShuttleSet22 provide stroke-level metadata and a forecasting track, with baselines and public code enabling reproducible evaluation and iterative improvement<cite id="22"></cite>.

# Evaluation and Deployment Considerations

- Datasets: Use ShuttleSet for stroke-level labels and ShuttleSet22 for forecasting benchmarks; consider FineBadminton for multi-level annotations and MLLM evaluation<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="22"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>.
- Metrics: Report stroke-type accuracy, influence scores, forecasting metrics (e.g., mAP@δ), and movement forecasting errors; leverage visualization platforms for interpretability<cite id="16"></cite><cite id="28"></cite>.
- Real-time constraints: Adopt lightweight pose and object detectors (YOLOv8, TrackNet) and top-view conversion for court-aware analysis, validated in real-time deployments<cite id="20"></cite><cite id="18"></cite><cite id="71"></cite>.
- Uncertainty: While shuttlecock detection remains challenging (CoachAI 2023 Track1 scores), active learning and noise reduction pipelines can mitigate errors and improve precision<cite id="19"></cite>.

# Conclusion

By structuring the project around rally segmentation, skeleton and shuttlecock trajectories, and stroke-level annotations, the four components become tightly coupled and data-driven. Transformer-based stroke recognition and forecasting, combined with rally-aware fusion and multi-level annotations, offer a robust path to accurate technical and tactical analysis, with public benchmarks and visualization tools enabling evaluation and interpretation<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="28"></cite><cite id="30"></cite><cite id="17"></cite><cite id="16"></cite>.

This study aims to demonstrate an innovative and higher-level video comprehension framework (ChatMatch), which integrates computer vision technologies with the cutting-edge large language models (LLM) to enable intelligent analysis and inference of racket sports videos. To examine the feasibility of this framework, we deployed a prototype of ChatMatch in the badminton in this study. A vision-based encoder was first proposed to extract the meta-features included the locations, actions, gestures, and action results of players in each frame of racket match videos, followed by a rule-based decoding method to transform the extracted information in both structured knowledge and unstructured knowledge. A set of LLM-based agents included namely task identifier, coach agent, statistician agent, and video manager, was developed through a prompt engineering and driven by an automated mechanism. The automatic collaborative interaction among the agents enabled the provision of a comprehensive response to professional inquiries from users. The validation findings showed that our vision models had excellent performances in meta-feature extraction, achieving a location identification accuracy of 0.991, an action recognition accuracy of 0.902, and a gesture recognition accuracy of 0.950. Additionally, a total of 100 questions were gathered from four proficient badminton players and one coach to evaluate the performance of the LLM-based agents, and the outcomes obtained from ChatMatch exhibited commendable results across general inquiries, statistical queries, and video retrieval tasks. problem: Please prepare a market research analysis of the global video editing and creation software/tool market. Include major products like those from Adobe (Premiere Pro, After Effects), CapCut, DaVinci Resolve, Final Cut Pro, and others relevant in the current landscape.
final_response:

<answer>
Executive summary

The global video editing and creation software market is highly segmented across desktop and mobile, with professional non-linear editors (NLEs) on desktop and social-first mobile apps driving growth. In 2024, Adobe Premiere Pro led the professional desktop market with a 35% share, while Apple’s Final Cut Pro held 25%, reflecting strong Mac ecosystem adoption and performance on Apple Silicon. Mobile video editing software reached $4.2 billion globally, with a projected 12.45% CAGR, and Canva dominated mobile app downloads and active users, underscoring the rise of AI-augmented editing in the social-creator economy<cite id="33"></cite><cite id="41"></cite><cite id="56"></cite>. Professional NLEs saw continued growth, with the market valued at $10.1 billion in 2024 and expected to rise to $14.5 billion by 2027, and DaVinci Resolve’s free tier and industry-grade color correction capabilities helped it capture 15% of the professional market<cite id="27"></cite><cite id="100"></cite>.

Market size and growth

The global video editing software market was valued at $10.1 billion in 2024 and is forecast to grow to $14.5 billion by 2027, representing a CAGR of 9.4% over that period<cite id="27"></cite>. Mobile video editing software was estimated at $4.2 billion in 2024, with a CAGR of 12.45% through 2031, reflecting faster adoption of advanced mobile editing features on smartphones<cite id="56"></cite>. The broader photo and video editor market is also expanding, with Canva’s mobile video editor positioned as a key growth driver in the mobile segment<cite id="45"></cite>.

Professional desktop NLEs

Adobe Premiere Pro remains the dominant desktop NLE, holding 35% of the professional video editing market in 2024, with a large user base that expanded from about 5 million in 2019 to nearly 30 million by 2024<cite id="33"></cite><cite id="36"></cite>. Apple’s Final Cut Pro X captured 25% of the market, with strong adoption among Mac users due to its performance on Apple Silicon and ease of use<cite id="40"></cite><cite id="42"></cite>. DaVinci Resolve’s free version has grown to over 2 million users as of January 2019, and it commands 15% of the professional market, favored for color grading and available in a free tier alongside a full-featured Studio edition<cite id="99"></cite><cite id="100"></cite>. Avid Media Composer holds 10% of the professional market and remains the tool of choice for film and TV production houses due to its collaborative features<cite id="98"></cite><cite id="100"></cite>.

Professional workflows and trends

Professional editors increasingly rely on integrated toolchains. For example, 78% of professional editors use Adobe products across their workflow, and 64% of those use multiple Adobe products, highlighting Premiere Pro’s integration with other Adobe Creative Cloud apps<cite id="103"></cite>. DaVinci Resolve’s adoption among professionals rose to 27% in 2021, driven by its free, feature-rich offering and industry-leading color science<cite id="101"></cite>. Apple’s transition to Apple Silicon in 2023–2024 improved performance for Final Cut Pro workflows, particularly with high-resolution RAW and ProRes footage, reinforcing the hardware–software synergy that attracts professionals from Windows and Avid environments<cite id="41"></cite>.

Mobile-first editing and social creators

Mobile video editing apps are the fastest-growing segment, with Canva’s mobile video editor leading in app downloads and active users. In the U.S., Canva surpassed 1.16 million downloads in November 2024, and AppTweak reported CapCut as the most downloaded photo/video app globally with about 509 million downloads and an estimated 8.6% share of top 500 app downloads<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="92"></cite>. Sensor Tower data shows CapCut reached 66 million Android downloads in Q2 2025 and had more than 442 million monthly active users, with reports of a 81% mobile video editing market share among users (though this figure should be interpreted cautiously given the source context)<cite id="94"></cite><cite id="93"></cite>. CapCut’s integration with TikTok—where over 80% of TikTok爆款 videos are edited with CapCut—creates a closed-loop for content creation and user acquisition, further fueling its growth<cite id="95"></cite>.

AI-augmented editing and creator tools

AI is reshaping both professional and consumer workflows. Canva’s Magic Studio suite reported over 5 billion cumulative uses since launch, with 800 million AI interactions per month in 2026, and users completing projects 28% faster when using Magic Write<cite id="48"></cite><cite id="52"></cite>. CapCut has also expanded AI features, including a “Magic AI” tool for removing objects and background noise, which has been widely adopted by creators<cite id="102"></cite>. These trends indicate a shift toward AI-powered templates, auto-cutting, and smart transitions that lower the barrier to high-quality content creation<cite id="102"></cite>.

Key players and market positioning

Adobe’s ecosystem remains the strongest for professional video workflows, with Premiere Pro tightly integrated with After Effects and other Creative Cloud apps, and with a large, growing user base<cite id="33"></cite><cite id="36"></cite><cite id="103"></cite>. Final Cut Pro continues to be the preferred NLE among Mac users, supported by Apple’s hardware and optimized performance<cite id="42"></cite>. DaVinci Resolve is the go-to tool for color grading and visual effects, with a free tier that appeals to independent filmmakers and a Studio edition used in Hollywood productions<cite id="100"></cite>. CapCut is the fastest-growing mobile editor, leveraging TikTok’s ecosystem and aggressive feature updates<cite id="93"></cite><cite id="95"></cite>. iMovie retains a solid position among entry-level users on macOS, with a simple interface and strong iCloud integration<cite id="64"></cite><cite id="65"></cite>.

Regional and demographic insights

Professional adoption varies by region, with the U.S. and U.K. historically leading in desktop NLE usage. A 2017 study identified the U.S. and U.K. as the top two markets for Premiere Pro and Final Cut Pro, with analysts forecasting 4.3% growth in the U.K. and 2.7% in the U.S. for the post-production market<cite id="77"></cite>. Mobile adoption is more globally diffuse, with Canva’s large user base spanning multiple regions and AppTweak’s rankings indicating CapCut’s global dominance<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="92"></cite>.

Challenges and outlook

Professional editors face rising costs and complexity in hardware and software stacks, with 78% using Adobe products and 64% using multiple Adobe apps, underscoring integration needs<cite id="103"></cite>. Mobile editors must balance feature breadth with performance on diverse devices; while Canva and CapCut lead in downloads and active users, performance on lower-end hardware remains a constraint for some mobile NLEs<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="93"></cite>. The market is expected to continue growing, with mobile video editing software expanding at a faster rate than desktop NLEs, and AI-driven tools likely to accelerate adoption among both professionals and casual creators<cite id="56"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>.

Recommendations

For professional studios, maintaining integration with Adobe’s ecosystem while exploring AI-powered color grading and auto-editing in Resolve can improve efficiency<cite id="33"></cite><cite id="100"></cite><cite id="103"></cite>. For mobile-first creators, leveraging AI-augmented editors like Canva and CapCut can reduce production time and expand reach, especially within TikTok’s ecosystem<cite id="92"></cite><cite id="93"></cite><cite id="95"></cite>. Hardware vendors should optimize NLEs for Apple Silicon and cloud workflows to meet demand from professionals and entry-level users alike<cite id="41"></cite><cite id="27"></cite>.

While simple video editing can be done even on modern smartphones, complex projects containing media from multiple sources and requiring more processing power are done on desktop with non-linear editors (NLEs), editing software that allows the user to easily adjust any part of the sequence. This is a task that requires both creativity and technical knowledge to solve the problem of storytelling and the idea into the final cuts. A control surface is a physical user interface that facilitates the use of a specific software, and for video editing the most common control surfaces are the keyboard and mouse.
This Master's thesis examines video editing control surfaces from a human-centred perspective through a human-centred design process. The research problem consists of three research questions: (1) What is important to the user in a video editing control surface, (2) What is the right degree of specificity for a control surface and (3) What design considerations does the task of video editing cause. The questions were answered by developing a new control surface concept using the human-centred design process, and evaluating both the process and its results.
Initial context were gathered via a literature review and a contextual inquiry, which produced personas for the potential user and some tentative heuristics that could be used to evaluate the UX of existing control surfaces. The heuristics were developed into a full set through a formalized process and three different control surfaces were evaluated to find potential issues and ideas for a new product concept. A prototype of a new control surface was created and evaluated through an online survey, and finally, the design guidelines for video editing control surfaces were formed.
The results of the research indicate that there might not be a need for editing-specific control surfaces as the keyboard and mouse are sufficient for most users, even experienced professional editors. The actions of modern NLEs are designed to be completed without specialized control surfaces and for many tasks, a button press is already an efficient interaction. The users are willing to spend time building muscle memory for their tasks, so the creative problem-solving becomes the bottleneck instead of the execution of each action.
The heuristics created during the research worked well and could be used to evaluate physical user interfaces in other contexts as well. If a new video editing control surface is designed, the most important considerations are customizability, well-working combination of hardware, software and integration with the NLE, and allowing the user to memorize the most common actions while being able to find less common actions easily. The users' deep level of expertise with their current software interfaces and while novel interaction types were not found to be interesting in this research, the result may change if NLEs with better support for new controls are created.
Keywords: video editing, control surface, controller, physical user interface, human-centered design, heuristic evaluation, design guidelines
